cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — AI for Good

The Empowerment Test (apply first, to any AI proposal)

Who does this empower? A teacher customizing lessons for thirty students ≠ a company eliminating teachers. A doctor spotting patterns in scans ≠ an insurer denying claims. Back the amplifier, resist the replacer.

Should you build it? — decision path

  • Is there a specific problem that matters, named by someone who lives with it?
  • No → stop. Solution-in-search-of-a-problem is the book's most common failure.
  • Yes ↓
  • Does a specific AI capability map to it (predict / classify / optimize / generate)?
  • No → the answer is process or staffing, not AI.
  • Yes ↓
  • Is there an owner whose reputation is staked on the outcome?
  • No → find your Buffington first. Championless pilots die.
  • Yes ↓
  • Can you standardize the data first?
  • No → that IS the project (Perna: "see myself" before you optimize).
  • Yes → build, quietly, on notional data if real data is blocked.

Consequence of being wrong → deployment posture

If wrong, the cost is…Posture
Trivial / reversibleShip; learn from usage
Wasted timeHuman reviews output
Clinical or legal harmHuman-in-the-loop mandatory; overrides logged as training data
Irreversible to a personDon't automate the decision; automate the surfacing

Vendor selection — tells

Green flagRed flag
Restates your problem more precisely than you didDemos before defining
Commits to a decision you'll makeCommits to a technology
Small enough that you have leverageYou are a rounding error to them
Works on your dataWorks on their slideware

Institutional-resistance diagnosis

SymptomName itMove
Good strategy, willing leadership, nothing changesFrozen middleFix incentives, not people
Rules nobody can explainGall's Law limitAudit unused authorities before seeking new ones
Six-month review for a routine stepBureaucratic tortureDe facto ban — route around or get cover
Sixteenth report, same findingsDiagnosis is doneWork ratification + execution, not analysis
Reformers vs. civil servantsCollaboration gate failureBuild with, or lose the institutional knowledge

Adoption sequence for professionals (clinicians, teachers)

  1. Volunteers only — never open with a mandate
  2. Bake-off — competing tools, usage data decides
  3. Confidence first — let them win before you ask them to change
  4. "You're the final check" — preserve authority explicitly
  5. Mandate — only after voluntary adoption plateaus

Thresholds & numbers the book commits to

  • Prompt validation: 10+ runs, judge the worst output, not the best
  • Admin burden in US healthcare: 25–30% of spend
  • Federal acquisitions workforce: ~30,000 people
  • Prior military software studies since 1982: 15, same conclusions
  • Rule of thumb: four singles > one home run on politically exposed projects

Failure tells — you are in trouble if…

  • Evaluation is "vibes-based"
  • The pilot was announced before it worked
  • The champion is a title, not a person
  • Success is measured in transactions, not outcomes (transaction-count fallacy)
  • The model is fluent and nobody has checked whether it's right (Eliza effect)
  • It agrees with you when you push back (sycophancy)
  • The plan requires the frozen middle to volunteer for extra risk

Personal protocol (Epilogue)

  1. Flirt with the tools — know capability vs. claim
  2. Decline what feels wrong; non-use is the strongest feedback tech has
  3. Price the swap: what data, what attention, worth it?
  4. Say loudly where AI should go — money follows taxes, purchases, votes
  5. Or build it yourself; most people in this book had no software expertise

glossary.md

Glossary — AI for Good

Accelerationists — camp arguing AI should be built as fast as possible to reap benefits and beat global competition (Ch 1)

Administrative burden — the 25–30% of US healthcare spending (~$5B at Cleveland Clinic scale) consumed by non-clinical work (Ch 8)

AGI (artificial general intelligence) — theoretical synthesis of AI capabilities surpassing human intellect across domains (Ch 1)

Alert fatigue — clinician desensitization from too many low-precision automated warnings (Ch 13)

Ambient scribe — AI that listens to a clinical visit and drafts the note, with doctor-in-the-loop review (Ch 11)

Bayesian Health — vendor whose sepsis model tiers alerts by probability rather than firing uniformly (Ch 13)

Bonini's paradox — a model detailed enough to be fully accurate becomes as hard to understand as the thing modeled (Ch 26)

Bullshit umbrella — senior cover that shields a team from bureaucratic interference during a crisis (Ch 16)

Case mix index (CMI) — severity-weighted measure of a hospital's patient population (Ch 12, 13)

Character.ai — companion chatbot platform built on an attention-based engagement model (Ch 22)

Classifier — AI that labels or sorts: images, email, tumors on an MRI (Ch 1)

Context stuffing — loading a model's context window with source material to constrain its answers (Ch 4)

Context window — the span of text a model can consider at once (Ch 3, 4)

Digital twin — a live data model mirroring a physical system, from a supply chain to a patient's anatomy (Ch 9, 15)

DOGE — initiative Tyrangiel treats as the cautionary counterexample: provocation over collaboration (Ch 21)

Doomers — camp arguing AI risks catastrophe or extinction and must be slowed (Ch 1)

Ed — the failed Los Angeles schools chatbot; shorthand for edtech deployed ahead of its competence (Ch 2)

Eliza effect — human tendency to attribute understanding to a system that merely reflects language back (Weizenbaum, 1966) (Ch 22)

Epic — dominant electronic health record system; its closed nature shapes what hospital AI can do (Ch 11, 13)

FASA (Federal Acquisition Streamlining Act, 1994) — statute requiring agencies to consider commercial products; the basis of Palantir's suit (Ch 17)

Frozen middle — the acquisition/program layer between leadership intent and execution, not incentivized to move (Ch 18, 20)

Gall's Law — every complicated working system evolved from a simple working system (Ch 18)

God view — a single synthesized real-time picture of a whole problem space (Ch 1, 15)

Hallucination — fluent, confident, false model output (Ch 2, 3)

Human-in-the-loop — required human review of AI output; also functions as legal and political cover (Ch 11, 20)

IMS (Integrated Master Schedule) — Operation Warp Speed's synchronized plan across all agencies and vendors (Ch 15)

Inherently governmental — legal category of work that may not be delegated to machines or contractors (Ch 20)

Iron triangle — the closed loop of agencies, incumbent contractors, and Congress that resists new entrants (Ch 17)

Notional data — placeholder data used to build and demo a system before real data arrives (Ch 16)

Ontology — Palantir's core abstraction: a shared model of an organization's entities and relationships (Ch 16)

Operation Warp Speed — the COVID vaccine distribution effort; the book's origin story (Ch 1, 14, 15)

Optimizer — AI making split-second decisions to improve logistics, pricing, or allocation (Ch 1)

p(doom) — self-reported probability of AI-caused human extinction (Ch 1)

POSIWID — "the purpose of a system is what it does" (Anil Dash) (Ch 21)

Productive struggle — the difficulty a learner must experience for learning to occur; the thing a tutor must not short-circuit (Ch 7)

Prompt drift — degradation of a tuned prompt when the underlying model is updated (Ch 3)

Red teaming — adversarially attacking your own system to find failures before users do (Ch 4)

Sepsis — fast-moving infection response; the canonical case for probabilistic clinical alerting (Ch 13)

SERT (Sepsis Emergency Response Team) — the human team an alert is designed to mobilize (Ch 13)

Sycophancy — a model's tendency to agree with the user under pressure, abandoning correct answers (Ch 2)

SWAP Study — Defense Innovation Board's Software Acquisition and Practices report; named the frozen middle (Ch 18)

Team Human — Tyrangiel's shorthand for AI that amplifies human judgment rather than replacing it (Ch 27)

Vibes-based evaluation — judging model output by impression instead of a repeatable test; the default failure (Ch 4)

Zero-shot translation — translating a language pair the model was never explicitly trained on (Ch 24, 26)

Zone of proximal development — the band just beyond current ability where learning happens; applied to device design (Ch 23)

patterns.md

Patterns — AI for Good

Techniques practitioners in this book actually used. Each is attributed to the person who ran it.

Hillis's Reframe

When: you cannot tell what AI is good for because vendor noise dominates.

How: "Try to imagine the tech without the tech companies." Ask what the capability enables for someone with a real problem, stripped of who profits from the answer.

Trade-offs: clarifies use, ignores cost and vendor lock-in — reintroduce those after.

Perna's "See Myself" Principle

When: coordinating anything across organizations that don't share data.

How: before optimizing, build one live standardized picture of positions, supplies, and flows. Reduce complexity to a single tracer material (Perna used plastic) to test whether the picture is real.

Trade-offs: data standardization is the expensive, unglamorous majority of the work.

The Definition-First Vendor Test

When: selecting an AI vendor.

How: give each an hour. Reject any who cannot state the problem back to you more precisely than you stated it. Hire the ones who commit to a decision you'll be able to make, not a technology.

Trade-offs: filters for clear communicators, which correlates with but does not guarantee capability.

The Ten-Run Prompt Test (DiCerbo)

When: validating any prompt before it faces users.

How: run the same prompt ten-plus times and inspect the spread, not the best output. Ship only if the worst run is acceptable.

Trade-offs: slow and manual; replaces vibes-based evaluation, which is worse.

The Role-Constraint Prompt Pattern

When: a model must refuse to do the user's work for them.

How: specify role, what it must never do, and the recovery move when pushed. Khan's tutoring script: ask what the student thinks first, never give the answer, decompose into the next smallest step.

Trade-offs: constraints erode under adversarial pressure and after model updates — retest on every version bump.

Context Stuffing

When: you need answers anchored to your material, not the model's priors.

How: load authoritative source content into the context window and instruct the model to answer only from it.

Trade-offs: bounded by window size; does not eliminate hallucination, only reduces it.

Zubovic's Pilot-Site Selection Rule

When: choosing where to run a first deployment.

How: pick the site with a leader who will personally champion it and whose reputation is staked on the outcome — not the easiest or largest site. "Get Buffington."

Trade-offs: success may not generalize to sites without a champion; plan the second site deliberately.

Quiet Pilot Containment

When: piloting anything that could be politically destroyed by early failure.

How: keep the pilot small and unpublicized until the failure modes are known. Announce after it works.

Trade-offs: limits learning volume and can read as secrecy if discovered.

The Voluntary Bake-off (Boose)

When: introducing a tool into a professional workforce that resents mandates.

How: let clinicians volunteer, run competing vendors side by side, let usage data pick the winner. Escalate to a mandate only after voluntary adoption plateaus (Mihaljevic's Mandate Threshold).

Trade-offs: volunteers self-select as enthusiasts; ghosting is common, so recruit more than you need.

The Sepsis Alert Triage Ladder

When: an automated alert system is being ignored.

How: tier alerts by probability instead of firing uniformly; route each tier to a different response. Treat every clinician override as training data (the Override-as-Training-Data Loop).

Trade-offs: tiering requires a calibrated model; miscalibration moves harm rather than removing it.

Build-With, Don't Buy-Out-of-the-Box (Pappas)

When: deploying into a workflow whose practitioners must trust the output.

How: co-build with the people who will use it; ship the reassurance that they remain the final check.

Trade-offs: slower than procurement, and the result is harder to resell elsewhere.

Four Singles Instead of a Home Run (Jaffe)

When: the full problem is too large or too political to solve at once.

How: ship four small, independently useful wins rather than one transformative system. Start on notional data so building begins before real data clears.

Trade-offs: risks a pile of tools with no coherent ontology unless the data model is planned up front.

Werfel's Five-Degree Turn Doctrine

When: reforming an institution that cannot survive visible upheaval.

How: make small course corrections continuously, keep the work below the threshold of political attention (the Invisibility Shield), and let compounding do the rest.

Trade-offs: invisibility forfeits the credit and the mandate that would let you move faster.

Pandya's "Why You Should Care" Rule

When: pitching technical work to non-technical stakeholders.

How: lead with the consequence for the listener's constituency, never the architecture.

Trade-offs: none; the omission is the common error.

The Collaboration Gate for Public-Sector AI

When: judging whether a government AI effort will help or damage.

How: ask whether the team is building with the civil servants who run the system or against them. Provocation-first efforts (Ch 21) destroy the institutional knowledge they need.

Trade-offs: collaboration is slower and dilutes the reformer's narrative.

Johnson's Burden-Side Rule

When: designing for someone who cannot easily self-report.

How: put the sensing and interpretation burden on the technology and the caregiver's observations, not on the person being helped. Meet him at the what — start from observed behavior, not a diagnostic label.

Trade-offs: caregiver-labeled signal carries the caregiver's interpretation; validate against outcomes.

Shah's Rope-and-Car Principle

When: a system must survive real-world conditions it wasn't trained on.

How: design the protocol so it can be perturbed and still function, rather than optimizing for clean-condition accuracy.

Trade-offs: costs benchmark performance to buy field robustness.

Tyrangiel's Four-Step Civic Protocol

When: you are a non-expert deciding how to engage with AI.

How: (1) flirt with the tools enough to know real capability vs. claim; (2) decline features that feel like a solution seeking a problem — non-use is the strongest feedback signal; (3) price the swap (data, attention) and read the terms; (4) back AI that amplifies human judgment, oppose AI that replaces it.

Trade-offs: individually slow; the mechanism is aggregate, not personal.

Atomic Habits: An Easy & Proven Way to Build Good Habits & Break Bad Ones

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Atomic Habits (decision aid)

The core decision: build or break?

StepTo BUILD a good habitTo BREAK a bad habit
1. CueMake it ObviousMake it Invisible
2. CravingMake it AttractiveMake it Unattractive
3. ResponseMake it EasyMake it Difficult
4. RewardMake it SatisfyingMake it Unsatisfying

Which law do I reach for? (diagnose the failing step)

  • "I keep forgetting / never get around to it" → 1st Law: implementation intention, habit stacking, environment cue.
  • "I don't feel like doing it" → 2nd Law: temptation bundling, join a culture where it's normal, reframe "get to."
  • "It's too much effort / I start too big" → 3rd Law: Two-Minute Rule, reduce friction, prime the environment.
  • "I do it once then drop it" → 4th Law: immediate reward, habit tracking, never miss twice, accountability.

Fill-in formulas (memorize these)

  • Implementation intention: "I will [BEHAVIOR] at [TIME] in [LOCATION]."
  • Habit stacking: "After [CURRENT HABIT], I will [NEW HABIT]."
  • Temptation bundling: "After [HABIT I NEED], I will [HABIT I WANT]."
  • Identity: "I am the type of person who [does X]." → prove with small wins.

Rules of thumb & thresholds

  • 1% better/day ≈ 37× in a year; 1% worse/day ≈ near zero.
  • Two-Minute Rule: any new habit must start in < 2 minutes.
  • Never miss twice: one miss = accident; two = new habit. Recover next day.
  • Goldilocks / sweet spot: aim for ~50% success rate; flow ≈ ~4% beyond current skill.
  • Immediacy > magnitude: a small instant reward beats a big delayed one.
  • Frequency > time: count reps, not days, to build automaticity.

Tells & smells (recognize the trap)

  • You're reading/planning/researching a lot but not doing → motion, not action (Ch 11).
  • "I'll start Monday / when I'm ready" → readiness is a byproduct of reps, not a prerequisite.
  • Relying on willpower to resist a visible cue → self-control is short-term; remove the cue instead.
  • "No thanks, I'm trying to quit" → still the old identity; say "I'm not a [X]."
  • One slip → "I've blown it" → all-or-nothing thinking; apply never-miss-twice.
  • Habit feels boring so you seek novelty → boredom is the threshold pros push through, not a stop sign.

Goals vs. Systems

  • Goal = direction (fine for setting aim). System = the process (what actually moves you).
  • "You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems."
  • If you keep resetting the same goal → fix the system/inputs, not the outcome.

The three questions to find your fit (Ch 18)

  1. What feels like fun to me but work to others?
  2. What makes me lose track of time?
  3. Where do I get greater returns than the average person?

→ If you can't win by being better, win by being different.

Sustaining loop (Advanced)

Mastery = Habits + Deliberate Practice, kept honest by Reflection & Review (Annual Review + midyear Integrity Report). Keep identity flexible so growth doesn't threaten who you are.

glossary.md

Glossary — Atomic Habits

Aggregation of Marginal Gains — the philosophy of improving every component of a system by ~1%; small gains compound into decisive results (Ch 1).

Annual Review — yearly reflection: what went well, what didn't, what I learned (Ch 20).

Atomic Habit — a tiny, easy routine that is also a building block of a larger system of compound growth (Ch 1).

Automaticity — the state where a behavior runs without conscious thought, reached through repetition (Ch 3, 11).

Cardinal Rule of Behavior Change — what is immediately rewarded is repeated; what is immediately punished is avoided (Ch 15).

Commitment Device — a present choice that controls your future actions, locking in good behavior in advance (Ch 14).

Craving — the motivational force behind a habit; the anticipation of a reward / desire for a change in state (Ch 3, 8).

Cue — the trigger that initiates a habit by predicting a reward (Ch 3).

Decisive Moments — small daily forks (cook vs. takeout) that set the options available to your future self (Ch 13).

Deliberate Practice — focused effort to improve specific weaknesses; paired with habits it produces mastery (Ch 20).

Diderot Effect — obtaining something new spirals into further consumption/behaviors; behaviors chain (Ch 5).

Environment Design — arranging surroundings so good-habit cues are obvious and bad-habit cues invisible (Ch 6, 7).

Explore/Exploit Trade-off — sample options early (explore), then double down on the best fit (exploit) (Ch 18).

Fall in Love with Boredom — pros stick to the schedule when it's dull; boredom is the main threat to lasting habits (Ch 19).

Fit — the match between a habit/field and your natural temperament; good fit multiplies returns (Ch 18).

Flow State — full immersion "in the zone," reachable when challenge is ~4% beyond current ability (Ch 19).

Four Laws of Behavior Change — Make it Obvious, Attractive, Easy, Satisfying (build); invert to break (Ch 3).

Frequency, Not Time — habits form from number of repetitions, not days elapsed (Ch 11).

Gateway Habit — the ≤2-minute entry point on the path to a larger goal (Ch 13).

Goldilocks Rule — peak motivation comes from tasks of just manageable difficulty — not too hard, not too easy (Ch 19).

Habit — a behavior repeated enough to become automatic; a reliable solution to a recurring problem (Ch 3).

Habit Contract — a written, witnessed agreement stating a habit and the penalty for failing (Ch 17).

Habit Loop — Cue → Craving → Response → Reward, the neurological feedback cycle of every habit (Ch 3).

Habit Shaping — scaling a two-minute habit up in stages, mastering the first two minutes of each level (Ch 13).

Habit Stacking — pairing a new habit with a current one: "After [CURRENT HABIT], I will [NEW HABIT]" (Ch 5).

Habit Tracking — measuring whether you did a habit; obvious, attractive, and satisfying at once (Ch 16).

Habits Scorecard — listing daily habits and scoring each +/–/= against your desired identity (Ch 4).

Identity-Based Habits — habits chosen from who you wish to become rather than what you want to achieve (Ch 2).

Immediate-Return vs. Delayed-Return Environment — ancestral rewards were instant; modern good habits pay off later (Ch 15).

Implementation Intention — a pre-set plan: "I will [BEHAVIOR] at [TIME] in [LOCATION]" (Ch 5).

Integrity Report — midyear reflection on core values and whether you're living them (Ch 20).

Inversion of the Four Laws — Make it Invisible, Unattractive, Difficult, Unsatisfying (to break habits) (Ch 3, 7, 10, 14, 17).

Lagging Measure — an outcome (weight, net worth) that trails the habits producing it (Ch 1).

Law of Least Effort — behavior gravitates to the option requiring the least energy (Ch 12).

Motion vs. Action — motion is planning/preparing; action is the rep that produces results (Ch 11).

Never Miss Twice — a slip is fine; two in a row starts a bad habit — recover immediately (Ch 16).

One Space, One Use — give each context a single association so cues don't compete (Ch 6).

Plateau of Latent Potential — the phase where effort is "stored" before results appear (Ch 1).

Pointing-and-Calling — saying actions aloud to make automatic behavior conscious (Ch 4).

Priming the Environment — pre-arranging surroundings so the next good action is ready to go (Ch 12).

Reflection and Review — periodic review that prevents habits from becoming mindless and off-course (Ch 20).

Reward — the end of the loop that satisfies the craving and teaches the brain to repeat the cue (Ch 3).

Sweet Spot of Desire (50/50) — motivation peaks near a 50/50 split of success and failure (Ch 19).

Systems vs. Goals — goals set direction; systems drive progress. "You fall to the level of your systems" (Ch 1).

Temptation Bundling — linking a wanted action to a needed one: "After [NEED], I will [WANT]" (Ch 8).

Three Layers of Behavior Change — Outcomes → Processes → Identity; change from the inside out (Ch 2).

Three Social Groups We Imitate — the Close, the Many, the Powerful (Ch 9).

Two-Minute Rule — a new habit should take less than two minutes to start (Ch 13).

Valley of Disappointment — the stretch where effort feels wasted before results surface (Ch 1).

Votes (for an identity) — each habit is a piece of evidence for the type of person you're becoming (Ch 2).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Atomic Habits

Concrete, reusable techniques with their fill-in formulas. Organized by which Law they serve.

Implementation Intention (1st Law)

When to use: any habit you keep forgetting or postponing.

How: write I will [BEHAVIOR] at [TIME] in [LOCATION].

Trade-offs: requires specificity up front; vague versions don't fire.

Habit Stacking (1st Law)

When to use: you have reliable daily habits to anchor to.

How: After [CURRENT HABIT], I will [NEW HABIT]. Chain several into a routine.

Trade-offs: the anchor habit must itself be rock-solid, or the chain breaks.

Environment Design / Make the Cue Obvious (1st Law)

When to use: any good habit you want automatic.

How: place the cue in your line of sight; give each space one dedicated use.

Trade-offs: only as strong as the most obvious competing cue.

Habits Scorecard (1st Law — awareness)

When to use: before changing anything.

How: list every daily habit → mark +/–/= vs. your desired identity.

Trade-offs: awareness only; no change without follow-through.

Pointing-and-Calling (Inverted 1st Law)

When to use: catching an automatic bad habit in the act.

How: say the action and its consequence aloud.

Trade-offs: works in the moment; doesn't remove the cue.

Remove the Cue / Make It Invisible (Inverted 1st Law)

When to use: breaking an environment-triggered bad habit.

How: delete the trigger — phone in another room, snack out of the house.

Trade-offs: requires controlling the environment; harder in shared/public spaces.

Temptation Bundling (2nd Law)

When to use: a good habit that isn't intrinsically appealing.

How: After [HABIT I NEED], I will [HABIT I WANT]. Allow the craved thing only with the needed thing.

Trade-offs: pick a "want" that doesn't cancel the habit's benefit.

Join the Right Culture (2nd Law)

When to use: making a habit socially attractive.

How: join a group where the desired behavior is normal and you share common ground.

Trade-offs: the same force works against you in the wrong group.

Reframe / Highlight Benefits (2nd Law & inverted)

When to use: making good habits attractive, bad habits unattractive.

How: "get to" not "have to"; associate a bad habit with its true hidden costs.

Trade-offs: mindset shift takes repetition to stick.

Reduce Friction / Prime the Environment (3rd Law)

When to use: any good habit.

How: cut steps and decisions; set up in advance (clothes out, gear ready).

Trade-offs: setup effort now for effortlessness later.

Two-Minute Rule (3rd Law)

When to use: starting or reviving any habit.

How: scale it to <2 minutes (the gateway habit); master showing up, then use habit shaping to scale up.

Trade-offs: risk of staying at two minutes forever — shape upward once established.

Add Friction / Commitment Device (Inverted 3rd Law)

When to use: bad habits you'll rationalize away in the moment.

How: increase steps for bad habits; lock in good ones with a present decision (auto-transfer savings, delete the app, one-time purchases).

Trade-offs: must set it up while willpower is high.

Add an Immediate Reward (4th Law)

When to use: good habits with delayed payoff (saving, exercise).

How: attach a small instant reward that reinforces your desired identity.

Trade-offs: reward must not contradict the habit (no ice cream after the gym).

Habit Tracking / Don't Break the Chain (4th Law)

When to use: sustaining consistency.

How: mark each completion (calendar X, jar, app); keep the streak alive.

Trade-offs: don't let the metric become the goal; keep it simple.

Never Miss Twice (4th Law)

When to use: recovering from a slip.

How: the day after a miss, do at least the two-minute version.

Trade-offs: none — the key defense against all-or-nothing collapse.

Habit Contract / Accountability Partner (Inverted 4th Law)

When to use: high-stakes bad habits needing external teeth.

How: write the habit, schedule, and immediate penalty; have partners co-sign.

Trade-offs: needs a trustworthy partner who'll enforce it.

Explore/Exploit + Pick the Right Game (Advanced)

When to use: choosing which habits/fields to commit to.

How: sample broadly, then double down where you have natural fit; if you can't be better, be different.

Trade-offs: over-exploring delays mastery; over-exploiting too early risks the wrong game.

Goldilocks Tuning (Advanced)

When to use: sustaining long-term motivation.

How: keep difficulty at just-manageable (~50% success); raise the bar in small steps.

Trade-offs: too easy → boredom; too hard → discouragement.

Habits + Deliberate Practice + Review (Advanced)

When to use: pursuing mastery, not just consistency.

How: automate fundamentals via habit, deliberately push weaknesses, run Annual Review + Integrity Report.

Trade-offs: reflection takes scheduled time; skipping it invites complacency.

Death by Meeting: A Leadership Fable About Solving the Most Painful Problem in Business

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Death by Meeting — Cheatsheet

Diagnose first: which problem is this?

SymptomRoot problemFix
Meeting is boring, disengaged, politeLack of dramaMine for conflict; add the hook
Meeting is ineffective, nothing decidedLack of contextual structureSplit into the four meetings
People want different things from one meetingMeeting stewSeparate by purpose/format/timing
Lots of post-meeting email/hallway clarifyingSneaker timeGet clarity/closure/buy-in in the room

The Four Meetings — pick by purpose

If you need to…UseTimeCadence
Coordinate today's activitiesDaily Check-in5 min, standingDaily
Resolve this week's tacticsWeekly Tactical45–90 minWeekly
Decide a big long-term issueMonthly Strategic~2 hrs/topicMonthly
Decide a big issue that can't waitAd Hoc Strategicas neededOn demand
Step back & review the whole businessQuarterly Off-Site1–2 daysQuarterly

Weekly Tactical — run it in this order

  1. Lightning Round — each person, 2–3 priorities, ≤60 sec (~10 min)
  2. Progress Review — 4–6 key metrics, clarify only (~5 min)
  3. Real-Time Agenda — set now, from what's actually happening (~15 min in)

Rule: strategic topic raised? Park it for the Monthly Strategic. Don't discuss.

Decision rules

  • When a meeting feels flat → mine for conflict. Surface the disagreement everyone

is avoiding; politeness is the disease, not the cure.

  • When first conflict gets tense → grant real-time permission. Interrupt: "this is

exactly the debate we need — keep going."

  • When a strategic issue erupts in a tactical meeting → park it, don't solve it.
  • When a strategic issue truly can't wait → call an Ad Hoc Strategic, separate from

the Weekly Tactical.

  • When tempted to pre-write the Weekly agenda → don't. Use disciplined spontaneity.
  • When someone says "too many meetings" → count the sneaker time the bad meetings

create. Better meetings save net time.

  • When the Daily Check-in runs long → stay standing, end hard, park the rest.

Thresholds & defaults

  • Daily Check-in: 5 min (hard-cap ~10), standing, never cancel.
  • Lightning round: 60 sec/person; 2–3 priorities.
  • Progress review: ~5 min, 4–6 metrics max.
  • Monthly Strategic: ≥2 hrs/topic, 1–2 topics only, prep required.
  • Off-site: 1–2 days, ~1 hour's drive away (not Hawaii), no outsiders

(except a trusted facilitator).

  • New meeting type: commit ~2 months before judging it.

Tells & smells (you're in trouble if…)

  • The leader optimizes for ending on time and avoiding tension.
  • The agenda was emailed 48 hrs early and no one replied.
  • One 2–3 hour "staff meeting" covers tactics + strategy + admin + culture.
  • People lobby to end the meeting to "go do real work."
  • Disagreements happen in the hallway, never in the room.
  • The off-site is mostly slides or mostly golf.

Off-Site: four reviews to cover

Strategy · Team · Personnel (stars & poor performers) · Competition/Industry

Genre cheat (for buy-in)

Headline News = Daily · Sitcom/Crime Drama = Weekly · Feature Film = Monthly ·

Mini-Series = Quarterly

glossary.md

Glossary — Death by Meeting

Ad Hoc Strategic Meeting — a separately convened strategic meeting for a critical

issue that can't wait for the next Monthly Strategic; kept distinct from the Weekly

Tactical so minds reset and enough time is allotted (Ch 5).

Boondoggle — a self-indulgent, socially-driven off-site that wastes the

opportunity for critical conversations; an anti-pattern for the Quarterly Off-Site (Ch 5).

Cascading Messages — agreeing at meeting's end on what to communicate downward to

the rest of the organization; a field on the Weekly Tactical guide (Ch 5).

Contextual Structure — clearly distinguishing the purpose, format, and timing of

each meeting type so participants know what mode they're in; the cure for Problem #2 (Ch 4).

Daily Check-in — ~5-minute, stand-up daily meeting to share schedules/activities

and keep priorities aligned; genre: Headline News (Ch 5).

Disciplined Spontaneity — planning the meeting's structure while letting the

agenda emerge live from real activity and progress; basis of the Real-Time Agenda (Ch 5).

Drama — legitimate, constructive ideological conflict that keeps people engaged;

its absence makes meetings boring (Problem #1) (Ch 2–3).

Fear of Conflict — reluctance to engage in unfiltered ideological debate; a named

challenge that undermines Monthly Strategic and Off-Site meetings (Ch 3, 5).

The Four Meetings — Daily Check-in, Weekly Tactical, Monthly Strategic, Quarterly

Off-Site Review; the structural solution to meeting stew (Ch 5).

The Hook — jolting participants in the first ten minutes by making the stakes

vivid, so they have a reason to care (Ch 3).

Huddle — Verne Harnish's term (from Mastering the Rockefeller Habits) for the

short daily meeting Lencioni adapted into the Daily Check-in (Ch 5).

Ideological Conflict — disagreement about ideas/issues (productive), as opposed to

personal or political conflict (destructive) (Ch 3).

Lightning Round — opening segment of the Weekly Tactical where each person states

their 2–3 weekly priorities in ≤60 seconds; sets the tone and surfaces issues (Ch 5).

Lack of Contextual Structure — Problem #2: cramming all issue-types into one

meeting, leaving no clear context for any discussion → ineffective meetings (Ch 4).

Lack of Drama — Problem #1: removing conflict, the ingredient that makes meetings

engaging → boring meetings (Ch 3).

Magnitude Mismatch — the difficulty of shifting between decisions of very

different weight (e.g., travel policy vs. a merger) in one meeting (Ch 4).

Meeting Paradox — meetings are simultaneously critical and painful; resolvable by

fixing attitude and design, not by avoiding meetings (Ch 2).

Meeting Stew — the structural error of throwing every issue-type into one

undifferentiated staff meeting "like a bad stew" (Ch 4).

Meetings vs. Movies — meetings should beat movies for engagement because they're

interactive and directly relevant, while movies are passive and irrelevant (Ch 2–3).

Mining for Conflict — the leader's deliberate act of seeking out and surfacing

buried disagreements, even at the cost of being temporarily unpopular (Ch 3).

Monthly Strategic — 2+ hours/topic meeting (monthly or biweekly) to debate and

decide a few critical long-term issues; genre: feature film (Ch 5).

Parking Lot — capturing an out-of-context (usually strategic) issue raised in a

tactical meeting so it gets the right forum later; the Monthly Strategic is the

standing parking lot (Ch 4–5).

Progress Review — Weekly Tactical segment reviewing a handful (4–6) of key metrics

quickly, without deep discussion (Ch 5).

Quarterly Off-Site Review — 1–2 day quarterly meeting to review strategy, team,

personnel, and competition holistically; genre: mini-series (Ch 5).

Real-Time Agenda — setting the Weekly Tactical's agenda only after the lightning

round and progress review, based on actual current activity (Ch 5).

Real-Time Permission — the leader interrupting a first tense exchange to affirm the

conflict is good and wanted, separating ideological passion from fear of rejection (Ch 3).

Sneaker Time — uncounted hours spent after bad meetings clarifying via email,

voicemail, and hallway visits; the hidden cost good meetings eliminate (Ch 6).

TV/Film Genre Analogy — mapping each meeting type to a media format (Headline News,

sitcom, feature film, mini-series) so context sets expectations (Ch 1).

Weekly Tactical — 45–90 minute weekly meeting to review activities/metrics and

resolve tactical obstacles; goals: resolution of issues + reinforcement of clarity (Ch 5).

Will's White Board — the fable's artifact where Will maps the four meetings to TV/

film genres and diagnoses the missing elements of meetings (Ch 1).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Death by Meeting

The Hook (First Ten Minutes)

When to use: opening any important meeting, especially a dry-sounding one.

How: in the first ~10 minutes, make the stakes vivid — name a competitive threat,

the cost of a bad decision, or the mission's impact on customers/employees/families.

Give people "a reason to care."

Trade-offs: requires the leader to prepare a genuine stake; overuse or manufactured

urgency reads as manipulation. The conflict/stakes must be legitimate.

Mining for Conflict

When to use: real disagreement exists but is being politely buried.

How: as leader, prioritize uncovering unresolved disagreements; when people dodge,

force the issue onto the table. Both leaders and participants should act as "miners."

Trade-offs: temporarily unpopular; risks tipping into personal conflict if not kept

ideological. The cost of not doing it is worse — buried conflict returns as politics.

Real-Time Permission

When to use: the tense moment a team unaccustomed to conflict first debates openly.

How: interrupt, name that the conflict is exactly what's wanted, encourage both

parties to continue, remind them questioning each other improves the outcome.

Trade-offs: feels "paternal," but is "remarkably effective" at separating

ideological passion from interpersonal fear so debate can continue.

The Lightning Round

When to use: opening of every Weekly Tactical.

How: go around the table; each person names 2–3 priorities for the week in ≤60

seconds. ~10 minutes total even for a large team.

Trade-offs: strict 60-second cap can feel rushed, but over-detail loses the room

and obscures the real issues. Sixty seconds is "a lot longer than it seems."

Progress Review

When to use: right after the lightning round in the Weekly Tactical.

How: quickly review a handful (4–6) of key metrics; clarifying questions only.

~5 minutes. Avoid deep discussion of underlying issues here.

Trade-offs: reviewing too many metrics drowns the signal; pick the few that define

success.

Real-Time Agenda (Disciplined Spontaneity)

When to use: setting the Weekly Tactical agenda.

How: do not pre-set the agenda. After the lightning round + progress review

(~15 min in), let the agenda emerge from what people are actually working on and how the

company is actually performing. Plan the structure; improvise the content.

Trade-offs: sacrifices some control and predictability; requires leader discipline

to resist preparing an agenda 48 hours early. Payoff: the meeting addresses what

actually matters this week.

Parking Lot (Park Strategy in Tactical Meetings)

When to use: a strategic/long-term issue surfaces during a Weekly Tactical.

How: take it off the table and add it to a list for the next Monthly (or Ad Hoc)

Strategic. Don't discuss it now.

Trade-offs: feels like deferring something important, but mixing magnitudes wrecks

both topics; a trusted parking lot gives people confidence to table issues.

Ad Hoc Strategic Meeting

When to use: a critical strategic issue genuinely can't wait for the next Monthly

Strategic.

How: convene a separate, clearly delineated meeting (even later the same day);

allot enough time for real analysis. Keep it distinct from the Weekly Tactical.

Trade-offs: disrupts schedules — justified only for truly critical issues, but

those are exactly when great teams outmaneuver competitors.

The Trial-Period Commitment

When to use: introducing a new meeting type (especially the Daily Check-in).

How: commit to running it consistently for a set period (~2 months) before judging

whether it works; keep time/place consistent and never cancel.

Trade-offs: forces persistence through early awkwardness when abandonment is

tempting.

Outside Facilitator (Off-Site Exception)

When to use: a Quarterly Off-Site where the leader wants to participate fully.

How: bring in a trusted facilitator who knows the business and serves the team's

objectives — not an outsider who changes team dynamics.

Trade-offs: the only sanctioned exception to "no outsiders at the off-site";

choose someone driven by the team's goals, not their own.

Genre-Tagging Meetings (TV/Film Analogy)

When to use: teaching/enforcing the four-meeting structure.

How: label each meeting by its genre so attendees bring the right expectations —

Headline News (Daily), sitcom (Weekly), feature film (Monthly), mini-series (Quarterly).

Trade-offs: an explanatory device, not a rule; useful for buy-in and for keeping

meetings in their lane.

Deep Work: Rules for Focused Success in a Distracted World

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Deep Work — Cheatsheet (decisions, defaults, tells)

The one formula

High-Quality Work Produced = (Time Spent) × (Intensity of Focus) → to produce more, raise intensity, not just hours.

Pick your depth philosophy (decision tree)

  • Can you shed almost all shallow duties? → Monastic
  • Can you clear whole days/seasons but need open time too? → Bimodal (min unit ≈ 1 day)
  • Regular job, need a reliable daily habit? → Rhythmic (same time daily, keep the streak) ← default for most
  • Already have trained, on-demand focus and an unpredictable schedule? → Journalistic (not for beginners)

Is this task deep or shallow?

Ask: "How many months to train a smart recent college grad (no field training) to do it?"

  • Few months → shallow → batch it, minimize it, fit it in the budget
  • Years of expertise → deep → protect a dedicated block for it

Keep or kill a tool? (craftsman test)

  1. List the few goals that define success (work + life).
  2. Does the tool substantially help the key activities behind them?
  • Yes → keep · "some benefit" / "might miss out" → kill (that's any-benefit reasoning)
  1. Unsure? Run the 30-day quit: gone 30 days — would it have been notably better? Did anyone care? Both must be a clear yes to readopt.

Willpower rule

Willpower is finite → never rely on resolve; rely on rituals, fixed times, and pre-decisions. If starting deep work requires a burst of willpower, your system is wrong.

4DX for depth (run all four)

DisciplineIndividual version
Wildly Important1–2 ambitious goals; say yes to the compelling goal, not no to distractions
Lead MeasureTrack deep-work hours (not papers/revenue — those are lag)
Compelling ScoreboardVisible tally; circle the hour that produced a result
Cadence of AccountabilityWeekly review confronting the scoreboard

Defaults & thresholds

  • Shallow-work budget: aim ~30–50% max; anything over → decline with the budget as reason.
  • Fixed endpoint: set when you stop (e.g., 5:30, no nights/weekends), then prune backward.
  • Internet blocks: schedule allowed windows; offline between them; need it early → move the next block a few min out, never jump online on impulse.
  • Schedule every minute: ~30-min blocks; rebuild the remaining day when derailed (thoughtfulness > obedience).

Email: become hard to reach

  • Sender filter → put the burden on them ("reply only if it's a good match").
  • Process-centric reply → answer the whole project in one message; kill the back-and-forth.
  • Don't respond → ambiguous / uninteresting / disproportionately costly = professionally ignorable.

Tells & smells (you're in trouble if…)

  • You "just quickly check" your inbox mid-task → attention residue is taxing every hour.
  • Your calendar is full but you can't name what you produced → busyness as proxy for value.
  • You reach for your phone at every micro-boredom (line, elevator) → training distraction addiction; your focus muscle is atrophying.
  • You justify a tool with "it has some benefit" → any-benefit trap.
  • Work thoughts loop at night → no shutdown ritual (Zeigarnik effect).
  • You default to the easiest task available → Principle of Least Resistance running your day.

End-of-day shutdown (algorithm)

inbox check → capture loose tasks → skim all lists + next few days' calendar → rough plan for tomorrow → say "Shutdown complete."

glossary.md

Glossary — Deep Work (Cal Newport)

Any-Benefit Approach — The flawed rule that a network tool is justified if it offers any possible benefit or you might miss anything by not using it; approves everything because every tool has some benefit (Ch 7).

Attention Residue — Sophie Leroy's finding that after switching from Task A to Task B, part of your attention stays stuck on A, degrading performance on B; worse when A is left unfinished (Ch 2).

Attention Restoration Theory (ART) — Directed attention is a finite resource that depletes; time in nature (or restful downtime) replenishes it, aiding subsequent deep work (Ch 5).

Bimodal Philosophy — Divide time into clearly defined deep stretches (days or a season) and open shallow periods; minimum deep unit usually a full day (e.g., Jung, Adam Grant) (Ch 5).

Busyness as a Proxy for Productivity — Doing lots of visible stuff as a stand-in for value, used when knowledge work lacks clear productivity metrics (Ch 3).

Cadence of Accountability — 4DX Discipline #4: a regular (weekly) review confronting your scoreboard and committing to next actions (Ch 5).

Compelling Scoreboard — 4DX Discipline #3: a physical, visible tally of your lead measure (deep-work hours); "people play differently when they're keeping score" (Ch 5).

Craftsman Approach to Tool Selection — Adopt a tool only if its positive impact on your core success/happiness factors substantially outweighs its negatives (Ch 7).

Cult of the Internet — Treating any new technology as inherently good/necessary, branding skeptics Luddites, so tools spread unchecked (Ch 3).

Deep Work — "Professional activities performed in a state of distraction-free concentration that push your cognitive capabilities to their limit. These efforts create new value, improve your skill, and are hard to replicate" (Intro).

Deep Work Hypothesis — The ability to do deep work is becoming rarer and more valuable; the few who cultivate it and center their work on it will thrive (Intro).

Deliberate Practice — Ericsson's mechanism of skill acquisition: focused, feedback-driven strain on a specific ability just beyond current reach; incompatible with divided attention (Ch 2).

Depth Philosophy — Your chosen pattern for integrating deep work: Monastic, Bimodal, Rhythmic, or Journalistic (Ch 5).

Eudaimonia Machine — David Dewane's conceptual building whose architecture channels occupants from social space into progressively deeper chambers ending in isolated deep-work rooms; a metaphor for engineering depth (Ch 5).

Fixed-Schedule Productivity — Fix a firm workday endpoint, then work backward, ruthlessly pruning shallow obligations to fit deep work into the constrained hours (Ch 8).

Flow — Csikszentmihalyi's state of full absorption when mind/body is stretched to its limits on a worthwhile task; the reliable source of satisfaction (Ch 4).

Grand Gesture — A radical change to environment or investment that raises a task's perceived importance and mobilizes focus (e.g., Rowling's hotel suite) (Ch 5).

Hub-and-Spoke — Architecture of collaboration: expose yourself to "hub" spaces for serendipitous idea exchange, then retreat to isolated "spoke" spaces for deep execution (Ch 5).

Journalistic Philosophy — Fit deep work into any open gap on demand; requires trained concentration and confidence (e.g., Walter Isaacson); hard for beginners (Ch 5).

Lag Measure — A metric describing the outcome you ultimately want (papers published, revenue); arrives too late to steer daily behavior (Ch 5).

Law of Productivity — High-Quality Work Produced = (Time Spent) × (Intensity of Focus); raise intensity to produce more per hour (Ch 2).

Law of the Vital Few — ~80% of a desired effect comes from ~20% of possible causes; concentrate effort on the high-impact minority (Ch 7).

Lead Measure — A metric for the controllable behavior that drives the lag measure (for depth: hours spent in deep work); movable day-to-day (Ch 5).

Metric Black Hole — The impact of distraction/depth on productivity is real but hard to measure, so it goes unmanaged (Ch 3).

Monastic Philosophy — Maximize depth by radically eliminating or minimizing shallow obligations (e.g., Knuth, Stephenson) (Ch 5).

Myelination — Growth of insulating myelin around repeatedly-fired neural circuits; the physical basis of skill, triggered by isolated intense focus (Ch 2).

Principle of Least Resistance — Without clear feedback on bottom-line impact, we default to whatever behavior is easiest in the moment (Ch 3).

Process-Centric Email — A reply that resolves the whole underlying project/loop in one message to minimize future back-and-forth (Ch 8).

Productive Meditation — Focusing attention on a single well-defined professional problem during physical-but-not-mental activity (walking, driving); redirect from distraction and looping (Ch 6).

Rhythmic Philosophy — Make deep work a daily habit at a fixed time, sustained via a streak/chain ("don't break the chain") (e.g., Brian Chappell) (Ch 5).

Ritual (Deep Work Ritual) — A preset answer to where/how long you'll work, how you'll work (rules/metrics), and how you'll support the work — to minimize willpower cost of starting (Ch 5).

Roosevelt Dash — A burst of maximal-intensity focus on one task under a deadline far shorter than normal, used to stretch your concentration ceiling (Ch 6).

Sender Filter — Published expectations shifting the burden of contact to the sender, reducing inbound email you must handle (Ch 8).

Shallow Work — "Noncognitively demanding, logistical-style tasks, often performed while distracted... tend not to create much new value and are easy to replicate" (Intro / Ch 8).

Shallow Work Budget — An explicit agreed percentage of time (often 30–50%) allowed for shallow work, defended against overrun (Ch 8).

Shutdown Ritual — An end-of-day algorithm confirming every incomplete task has a trusted plan or is captured, ending in a set phrase ("Shutdown complete") (Ch 5).

The Great Restructuring — Economic split by intelligent machines/connectivity into those who work with depth (winners) and those who don't (Intro).

Willpower Depletion — Willpower is finite and drains with use; hence rely on rituals, not resolve, to sustain deep work (Ch 5).

Zeigarnik Effect — Incomplete tasks dominate our attention; the shutdown ritual neutralizes it by capturing/planning open loops (Ch 5).

4DX (Four Disciplines of Execution) — Framework applied to individual depth: focus on the wildly important → act on lead measures → keep a compelling scoreboard → create a cadence of accountability (Ch 5).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Deep Work (Cal Newport)

Choose a Depth Philosophy

When to use: Setting up how deep work fits your life; do this before any scheduling tactic.

How: Pick the one matching your constraints — Monastic (eliminate shallow entirely), Bimodal (deep in day/season blocks), Rhythmic (same time daily, keep a streak), Journalistic (any open gap, on demand).

Trade-offs: Monastic needs a job that tolerates it; Journalistic needs pre-trained focus. Rhythmic is the safe default for most jobs. A mismatch derails the habit.

Deep Work Ritual

When to use: Every deep session, to spend minimal willpower starting.

How: Pre-decide (1) where and for how long; (2) how you'll work (rules — no internet; metrics — words/20min); (3) how you'll support it (coffee, food, walk, tidy space).

Trade-offs: Feels mechanical, but that's the point — remove in-the-moment decisions that leak willpower.

4DX for Individual Depth

When to use: To translate "work more deeply" into a driven, tracked habit.

How: (1) Set a small number of wildly important goals; (2) track the lead measure — deep-work hours — not lag outcomes; (3) keep a compelling scoreboard (visible tally, circle hours that produced results); (4) run a weekly cadence of accountability review.

Trade-offs: Requires honest daily tracking; the scoreboard only motivates if you actually confront it.

Shutdown Ritual

When to use: End of every workday.

How: Algorithm — check inbox for anything urgent → capture loose tasks into master lists → skim every list + next few days' calendar → make a rough plan for tomorrow → say a closing phrase ("Shutdown complete").

Trade-offs: Takes 10–15 min; defeats the Zeigarnik effect so evenings truly restore attention.

Grand Gesture

When to use: A high-stakes project that deserves a jolt of importance.

How: Make a conspicuous investment/change of environment (a hotel room, a trip, a paid retreat) that raises the psychological stakes and mobilizes focus.

Trade-offs: Costs money/effort; overuse dilutes the effect. Reserve for projects that warrant it.

Hub-and-Spoke Collaboration

When to use: When ideas benefit from exchange but execution needs isolation.

How: Spend time in shared "hub" spaces for serendipitous encounters, then retreat to isolated "spoke" spaces to work deeply on what surfaced. The whiteboard effect: working with someone on a hard problem can push depth further.

Trade-offs: Pure isolation misses cross-pollination; pure openness kills focus. Alternate deliberately.

Scheduled Internet Blocks (Embrace Boredom)

When to use: Default operating mode to rebuild concentration.

How: Schedule the blocks when internet use is allowed; stay fully offline between them. If you need it sooner, reschedule the next block a few minutes out — never jump online impulsively.

Trade-offs: Uncomfortable at first; the discomfort is the training. Works at home too, not just at work.

Roosevelt Dash

When to use: To stretch your focus ceiling, or to blast through an important task.

How: Estimate the time a task needs, set a deadline well under it, work at total intensity (no email, no drift) to make it.

Trade-offs: Exhausting; use occasionally as interval training, not constantly.

Productive Meditation

When to use: During walks, commutes, showers — physical-but-not-mental time.

How: Hold one well-defined work problem in mind; when you notice distraction (drift to easier thoughts) or looping (rehashing knowns), gently redirect. Structure it: identify variables → determine next-step question → consolidate the gain.

Trade-offs: Frustrating early; builds both focus and problem-solving output over time.

Craftsman Tool Selection + Law of the Vital Few

When to use: Deciding whether to keep any network/social tool.

How: (1) Name the few high-level goals defining professional and personal success. (2) List the 2–3 key activities supporting each. (3) Keep a tool only if it substantially helps those (not "any benefit"). Concentrate on the ~20% of activities driving ~80% of results.

Trade-offs: Requires honesty about what actually matters; you'll drop tools that feel socially expected.

30-Day Quit (Packing-Party Test)

When to use: To measure a tool's real value.

How: Quit it quietly for 30 days. Then ask: (1) Would these 30 days have been notably better with it? (2) Did anyone care I wasn't using it? Readopt only on a clear yes to both.

Trade-offs: Mild FOMO; usually reveals the tool was justified only by the any-benefit standard.

Schedule Every Minute

When to use: Every workday, to prevent shallow drift.

How: Block the day in ~30-min chunks with an assigned task each; keep an overflow column; when reality derails a block, rebuild the remaining schedule rather than abandoning it.

Trade-offs: Not about rigid obedience — about staying thoughtful. Expect frequent revision.

Quantify Depth (College-Grad Heuristic)

When to use: To classify any ambiguous task as deep or shallow.

How: Ask "How many months to train a smart recent college grad with no field training to do this?" Few months → shallow; years → deep.

Trade-offs: A heuristic, not a law; but surprisingly clarifying for borderline tasks.

Shallow Work Budget + Fixed-Schedule Productivity

When to use: To cap shallow work and force prioritization.

How: Ask your boss what % of time should be shallow (often 30–50%); defend the budget. Separately, fix a hard workday endpoint and prune obligations backward to fit deep work into fewer hours.

Trade-offs: Requires saying no often; the constraint is the mechanism, not a limitation.

Become Hard to Reach

When to use: To reclaim attention from email.

How: (1) Sender filters — publish expectations that put the burden on the sender; (2) do more work per email — send process-centric replies that close the whole loop; (3) don't respond to ambiguous/uninteresting/disproportionately costly messages.

Trade-offs: Some senders bristle; net attention reclaimed is large. Not for messages where non-response has real cost.

Executive Presence: The Missing Link Between Merit and Success

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Executive Presence — Cheatsheet

Decision-ready rules from Hewlett. Keep beside you before a high-stakes moment.

The Three Pillars (weight & rule)

Pillar"How you…"Exec weightRule
Gravitasact67% (core)Fix first — without it, no title makes you a leader
Communicationspeak28%It's how not what; content persuades only ~15%
Appearancelook5%The filter — fail it and no one assesses the rest

Rule of thumb: Don't aim for straight A's. Nail ~3 top picks in each pillar to your natural strengths and avoid serious blunders.

Decision Rules

  • When merit isn't translating into advancement → audit all three pillars; the gap is almost always EP, not competence.
  • When in a crisis → own the mistake publicly and fast; handling catastrophe > avoiding it. Never deflect blame.
  • When a decision is being avoided → render a decision (not necessarily the perfect one) when no one else dares — but only after listening and finding the timely opening.
  • When you must show teeth as a woman/minority → frame it around the team/company; take the "I" out.
  • When speaking truth to power → come from a core of values (not grievance); leaven with humor to widen receptivity.
  • When opening a talk → connect in 5 seconds with a short personal story; then lose the props and make eye contact.
  • When you have a point in a meeting → snipe, don't spray: wait for a strong counterpoint or insightful question. But if you're leading, open with a bold agenda-setting statement.
  • When dressing → "appropriate for your environment, authentic to you." Dress for the job you want.
  • When told "you're doing great" → distrust it; ask for specific/timely/prescriptive feedback on a named recent encounter.
  • When given vague criticism ("be more vulnerable") → ask "How is what I'm doing getting in the way of my job?" It's usually the culture, not you.
  • When you hit the fork (conformity costs your identity) → distinguish "playing the game" from "selling out." Only you draw the line; don't put your soul in play.
  • When a culture violates a non-negotiable → walk away. "Nothing is worth that."
  • When you feel slighted → assume ignorance before bigotry; engage rather than withdraw.

Voice & Delivery Thresholds

  • Optimal voice frequency ≈ 125 Hz; lower reads as smart/successful. (−22 Hz ≈ +$187K CEO comp.)
  • Persuasion mix: passion 27% · voice 23% · presence 15% · content 15%.
  • Judgments of competence/likability/trust form in 250 milliseconds.
  • Kill: uptalk, "um/like/you know," shrillness, breathlessness, list-reading, phone-checking.
  • Use: pauses/silence, slowed pace, "phrasing off," narrative over bullet points, succinctness.

The Great Feedback Formula

Timely + Specific + Prescriptive + Business-framed. After it, the receiver knows what the problem is, why it matters, exactly what to do.

  • Give: frequent discrete pointers · never while angry (wait 24h) · good things first · embed correctives · catch people getting it right · "I want you to be successful."
  • Get: request it on a named encounter · thick skin · coach if needed · peer circle · sponsor · don't cry/burn bridges.

Six Gravitas Behaviors (self-audit)

Confidence under fire (79/76%) · Decisiveness (70%) · Integrity/truth-to-power (60%+) · EQ (~60%) · Reputation (56/57%) · Vision (50–54%).

Six Communication Traits

Superior speaking · Command a room · Assertiveness · Read the room · Humor/banter · Body language & posture.

Five Appearance Aspects

Polish & grooming (top) · Fit/wellness (not thinness) · Stylish clothes for your next job · Height (compensable) · Youth/vigor. Golden rule: minimize distractions from your competence.

Blunder Watch (career-enders in bold)

  • Gravitas: lack of integrity, sexual impropriety, bullying, lack of depth.
  • Communication: crying, phone-checking, long-windedness, notes/props, breathlessness.
  • Appearance: provocative dress (women), disheveled/unkempt (men), bling that steals thunder.

The Double Binds (tightrope — recognize, don't internalize)

Bind"Too much""Too little"
Forcebossy / bitch (31%)passive (31%)
Horntooting (29%)self-deprecating (24%)
Warmthtoo niceno empathy
Voiceshrilltentative
Age (women)too oldtoo young (sweet spot 39–42)

Contradictory feedback = hidden bias, not your defect. Widen latitude: team-framed arguments, humor, sniping, a bold brand, credentials, visible care.

glossary.md

Glossary — Executive Presence

250-millisecond judgment — The speed at which colleagues assess your competence, likability, and trustworthiness from appearance alone; these flash judgments stick (Ch 1, Ch 4).

Air cover — Sponsor protection secured before you step out to assert authenticity or take the spotlight; without it, visibility invites attack (Ch 7).

Always on — The principle that every verbal encounter (email, hallway chat, pitch) is a chance to build or erode your EP; you are never not presenting (Ch 3).

Appearance — The third EP pillar ("how you look"); rated least important long-term (5%) but the filter through which the other pillars are evaluated (Ch 1, Ch 4).

Bleached-out professional — Someone who scrubs away ethnic, religious, socioeconomic, or educational identifiers to be seen as "professional"; a lose-lose costing authenticity and visibility (Ch 7).

Command a room — Grabbing and holding an audience's attention; a core communication trait — "never be boring" (Ch 3).

Cracking the EP code — Learning and delivering the (often unwritten) rules of what bosses and coworkers look for (Ch 1).

Diversity dividend — The measurable bottom-line impact when leaders harness gender, ethnicity, culture, and nationality; your difference as a business asset (Ch 7).

Emotional intelligence (EQ) — Reading and acting on others' feelings (self- + situational awareness); a gravitas component and a muscle built by experience, not inborn (Ch 2).

Executive presence (EP) — The amalgam of confidence, poise, and authenticity that telegraphs you're in charge or deserve to be; the missing link between merit and success (Ch 1).

First language / second language — Trevor Phillips's model: your authentic identity (first) vs. the conventions of the dominant world you learn to survive (second) (Ch 7).

Fork in the road — The career rung where suppressing your difference no longer feels worth it (Ch 7).

Goldilocks syndrome — Being perpetually "too this, too that," never "just right" — the signature of hidden bias against those who don't fit the leader stereotype (Ch 6).

Grace under fire — Composure and confidence at the center of a crisis; the #1 gravitas behavior (79% women / 76% men) (Ch 2).

Gravitas — The first and core EP pillar ("how you act"); the "heft that marks you as worth following into the fire" (Ch 1, Ch 2).

Great Feedback Formula — Feedback that is timely + specific + prescriptive + framed in business outcome (Ch 5).

Invisible knapsack — The kit of inborn privileges the dominant group can't perceive it carries (Ch 6).

Iron core — The deep self-confidence you reach for to "lean into the wind" in a crisis (Ch 2).

Likability vs. competence trade-off — The most tenacious double bind: successful women (unlike men) suffer social rejection and lost trust (Ch 6).

Marzipan layer — The rich, sticky talent layer just below top management where qualified women and minorities stall for lack of EP feedback (Ch 5).

Narrow band of acceptability — The constrained range of behavior/appearance women (and minorities) are allowed before being penalized in one direction or the other (Ch 5, Ch 6).

Non-negotiables — The values or cultures that don't deserve your compliance; know them and walk away (Ch 7).

Personal brand / right-sizing your reputation — Proactively managing how you're perceived before others do it for you; a gravitas component (Ch 2).

Playing the game vs. selling out — Distinguishing benign conformity from a compromise of your soul; only you can draw the line (Ch 7).

Props — Notes, slides, lists, glasses, podiums — anything that blocks eye contact and signals you don't command your material (Ch 3).

Reading a room — Sensing mood and cultural cues and course-correcting on the spot; EQ applied to communication (Ch 3).

Shrillness — A high-pitched, emotion-raised voice; the most-cited destroyer of a woman's EP — the "hint of hysteria" (Ch 3).

Showing teeth — Being (and appearing) decisive; imposing direction and owning it — but do it discriminately (Ch 2).

Signature look — A consciously built, personalized appearance/brand that telegraphs you embrace the code yet channel individuality (Ch 4).

Speaking truth to power — Voicing convictions upward from a core of unshakable values; a gravitas component (Ch 2).

Sponsor — A powerful leader vested in your success who advocates, steers assignments, protects you, and gives the blunt EP feedback mentors won't (distinct from a mentor) (Ch 5, Ch 7).

Telegraph — To signal (vs. perform); EP is a measure of image you telegraph, not of performance (Ch 1).

The three pillars — Gravitas (act), communication (speak), appearance (look); the universal structure of EP (Ch 1).

Uptalk — Ending declarative statements on a rising note as if questioning; denies closure and undermines the message (Ch 3).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Executive Presence

Concrete, repeatable moves drawn from the book. Grouped by situation.

Deepening Gravitas

When to use: You're not yet perceived as leadership material despite the credentials.

How: Surround yourself with people better than you; be generous with credit; stick to what you know (back claims with firsthand examples); show humility (admit failings); smile more; empower others' presence to build your own; drive change rather than be changed.

Trade-offs: Humility disarms detractors but requires security; over-deference reads as weakness.

Grace Under Fire (Crisis Composure)

When to use: A crisis, a mistake (yours or others'), a hostile grilling.

How: Reach for your "iron core"; own mistakes publicly and fast; lay out concrete steps; never break eye contact; speak with empathy. Handling catastrophe > avoiding it.

Trade-offs: Deflecting blame to look clean (Hayward) is catastrophic; owning it (Dimon) bolsters gravitas.

Show Teeth Discriminately

When to use: A decision everyone is avoiding.

How: Listen, gather info, weigh options, wait for the opening (when others writhe in indecision), then demand action. Hide your teeth more often than you bare them; pair every hard call with EQ.

Trade-offs: For women, decisiveness risks the "bitch"/"not a team player" penalty — frame around the team.

Establish Connection in 5 Seconds

When to use: Opening any talk or presentation.

How: Unveil just enough of your inner core (a personal story) that the audience starts pulling for you — without oversharing. Give the impression you don't need to be liked.

Trade-offs: Over-revelation reads as neediness; too withheld reads as cold (especially penalizing for women).

Deliver Words as a Musician Delivers Notes

When to use: High-stakes speaking; when you want a point to land.

How: Vary phrasing, inflection, pace. "Phrase off" the ends of sentences for closure (kills uptalk). Slow down. Surround key words with silence — "a musician's impact lies in the rests."

Trade-offs: None if practiced; silence feels risky but reads as confidence.

Lose the Props → Make Eye Contact

When to use: Any presentation or important meeting.

How: Know your material cold so you can ditch notes, slides, and glasses. Prepare until the arc is "muscle memory." Move the podium; use a lavaliere mic to roam.

Trade-offs: Requires heavy prep; but reliance on props signals a lack of command.

Be a Sniper, Not a Machine Gun

When to use: A meeting where you want your voice to carry weight.

How: Don't speak unless you have a strong point; wait to make a counterpoint or ask an insightful question. When leading, invert: open immediately with a bold, agenda-setting statement.

Trade-offs: Silence early can be mistaken for having nothing to say — so land a strong first contribution.

Assert with the Company's Interest (Take Out the "I")

When to use: Pushing back, negotiating, or disagreeing upward.

How: Frame the demand around what's best for the company/team, not what you want. Mind tone and body language. Ask, "How will this be heard by those in power?" Follow a confrontation privately to reframe intent.

Trade-offs: Slower than blunt assertion, but avoids the "not a team player" brand.

Achieve Polish (Golden Rule: Minimize Distractions)

When to use: Always; especially first impressions and client meetings.

How: Regular nails/hair; well-cut attire for your body type; accessorize without billboarding; never let clothing advertise your body; look "appropriate for your environment, authentic to you."

Trade-offs: Provocative dressing distracts and costs credibility; disheveled reads as poor judgment.

Dress for the Job You Want

When to use: Angling for a promotion or stretch role.

How: Study the leaders above you; upgrade to their register; build a signature look with one distinctive style piece. Get "over the bar" first, then earn latitude to set your own code.

Trade-offs: Inauthentic clothing saps confidence — the look must still be you.

Great Feedback (Give)

When to use: Developing talent; a core leadership competency.

How: Timely (right before/after the blunder) + specific (one behavior) + prescriptive (what to do) + framed in business outcome. Frequent discrete pointers, not semi-annual downloads. Never while angry (wait 24h). Good things first. Embed correctives. Catch people getting it right. Preface: "I'm telling you this because I want you to be successful." For appearance, route through personal brand. Enlist a third party if litigation is a risk.

Trade-offs: Uncomfortable, but withholding stalls the marzipan layer and questions your own leadership.

Get the Feedback You Need (Receive)

When to use: You suspect an EP gap but keep hearing "you're doing great."

How: Recognize you need it; develop a thick skin; request specific, timely, prescriptive feedback on a recent high-EP encounter; if superiors won't, hire a coach (even on your own dime); build a peer feedback circle; cultivate a sponsor; listen for the "ring of truth"; demonstrate you'll act; don't cry or burn bridges.

Trade-offs: Vulnerable and painful — but far less painful than learning your blunders too late.

Widen Your Latitude (Tightrope Strategies)

When to use: You face the narrow band of acceptability (women/minorities).

How: Show teeth for the team; speak truth with humor; snipe don't spray; build a latitude-granting personal brand (Branson); wield credentials consciously ("Dr."); show you care (public good works).

Trade-offs: Doesn't erase the bias — navigates it while preserving authenticity.

Own Your Authenticity (Resolve the Tension)

When to use: At the "fork in the road" where conformity costs your identity.

How: Know your non-negotiables and walk away from cultures that don't deserve compliance; never fake a style that isn't you; play the long game (traditional role, untraditional execution); read slights as ignorance not bigotry; leverage and differentiate by your difference; secure air cover (a sponsor) before stepping out.

Trade-offs: Asserting difference invites bias — but bleaching out costs you personally and professionally, and difference is now a diversity dividend.

Factfulness: Ten Reasons We're Wrong About the World — and Why Things Are Better Than You Think

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Factfulness — Cheatsheet

The 10 Instincts → Warning Sign → Control Rule

#InstinctWarning sign (the "tell")Control rule
1Gap"the gap," two opposed groups, us/them, developed/developingLook for the majority
2Negativity"things are getting worse," bad news, nostalgiaExpect bad news
3Straight linea trend assumed to continue straightLines might bend (5 shapes)
4Fearfrightening images, "in times like these"Calculate the risk = danger × exposure
5Sizea lonely big number, one vivid victimCompare & divide (+ 80/20)
6Generalization"they," one example → whole group, "their culture"Question your categories
7Destiny"it will never change," "it's their culture"Slow change is still change
8Single perspectiveone cause/solution for everythingToolbox, not a hammer
9Blamea clear villain (or hero)Causes, not villains; systems, not heroes
10Urgency"now or never," "act today"Take small steps

The Four Income Levels (memorize this first)

LevelIncome/dayPeopleLife looks like
1~$1~1bnbarefoot, walk for dirty water, ~5 kids, extreme poverty
2~$4~3bnbike, sandals, gas stove, kids in school, unstable power
3~$16~2bncold tap, fridge, motorcycle, multiple jobs, high school
4>$64~1bncar, 12+ yrs education, hot water, air travel (you)

Each step up ≈ 4× income. PIN code of the world: 1-1-1-4 (Americas-Europe-Africa-Asia) → 1-1-4-5 by 2100.

Decision rules

  • See a lonely number? → Never trust it alone. Compare (vs. last year / a comparable place) AND divide (per person). Then judge.
  • See a doubling/tripling number? → Look closer (Ebola, terrorism), but get a 3rd data point before extrapolating.
  • Scared by a news event? → Ask: what's the actual death toll / proportion? Is this frightening or dangerous? Get calm before acting.
  • Tempted to extrapolate a line? → Which curve shape? Need 3 points. Does my Level-4 view apply to Levels 1–3?
  • Hear "majority"? → Ask 51% or 99%?
  • Hear "it's their culture / they'll never change"? → Feeling disguised as fact. Find a counterexample; talk across generations.
  • Offered one cause/solution for everything? → Get a toolbox. Test it against someone who disagrees.
  • Reaching for a villain? → You've stopped thinking. Find the system. Look in the mirror.
  • Told "act NOW or never"? → Almost always manipulation. Ask for time + data. Demand a range of scenarios, not one.
  • Forecasting? → Show mid + best + worst; round to your own disadvantage to protect credibility.

The "safe bet" heuristic

On Rosling's fact questions, the most positive answer is usually correct. When unsure about a global trend, guess that things are better than your instinct says.

Proportions people get wrong (reality is ~80–90%, guessed ~20%)

Vaccinated 1-yr-olds 88% · electricity access 80% · girls in primary school 90% · world life expectancy ~72 · extreme poverty (last 20 yrs) halved (29%→9%).

Thresholds & rules of thumb

  • 80/20: ~20% of a list's items = ~80% of the total — handle those first.
  • Rule of 70: years to double ≈ 70 ÷ growth%. (1%→70yr, 2%→35yr, 3%→24yr.)
  • Statistics caution: ignore differences smaller than ~10% — likely noise.
  • Forecast accuracy tracks system simplicity: demographics (decades) ≫ economics ≫ weather (a week).

The 5 global risks worth real urgency

Global pandemic · financial collapse · World War III · climate change · extreme poverty (+ the unknown risk). Approach all with cool heads, robust independent data, baby steps — never cry wolf.

Two foundational values

Humility (it's hard to get facts right; say "I don't know"; change your mind) + Curiosity (seek disconfirming facts; "how interesting that I was wrong"). Be a possibilist, not an optimist or pessimist.

glossary.md

Factfulness — Glossary

80/20 rule — Find the few largest items in any list; usually ~20% of items make up ~80% of the total. Deal with those first. (Ch 5)

Attention filter — A mental shield with ten instinct-shaped holes; only drama-fitting information passes, so we believe the unusual is usual. (Ch 4)

Bad and better — Holding two thoughts at once: a level can be bad while its direction is improving. (Ch 2)

Blame instinct — The urge to find a simple, guilty individual or group for a bad event; it stops thought and blocks systemic understanding. Control: look for causes, not villains. (Ch 9)

Chimpanzee benchmark — Random guessing scores 33% per 3-option question (~4/12); humans average ~2/12, i.e., worse than random. (Intro)

Chemophobia — Exaggerated fear of invisible chemical contamination, generalized from a few vivid examples; blocks data-driven argument. (Ch 4, Ch 6)

Compare and divide — The two "magic tools" for proportion: never trust a lonely number — compare it (over time/place) and divide it into a rate (per person). (Ch 5)

Cool chains — Refrigerated logistics keeping vaccines cold from factory to child; require the same infrastructure as new factories. (Ch 6)

Curve shapes — Trends come in five shapes: straight line, S-bend, slide, hump, doubling line. Three points are needed to tell them apart. (Ch 3)

Destiny instinct — Belief that innate traits fix the unchanging destiny of people/cultures/nations. Control: remember slow change is still change. (Ch 7)

Dollar Street — Project photographing ~300 families across 50+ countries by income, showing that income (not culture/religion/country) is the main factor in how people live. (Ch 1, Ch 6)

Dramatic instincts — The ten evolved mental shortcuts (gap, negativity, straight line, fear, size, generalization, destiny, single perspective, blame, urgency) that crave drama and distort the worldview. (Intro)

Doubling income scale — Comparing income by doublings ($1→$2→…→$64) because each extra dollar matters far more at low levels; six doublings span the four levels. (Ch 3)

Fear instinct — Attention to frightening things, which aren't necessarily the most dangerous (harm, captivity, contamination). Control: calculate the risks. (Ch 4)

Fill-up effect — Population grows ~3 billion more not from more births but from already-born children growing into adults over three generations, then stops. (Ch 3)

Four Income Levels — The book's master framework replacing developed/developing: Level 1 (~$1/day, ~1bn), Level 2 (~$4, ~3bn), Level 3 (~$16, ~2bn), Level 4 (>$64/day, ~1bn). Each step ≈ 4× income. (Ch 1)

Frightening vs. dangerous — Frightening = perceived risk; dangerous = real risk. Direct fear at the dangerous. (Ch 4)

Gap instinct — The urge to split things into two conflicting groups with a gap between; reality is usually a continuum with the majority in the middle. Control: look for the majority. (Ch 1)

Generalization instinct — Lumping together different things/people, or judging a category from one example. Control: question your categories. (Ch 6)

Hammer and nails — Overusing your favorite tool/expertise where it doesn't fit. Get a toolbox, not a hammer. (Ch 8)

Konzo — Incurable paralytic disease from improperly processed cassava that Rosling researched; central to the Nacala and Makanga stories. (Ch 10, Ch 11)

Mega misconception — A wrong belief so basic it distorts all global proportions. The three: world divided in two (Ch 1), world getting worse (Ch 2), population just increasing (Ch 3).

Negativity instinct — Noticing the bad more than the good, from misremembered pasts + selective reporting + feeling. Control: expect bad news. (Ch 2)

Overdramatic worldview — The instinctive, too-negative picture: world divided, worsening, gap widening. Opposite of the fact-based worldview. (Intro)

Peak child — The point (now reached) where the number of children worldwide stops increasing. (Ch 3)
