How: Find a comparable situation the audience already understands and map your idea onto it (software as supermarket vs. restaurant; weekly sales meetings as early Christian gatherings). Lead or close a point with one relevant statistic; never recite strings of numbers.

Trade-offs: A strained analogy is worse than none; test it on someone outside the project.

Emotional Matchmaking

When to use: Before any high-stakes internal presentation (Ch 5).

How: Canvass key individuals who have a pulse on the room's mood; ask how your proposal will land emotionally. Match your fervor to their receptivity. If they need recognition first, give it in a separate session before delivering bad news. End with hope rather than doom.

Trade-offs: Splitting recognition and warning across two meetings costs time and momentum, but combining them can produce open resentment.

The Seven-Tactic Issue-Selling Campaign

When to use: Selling any idea upward over weeks or months (Ch 7).

How: Tailor the pitch to each decision maker's goals; frame in business benefits and opportunity; regulate your emotions and protect the boss's standing; time it to a trend or decision window; build a coalition including people the target trusts; follow house norms; always bring a solution or a process for finding one. Start informal to gauge interest, then go formal.

Trade-offs: All seven combined explain ~40% of the difference between success and failure, but campaigns cost social capital — choose battles by asking how important the issue is to the company and to you.

Motivating Language Mix

When to use: Any pre-performance moment, one-on-one or to a crowd (Ch 6).

How: Include direction giving, empathy, and meaning making, then weight by need. Unknown challenge → more direction. Underdog or high stakes → more empathy and meaning. Obvious purpose → less meaning making. Sequence that works (McChrystal): direction → meaning → empathy → recap. Continue all three one-on-one after the speech.

Trade-offs: Veterans mid-operation want the plan, not reassurance; over-emphasized empathy reads as doubt in their capability.

Organizational Apology Execution

When to use: After the four diagnostic questions indicate an apology is warranted (Ch 8).

How: Match apologizer seniority to violation severity; address the actual victims; include candor, remorse, and a concrete commitment to change; choose a setting proportional to the harm; move fast, with a placeholder if facts are pending; use plain, self-implicating language, preferably spoken.

Trade-offs: On-site, in-person apologies maximize sincerity signals but are uncontrolled — rejection becomes a public confrontation.

Coherent Transition Story

When to use: Career change, interviews, networking, internal moves (Ch 9).

How: Ground the reasons in character ("I discovered I'm good at that"), cite multiple complementary reasons, extend the goal back in time and explain what blocked it, reframe past experience to surface the connecting pieces, and choose a familiar plot (maturation or education). Acknowledge the size of the jump explicitly.

Trade-offs: External causes ("I got fired") must be incorporated but never carry the justification; downplaying discontinuity to seem safe makes you dull and untrustworthy at once.

Multiple Stories for Multiple Selves

When to use: Early transition, when several paths are live (Ch 9).

How: Develop a distinct coherent story per possible self and test each with the audience that relates to it. Let responses tell you which to pursue hardest.

Trade-offs: Not deception, but requires discipline — airing all options with one audience destroys coherence.

The Story-Shaped Résumé

When to use: Whenever your target role differs from your last one (Ch 9).

How: Three parts, all pointing at one goal — (1) the position you want, (2) bulleted experience highlights proving you can do it, drawn from all experience including volunteer work, (3) a reverse-chronological professional summary phrased in the same terms, so every highlight claim is supported below. Build a separate version per target.

Trade-offs: A CV is exhaustive and neutral; a résumé is interpretive and must be rebuilt for each direction.

The Dataviz Two Questions

When to use: Before opening any charting tool (Ch 10).

How: Ask whether the information is conceptual or data-driven, and whether you're declaring or exploring. The quadrant tells you which skills to bring: editing and design (idea illustration), facilitation (idea generation), BI and programming (visual discovery), design and storytelling (everyday dataviz).

Trade-offs: Slower than clicking a chart type, but convenience produces charts that visualize a spreadsheet rather than an idea.

Subtractive Chart Design

When to use: Any chart destined for a live presentation (Ch 10).

How: One message, few variables. Cut historical context the decision doesn't need. If it takes more than a few seconds to digest, move it to paper or a personal screen instead of a slide.

Trade-offs: Requires courage — busy charts advertise your effort, clean ones advertise only the idea.

What Is / What Could Be Oscillation

When to use: Structuring any presentation intended to change behavior (Ch 11).

How: Open by describing the audience's reality until they nod, then introduce the alternative. Alternate the two poles through the middle, pairing every obstacle with its answer. Close with a call to action, then new bliss — concrete future rewards.

Trade-offs: Requires naming problems out loud; hiding them collapses the tension the pattern runs on.

Cheatsheet — Decision Rules

Core if/then rules

Current behavior contradicts the value you wantAmplify existing good behavior; do NOT announce the idealWhen norms and ideals clash, people follow what others do (Ch 3)
Someone resists needed learningDiagnose the attribute first, then swap the self-talk"No time / not relevant" is an aspiration symptom, not an argument (Ch 4)

Pitching your bossOne frame only, in private, tied to their stated goalsMixed opportunity+threat framing gets the least support of any option (Ch 6)

Feedback loop by team maturity (Ch 7)

  • Never exchanged feedback → one-to-one chats, private
  • Some trust established → speed-dating, 3 min each way, rotate, each names one action
  • Mature, strong relationships → live 360 circle over a meal; recipient listens and says thank you

Thresholds & numbers the authors commit to

Tells & smells

  • You're being clueless: you're technically strong, people avoid you, and when told, you blame back (Ch 2)
  • You've hit a phantom norm: the attitude you think is dominant belongs to the loudest one or two people (Ch 3)
  • It's an aspiration problem, not a time problem: the objections are "too long," "old way works," "flash in the pan" (Ch 4)
  • Your ask will fail: you opened with "May I ask you a favor?", apologized profusely, offered reciprocity, or minimized the need (Ch 5)
  • Your pitch will fail: it names both the upside of acting and the risk of not acting (Ch 6)
  • Your feedback will land as dominance: majority member → underrepresented colleague, unasked (Ch 7)
  • You're listening to protect: you're rehearsing your reply and guarding your position (Ch 8)
  • Confirmation bias has set in: a colleague's occasional missteps have hardened into "X is difficult" (Ch 9)
  • You're coaching for compliance: you're doing most of the talking and naming gaps (Ch 10)
  • You're rationalizing: "everyone does this," "just following orders," "not like I'm robbing a bank" (Ch 13)
  • Your environment is eroding self-control: high uncertainty, cognitive overload, late nights, back-to-back stretch goals (Ch 13)

Defaults

  • Assume your view is a view; ask the challenge questions anyway (Ch 9)
  • Assume the quiet majority is already empathic; your job is volume (Ch 3)
  • Assume people will help; the constraint is how you ask (Ch 5)
  • Assume delivery, not content, decides whether feedback lands (Ch 7)
  • Assume your future self is less virtuous than you think (Ch 13)
  • Set your relationship goals low if needed — "functional" is a legitimate target (Ch 9)

glossary.md

Glossary

Affinity bias — Unconscious tendency to align with people similar to you in appearance, beliefs, and background (Ch 9)

Anticipatory utility — The pleasure of expectation itself; readers' reward circuits peak before a passage's high point (Ch 11)

Aspiration — The wanting-to-learn attribute; raisable by shifting focus from challenges to future benefits (Ch 4)

Attentional blink — Momentary lapse causing missed words in a list; emotionally significant words produce none (Ch 11)

Automated social hierarchy detection — Inferring org standing from response latency; slower repliers hold more power (Ch 2)

Coachable moment — An opening for development: an evident challenge, a wake-up call, or a vague unease (Ch 10)

Coaching for compliance — Drilling into problems and targets; works for predetermined goals, fails for behavioral change (Ch 10)

Coaching with compassion — Coaching from the person's dreams and vision; activates brain regions for openness and learning (Ch 10)

Cognitive control — Putting attention where you want it and holding it against temptation; colloquially, willpower (Ch 2)

Cognitive empathy — Understanding another's perspective by thinking about feelings rather than feeling them (Ch 2)

Confirmation bias — Reading new evidence as proof of existing beliefs, making it harder for others to disprove you (Ch 9)

Connectors — The most-connected people in a group, through whom information, ideas, and values flow (Ch 3)

Developmental network — The extended circle supporting someone's change; a personal board of advisers (Ch 10)

Downgraders — Words that soften criticism ("kind of," "a little," "maybe") plus deliberate understatement (Ch 7)

Effectiveness (reinforcement) — Making clear what you need and what impact the help will have (Ch 5)

Emotional empathy — Feeling what another feels; used for mentoring, clients, and reading group dynamics (Ch 2)

Empathic concern — Sensing what another person needs from you; requires managing distress without numbing (Ch 2)

Ethical mirage — Overestimating the virtuousness of your future self (Ch 13)

Eulogy virtues — What people praise after you've died: character and what you did for others (Ch 13)

Fair witness — An inner voice that reports the facts of a situation in balance, neither defensive nor punishing (Ch 4)

Fundamental attribution error — Attributing others' behavior to personality and your own to circumstances (Ch 9)

Humble inquiry — Setting aside your own assumptions and letting the other person do 80% of the talking (Ch 10)

Identity segmentation — Compartmentalizing personal and professional life under different moral codes (Ch 13)

Ideals vs. norms — What a group says people ought to do vs. what most members actually do; norms win (Ch 3)

Implementation intentions — "If X happens, then I will do Y," specified in advance and voiced aloud (Ch 13)

In-group (reinforcement) — Assuring a potential helper you're on the same team and the team matters (Ch 5)

Intentional Change Theory — Ideal self → real self → learning agenda → experimenting and practicing (Ch 10)

Job crafting — Proactively reshaping your tasks, relationships, and view of your job to make it meaningful (Ch 13)

Know-it-all vs. learn-it-all — Status-seeking expertise display vs. humility to hear criticism and diverse views (Ch 7)

Learning agenda — A road map from strengths and passions toward the ideal self; not a performance improvement plan (Ch 10)

Listening to co-create — Listening to connect and explore, with psychological safety (Ch 8)

Listening to protect — Defensive listening that guards your identity; the speaker feels ignored (Ch 8)

Manvising — Men giving women advice they neither asked for nor want (Ch 7)

Mirror test — Would you like the person in the mirror after this decision? (Ch 13)

Moral humility — Recognizing that anyone can transgress without vigilance (Ch 13)

Naive realism — Believing you see an issue objectively, so dissenters must be uninformed or biased (Ch 9)

Open awareness — Noticing broadly without judging, censoring, or getting swept up in any one thing (Ch 2)

Personal balance sheet — Strengths, weaknesses, and enduring distinctive qualities, weighed against a long-term vision (Ch 10)

Personal vision statement — A short written statement of the ideal self, kept present as a daily reminder (Ch 10)

Phantom norms — Behaviors that seem dominant only because a few loud or prominent people display them (Ch 3)

Positive identity (reinforcement) — Framing the helper as a helpful person uniquely placed to assist (Ch 5)

Prevention focus — Orientation toward vigilance, downside management, and playing not to lose (Ch 6)

Processing fluency — How little brainpower a reader spends extracting your meaning (Ch 11)

Promotion focus — Orientation toward aspirations, ideals, the future, and playing to win (Ch 6)

Psychic attrition — Erosion of attention to others that accompanies rising rank and power (Ch 2)

Publicity test — Would you be comfortable with this choice on the newspaper's front page? (Ch 13)

Radical candor — Kim Scott's argument that blunt feedback beats withholding it ("ruinous empathy") (Ch 7)

Readiness to change — Whether someone is open to the reflection and experimentation coaching requires (Ch 10)

Resonant relationship — The caring, trusting bond that makes coaching effective (Ch 10)

Résumé virtues — Listable skills, abilities, and accomplishments; largely what you've done for yourself (Ch 13)

Reward circuit — Midbrain neurons that light up in response to pleasurable stimuli, including good prose (Ch 11)

Self-talk — Internal narration about yourself; the lever for aspiration, self-awareness, curiosity, and vulnerability (Ch 4)

Social skills (C-suite sense) — Self-awareness, listening/communication, cross-group facility, and theory of mind (Ch 1)

Somatic markers — Gut sensations from the insula and amygdala signaling that something feels right or wrong (Ch 2)

Status incongruence — When your role's societal status doesn't match the role you play in context (Ch 7)

Systems effect — One weak team member degrading the whole group's performance (Ch 1)

The Eight S's — Simplicity, specificity, surprise, stirring language, seductiveness, smart thinking, social content, storytelling (Ch 11)

The Third Entity — You, your colleague, and the dynamic between you; work on the third thing (Ch 9)

Theory of mind — Inferring how others think and feel; the hardest-to-fake social skill (Ch 1)

Three A's of feedback — Assist, actionable, asked for (Ch 7)

Triad of Awareness — Focus on yourself, on others, and on the wider world (Ch 2)

True North groups — Small trusted groups where self-knowledge begins with self-revelation (Ch 2)

Upgraders — Words that intensify criticism ("absolutely," "totally," "completely") (Ch 7)

Vulnerability (learning attribute) — Tolerating your own beginner mistakes on the way up the curve (Ch 4)

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques

Decompose "Soft Skills" Before Assessing (Ch 1)

When to use: Hiring, promoting, or developing anyone where "good with people" is the criterion.

How: Score separately on self-awareness, listening/communication, cross-group facility, and theory of mind. Place high-potentials in roles that force contact with varied constituencies and monitor performance there.

Trade-offs: Slower than a résumé screen; no established tool exists at the executive level, so you must build one.

The Triad Diagnostic (Ch 2)

When to use: A capable leader is failing and you can't name why.

How: Map symptom to missing focus — rudderless (inward), clueless (others), blindsided (outward).

Trade-offs: Diagnostic only; each focus is trained differently, and strength in one doesn't transfer.

Pick the Right Empathy (Ch 2)

When to use: Any high-stakes interpersonal moment.

How: Cognitive empathy to explain yourself and to de-escalate an overheated conversation; emotional empathy to mentor and read a room; empathic concern to judge what someone needs from you.

Trade-offs: Too much emotional empathy causes compassion fatigue; too little numbs you.

Attention Reps (Ch 2)

When to use: Building focus as a trainable capacity.

How: Notice the mind has wandered, return it to the chosen object, hold. Protect uninterrupted reflection time to enable exploration.

Trade-offs: Sleep loss, stress, and overload disable the switch from exploitation to exploration.

Amplify Existing Norms Instead of Announcing Ideals (Ch 3)

When to use: Any culture change, especially when current behavior contradicts the target.

How: Measure the actual norm; find where the desired behavior already happens; make it visible via recognition and incentives; identify connectors and co-create the initiative with them.

Trade-offs: Slower and less visible than a values launch — but a values launch that outruns the norm produces cynicism.

Self-Talk Substitution (Ch 4)

When to use: You or someone you coach is resisting required learning.

How: Diagnose which attribute is blocked, then swap the phrase. "I don't need to learn this" → "What would my future look like if I did?" "I'm already fine" → "Am I really? How do I compare with peers?" "This is boring" → "I wonder why others find it interesting." "I'm terrible at this" → "I'm making beginner mistakes, but I'll get better."

Trade-offs: Requires catching the thought in flight; not a substitute for real capability gaps.

Import Curious Language (Ch 4)

When to use: A required topic bores you.

How: Notice the How…? Why…? I wonder…? phrasing you use about a genuine interest; aim it at the boring topic; take exactly one action to answer one question.

Trade-offs: You only need one spark, but arguing someone into interest never works.

The Three Reinforcements (Ch 5)

When to use: Asking anyone for help, and in day-to-day priming.

How: In-group (shared experience over shared trait); positive identity (identity nouns, tailored, plus pre-emptive gratitude); effectiveness (state the need and the impact, follow up afterward, allow alternative forms of help).

Trade-offs: Reciprocity framing, apology, and minimizing all backfire; ask individually, never by group email.

Single-Frame Pitching (Ch 6)

When to use: Proposing anything upward.

How: Read the boss's tells for promotion vs. prevention focus, then pitch opportunity or threat — never both. Pitch in private, tie it to their stated goals, and pre-answer resources, coalition difficulty, and political cost.

Trade-offs: Raises endorsement 15–18%; mixed frames get the least support of any framing.

Recruit Allies Before Pitching (Ch 6)

When to use: Before raising anything contentious.

How: Socialize with colleagues first; ask to cite their support or have them co-present; ideally let a well-positioned colleague who won't benefit make the case.

Trade-offs: Speaking on behalf of others is 57% more influential — but takes time and cedes some ownership.

The Three A's Filter (Ch 7)

When to use: Before any unsolicited feedback, mandatorily across power or identity lines.

How: Is it meant to assist? Is it actionable? Was it asked for — and if not, ask for feedback on your own work first.

Trade-offs: The third A costs a step but neutralizes the power transfer that makes advice read as dominance.

Match Upgraders and Downgraders (Ch 7)

When to use: Cross-cultural feedback.

How: Listen for the intensity words your counterpart uses and mirror them. In indirect cultures, praise the good specifically and omit the bad; the silence carries the message.

Trade-offs: Feels evasive to direct-culture speakers and blunt to indirect ones — calibrate to the recipient, not your comfort.

Feedback Loops by Team Maturity (Ch 7)

When to use: Building a candid culture on a diverse team.

How: One-to-one chats (new teams) → speed-dating rounds, three minutes each way (closer teams) → live 360 circles over a meal (mature teams). Structure content as one strength + one improvement, or start/stop/continue.

Trade-offs: Public formats require courage but prevent backchannel gossip and normalize feedback.

Choose Your Listening Attitude (Ch 8)

When to use: Any conversation where the relationship matters.

How: Name whether you're listening to protect, to judge, or to co-create. In co-create mode hold four questions: What are they trying to say? What are they thinking? What do they expect to explore with me? How can I connect to their world?

Trade-offs: Costs attention up front; the alternative is a threat response you then have to repair.

The Third Entity Reframe (Ch 9)

When to use: A conflict has become personal and polarized.

How: Imagine three parties — you, them, and the dynamic. Make progress on the dynamic (a decision, an assignment, the tension itself) rather than trying to change the person.

Trade-offs: Doesn't fix genuinely abusive behavior; sometimes you must cut losses.

Conflict Experiments (Ch 9)

When to use: A difficult relationship you haven't been able to shift.

How: Pick two or three tactics, define what you'll do differently, set a time period, observe. Keep, tweak, or abandon. Do something the other person doesn't expect to interrupt the pattern.

Trade-offs: Treat failures as information; repeating a dead tactic is the real error.

Compassionate Coaching Sequence (Ch 10)

When to use: Helping someone through a real behavioral or career change.

How: Check readiness → ask ideal-self questions and let them talk 80% → write a short personal vision statement → build a personal balance sheet including enduring qualities → set a learning agenda from strengths → experiment, review regularly, and surround them with a developmental network.

Trade-offs: Slower than advice-giving; advice is faster but triggers stress and blocks learning for broad goals.

The Eight S's Revision Pass (Ch 11)

When to use: Revising any business writing.

How: Ask which S is missing. Simplicity (cut, activate, drop tangents); specificity (concrete nouns, memorable shorthand); surprise (novelty, wordplay); stirring (emotional verbs, metaphor); seductiveness (open with a question or mystery); smart (fresh distinction, universal truth); social (people, your own voice, second person); story.

Trade-offs: Passive voice can cut comprehension accuracy 10%; nested clauses slow reading and add errors.

Five Voices Selection (Ch 12)

When to use: Choosing how to show up in a given moment.

How: Character before hard conversations; context before details and when presenting up; clarity when the team is scattered (including empowering them to say no); curiosity when work is interdependent, when coaching, or when emotions run high; connection to stay visible as your span grows.

Trade-offs: Requires the self-awareness to notice which voice the moment wants.

The Newspaper Headline Question (Ch 12)

When to use: Annual or quarterly prioritization with a direct report.

How: Ask, "If we were to publish this in a newspaper, what would you want the big headlines to be for you and your team at the end of the year?" Then use the answer as the reference point for later re-prioritization.

Trade-offs: Forces hard trade-offs some people would rather defer.

Ethical Pre-Commitment (Ch 13)

When to use: Before you face a moral challenge — which is the only time it works.

How: Write eulogy-virtue goals; make specific if-then plans aloud; recruit ethical mentors inside and outside; screen employers for moral fit and ask about it in interviews; signal your standards subtly.

Trade-offs: Feels theoretical until needed; that's precisely the ethical mirage it counters.

The Three Rationalization Tests (Ch 13)

When to use: Any decision where you notice yourself constructing a justification.

How: Publicity (front page?), generalizability (precedent for everyone?), mirror (would you like that person?). Also run rules / consequences / virtues. If any answer is no, stop.

Trade-offs: Requires slowing down — and rushing is itself a strong predictor of unethical action.

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Grove's Decision Rules

Thresholds & Defaults

QuantityGrove's number
Direct reports (supervisory manager)6–8; 3–4 too few, 10 too many
Time budget per subordinate~½ day/week (2 days → meddling; 1 hour → can't monitor)
Coordinating-group membership½ day/week = one subordinate-equivalent
One-on-one length1 hour minimum
One-on-one frequencyWeekly (low TRM) → every few weeks (veteran)
Decision-meeting size≤6–7; 8 absolute cutoff
Ad hoc mission-oriented meetings>25% of your time = malorganization
Problems absorbed by regular meetingsTarget 80%
Work simplification, round one30–50% of steps eliminated
MBO objective difficulty50/50 odds of hitting it
MBO cycle if planning annuallyQuarterly or monthly
Pipeline loss factor~20% (semiconductor benchmark)
Visual aid pacing4 min presentation + discussion per aid
Interview talk ratioCandidate 80%
Performance bonus~50% senior / 10–25% middle manager
Training time2–4% of employee hours (Intel)
Training leverage12 hrs prep → 200 hrs returned at 1% improvement
Long-range plan horizon vs. commitmentLook 5 years, commit 1

Decision Rules

  • If a step isn't the limiting step, don't optimize it. Find the longest/hardest/costliest step and schedule backward from delivery.
  • If a defect can be caught earlier, catch it there — cost compounds with every stage it survives. Exception: reliability defects admit no economic trade-off at all.
  • If big problems are unlikely, monitor rather than gate. Same money buys far more coverage.
  • If you have only one indicator, you have none. Pair every quantity with a quality, every effect with its counter-effect.
  • If you wouldn't act on a leading indicator, don't track it — you've bought anxiety, not control.
  • If you're measuring calls instead of orders, you're measuring activity, not output.
  • If value can be priced → market. If not, and CUA is low → contract. If CUA is high and interests are shared → culture. If CUA is high and interest is self → chaos (lower the CUA or build group-interest; trying harder won't work).
  • If you say yes to something, name what you just said no to. Time is the only truly finite resource.
  • If you're free and have no discretionary project inventory, you will meddle. Keep one stocked.
  • If two people are debating something that affects only them, break it off and move the staff meeting on.
  • If you don't know what decision the meeting must produce, don't call it.
  • If a decision is controversial, be more explicit, not less — obscuring only postpones the argument and deepens the anger.
  • If no consensus has formed and the deadline has arrived, the senior person decides. Using position power before that point is destructive; refusing to use it after is equally so.
  • If peers are circling, insert a peer-plus-one — or let whoever has most at stake take charge.
  • If you're forecasting demand, don't discount it by what you think you can deliver — you'll never tool up for the real demand.
  • If your subordinate's task changed, their TRM just reset. Revert to structured direction immediately, without embarrassment.
  • If you're delegating, monitor at the rough-draft stage, sample partially, and set frequency by TRM. No monitoring = abdication. Full checking = meddling.
  • If a review has more messages than the person can remember, cut some. What you drop keeps until next time.
  • If you uncover a surprise while preparing a review, deliver it anyway. Swallow hard.
  • If the subordinate is still denying or blaming, do not propose the solution — nothing can happen until they assume responsibility.
  • If you get commitment without agreement, take it. Don't confuse emotional comfort with operational need.
  • If a manager's organization failed, his rating cannot exceed theirs — no matter how well he presents.
  • If your best review effort goes to your worst performers, you have it backwards. Stars carry disproportionate output; improving them is the high-leverage move.
  • If someone valuable says "I quit," drop everything now. Deferring confirms exactly the feeling that produced it.
  • If a promotion went too far, recycle — don't fire. It was management's misjudgment.
  • If the training contradicts how you actually operate, it does damage, not nothing.

Choosing a Management Style (TRM)

Subordinate's TRM on this taskStyleAlways
LowStructured; tell what, when, howMonitor
MediumTwo-way communication, support, mutual reasoningMonitor
HighMinimal: set objectives, monitorMonitor

Trap: managers skip the medium row, choosing full immersion or full absence. And 90% rate their own style as more delegating than their subordinates do.

Choosing a Control Mode

Low CUAHigh CUA
Self-interestMarketCHAOS
Group-interestContractCulture

Tells & Smells

What you seeWhat it means
Output great, but turnover up and people grumblingLight from distant stars — you're seeing last year's work. Trust the internal measures.
A unit that hits monthly goals only in the final weekPoor manpower/equipment use; one breakdown from missing entirely
People waiting to hear the boss's view before speakingFree discussion has already failed; decisions will be worse than your information allows
"I think our position seems to be…"Peer-group syndrome — consensus-hunting, not thinking
A queue choking a process that passes 98% of casesYou're inspecting 100% where sampling would do. Sorting the queue is overhead; shrinking inspection is throughput.
Salespeople chasing commissions you designedYou built a market inside your org. Audit incentives before blaming people for responding to them.
A manager who wafflesNegative leverage: no green light is a red light, and a whole org can stop
A visibly depressed managerPervasive, elusive, and very hard to counter — worse than a bad training session
Someone quits saying money and perksPossibly fine. Someone quits feeling unappreciated → you failed as their manager
A candidate who impresses you enormouslyNo signal. Grove hired one such person who "failed badly on the job."
Interview answers you can't evaluateYou're not in shared vocabulary — steer to subjects familiar to both
A "meets requirements" performerTwo kinds: noncompetitor (settled, unchallenged) vs. competitor (just promoted, will exceed again). Same rating, opposite meanings.
A high performer given no new challengeThey will atrophy back to "meets" and stay there
Objectives you're confident of hittingSet too low — you're leaving output on the table
Review comments that are general, avoid negatives, or contradict the raiseFour of the seven things managers hate about their own reviews

Fast Diagnostics

  • Underperformance: If their life depended on it, could they do it? Yes → motivation. No → training.
  • Where someone sits on Maslow: Does the absolute raise matter, or the relative one? Absolute → physiological/safety. Relative → esteem/self-actualization (money as measure).
  • Whether to befriend a subordinate: Imagine delivering a tough review to them. Do you cringe? Yes → don't.
  • Whether a meeting is justified: Necessary? Desirable? Justifiable? Anything but yes on all three → don't call it.
  • Whether you're delegating or abdicating: Are you monitoring?
  • Whether it's monitoring or meddling: Are you sampling, or checking everything?

Grove's Named Laws

  • The output equation — A manager's output = the output of his organization + the output of the neighboring organizations under his influence.
  • Grove's Law — All large organizations with a common business purpose end up in a hybrid organizational form.
  • Grove's Principle of Didactic Management — "Ask one more question!"
  • Grove's malorganization test — >25% of time in ad hoc meetings (not meetings generally).
  • The motto — "Let chaos reign, then rein in chaos."

glossary.md

Glossary — High Output Management

Abdication — Delegating a task and then dropping the monitoring. "Delegation without follow-through is abdication." (Ch 3, Ch 12)

Achiever — In the ring-toss experiment, the person who stands just far enough away that success is a genuine challenge, working at the boundary of capability. Contrasted with gamblers (high risk, no influence) and conservatives (minimal risk). (Ch 11)

Achievement-driven — One of two roads to self-actualization: an abstract need to achieve in everything, held by a minority. Compare competence-driven. (Ch 11)

Assembly — Production operation combining components into a new entity. One of the three fundamental operations. (Ch 1)

Batching — Grouping similar tasks so one mental set-up cost serves many transactions: reading all reports in a block, accumulating one-on-one items in a hold file. (Ch 3, Ch 4)

Beauty contest — The failure mode of a performance bonus based on subjective elements. (Ch 15)

The blast — A performance review for someone who could be fired unless turned around; essentially conflict resolution. (Ch 13)

Black box — Representation of any production-like activity as inputs + labor → output, into which you cut "windows" to see internal workings and predict future output. (Ch 2)

Build to forecast — Committing resources against "a contemplation of future orders," accepting inventory risk. Necessary when throughput time exceeds the customer's tolerable wait. (Ch 2)

Build to order — Waiting for the order, then finding a hole in the schedule. No inventory risk, long customer wait. (Ch 2)

Building czar — The resident senior manager who periodically scores a building's upkeep against other buildings — Grove's example of manufacturing a racetrack. (Ch 11)

Can't/won't diagnostic — Underperformance has only two causes. Test: if their life depended on it, could they do it? Yes → not motivated (motivation). No → not capable (training). (Ch 11)

Competence-driven — One of two roads to self-actualization: task mastery pursued for its own sake, like the violinist or the skateboarder. (Ch 11)

Conservatives — Ring-toss participants who stood over the pegs and dropped the rings; minimal risk. Punishing failure converts achievers into these. (Ch 11)

Constructive confrontation — Intel's favored problem-solving approach, taught in its management courses. (Ch 16)

Continuous operation — Automated high-volume flow buying lower cost and predictable quality at the price of flexibility; a continuous egg-boiler cannot make a four-minute egg. (Ch 1)

Contractual obligations — The control mode based on agreed rules defining work and standards, plus generalized authority to monitor, evaluate, and correct. Requires overhead: supervisors, police, auditors. (Ch 10)

Corporate citizenship — Treating a valued employee as the company's asset, pursuing every avenue to retain them even by transferring them to a peer's department. (Ch 14)

CUA factor — Composite index of an environment's Complexity, Uncertainty, and Ambiguity, which together with individual motivation determines the appropriate control mode. (Ch 10)

Difference analysis — Comparing what the environment demands now against what it will demand in about a year; the gap defines what new work must exist. (Ch 6)

Dual reporting — Reporting jointly to a mission-oriented supervisor (priorities, daily monitoring) and a functional one (standards, technical oversight, career). The practice that makes hybrid organizations work. (Ch 9)

Free discussion → clear decision → full support — The three-stage ideal decision-making model. Free and clear matter most exactly where disagreement is greatest. (Ch 5)

Free-market forces — The control mode based on price, requiring clearly defined dollar value and no supervision. (Ch 10)

Functional organization — Totally centralized form: each function serves all units. Wins on scale, reallocation, specialist leverage, and focus. (Ch 8)

Functional test — A test that consumes or destroys the unit tested. Prefer in-process inspection. (Ch 1)

Gamblers — Ring-toss participants who casually tossed rings at faraway pegs: high risk, no influence on outcome. (Ch 11)

Gate-like inspection — Holding all material until tests complete. Slows throughput but limits escapes. Compare monitoring. (Ch 2)

Grove's Law — "All large organizations with a common business purpose end up in a hybrid organizational form." The one exception is the conglomerate, which lacks that common purpose. (Ch 8)

Grove's Principle of Didactic Management — "Ask one more question!" When you think the subordinate has said all he wants, ask another — until both feel you've reached the bottom. (Ch 4)

Hold file — Where supervisor and subordinate accumulate important-but-not-urgent items for the next one-on-one; batching applied to a relationship. (Ch 4)

Hybrid organization — A mix of mission-oriented business divisions and centralized functional groups. Balances responsiveness and leverage. (Ch 8)

In-process inspection — Monitoring a process variable instead of destroying product — a thermometer in the egg-boiler water. Always preferred to destructive testing. (Ch 1, Ch 2)

Incoming (receiving) inspection — Testing raw material at the moment of receipt; the lowest-value inspection point. (Ch 1, Ch 2)

Indicator — A measurement focused on a specific operational goal. Must cover output not activity, be physical and countable, and be paired. Any measurement beats none. (Ch 2)

Information hierarchy — Verbal (fastest, sketchiest — the headline) → written report (the article) → reiteration and perspective (the news magazine). Sources should complement each other and be deliberately redundant. (Ch 3)

Internal measures — What goes on inside the black box — including what sets the stage for future periods' output. Weighed against output measures in a review. (Ch 13)

Internal subcontractor — How to think of a functional group: providing services to all business units, presumably cheaper and more responsive than an outside vendor. (Ch 8)

Key result — A dated, unambiguous milestone that paces you toward an objective. "Reaching towns A, B, and C in 10, 20, and 30 minutes." (Ch 6)

Knowledge power vs. position power — In know-how businesses these diverge rapidly because managers "get a little more obsolete every day." The middle manager's job is to mesh them. (Ch 5)

Know-how manager — An individual contributor who gathers and disseminates knowledge, exerting great influence on neighboring organizations. A middle manager by influence, not authority. (Intro, Ch 3)

Leverage — The output generated by a given work activity. Can be positive or negative. Raised by breadth (many people affected), duration (brief act, long effect), or uniqueness (key knowledge). (Ch 2, Ch 3)

Light from distant stars — Output indicators reflecting work done in earlier periods, masking a manager's current performance. Grove's own review error. (Ch 13)

Limiting step — The longest, most difficult, most sensitive, or most expensive step in a flow. Design the whole flow around it, working backward from delivery. (Ch 1)

Linearity indicator — Cumulative actual progress plotted against the ideal straight line to target; flashes an early warning while correction is still possible. (Ch 2)

Lowest competent level — Where a decision should be made: closest to the situation, combining technical knowledge with judgment earned from errors. (Ch 5)

Lowest-value-stage rule — Detect and fix problems at the lowest-value stage possible. "Reject before investing further value." (Ch 1, Ch 2)

Malorganization test (Grove's) — Not total meeting time (Drucker's 25%), but the share of time in ad hoc, mission-oriented meetings. Over 25% signals malorganization. (Ch 4)

Managerial meddling — A supervisor exploiting superior knowledge to assume command of a subordinate's situation. Negative leverage: the subordinate narrows his view of what's expected and shows less initiative. (Ch 3)

MBO (Management by Objectives) — Planning applied to daily work, answering two questions: where do I want to go (objective) and how will I pace myself (key results). A stopwatch, not a legal document. (Ch 6)

Messages — The consolidated themes a performance review actually delivers, distilled from raw observations on the worksheet. (Ch 13)

Mission-oriented meeting — Ad hoc, held to produce a specific output, usually a decision. Cap at eight attendees; the chairman does most of the work before it starts. (Ch 4)

Mission-oriented organization — Totally decentralized form: each unit pursues its mission independently. Has exactly one advantage — responsiveness — which is decisive. (Ch 8)

Monitoring (inspection) — Sampling while the bulk keeps moving; stop the line after repeated failures. Far more coverage per dollar than gate inspection. Lean toward it when big problems are unlikely. (Ch 2)

Monitoring (managerial) — Checking that an activity proceeds in line with expectations. The presence or absence of it is what separates delegation from abdication. Not meddling. (Ch 3, Ch 12)

Nudging — Advocating a course of action without commanding — a call, a note, a comment. "For every unambiguous decision we make, we probably nudge things a dozen times." (Ch 3)

Objective — Where you want to go. Nests: a subordinate's objective is often the supervisor's key result. (Ch 6)

Offset (time offset) — Deliberately delaying a shorter step so it completes in sync with the limiting step. Also, the lag between a manager's activity and his organization's output. (Ch 1, Ch 13)

One-on-one — A regularly scheduled supervisor-subordinate meeting for mutual teaching and information exchange. The subordinate's meeting: his outline, his agenda, his work area, minimum one hour, frequency set by task-relevant maturity, scheduled on a rolling basis. (Ch 4)

Operation review — Formal presentations by managers to managers who are not their immediate supervisors, carrying teaching across organizational levels. Four roles: organizing manager, reviewing manager, presenters, audience. (Ch 4)

Operational values — The shared sense of how things are done that lets structure become internally given rather than externally imposed, and without which a supervisor cannot effectively delegate. (Ch 12, Ch 14)

Opportunity at risk — What a shutdown would actually cost: lost customers plus the cost of luring them back. The real justification for inventory. (Ch 1)

Output measures — The black box's output: completed designs, sales quotas met, yield increases. Weighed against internal measures. (Ch 13)

Paired indicators — Measuring both effect and counter-effect, because indicators direct behavior. Inventory level ↔ shortages; vouchers processed ↔ errors found. (Ch 2)

Peer-group syndrome — A group of organizational equals going in circles without noticing, because people fear differing from the group. (Ch 5)

Peer-plus-one — The remedy: adding one hierarchical level above a peer group, who acts as "a godfather, a repository of knowledge about how decisions should be made." (Ch 5)

Performance bonus — The variable portion of pay, scaled up with total compensation: ~50% for senior managers, 10–25% for middle managers. (Ch 15)

Potential trap — Rating form rather than substance. "The performance rating of a manager cannot be higher than the one we would accord to his organization." Deliberately inverted when hiring. (Ch 13, Ch 14)

Present value (applied to reviews) — Weighing long-term-oriented work against short-term: how much will the future-oriented activity pay back, and what is that worth today? (Ch 13)

Process — Production operation that physically or chemically changes material. One of the three fundamental operations. (Ch 1)

Process-oriented meeting — Regularly scheduled, held to share knowledge and exchange information. Should absorb ~80% of problems. Three types: one-on-one, staff meeting, operation review. (Ch 4)

Programmed visit — A formal errand ("Mr. Clean" inspections) that creates the occasion for informal ad hoc information-gathering. (Ch 3)

Racetrack — A deliberately created arena of measured competition — rules of the game plus a way to measure yourself. (Ch 11)

Recycling — Returning an over-promoted person to the job they did well, openly and with support, naming management's misjudgment rather than forcing them out. (Ch 15)

Reliability problem — A defect that could cause complete failure at the customer. Accept/reject is normally economic; reliability is the exception where no compromise is allowed. (Ch 2)

Role model — The manager's pervasive, unavoidable activity. "Nothing leads as well as example." How you handle your own time is the most important aspect of it. (Ch 3, Ch 10, Ch 16)

Self-actualization — "What I can be, I must be." The only need that does not extinguish itself on satisfaction, and therefore the only limitless source of motivation. (Ch 11)

Six questions (decision-making) — What decision? When? Who decides? Who is consulted? Who ratifies or vetoes? Who is informed? Settled before the fact, they prevent the surprise veto and the appearance of politics. (Ch 5)

Six-to-eight rule — The right span of control for a supervisory manager, derived from allocating about a half day per week to each subordinate. Half-day-per-week coordinating-group memberships count as equivalents. (Ch 3)

Slack — Deliberate looseness — in inventory, absorbing mismatch between the sales and manufacturing flows, or in a calendar, so one unanticipated call doesn't ruin the day. (Ch 2, Ch 3)

Stagger chart — A multi-month forecast re-issued monthly alongside all prior forecasts with actuals marked, showing not just the outlook but how the outlook is changing. Grove's best indicator of business trends. (Ch 2)

Stages of problem-solving — Ignore → deny → blame others → assume responsibility → find the solution. The move from blaming to assuming is emotional; from assuming to solving is intellectual and easier. (Ch 13)

Strategy / tactics — Strategy is "the most abstract and general summary of those actions meaningful to you"; tactics is what you do to implement it. "A strategy at one managerial level is the tactical concern of the next higher level." (Ch 6)

Task-relevant feedback — Measures tied to the actual work and the organization's workings, letting a person gauge progress. The performance review is its most important form; compensation is another. (Ch 11, Ch 13, Ch 15)

Task-relevant maturity (TRM) — Achievement orientation and readiness to take responsibility, plus education, training, and experience — specific to the task at hand. Determines the effective management style, one-on-one frequency, and monitoring intensity. (Ch 3, Ch 4, Ch 12)

Test — Production operation examining characteristics. One of the three fundamental operations. (Ch 1)

Three L's — Level, listen, leave yourself out. The delivery discipline for a performance review. "Listen" means verifying your message landed, using all your sensory capabilities. (Ch 13)

Throughput time — Total elapsed time from starting the first step to delivering the finished product. (Ch 1)

Transitory team — A temporary task force or informal group formed faster than the formal organization can change; dissolves once the problem is handled. (Ch 9)

Trend indicator — Output measured against time and against a standard, forcing extrapolation and forcing you to think through why results differed from expectation. (Ch 2)

Tuition principle — "The subordinate's tuition is paid by his customers. And that is absolutely wrong." Teaching is the supervisor's job, not the customer's expense. (Ch 12)

Two-plane (multi-plane) organization — One person on two org charts serving two purposes — operating a unit and coordinating across units. Rank can reverse across planes. (Ch 9)

Variable inspection — Varying inspection frequency with observed quality. Applied to management, it is what makes a manager's deep dive sampling rather than meddling. (Ch 2)

Voluntary surrender of individual decision-making — What membership in a peer decision body requires. Underwritten by trust, which is a property of culture, not structure. (Ch 9)

Waffling — Putting off a decision that affects others' work. "The lack of a decision is the same as a negative decision; no green light is a red light." Unlimited negative leverage. (Ch 3, Ch 10)

Windows — Cuts into the black box that reveal internal workings and predict output: leading indicators, linearity indicators, trend indicators, stagger charts. (Ch 2)

Work simplification — Flow-chart every real step, count them, target a 30–50% reduction, and question why each exists. Intel achieved ~30% across administrative activities. (Ch 2)

Worksheet (review) — Blank-paper method for a review: dump everything without editing, find relationships, distill into "messages," then cut what the subordinate won't remember. (Ch 13)

Zinger — A heart-to-heart issue raised at an awkward time, usually near the end of a one-on-one, leaving no time to handle it. (Ch 4)

patterns.md

Patterns — Techniques from High Output Management

Concrete, repeatable procedures. Each is stated as: when to use, how, trade-offs.

Limiting-Step Flow Design

When to use: Designing or debugging any process, or scheduling your own week.

How: (1) Identify the longest, hardest, most sensitive, or most expensive step. (2) Start at the committed delivery time and work backward. (3) Offset each shorter step to finish in sync. (4) Recheck when capacity changes — the limiting step moves.

Trade-offs: Optimizing anything else is wasted while the limiting step governs. Requires knowing real throughput times, which most organizations don't measure.

Lowest-Value-Stage Rejection

When to use: Placing any quality gate — code review, hiring screens, design approval, incoming materials.

How: Find the point where accumulated value is lowest and still detectable. Reject the rotten egg at receiving, screen the candidate on campus, catch the defect at unit test.

Trade-offs: Earlier gates are cheaper per defect but see less information, so false rejections rise. Never applies to reliability defects — those admit no economic trade-off at all.

Gate vs. Monitor Inspection

When to use: Whenever inspection interferes with flow.

How: Gate — hold everything until tests pass. Monitor — sample while the bulk keeps moving, stop the line after N successive failures. Rule of thumb: lean toward monitoring when experience says big problems are unlikely.

Trade-offs: Gates add throughput time; monitors let some bad material escape to a higher-value stage. For the same money you get far more monitoring than gating.

Variable Inspection

When to use: Any recurring check whose subject's quality varies over time — including a manager's deep dives into a subordinate's work.

How: Check less often after a clean stretch; ramp up when problems appear.

Trade-offs: Cheapest and least disruptive, but rarely adopted "because we are creatures of habit." Applied to management, it is what separates sampling from meddling.

Paired Indicators

When to use: Designing any metric or dashboard.

How: Pair every quantity measure with a quality counterpart, and every effect with its counter-effect. Inventory ↔ shortages. Vouchers processed ↔ errors found by audit or supplier. Square feet cleaned ↔ a manager's quality rating. Software delivery date ↔ capability delivered.

Trade-offs: Doubles measurement work, and the quality half is often partly subjective. Without it, indicators get over-optimized — "you will steer the bicycle where you are looking."

Cutting Windows in the Black Box

When to use: Any opaque process whose failures currently surprise you.

How: Name inputs, output, and labor. Then install: leading indicators (early warnings you actually believe and will act on), a linearity indicator (cumulative actual vs. the straight line to target), trend indicators (vs. history and vs. a standard), and a stagger chart (rolling multi-month forecast re-issued monthly beside all prior forecasts, with actuals marked).

Trade-offs: A leading indicator you won't act on produces anxiety, not control. Stagger charts expose forecasters, which is the point and also the resistance.

Work Simplification

When to use: Any tedious, time-consuming recurring task; whole administrative processes.

How: (1) Flow-chart every step as actually performed — omit nothing to make it look better. (2) Count the steps. (3) Set a reduction target: expect 30–50% in round one. (4) Question why each step exists; discard those surviving only on tradition or formal procedure.

Trade-offs: The mapping is tedious and politically uncomfortable. Some discarded steps turn out to have had non-obvious reasons — reintroduce deliberately, not by default.

Calendar as Production Plan

When to use: Any week where others' requests fill your time.

How: Identify your genuinely immovable limiting steps and schedule around them. Batch similar work to reuse mental set-up. Actively fill gaps with non-time-critical work rather than waiting for incoming "orders." Say no at the start level, early. Build in slack. Keep a raw-material inventory of discretionary projects.

Trade-offs: Requires refusing work, and your capacity indicators are less credible than a factory's. Without the discretionary-project inventory, free time becomes meddling.

Standard Responses to Interruptions

When to use: When the same questions keep reaching you.

How: Catalogue the recurring interruptions; prepare standard answers; delegate them to less experienced people. Batch the rest into regular one-on-ones and staff meetings. Keep an indicator archive so answers don't require fresh research. Post an explicit boundary ("don't interrupt unless it can't wait until 2:00") paired with a genuinely open office hour.

Trade-offs: Hiding fails — the problems are legitimate and accumulate. Regularity requires coordination with others (Intel reserved Monday mornings company-wide for planning groups).

The One-on-One

When to use: With every professional who reports to you, permanently.

How: Subordinate owns it — he prepares a written outline and walks you through it. Minimum one hour. Held in or near his work area. Frequency set by his task-relevant maturity for current tasks and the pace of change in his area. Cover indicators (especially those signalling trouble), what's happened since last time, people and organizational issues, and potential problems. Both take notes on the outline. Keep a hold file. Invite heart-to-heart issues early. Schedule the next one as this one ends.

Trade-offs: Costs you ~90 minutes per subordinate per cycle, which is exactly why six-to-eight reports is the ceiling. Watch for the zinger.

Ask One More Question

When to use: Any one-on-one, review, or diagnostic conversation.

How: When you think the subordinate has finished on a subject, ask another question. Keep prompting until both of you feel you've reached the bottom.

Trade-offs: Can feel like interrogation if the relationship is weak. The alternative — talking about your problems instead of surfacing theirs — is worse.

Chairing a Mission-Oriented Meeting

When to use: Any meeting convened to produce a decision.

How: Before — know the decision needed, confirm a meeting is necessary/desirable/justifiable, secure commitments from attendees (or a proxy with power to speak), cap at eight, send an agenda stating the purpose and each person's role, handle logistics. During — enforce time discipline, confront lateness. After — send fast, specific minutes: what, who, when.

Trade-offs: Feels like regimentation to attendees until they're the one whose time got wasted. Price it: ten managers for two hours is a real, approvable expenditure.

The Six-Question Decision Structure

When to use: Before any significant decision process starts.

How: Answer, in writing: (1) What decision needs to be made? (2) When? (3) Who will decide? (4) Who will be consulted first? (5) Who will ratify or veto? (6) Who will be informed? Give competing interest groups roughly equal representation on the deciding body.

Trade-offs: Slower to start. Prevents the late veto that demoralizes teams and creates the appearance of political maneuvering.

Free Discussion → Clear Decision → Full Support

When to use: Any decision where knowledge and position power are separated.

How: Insist all views are voiced as equals with status ignored; withhold position power entirely during discussion. Then state the decision with utter clarity, especially when controversial. Then require commitment to support — not agreement. If no consensus arrives on time, the senior person decides.

Trade-offs: Onerous — Sloan's warning about the temptation to skip it. Demands that people be taught "nobody ever died from making a wrong business decision."

The Peer-Plus-One Intervention

When to use: A peer group circling without converging.

How: Add one hierarchical level — someone who need not be the most knowledgeable, functioning as a repository of how decisions get made. Absent a formal chair, the person with the most at stake takes charge; failing that, the senior person present.

Trade-offs: Risks importing position-power distortion into free discussion; the plus-one must moderate, not decide, until the decision stage.

Three-Step Planning

When to use: Annual planning, team planning, or personal roadmapping.

How: (1) Establish projected environmental demand — without discounting it by what you think you can deliver. (2) Establish present status in the same "currency," including timing and a realistic loss factor for work in flight (~20% in semiconductors). (3) Ask separately "what do I need to do?" and "what can I do?", then decide what you will do and when. The resulting action set is your strategy.

Trade-offs: The un-discounted demand forecast feels unrealistic to the people producing it — but pre-constraining it means never tooling up for real demand.

MBO (Objectives and Key Results)

When to use: Translating plans into work you can steer by, at least quarterly.

How: Two questions — where do I want to go (objective), how will I pace myself (key results with specific wording and dates). Keep objectives few. Nest them so a subordinate's objective supports the supervisor's. Set them at roughly 50/50 odds of success.

Trade-offs: It is a stopwatch, not a contract. Mechanical use by the supervisor (as a review basis) or the subordinate (refusing an unlisted opportunity) is "petty and unprofessional."

Delegation with Quality-Assurance Monitoring

When to use: Every delegated task.

How: Share the information base and operational values first. Prefer delegating what you know best (easier to monitor). Check at the lowest-added-value stage — review the rough draft. Sample randomly and partially. Set frequency by the subordinate's TRM on that specific task, decreasing as performance improves. To delegate a decision, monitor the decision-making process by asking probing questions about the request.

Trade-offs: Delegating what you know best goes against emotional grain. Under-monitoring is abdication; 100% checking is meddling.

Matching Style to Task-Relevant Maturity

When to use: Continuously, and immediately after any promotion, transfer, or change of pace.

How: Low TRM → structured, tell what/when/how. Medium → individual-oriented, two-way communication, mutual reasoning. High → minimal involvement, objectives and monitoring. Monitor at every level. Revert instantly when the task or pace changes.

Trade-offs: Managers systematically skip the medium row and overrate their own delegation (90% rated themselves higher than their subordinates did). Reverting feels regressive to both parties.

Dual Reporting

When to use: Any hybrid organization where a manager cannot technically supervise what reports to him.

How: Split supervision — mission supervisor gives priorities and daily monitoring; functional supervisor gives standards, technical oversight, and career ownership. The functional half may be a peer group rather than an individual, chaired by a coordinating manager.

Trade-offs: Ambiguity, which most people dislike, and patience-taxing cross-peer negotiation. Requires trust — a cultural property, not a structural one — and voluntary surrender of individual decision-making.

Choosing a Control Mode

When to use: Deciding how to govern any activity, team, or new hire.

How: Score individual motivation (self- vs. group-interest) and the environment's CUA factor (low/high). Self-interest + low CUA → market. Group-interest + low CUA → contract. Group-interest + high CUA → culture. Self-interest + high CUA → chaos: lower the CUA or build group-interest, but don't try harder.

Trade-offs: Culture is not universally superior — it can't govern tire purchases or a tax system. Building it requires accumulated shared experience, which takes years.

Building a Racetrack

When to use: Any group whose performance is mediocre and unresponsive to pressure or inducement.

How: See the work as the people doing it see it. Define rules of the game and a way for people to measure themselves against peers doing the same work. Score periodically, by someone whose esteem that group values, and publish comparative results.

Trade-offs: Removing the competition removes the motivation. Contests between internal groups for a shared resource (e.g. divisions bidding for salespeople's time) produce exactly the self-interested behavior you'll later resent.

The Performance Review Worksheet

When to use: Preparing any review.

How: (1) Scan progress reports, performance against quarterly objectives, one-on-one notes. (2) Blank paper — write everything down without editing, major to trivial, no order. (3) Put documentation away and find relationships: which items are manifestations of the same phenomenon, and why the strength or weakness exists. (4) Name those "messages." (5) Gather specific examples. (6) Apply the memory test — delete anything the subordinate won't remember; it can wait for next time.

Trade-offs: Deleting true observations feels like dishonesty. It isn't: "the purpose is not to cleanse your system… but to improve his performance."

Delivering a Review — The Three L's

When to use: Every review delivery.

How: Level — total frankness, including in praise. Listen — use every sensory capability to verify the message landed; watch the person; if their verbal and nonverbal responses don't assure you, it is your responsibility to keep at it. Leave yourself out — it is the subordinate's day in court.

Trade-offs: Verification takes time and can feel repetitive. A paraphrase is not sufficient evidence of receipt.

Moving Someone Through the Problem-Solving Stages

When to use: A review or confrontation with a serious performance problem.

How: Track which stage you're in — ignore → deny → blame others → assume responsibility → find the solution. Supply facts and examples against ignoring and denial. Do not attempt the solution while they are still denying or blaming. Get them to assume responsibility (the emotional step); then solve jointly (the intellectual step, and easier).

Trade-offs: The blame-others stage is where things stick. If they won't move, invoke position power explicitly, secure a commitment without agreement, and monitor performance against it.

Interviewing

When to use: Every hire.

How: Let the candidate talk 80% while you control by active listening and interruption. Steer to subjects familiar to both, in your vocabulary. Mine four categories: technical skill; what he did with it; discrepancies between the two; operational values. Ask blunt direct questions. Use a hypothetical when domains don't overlap — supply the domain yourself and watch the derivation. Ask what he wants to know about you. Build a personal bond with references (the last ten minutes beat the first ten), then re-interview.

Trade-offs: Hiring is the one deliberate exception to the potential trap. Even done well it "merely increases your odds of getting lucky." No tricks — the candidate is forming durable first impressions.

The "I Quit!" Response

When to use: The moment a valued, dedicated employee says they're leaving.

How: Drop everything immediately — the delay itself confirms the reason they're going. Sit them down, ask why, let the rehearsed speech run without arguing. Then ask more questions; the real issues surface after the prepared points. Don't lecture, don't panic, don't try to change their mind — buy time and commit to follow through. Escalate to your supervisor and make it his problem too. Pursue every retention avenue including transfer, project-managing it yourself.

Trade-offs: You may lose them from your own org to keep them in the company. Answer the blackmail objection ("you shook us up and made us aware of the error of our ways") and the accepted-offer objection (two commitments, and the one to daily colleagues is stronger).

Designing a Performance Bonus

When to use: Structuring variable pay for managers.

How: Scale the bonus percentage with total compensation (~50% senior, 10–25% middle). Split across three factors — individual performance judged by the supervisor, immediate team's objective performance, overall corporate financial performance. Answer five questions: team or individual, which team, what period (close enough that they remember the work), what basis (avoid the beauty contest), and what floor (never pay lavishly into bankruptcy).

Trade-offs: "No matter what way you choose, none gives you exactly what you want." Splitting dilutes each signal but calls attention to all three.

Recycling an Over-Promoted Person

When to use: Someone performing below average for too long after a promotion.

How: Return them to the job they previously did well. Name management's misjudgment openly rather than theirs. Support them through the embarrassment. Do it visibly.

Trade-offs: Society reads it as personal failure, which is why the default is a forced exit rationalized as "for his own sake." Done openly, the embarrassment is short-lived — and these people often succeed on a later promotion.

Manager-Delivered Training

When to use: Any recurring capability gap; continuously as a process.

How: List everything your people should be trained in, from trivial to value-system level; ask them what they need. Inventory available teachers and materials. Prioritize. Build one three-to-four-lecture course on the most urgent topic. Set deadlines; outline the whole, write lecture one, and go — write lecture two after delivering one. Treat the first delivery as a throwaway and give it to your most knowledgeable subordinates for critique. If many repetitions are needed, train instructors from your first set. Collect anonymous numerical plus open-ended feedback.

Trade-offs: Costly — Intel priced one new one-day middle-management course at over a million dollars in student time alone. Canned outside courses that contradict your practice demoralize rather than merely fail. Expect feedback split evenly between "too detailed," "too superficial," and "just right."

How Great Ideas Happen: The Hidden Steps Behind Breakthrough Success

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — How Great Ideas Happen (Newman)

Which stage am I in? (diagnose, then act)

TellStageDo thisMode
No idea where to look; scanning randomlySurveyingExpand influences; low-res survey many domains; find the problemDeep → surface
Have a direction, no mapGriddingWrite the guiding question; build the What/Why GridDeep
Have a mapped cell, few ideasDiggingVolume; evaluation-free; double your targetSurface
Too many ideas, can't chooseSiftingDistance + subtraction; others pickDeep

Decision rules

  • When your idea feels strikingly original, cut the novelty — audiences penalize excess originality; hits cluster at ~90–95% conventional / 5–10% novel.
  • When you feel tapped out mid-session, run another round — the creative cliff is an illusion; late ideas rate higher.
  • When you must judge your own ideas, don't — the creative endowment effect is immune to warnings and examples; only elapsed time or another person's eyes fix it.
  • When the brief feels impossibly constrained, stop negotiating the constraints — the most-constrained groups produce the highest-rated work.
  • When an idea makes you uncomfortable, develop it 10–15 min before discarding — discomfort marks an information gap, which is where curiosity (and value) peaks.
  • When editing, ask what to remove first — people default to adding; subtraction has to be prompted explicitly.
  • When the work underperforms, tweak and ship again — don't restart — Wright's law: ~10–15% improvement per doubling of cumulative output.
  • When everyone around you agrees, go to weak ties — strong ties know what you already know.
  • When you notice a cross-domain analogy, don't stop at Recognition — map Relevance element-by-element, or it's decoration.
  • When you're stuck and working harder, change inputs instead of effort — read others' work, adjacent fields, new places.
  • Never say "be creative" — the instruction itself cuts idea productivity ~20%. Say "as many ideas as possible."

Guiding question — four-criteria gate

Keep it only if it is specific · open-ended · motivating · measurable.

Template: "What is a [project type] that [unique value/meaning] for [audience] in [context], despite [obstacle]?"

  • Bored delivering your own one-minute pitch? → the idea is wrong, not the pitch.
  • Starting from what you want to say? → flip inside-out → outside-in: what will they think about on the drive home?

Three Roadblocks (Conclusion) — pick the diagnosis

  • Stuck with nothing → not enough work up front. Missing why/guiding question or grid. Go back to Gridding.
  • Stuck with a mediocre idea → settled too early. "Ideas are cheap" is false; breakthrough ideas are rare. Go back to Digging.
  • Stuck defending an idea → in love with the idea, not the process. Also applies to being attached to finishing. Go to Sifting-with-others.

Transplanting: the Three R's — where it fails

RQuestionFailure mode
RecognitionWhat in another domain resembles this?Stopping here (most common)
RelevanceWhich elements map, exactly?Metaphor mistaken for mapping
RefinementDoes it survive prototyping here?Skipping domain experts

Different people are good at different R's — staff each stage separately.

Tower vs. Raft (Sifting posture)

Building a TowerFloating a Raft
StanceCram everything in, defendAudience hunts for holes
MoveAddSubtract
Test"Look what I made""What does this element contribute to my guiding question?"

Default is Tower. Force the Raft frame deliberately.

Feedback triage

  • Weight the tails, not the agreeable middle — outlier comments carry the signal.
  • Then apply the frequency rule to the middle: many people tripping on the same thing is real, however badly they explain it.
  • Ask "What specific aspects are strong / could be improved?" and "Does this remind you of things you've seen?" — never "Do you like it?"
  • State your guiding question as context first, and pre-declare what you will not change.
