glossary.md

Glossary — How Great Ideas Happen (George Newman)

5% Novelty Rule — Hit ideas sit at roughly 90–95% conventional and 5–10% novel; make a small, sharp departure from an established concept rather than a wholesale one (Ch 2).

Adjacent possible — The set of moves reachable from where you currently stand; ideas arrive only when their neighboring components already exist (Ch 6).

Analogical reasoning — Using a familiar concrete case to unlock the abstract relational structure of a new problem; Hofstadter's "engine of cognition" (Ch 6).

Attending to negative space — Deliberately examining what is absent or unmarked in a scene, rather than the labeled objects (Ch 3).

Bottom-up processing — Building a representation from the sensory data actually present, rather than from expectation (Ch 3).

Brick-counting fallacy — Mistaking accumulation of facts for progress toward an idea; volume of detail is not directed thinking (Ch 11).

Brilliance-focused culture — An environment that prizes innate genius; signals belonging to a narrow group and drives talent out (Ch 11).

Broker — A person who connects otherwise disconnected clusters of a network, and therefore sees combinations no one inside either cluster can (Ch 6, Burt).

Building a Tower — The creator's default posture: cram in every element you built, defending the whole (Ch 10). Contrast Floating a Raft.

Close looking — Sustained 30–60 minute examination of a single object or scene, past the point where the inner explainer stops you (Ch 3).

Collective intelligence — A team's general problem-solving capacity; driven by emotional intelligence and turn-taking, not average member IQ (Ch 8).

Creative Cliff Illusion — The false belief that idea quality collapses after the first couple of minutes; in fact late-session ideas rate higher (Ch 7, Lucas & Nordgren).

Creative Endowment Effect — Overvaluing an idea because you authored it, which wrecks your ability to sift your own list (Ch 10).

Creative explorer — Newman's replacement for the genius myth: someone who searches for ideas that already exist in the landscape (Introduction).

Curation — Selecting with intent from a large generated set; the human half of working with AI (Ch 9).

Digging — Stage 3: generating many candidate ideas within the region you have gridded (Part III).

Directed thinking — Reasoning aimed by a structural question rather than by accumulating facts (Ch 11, Wertheimer on Einstein).

Early diversification — Sampling widely across styles/domains early in a career; predicts later hits via skill portfolio, transferable expertise, and better talent-matching (Ch 8, Berg).

Evaluation-free zone — A declared period in which no idea may be judged, protecting the Digging stage from premature Sifting (Ch 7, Ch 8).

Floating a Raft — Reframing your idea as something an audience will inspect for holes, which puts you in subtraction mode (Ch 10).

Gridding — Stage 2: sectioning the conceptual space so every combination gets examined, and you know where you haven't looked (Part II).

Guiding Question — The compass question fusing what you are making with why it matters; must be specific, open-ended, motivating, and measurable (Ch 4).

Identity trap — Refusing a needed change because the current version feels like you; blocks tweaks (Ch 12).

Information-gap theory of curiosity — Curiosity peaks for questions you sort of already know the answer to; discomfort marks the gap worth digging into (Ch 11, Loewenstein).

Inner explainer — The internal voice that labels a scene and thereby ends observation (Ch 3).

Inside-out method — Starting a project from your own goals and interests; Newman's own failure mode. Contrast outside-in method (Ch 4).

Kernel idea / the spark — The seed that cues something specific and complex — core idea, satellites, mood, energy, flow — and is therefore worth elaborating (Ch 9).

King of the Mountain — Tournament-style group selection: each person brings their top two ideas, and rounds narrow to a top three (Ch 8, Ex. 25).

Knowledge funnel — Deep expertise in one or two domains, shallow familiarity with many, plus skill at translating between them (Ch 3).

Low-resolution surveying — Knowing a little about a lot, deliberately; the input side of transplanting (Ch 2).

Mid-Stakes Event — A scheduled, dated exposure of work to a real but non-gatekeeping audience, used to force selection and test predictions (Ch 10, Ex. 32).

Multiple discovery — The same idea reached independently by several parties, often simultaneously; evidence that ideas are found, not conjured (Ch 1).

Narrative Reversal — Listing your assumptions and asking "what if the opposite were true?" (Ch 7, Knight).

Originality Ostrich — A creator who assumes originality only helps, blind to the fact that audiences penalize excess novelty (Ch 2).

Outside-in method — Starting from the audience's anticipated end experience and working backward (Ch 4).

Problem finding — Letting the problem emerge from close observation instead of importing a predefined one (Ch 3, Csikszentmihalyi & Getzels).

Psychological distance — Separation from your own work via elapsed time or other people's eyes; the prerequisite for subtraction (Ch 10).

Refinement — Third R: prototyping and iterating a transplanted concept in its new context, usually with other experts (Ch 6).

Recognition — First R: spotting a candidate cross-domain connection (Ch 6).

Relevance — Second R: mapping element-by-element what actually overlaps between the two domains (Ch 6).

Second-mover advantage — The tweak, not the original, is usually what breaks through (Ch 2).

Set of ideas — What to hunt for instead of "the right idea": a localized cluster of near-variants to compare (Ch 7).

Sifting — Stage 4: choosing which ideas to pursue, mostly by subtraction (Part IV).

Sleeping Beauty — A dormant idea that lies unused for years until a new domain awakens it (Ch 6).

Structural hole — The gap between disconnected network clusters that a broker spans (Ch 6, Burt).

Subtraction neglect — The robust human tendency to improve things only by adding, never by removing (Ch 10, Adams).

Surveying — Stage 1: reading the conceptual terrain to decide where to search (Part I).

The Three R's of Transplanting — Recognition, Relevance, and Refinement; skipping past Recognition is the standard failure (Ch 6).

The Unconscious Grid — The implicit constraint structure that produces the sensation that "the story writes itself" (Ch 5).

The What and Why Grid — A two-axis grid (what you make × why it matters) whose cells you fill to find unoccupied combinations (Ch 5).

Top-down processing — Perception driven by prior expectation; the source of seeing what you expected rather than what is there (Ch 3).

Transplanting — Taking an existing concept from one domain and applying it somewhere new and unexpected (Ch 6).

Turtling-up — Retreating into your existing strong-tie network when threatened, which starves you of new information (Ch 8).

Wright's law — Cost/effort per unit falls a predictable ~10–15% with each doubling of cumulative output; the most successful entrepreneurs are identifiable by adherence to it (Ch 12).

"Yes, and" — The improv rule adopted as a group Digging protocol: build on contributions rather than evaluating them (Ch 8).

patterns.md

Patterns — techniques from How Great Ideas Happen

The 5% Workshop

When to use: You have a domain and want a viable idea fast, without the originality penalty.

How: Copy a celebrated existing work verbatim (score it, rebuild it, retype it). Brainstorm ≥10 distinct modifications that alter roughly 5% of it. Implement one at a time and compare.

Trade-offs: Feels like cheating and produces no origin story. But it targets the 90–95% conventional / 5–10% novel band where hits actually cluster; pure originality reliably underperforms with audiences.

Close Looking

When to use: You need a problem worth solving and don't have one — or your read of a situation is running on assumption.

How: Pick one mundane scene from your actual work (people reacting to an idea, customers browsing, your own routine). Observe 10–60 minutes without labeling. When the inner explainer names the thing, keep going. Record what is absent, not just what's present.

Trade-offs: Slow and feels unproductive; there is no deliverable. It's the only reliable route from top-down assumption to bottom-up data.

The Guiding Question Template

When to use: Start of any project, and again whenever you feel directionless mid-project.

How: Fill in — "What is a [type of project] that [provides a unique form of value or meaning] for [a particular audience] in [a specific context/environment], despite [potential obstacles]?" Test it against four criteria: specific, open-ended, motivating, measurable. If you bore yourself delivering it as a one-minute elevator pitch, the idea needs work, not the pitch.

Trade-offs: A too-specific question forecloses search; too broad and it fails as a compass. Expect to sharpen it with data as you go — it's meant to be dynamic.

The Outside-In Flip

When to use: Your work is well-crafted but isn't landing.

How: Replace "What do I want to say?" with "What does my audience need to hear?" and "What will they be thinking about on the drive home?" Design backward from that end experience.

Trade-offs: Can slide into pandering if you skip the why. Pair with the guiding question so audience-fit doesn't erase point of view.

The What and Why Grid

When to use: You have a guiding question and need to map the search space before generating.

How: (1) Gather data — list existing successes in the space. (2) Derive what categories and why categories from that list. (3) Build the grid: what = columns, why = rows. (4) Fill every cell, weighting toward your expertise; delete barren rows/columns. (5) Pick the cell with the most branching options and narrow in.

Trade-offs: Overhead before any ideation, and the axes you choose bound what you can find. Its payoff is knowing where you didn't look — free brainstorming can't tell you that.

Constraints into Opportunities

When to use: The brief feels impossibly restrictive (budget, format, tech, time).

How: List every constraint. Invent one named audience persona with a history and goals. Convert each constraint into an advantage for that person. Repeat with a different persona.

Trade-offs: Requires taking the constraints as fixed, which is wrong sometimes. But the more rigid the box, the better people think inside it — the most-constrained groups produce the highest-rated work.

The Three R's of Transplanting

When to use: You've noticed a concept in another domain that might apply to yours.

How: Recognition — name the candidate connection. Relevance — map element to element what actually overlaps; be explicit, not metaphorical. Refinement — prototype in the new context with domain experts. Different people are often good at different R's; staff each stage separately.

Trade-offs: Stopping after Recognition is the default failure — a pleasing analogy that never gets tested. Relevance is where most transplants die, and should.

Push Past the Creative Cliff

When to use: Any Digging session, at the exact moment you feel tapped out.

How: Set a target and then double or triple it. Run a deliberate second and third round after the point where you'd normally stop. Sort output into at least 3 categories to expose thin regions.

Trade-offs: Uncomfortable and feels wasteful. The felt cliff is an illusion — later ideas rate higher in quality, and the first idea suppresses creativity while the ninety-seventh may enhance it.

Narrative Reversal Sweep

When to use: The idea set is competent but predictable.

How: List the assumptions your idea rests on. For each, ask "what if the opposite were true?" Keep the ones that are still coherent.

Trade-offs: Generates a lot of nonsense per usable reversal. Cheap enough that the ratio doesn't matter.

Group Digging Protocol

When to use: Ideation with more than one person.

How: Declare an evaluation-free zone. Separate Digging from Sifting into different sessions. Formalize turn-taking (randomize with cards or an RNG). Accept anonymous submissions. Purposely generate bad ideas. Let someone other than the senior person lead. Enforce "yes, and."

Trade-offs: Feels bureaucratic. Without it, the highest-status voice sets the frame and collective intelligence collapses.

Engaging Your Weak Ties

When to use: Your idea set is converging and everyone around you agrees with you.

How: Consult acquaintances outside your cluster — unprimed, without pre-explaining what you want to hear. Reach for people whose domain doesn't overlap yours.

Trade-offs: Weak ties give less committed help. But strong ties mostly know what you already know; turtling-up under pressure is the anti-pattern.

Sifting with Others

When to use: You must select from your own list — i.e., always, because the creative endowment effect makes self-selection unreliable.

How: Hand your list to someone else and compare their picks with yours. Or shelve the list for weeks-to-months and re-select with time-created distance. Warning yourself about the bias does not work; only distance does.

Trade-offs: Costs calendar time or social capital. Being told about the bias, or shown examples, demonstrably fails to correct it.

Floating a Raft (not Building a Tower)

When to use: Cutting an over-built piece of work.

How: Write out your guiding question. Go element by element and state what each contributes to it. Cut anything that doesn't serve it — including material you love. Ask what an audience inspecting this for holes would find.

Trade-offs: Painful; the tangent material is often the prettiest. People almost never edit by subtraction unless explicitly prompted to.

The Mid-Stakes Event

When to use: The work could drift indefinitely, and low-stakes feedback isn't forcing decisions.

How: Schedule a dated exposure to a real but non-gatekeeping audience. Before it, write down predicted reactions. After, audit your predictions against what happened.

Trade-offs: Manufactured deadlines can force premature closure. The prediction audit — not the feedback — is the durable payoff: it calibrates your taste.

Develop the Uncomfortable Idea

When to use: Sifting a list where one idea keeps making you uneasy.

How: Rank ideas most to least comfortable. Take the most uncomfortable and develop it for 10–15 minutes before discarding. Treat discomfort as an information gap, not a verdict.

Trade-offs: Most uncomfortable ideas are just bad. Cheap to test, and the ones that survive are disproportionately the interesting ones.

Planning for Feedback

When to use: Before every feedback conversation.

How: Decide the purpose of the feedback. Provide context — state your guiding question first. Ask better questions: replace "Do you like this?" with "What specific aspects are strong / could be improved?" and "Does this remind you of other things you've seen?" Pre-declare what you will not change.

Trade-offs: Framing the ask constrains what you'll hear. Unframed feedback is mostly noise about taste.

The Bell Curve of Feedback

When to use: Triaging a pile of responses.

How: Weight the tails — the outlier comments — over the agreeable middle. Then triage the middle by frequency: if many people trip on the same thing, it's real regardless of how they explain it.

Trade-offs: Tails include cranks. Frequency alone would have you optimize for the median and sand off everything distinctive.

Tweak, Don't Restart (Wright's law)

When to use: The work is underperforming and starting over feels attractive.

How: Pivot adjacent and ship again. Volume of iterations, not restarts, drives the improvement curve — roughly 10–15% better per doubling of cumulative output.

Trade-offs: Locks you into the current region of the space, so it only works after Surveying and Gridding were done honestly. Watch for the identity trap: refusing a tweak because the current version feels like you.

AI as Excavator

When to use: Digging within a region you have already mapped.

How: Guide it to the specific gridded region, solicit many candidates, then curate with intent. Keep the human on Surveying, Gridding, and Sifting.

Trade-offs: Powerful for volume, but produces a homogenization effect across users. Use it for surface work (Digging); keep deep work — deciding where to search and what to keep — yours.

How to Say It: Be Indispensable at Work

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Be Indispensable at Work (Griffin)

The one rule everything reduces to

When describing value, convert to money. Nouns and verbs beat adjectives; nouns and verbs linked to numbers beat everything. Your boss has exactly one motive: save and make money.

Decision rules

When…Do…Because
You feel an irritationRun FIDO — Forget It, Drive OnMost annoyances are transitory; acting enshrines them
FIDO failsAct on the situation, never the personSituations can be fixed; people are not readily fixable
You're about to describe yourselfConvert trait → verb → verb+object"I am persuasive" is a trait; "I persuade people" is a skill
You have a question for your bossBring an offer insteadIt's hard to feel persuasive with your hand out
You're offered a salary numberCounteroffer, even if it's goodThe number you name first caps your year; a counteroffer bonds you more than acceptance does
A raise is refusedAccept gracefully, then ask "When can we schedule another review?"Never express dismay or threaten to leave — he already assumes it
Business is bad and you want moreAsk for a promotion, not a raiseA raise rewards the past; a promotion is a proposal about the future, so it's easier to sell in a downturn
You miss a deadlineGive an explanation with a plan, never an excuseLate work is lost value; the plan is what restores the clutch brand
You errReport it yourself, fast: sorry → own it → empathize → remedyFar worse if the news reaches your boss any other way
Someone offers criticismThank them; listen ≠ agreeEven unfounded criticism tells you how you're coming across
You want to criticizeAsk permission, in private, one issue, with alternativesNever criticize anyone — only an issue, action, or outcome
You need helpAsk (don't apologize)A request is a vote of confidence that empowers the other person
You're about to say "my idea" to a bossSay "our idea"No idea sells easier than one he thinks he already owns
A bully attacks you personallyIgnore the question; answer with facts; show no emotionA bully cannot be a bully without a victim
Someone's complaint blocks workVerify merit first, then stop debating merits entirelyYou can't accuse a work-dodger before checking the assignment isn't genuinely impossible
You're about to share an ideaWrite and date it firstPoaching is the most common workplace scheme
The danger signs appearEngage more, not lessA stationary target is easier to hit (Patton's foxhole)
Target career differs in title and fieldChange one, then the otherBoth at once is a foot-long sandwich in one gulp
You're employed and job-huntingNever post your résuméYour boss surfs those sites too

Trade-off matrices

Which skill claim to make (People ladder — height = perceived value)

ClaimReads asPositions you for
Following directionsEntry levelNothing
CommunicatingCompetentYour current job
PersuadingSolidKeeping a sales role
NegotiatingStrongAccount executive
MentoringLeadershipVP of Sales

Effort vs. return on hours worked

Hours/weekLikely outcome

Career-change agencies

TypeWho paysBest for
Permanent employment agencyEmployerMost in-industry moves
HeadhunterEmployerSpecialized/senior roles

Thresholds & defaults

  • 25+ items per sheet in the People/Data/Things dig, unedited — then winnow to 8–10.
  • 3+ five-part achievement stories.
  • 10 seconds for a rehearsed self-introduction; 10 minutes max for an informational interview unless extended.
  • ~150 — Dunbar's ceiling on people you truly know; beyond that, connections have indirect value only.
  • Show up 10–15 minutes early, every day.
  • Two to three of the nine career components change in even a radical career switch.
  • One failure to share credit can undo months of goodwill.

Tells & smells

Your company is in trouble: stars leaving while back-benchers stay · the strategy stops making sense · lagging the industry · routinely missing numbers · repeat layoffs · cash out > cash in · management communicating in jargon.

You're the target: lost your boss · lost the space race (office → cube → basement) · a paper trail starts · frozen out of memos and meetings · handed scut work or doomed missions · merger or sale.

You're under assault: a less-qualified colleague promoted · people stop asking your advice · unwarranted criticism in meetings · you're not invited · you're gossip · people ask "is anything wrong?" · you're scapegoated · friends cool · you can't assemble a team anymore · emails go unanswered.

They're a passive aggressor: "Don't worry, I'm on it." It won't get done. Rely on it.

You're the problem: "I'm not a team player" (toxic, unlike "out-of-the-box thinker") · "That's not my job" · "There's no hurry" · "I'm working till I drop" · "I know my job" · "I'm efficient" (≠ effective) · "I did it, I did it" · "Modesty forbids me."

You're a thief (regardless of how normal it seems): office supplies taken home · padded expense reports · billing the estimated six hours for four hours' work.

Postures to hold by default

  • Fit in while standing out. Teamwork is a stage with more than one spotlight, not a mass grave.
  • Be task oriented, not time defined.
  • Wear the smile as discipline — Patton practiced his scowl; you practice your war face. Never walk through the open door to complain.
  • Always be looking for a job, even when secure.
  • Your commitment is to the firm, not the position you occupy — and your deepest loyalty is to yourself.

glossary.md

Glossary — How to Say It: Be Indispensable at Work

Achievement inventory — a list of what you did rewritten with dollar values and percentages attached, turning activity into quantified result (Ch 2)

Ambush / "gotcha" — publicly cornering a colleague; the satisfaction is momentary and the conflict long-term (Ch 6, Ch 9)

Blanket indictment — "You never come in at budget!" More provocative than helpful and rarely the whole truth (Ch 6)

Boss as customer — the frame governing every boss interaction: he trades value (a paycheck) expecting value (your productivity) (Ch 4, Ch 8)

Brand — a set of information, values, and expectations attached to a product, giving buyers confidence and loyalty (Ch 7)

Bully — a difficult type whose objective is to make you feel inadequate; requires a victim to exist (Ch 9)

Bumbler — the marginally incompetent boss; handled with patience, written confirmations, and no visible exasperation (Ch 8)

Career — a job with a future (Ch 3)

Career kryptonite — the strengths that make you exceptional and simultaneously vulnerable (Ch 10)

Chronic complainer — the difficult type who channels productive energy into whining to dodge work (Ch 9)

Clutch player — the person who reliably makes or beats hard deadlines; by definition indispensable (Ch 7)

Corporate karma — the workplace you help create by what you do, on the "what goes around comes around" model rather than "nice guys finish last" (Ch 5)

Creative austerity — devising ways to do more with less (Ch 7)

Cultivate, don't plow — rebuilding a drifting relationship with no agenda and no pushing (Ch 10)

Dunbar's number — ~150, the theorized ceiling on people you can truly know; connections beyond it have indirect value (Ch 11)

Efficiency vs. effectiveness — the cheapest path to a result vs. the one that actually produces it; confusing them can be fatal (Ch 10)

Eternal Truth (Part 1 / Part 2) — Part 1: there is no substitute for doing your job well. Part 2: being liked can outlast your numbers, and being a top performer guarantees nothing (Ch 8)

Exclusionary language — I, mine, you, yours plus words that negate, deny, contradict, reject, or refuse (Ch 5)

External customers — clients and consumers on the other side of the counter (Ch 7, Ch 8)

Feature vs. benefit — what the product is vs. how it makes the customer feel; FedEx's feature was overnight delivery, its advertised benefit was peace of mind (Ch 4)

FIDO — Forget It, Drive On; the first test applied to any workplace irritation (Ch 5)

Finger pointer — the blaming boss; answered by accepting responsibility without accepting blame (Ch 8)

Foxhole illusion — the felt safety of hunkering down, which turns a moving target into a stationary one (Ch 10)

Friction — necessary workplace physics: without it you can neither move nor stop (Ch 6)

Helping vocabulary — we, us, our plus collaboration verbs (brainstorm, collaborate, confer, cooperate, huddle, learn, listen, solve, team up, work together) (Ch 5)

High-maintenance employee — the real reason most people get fired; a problem creator (Ch 7)

Hub of the corporate wheel — what you become by convening the community rather than joining it (Ch 11)

Human capital — you as an asset with intrinsic, portable value, not an interchangeable plug in a socket (Ch 2)

In-house snake charmer — the reputation earned by consistently creating satisfaction in difficult people (Ch 9)

Informational interview — a knowledge hunt deliberately not framed as a job hunt (Ch 12)

Internal customers — subordinates, colleagues, and bosses, who expect value all of the time (Ch 7, Ch 8)

Internal networking — the neglected half of networking: connections inside your own company, including the next cubicle (Ch 11)

Language of business — money: money made, money saved, money your skills will make and save (Ch 2)

Lateral move — a change at roughly the same compensation made for a non-salary strategic gain; serial ones are career killers (Ch 4)

Leap gap — the distance between your current title+field unit and your target one (Ch 12)

Lever — an influential person through whom your idea reaches people you can't reach (Ch 10)

Musketeer Solution — "All for one, one for all"; the workplace cannot thrive as a zero-sum game (Ch 6)

Negative inventory — your honest list of deficiencies; essential to know, never to volunteer (Ch 2)

Office diplomat — the team player who brings the team together, keeps it together, and positions it to win — as opposed to the office politician, who manipulates to get ahead (Ch 6)

Passive aggressor — the difficult type characterized by reliable unreliability: procrastination, sulking, claimed helplessness (Ch 9)

Permission to fail — the concession that unblocks an evasive complainer, at the cost of extra work for you (Ch 9)

Plug-and-socket mentality — the boss's view of your job as a generic slot and you as an interchangeable plug (Ch 3)

Poacher — the difficult type who presents your idea as his own (Ch 9)

Poisoning the well — making an idea toxic before anyone evaluates it, e.g. "This is a joke, right?" (Ch 9)

Positioning — how a product, service, or person is perceived by its best potential customer; its three dimensions are Benefit, Target, and Competition (Ch 4)

Principle of Scarcity — a multitude of needs and wants against a shortage of resources; the structural root of most workplace conflict (Ch 6)

Problem solver — the one position that can never be filled redundantly (Ch 3, Ch 7)

Prospect pool — the universe of employers your current career reaches (Ch 12)

Proxemics — the anthropological study of how we define and use personal space (Ch 5)

Rapport — a relationship of mutual trust and emotional affinity; cumulative, built and eroded by interactions great and small (Ch 5)

Redundancy — the merger/acquisition euphemism that reliably precedes layoffs (Ch 1)

Responsibility without blame — owning a problem you didn't cause (Ch 8)

Schemer — the difficult type who uses gossip and rumor with malicious intent (Ch 9)

Skills vs. transferable (portable) skills — knowledge affixed to one job ("I know how to sell the Model A Widget") vs. know-how you own and carry ("I know how to sell") (Ch 2, Ch 3)

Task oriented, not time defined — measuring your day by the job done, not the clock (Ch 7)

Transferable Skills Ladder — skills ordered by complexity, where perceived height equals perceived value: following directions < communicating < persuading < negotiating < mentoring (Ch 3)

Trigger object — a pre-committed physical reminder to stop, listen, and think before reacting emotionally (Ch 6)

Two-stage career transition — changing job title or field first, the other later (Ch 12)

Utility player — someone who goes beyond the expected job description; more valuable in downsizing eras (Ch 7)

Vertical integration — why several apparently separate industries may now be one, making career changes possible without leaving your employer (Ch 12)

"I think I am a verb" — Grant's and Fuller's identical self-description; define yourself by what you actively do (Ch 3)

War face / work mask — a deliberately practiced expression worn as professional discipline; Patton practiced his scowl, you practice your smile (Ch 7)

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Be Indispensable at Work

The Three-Front Research Protocol

When to use: before any conversation with your boss about your future — raise, promotion, reassignment, or "how am I doing?"

How: (1) Company — unread memos and newsletters, your own job description and recent evaluations, the website's About Us / press releases / From the CEO / Investor Relations, a web search on the company name, legitimately available sales figures, 3–6 months of stock performance. (2) Industry — keyword searches, trade publications for trends, web searches on your boss and his bosses for moves and retirements, competitors' ads, whether the market is growing or contracting. (3) Yourself — the achievement inventory and skills dig.

Trade-offs: takes a week you'd rather spend working; converts the meeting from a plea into a pitch, which is the whole return.

Speak the Language of Business

When to use: any description of yourself, your work, or your value.

How: write the raw activity list without editing, then pass over it again attaching a dollar figure or percentage to each line. Nouns and verbs beat adjectives and adverbs; nouns and verbs linked to numbers beat everything.

Trade-offs: some real contributions resist quantification — attach the nearest proxy rather than dropping them.

The Verb Conversion

When to use: whenever you're about to claim a trait or a job title.

How: adjective → verb ("I am persuasive" → "I persuade"), then title → function by choosing People, Data, or Things ("sales rep" → "I persuade people").

Trade-offs: none; this is strictly additive precision.

The Three-Sheet Dig

When to use: to surface transferable skills you don't know you have.

How: three sheets headed PEOPLE / DATA / THINGS, each with "I am good at . . ."; target 25+ items per sheet with no editing; then winnow to your 8–10 highest-level skills and elaborate each as skill + object + benefit ("I am good at negotiating deals that please the buyer as well as the seller").

Trade-offs: the first pass feels wasteful; the buried items only appear because you didn't censor.

The Transferable Skills Ladder

When to use: deciding which skill to claim and which to develop next.

How: place your claim on the People ladder — following directions < communicating < persuading < negotiating < coaching/mentoring. Claim persuading and you keep a sales job; negotiating opens account executive; mentoring reads as VP material.

Trade-offs: overclaiming a rung you can't demonstrate is worse than accurately claiming a lower one.

The Five-Part Achievement Story

When to use: when raw inventory hasn't produced enough evidence; before any conversation requiring concrete proof.

How: write at least three, each following goal → obstacle → step-by-step solution → outcome with significance → objective evaluation quantified in dollars. Then map each story to your skill lists.

Trade-offs: slower than list-making; it's the only method that reliably surfaces skills you didn't know you had.

Feature → Benefit Translation

When to use: self-marketing to a boss or any employer.

How: state the skill (feature), ask what emotional state it creates in the customer, then reduce to a bottom-line factor. "I negotiate prices that satisfy both sides" → "I create satisfaction" → "repeat business, quarter after quarter."

Trade-offs: your job is easier than an ad agency's — your customer has one motive, to save and make money.

The Outside-Consultant Method

When to use: when no existing position fits, and you want to create one.

How: imagine you were hired externally to recommend improvements. (1) Consider what position should be added or replaced; (2) work out recommendations in detail; (3) decide what facts and figures support them and gather the data; (4) draw up benefit scenarios; (5) combine with your own performance record so you present as the ideal candidate.

Trade-offs: the company may be unable to act — but the exercise still markets your work ethic and identifies projects. No positive effort is wasted.

Let the Boss Own the Idea

When to use: selling a new or redefined role.

How: never proclaim a new position; describe the expanded role and let him name it. Use we / us / our, never I / me / you. Use "what if" language. Connect the proposal to something he already said he wanted, by date and detail.

Trade-offs: you forfeit credit. You buy the reality — which is what actually matters to your career.

The Helping Vocabulary

When to use: continuously, in every interaction.

How: move the conversation from I and you to we, us, our, then layer on collaboration verbs. "You've really got a problem" → "We've really got a problem" → "What should we do about it?"

Trade-offs: none; this is the cheapest rapport instrument in the book.

Asking for Help (in preference to offering it)

When to use: to build rapport faster than an offer of help does.

How: identify the best source first (who does what job, who has influence and respect, who's in the loop, who do others ask, who decides), then calibrate urgency: "Tom, I need your help" / "…when's a good time to talk?" / "…mind if I pick your brain?" Never apologize for asking; never belittle yourself; thank specifically.

Trade-offs: feels like taking; it's actually giving the opportunity to be helpful.

The 12 Rules of Constructive Criticism

When to use: any time you're about to correct someone.

How: never criticize a person, only an issue/action/outcome; confirm it's worth criticizing and fixable; ask permission; choose a private place and time; cite specifics; bring alternatives; use an informal tone, never command language; temper with praise; one issue at a time; follow up with positive feedback; no threats — but no sugarcoating either.

Trade-offs: slower than blurting. It's the difference between a correction and an enemy.

FIDO

When to use: as the first filter on any irritation or anger.

How: Forget It, Drive On. Act only when a situation — never a person — is damaging your work life or the organization's productivity.

Trade-offs: some real problems get deferred; most annoyances are transitory and acting on them enshrines them with destructive permanence.

The Four-Component Apology

When to use: as soon as you've erred; never wait to be asked.

How: (1) say you're sorry; (2) own the error; (3) express empathy for their feelings; (4) offer a remedy, shifting from I/you to we/us. Keep the tone sincere, not dramatic — the apology is about their feelings, not yours.

Trade-offs: none. It eases your guilt while giving the other person the chance to forgive.

The Trigger Object

When to use: preemptively, while calm, so it's available when conflict erupts.

How: choose an object always reliably on your desk (or a golfer's counter for your pocket, per Shapiro's Precision Nirvana). Say out loud that it is your signal to stop, listen silently, and think before responding to the issue rather than the personality.

Trade-offs: nothing is special about the object; it works only because you committed to it in advance.

Slap a Label on It

When to use: when emotion is fogging a dispute.

How: define the substantive issues, name each one, list them — then make yourself the public scribe: "Let's take an inventory of exactly what issues are in play. Alice, why don't you go first?" Enforce turns without interruption.

Trade-offs: costs meeting time; carefully describing a problem does roughly half the work of solving it.

The Six Questions Before You Engage

When to use: deciding whether a conflict is worth fighting.

How: Is the outcome worth the energy? Worth risking goodwill? Has the other side already decided, and is it reviewable? Can you live with them winning? Does letting them win buy future bargaining chips? Does this have to be solved now?

Trade-offs: the exception is a team about to choose a destructive course — that battle is always worth fighting.

Exploit Agreement, Transform Disagreement

When to use: converting a stalled dispute into progress.

How: build first in the areas everyone agrees on so everyone gains a stake, then split the remainder into what's working and what isn't, and name an owner for the path between. "We agree the project is feasible, but we need more data. Harry, can you get us the additional data?"

Trade-offs: none — but it is valueless without the action plan and follow-through.

The Action Plan + Executive Follow-Through

When to use: the moment any meeting produces agreement.

How: list the tasks; assign each to a defined owner; set objectives, measurable performance criteria, and timetables; get management buy-in. Then write the summarizing memo yourself, monitor within the deadlines, and encourage, cajole, nag, and goad as required.

Trade-offs: it's unglamorous work no one assigned you. An executive is someone who executes.

The Bully Protocol

When to use: under a personal attack that bypasses the merits.

How: ignore the illegitimate question, answer with facts; minimize contact and prefer email; maintain eye contact, don't interrupt, don't say "calm down"; assert and reassert without arguing or backing down; show as little emotion as possible.

Trade-offs: the bully wants a quick emotional skirmish. Deliver a slow war of attrition and the fire dies.

The Passive Aggressor Protocol

When to use: with anyone whose reliability you can rely on being absent.

How: stage-by-stage timetables with outcome criteria; take charge early and put the division of tasks in writing; demand facts and figures, not assurances; send tickler emails; repeat instructions as often as necessary and express no frustration.

Trade-offs: it is micromanagement, and it costs you time you shouldn't have to spend.

The Chronic Complainer Protocol

When to use: when whining is being used to dodge work.

How: verify the complaint has no merit first; then cease all discussion of merits; express no sympathy; state the assignment's importance; state that it is necessary; state it again; finally, grant permission to fail — promise to evaluate results and help make it right.

Trade-offs: step seven means agreeing to take on extra work. It may be the only route to usable output.

The Schemer Protocol

When to use: prevention always; confrontation only when damage control fails.

How: prevent with corporate karma, genuine human engagement, standing allies built before you need them, and never gossiping yourself. Respond to rumors with truth. If confronting: a planned meeting outside the office (never a hallway), broach issues not the person, no "gotcha," recruit their help stopping the talk, end looking forward — and never say the rumors hurt your feelings.

Trade-offs: involving your boss may work, but risks tagging you as part of a problem rather than the solution.

The Poacher Protection

When to use: before discussing any idea with anyone.

How: write and date the idea first, store it on a drive you control; distribute it marked as a draft with a comment deadline and a final-draft date; choose recipients carefully and let each know who else received it. If poached in a meeting, speak up immediately and persist politely.

Trade-offs: slows down casual idea-sharing, which collaboration requires; the dated draft is the cheapest insurance available.

Sell Your Influence

When to use: when the danger signs appear and you feel yourself being pushed out of the loop.

How: pick one proposal; identify a powerful person as a lever; sell the benefit to that person; shift from "my concept" to "our concept" as buy-in starts; recruit your critics rather than deflecting them.

Trade-offs: greater exposure at the moment you feel most like hiding — which is exactly the point.

The Two-Stage Career Change

When to use: when your target career differs from your current one in both title and field.

How: change one component to take a job; gain experience; change the other later. Either route works, and the first step is often easiest without leaving your current company.

Trade-offs: slower than a single leap, and far more likely to succeed.

The Informational Interview

When to use: after your immediate subsistence needs are handled, before applying anywhere.

How: identify the career → the companies → their product → the individuals producing it. Contact them explicitly not as a job applicant. Ask: how did you get started; what do you like most; what do you dislike most; what are the industry's prospects; who else should I talk to? Cap at ten minutes unless extended. Always send a thank-you email.

Trade-offs: no job comes of any single one. Enough of them broadcast your name across an industry before you apply.

How to Win Friends and Influence People

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — How to Win Friends & Influence People

The 30 Principles at a Glance

Part 1 — Handling People

  1. Don't criticize, condemn, or complain.
  2. Give honest and sincere appreciation.
  3. Arouse in the other person an eager want.

Part 2 — Make People Like You

  1. Become genuinely interested in others. 2. Smile. 3. Use the person's name. 4. Be a good listener; let them talk about themselves. 5. Talk in terms of their interests. 6. Make them feel important — sincerely.

Part 3 — Win to Your Thinking

  1. Avoid arguments. 2. Never say "You're wrong." 3. If wrong, admit it fast. 4. Begin friendly. 5. Get "yes, yes" early. 6. Let them talk most. 7. Let the idea be theirs. 8. See their viewpoint. 9. Sympathize with them. 10. Appeal to nobler motives. 11. Dramatize ideas. 12. Throw down a challenge.

Part 4 — Be a Leader

  1. Begin with praise. 2. Criticize indirectly. 3. Admit your own faults first. 4. Ask, don't order. 5. Let them save face. 6. Praise every improvement. 7. Give a reputation to live up to. 8. Make the fault seem easy to fix. 9. Make them happy to comply.

Decision Rules

SituationDo thisBecause
Tempted to point out a faultStop — say nothing, or correct indirectlyCriticism triggers defense, never change
Need someone to actReframe around their wantNo one is motivated by your want
Someone says "You're wrong" is on your lipsSay "I may be wrong — let's check"Contradiction locks the mind shut
You are wrongAdmit it loudly, first, before they doDisarms the critic completely
Facing resistance / an early "no"Open with questions earning "yes"Momentum carries them to your view
Must give feedbackPraise + "and" (never "but") + easy fix"But" cancels the praise
DelegatingPhrase as a questionPreserves initiative and pride
Someone is losing/wrong publiclyGive them a face-saving exitHumiliation costs the relationship
Want the idea adoptedLet them think they thought of itPeople back their own ideas
First meetingAsk about them, listen, use their nameInterested beats interesting

Tells & Smells

  • You feel the urge to say "Actually..." → you're about to trigger ego defense. Stop.
  • Your praise contains "but" → it will read as a set-up. Swap for "and."
  • You're explaining what you need → you've lost them. Reframe to their interest.
  • You "won" the argument → check whether you just lost the person.
  • Praise feels generic → it will read as flattery. Name the specific thing or don't say it.

The One-Line Test

Before any interaction: "What does the other person want, and how do I make them feel important — sincerely?" If you can't answer, you're not ready to persuade.

glossary.md

Glossary — How to Win Friends and Influence People

Appeal to the nobler motives — persuade by attributing a fine, unselfish reason to the other person and letting them live up to it (Ch 3, P10).

Appreciation (honest and sincere) — genuine, specific recognition of what is admirable in someone; the second Fundamental Technique. Opposite of flattery (Ch 1, P2).

Arouse an eager want — frame any request around the other person's desires so they want to act (Ch 1, P3).

Bait the hook to suit the fish — metaphor for speaking to the other person's self-interest, not your own (Ch 1).

Begin in a friendly way — open persuasion with warmth, not confrontation; "a drop of honey" (Ch 3, P4).

Creatures of emotion — Carnegie's premise that people are driven by pride and vanity, not logic (Ch 1).

Dramatize your ideas — make points vivid and showmanlike so they land and stick (Ch 3, P11).

Face-saving — protecting another's dignity even when they're wrong; a core leadership move (Ch 4, P5).

Flattery — insincere, generic praise; "from the teeth out." The counterfeit of appreciation (Ch 1).

Fundamental Techniques (the three) — don't criticize; give sincere appreciation; arouse an eager want (Ch 1).

Importance hunger — the deepest human craving to feel important and appreciated; root of most behavior (Ch 1).

"...and" not "...but" — replace "but" with "and" after praise so correction reads as encouragement, not a set-up (Ch 4, P2).

Indirect criticism — calling attention to a mistake by inference rather than direct rebuke (Ch 4, P2).

Nobler motives — the reason that "sounds good" (vs. the real reason); appeal to it to move people (Ch 3, P10).

Praise every improvement — reinforce the slightest progress specifically and lavishly (Ch 4, P6).

Reputation to live up to — assign someone a virtue so they strive to embody it (Ch 4, P7).

Save face — see Face-saving (Ch 4, P5).

Secret of Socrates — chain of small "yes" agreements that builds momentum toward your conclusion (Ch 3, P5).

Show respect for opinions — never say "You're wrong"; invite a joint look at the facts (Ch 3, P2).

Six Ways to Make People Like You — interest, smile, names, listening, their interests, feeling important (Ch 2).

Smile — low-cost signal of gladness; "act as if" until the feeling follows (Ch 2, P2).

Spotlight rule — aim attention at the other person, not yourself (Ch 2).

Throw down a challenge — spur people via competition and the desire to excel (Ch 3, P12).

"Yes, yes" response — see Secret of Socrates (Ch 3, P5).

patterns.md

Patterns — Carnegie's Techniques in Practice

Bait-the-Hook Reframe

When to use: any request or "ask" (email, delegation, sales, parenting).

How: delete every "I/we want" framing; rewrite the ask around what the other person already wants and show the path from their want to your request.

Trade-offs: requires genuinely knowing their interests — guessing wrong reads as manipulation.

Sincere Appreciation (not Flattery)

When to use: opening a relationship, motivating, before a hard conversation.

How: find something specific and genuinely admirable; name it concretely ("the way you handled X" not "good job"). Must be true.

Trade-offs: fails instantly if insincere or generic; over-use dilutes.

The "Yes, Yes" Ladder (Secret of Socrates)

When to use: overcoming resistance or an early "no"; onboarding, sales, negotiation.

How: begin with questions the other person cannot help but agree to; chain agreements toward the conclusion you want. Never open on the point of dispute.

Trade-offs: transparent if the questions are leading or gimmicky; keep them honest and relevant.

Admit-Your-Own-Fault-First

When to use: correcting a peer or junior; defusing a critic.

How: name your own similar mistake before mentioning theirs ("I got this wrong for years myself..."); or beat a critic to the punch by condemning yourself first.

Trade-offs: requires humility; loses power if the shared-fault claim is fabricated.

"And" Instead of "But"

When to use: any praise-then-correct message (feedback, reviews, coaching).

How: give sincere praise, then join the improvement with "and" — never "but," which cancels the praise.

Trade-offs: subtle; still needs the correction phrased as a forward-looking possibility, not a veiled criticism.

Order-as-a-Question

When to use: delegating, directing a team, changing behavior.

How: convert commands into questions — "Would it work to...?", "What do you think about trying...?" — so the person keeps initiative and ownership.

Trade-offs: slower than a direct order; unsuitable in true emergencies where speed > buy-in.

Reputation-to-Live-Up-To

When to use: motivating improvement, building trust, turning someone around.

How: publicly attribute a virtue to the person ("you've always been reliable"), then hand them the task that lets them prove it.

Trade-offs: manipulative if the virtue is fictional; works only when the person can plausibly own it.

Idea-Ownership Transfer

When to use: pushing a proposal that meets resistance.

How: plant the seed via question or partial suggestion; let the other person develop and voice the conclusion so it becomes their idea.

Trade-offs: requires ego restraint — you don't get public credit for the idea.

The Face-Saving Exit

When to use: someone is wrong, is losing, or must reverse course.

How: give them a dignified way out — attribute the error to circumstances, offer a graceful reframe, correct privately.

Trade-offs: means forgoing the satisfaction of being visibly right.

Interested-Not-Interesting Listening

When to use: any first meeting, networking, relationship-building.

How: ask about the other person's favorite subject and listen with full attention; talk about yourself as little as possible.

Trade-offs: none, provided the interest is genuine; feigned interest eventually shows.

Hyperfocus: How to Be More Productive in a World of Distraction

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Hyperfocus — Cheatsheet

The two modes (know which you need)

HYPERFOCUSSCATTERFOCUS
DirectionAttention outward, one thingAttention inward, nothing in particular
Best mode forProductivityCreativity
Fills attentional space withone complex taskfree space to connect dots
Fueled bymental energy (drains it)rest (restores it)
Boost withcaffeine, Biological Prime Timelow energy, Creative Prime Time, (occasional) alcohol

The Four Types of Tasks — where should you be?

AttractiveUnattractive
Productive✅ Purposeful (sweet spot; ~3–4 tasks)✅ Necessary (push yourself)
Unproductive⚠️ Distracting (small doses)❌ Unnecessary (active laziness)

Live in the top row. Sort your tasks here first.

Decision rules

  • What to focus on? → the most consequential task (the domino toppling a hundred others), not the most urgent/stimulating.
  • Analytical problem? → hyperfocus (+ caffeine). Creative/insight problem? → scatterfocus (low energy).
  • Am I productive? → Did I accomplish what I intended? (Busy ≠ productive. A planned lazy day = productive.)
  • Should I break? → If you're switching a lot, rereading, or drifting to mindless work — yes, and take it before you feel fatigued.
  • Worth consuming? → Treat it as a "pitch" for your attention. Useful > balanced > entertaining > trashy.

Hyperfocus in 4 stages

  1. Choose a purposeful object → 2. Eliminate distractions (in advance) → 3. Focus for a preset time → 4. Draw back when you wander (you will, 47% of the day).

Intention precedes attention. Make it an implementation intention (when/where/which action) → 62% vs 22% follow-through.

Key numbers (thresholds & defaults)

  • Attentional space: ~4 chunks / ~40 conscious bits per second.
  • Focus lasts ~40 seconds at a computer before interruption.
  • Never pair two complex tasks; only complex + habitual.
  • Task-switching makes work ~50% slower (attention residue).
  • Breaks: at least every 90 min, ~15 min per hour worked.
  • Sleep: 1 hr missed ≈ 2 hrs lost productivity; deficit shrinks attentional space up to 60%.
  • Caffeine: benefit up to ~200mg; avoid >400mg.

Where the wandering mind goes → why scatterfocus is productive

Past 12% · Present 28% · Future 48% (prospective bias). In scatterfocus you're 14× more likely to plan the future than when focused.

Three scatterfocus styles

  • Capture — roam free, write it down → clears the mind.
  • Problem-crunching — circle one problem → for a big decision (sparingly).
  • Habitual — simple enjoyable task + notepad → most powerful; recharges + connects most dots.

Tells you need to recharge

Frequent switching · losing grip on intentions · slower pace (rereading) · drifting to mindless work · slipping into scatterfocus unintentionally.

Master habit

Meta-awareness — hourly, ask "what's in my attentional space, and is it what I intended?" Meditation is the one proven way to enlarge that space.

glossary.md

Hyperfocus — Glossary

Active laziness — Staying busy with unnecessary work that produces nothing (Ch 1).

Attention residue — Fragments of a previous task lingering in attentional space after switching; makes work ~50% slower (Sophie Leroy) (Ch 2).

Attentional space — Bailey's term for working memory; the mental scratch pad ("RAM") holding what you're aware of now (~4 chunks, ~10-second lifespan) (Ch 2).

Autopilot mode — Managing attention reactively, without deliberate choice; fine for habits, toxic for attention (Ch 1).

Biological Prime Time (BPT) — Your peak-energy hours; best for focus/hyperfocus work (Ch 10).

Boredom — The restlessness of transitioning from high to low stimulation; "unwanted scatterfocus" (Ch 6).

Capture mode — Scatterfocus style: let the mind roam and write down whatever surfaces (Ch 6).

Chunking — Grouping information into meaningful units to hold more in attentional space (Ch 2).

Clustering — The brain's grouping of related dots; builds expertise and frees attentional space (Ch 9).

Creative Prime Time (CPT) — Your low-energy hours; best for creative/scatterfocus work (least-inhibited brain) (Ch 10).

Default network — The brain network active when unfocused; scatterfocus lights it up to connect dots (Ch 6).

Distraction-free mode — Eliminating every controllable distraction in advance to enable hyperfocus (Ch 4).

Dot — Any idea or piece of information in your mind; creativity = connecting dots (Ch 6, 8).

Flow — Total immersion when challenge ≈ skill (Csikszentmihalyi); often produced by hyperfocus (Ch 3, 5).

Four types of distractions — 2×2 of in/out-of-control × annoying/fun (Ch 4).

Four types of tasks — 2×2 grid: necessary, unnecessary, distracting, purposeful (Ch 1).

Hyperfocus — Keeping one important, complex object of attention filling your attentional space; the brain's most productive mode (Ch 3).

Habitual scatterfocus — The most powerful scatterfocus style: do a simple enjoyable task and capture rising ideas (Ch 6).

Hourly awareness chime — An hourly timer prompting you to check what's in your attentional space (Ch 3, 10).

Implementation intention — A specific when/where/which-action plan; doubles/triples follow-through (Gollwitzer) (Ch 3).

Insight trigger — A cue (from environment or wandering mind) that sparks a solution to an incubating problem (Ch 8).

Intention precedes attention — Decide what to accomplish before you begin; attention without intention is wasted (Ch 3).

Jobs to be done — Asking what "job" you "hire" each device to do (Christensen); redundant jobs = unnecessary device (Ch 4).

Meta-awareness — Noticing what's occupying your attentional space; the master attention skill (Ch 2).

Novelty bias — The prefrontal cortex rewards task-switching with dopamine, so busyness feels productive (Ch 2).

Open loops — Unresolved tasks/commitments held in your head that hijack attentional space (Ch 4).

Parkinson's Law — Work expands to fill available time; busywork can signal a lack of real work (Ch 5).

Positive affect — How good you feel; a good mood expands attentional space (Ch 10).

Problem-crunching mode — Scatterfocus style: hold one problem loosely and let thoughts circle it (Ch 6).

Productivity — Accomplishing what you intend to (not being busy) (Ch 2).

Prospective bias — The wandering mind's tendency to think about the future (48% of the time) (Ch 6).

Purposeful work — Attractive + productive tasks; the sweet spot; your ~3–4 highest-impact tasks (Ch 1).

Reduced-distraction mode — Taming the biggest distractions while staying reachable for collaboration (Ch 4).

Rule of 3 — Choose the three things you want accomplished by day's end (Ch 3).

Scatterfocus — Intentional mind-wandering; the brain's most creative mode (Ch 6).

Ten-thousand-hour rule — Rough length of deliberate practice to build expert-level dots (Ch 9).

Zeigarnik effect — Unfinished tasks weigh more heavily on the mind than finished ones (Ch 8).

40 bits / 4 chunks — We consciously process ~40 of 11M sensory bits/second, and hold ~4 chunks in short-term memory (Ch 2).

40 seconds — Average time we focus at a computer before being interrupted or self-interrupting (Ch 0, 2).

90/15 break rule — Break at least every 90 minutes, ~15 minutes per hour of work (Ch 7).

patterns.md

Hyperfocus — Patterns & Techniques

Sort Tasks into the Four Quadrants

When to use: Whenever you feel busy but unproductive.

How: Map monthly tasks by productive/unproductive × attractive/unattractive → necessary, purposeful, distracting, unnecessary. Live in the top two.

Trade-offs: A "stepping-back" activity — you must remove yourself from the trenches to do it (5–10 min).

The Four Stages of Hyperfocus

When to use: Any complex, purposeful task.

How: (1) Choose a meaningful object; (2) eliminate internal + external distractions in advance; (3) focus for a preset time; (4) draw attention back each time it wanders.

Trade-offs: For complex tasks only — full attention on a habit makes you choke.

Rule of 3

When to use: Every morning.

How: Pick the three things you want done by day's end; keep them visible. Optionally set 3 weekly and 3 personal intentions too.

Most Consequential Tasks

When to use: A long to-do list.

How: Rank by second/third-order consequences — which task is the domino that topples a hundred others? Combine with the quadrant grid.

Implementation Intentions

When to use: Any difficult or important intention.

How: Specify when/where/which-action ("Go to the gym" → "go on my lunch break"). Name the situational cue.

Trade-offs: Overkill for trivial goals; essential for hard ones. You must actually care about the goal.

Hourly Awareness Chime

When to use: To stay intentional moment-to-moment.

How: Set an hourly timer; when it rings, check whether you're on autopilot, how full your attentional space is, and whether you're on the most consequential thing. Pick 2–3 prompts.

Distraction-Free Mode

When to use: Before any hyperfocus block.

How: Block distracting sites/apps (Freedom, Cold Turkey, RescueTime), phone in Do Not Disturb in another room, noise-canceling headphones, maybe caffeine. When a new distractor slips through, add it to the block list.

Trade-offs: Impulsive people may find blockers stressful — use for the hardest tasks and treat yourself after.

Tame the Five Pain Points

When to use: Ongoing, to reduce baseline distraction.

How: Notifications (disable nonessential) · Phone (treat as "a more annoying computer"; stow it; second "distractions device"; phone swap) · Email (batch at set times, five-sentence rule, delete phone app, external to-do list, 20-min hyperfocus bursts) · Meetings (no agenda→no meeting; question recurring; challenge attendee list) · Internet (disconnect periodically).

Clear Your Mind (Externalize Open Loops)

When to use: When nagging thoughts fragment your focus.

How: Offload to a to-do list, calendar, distractions list, waiting-for list, worry list (Getting Things Done). Removes guilt (past), worry (future), doubt (present).

The Three Styles of Scatterfocus

When to use: To plan, recharge, or connect ideas.

How: Capture (roam free, write what surfaces — clear the mind); Problem-crunching (circle one big problem — use sparingly, 30–60 min); Habitual (simple enjoyable task + capture ideas — most powerful, most often). Keep a notepad.

Refreshing Breaks (90/15 Rule)

When to use: Throughout the workday.

How: Break at least every 90 min, ~15 min per hour; make it low-effort, wanted, and not a chore ("pleasurably effortless"). Not email/news. Take breaks before you need them.

Connect More Dots

When to use: Stuck on a creative or nonlinear problem.

How: Scatter in a richer environment; write the problem down; sleep on it; step back/unfocus; leave the task unfinished (stop mid-sentence); consume more valuable dots.

Consumption Audit

When to use: Periodically, to upgrade your inputs.

How: Log everything you consume into useful/balanced/entertaining/trashy. Cut trash, add a valuable item for each cut, veg out with intention, invest in serendipity.

Match Mode to Problem (with Substances)

When to use: Choosing how to attack a task.

How: Analytical → hyperfocus at Biological Prime Time (+ caffeine). Creative/insight → scatterfocus at Creative Prime Time (low energy; occasional drink for pure-creative). Caffeine narrows focus; alcohol widens wandering.

In the Line of Fire: How to Handle Tough Questions...When It Counts

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — In the Line of Fire

The one rule above all

Question → Buffer → Answer (head-on, ≤60s, with evidence) → Topspin. Skip the answer = evasive (politician's sin). Skip the Topspin = no influence (businessperson's sin). And: every answer must be true.

Decision tree: a question just landed

  • Do I understand it 100%? No → Return to Sender ("I'm sorry, I didn't follow; would you mind restating?"). Never interpret/speculate.
  • Is it factually inaccurate / an accusation? → Skip the Buffer; refute immediately ("No."), then support, then restate rebuttal.
  • Is the charge actually true? → Guilty-as-Charged: Buffer → Agree → "But…" → Evidence → Call to action+benefit.
  • Multiple unrelated questions? → Pick ONE; answer; then "You had another question."
  • Otherwise → Buffer (paraphrase or key word) → wait for head nod → answer → Topspin.

Buffer: pick your form

FormWhenCost
Paraphrase ("Why this price point?")hostile question; need thinking timeoveruse = stilted
"You" + paraphrase ("Your question is…")want Eye Connect + read the nodsounds like a "hoot owl" if every time
Key Words ("Our pricing rationale is…")Roman Column already crystal clearzero thinking time — must be sure

Cool-zone rule (positioning the Roman Column)

  • Repeat the charged question → land in "Guilty!" (left danger zone).
  • Reverse/invalidate it → land in "Contentious!" (right danger zone).
  • Neutral paraphrase of the bare key word → cool zone. ✅

Find the Roman Column — don't grab the wrapper

Hostile question ends with…Wrapper (wrong)Roman Column (right)
"…charging so much!"overpricing/expensiveprice
"…think you can survive?"survivecompete
"…you, a woman…old boy network?"sexismcapability
"…throw in your lot / get acquired?"mergeindependence

Tells & smells (read the room)

  • Involuntary head nod after your Buffer = you nailed the Roman Column → answer now. Frown / head-shake = wrong → Return to Sender.
  • Questioner's voice rises on "really" / "saying" ("What I'm really asking…") = "You're not listening!" alarm.
  • Your own slouch / hands-in-pockets / glance at watch = audience reads "bored, doesn't care" within ~5 seconds.
  • On camera, involuntary disdain (Scowl/Sigh) is fatal — assume you're always on a split screen.

Three ways to lose (diagnose fast)

Defensive (squirm/stammer) · Evasive (answer a different question) · Contentious (attack — the worst; = visible loss of control). All are Fight-or-Flight. Antidote: firm, calm resolve + the sequence.

Delete from your vocabulary

"Let me see if I have this right…" · "Could you repeat the question?" · "Does that answer your question?" · "Is what you're asking…?" · "The question is…" · "What you're really asking…" · "If I understand your question…" · "The issue/concern is…" · "As I said…" · "Why do you ask?"

Special questions — fast rules

  • Unknown → admit, promise follow-up, ask for a card (unless central — then answer).
  • Confidential → give a positive reason (policy/security/legality); never "I can't reveal that." Then Topspin.
  • Speculative/forecast → "It's impossible to say how long it'll take, but…" → Topspin to Point B + WIIFY.
  • Irrelevant → there's no such thing; Buffer the snicker away, then answer or take offline.

Topspin targets

Point B = what you want them to DO (call to action). WIIFY = WHY they should (their benefit). End on one or both — never on a negative. Earn it by answering first.

Prep checklist (before the session)

☐ List the questions you don't want to hear ☐ Position statement (press-release style) for each red-flag issue (Mgmt, Competition, Growth, Price, Contingencies, Timing, Problems, IP) ☐ Gather evidence ☐ Verbalize aloud Buffers + answers + a Topspin on each, with colleagues firing questions ☐ Set time expectations; plan the countdown.

Open-the-floor mechanics

Open hand, never point (one-plus-three). All names or no names — never selective. Raise your hand to invite hands — but not with investors/board.

glossary.md

Glossary — In the Line of Fire

Active Listening — Concentrating fully on the questioner to extract the Roman Column; the martial art of Concentration (Ch 4).

Agility counters Force — Core principle: beat a stronger/larger opponent (one-against-many) with skill and leverage, not brute force (Intro, Ch 9).

Anticipate — Pre-compile the worst questions you might face (questions only, not canned answers) (Ch 6, 8).

Back reference ("As I said…") — Citing earlier material; banned in Q&A as condescending. Use forward references only (Ch 5).

Buffer — A neutral restatement of a question that deflects negativity and tees up the answer; first line of self-defense. Three forms: paraphrase, "you"+paraphrase, Key Words (Ch 5).

Contentious — Combative reaction to a question (e.g., Perot's "You're lying!"); most damaging negative behavior (Ch 1, 9).

Control — The one-word thesis of the book; managing the question, answer, questioner, audience, time, and yourself (Intro).

Cool Zone — The neutral center where the Roman Column belongs; left zone = "Guilty!" (repeat), right zone = "Contentious!" (reverse) (Ch 5).

Defensive — Self-protective reaction (squirming, stammering) under a tough question (Ch 1).

Double Buffer — A buffer in front of the Buffer ("The question is…", "Glad you asked"); mostly useless fillers — fix by inserting "you" (Ch 5).

Effective Management (Perceived) — The positive subliminal impression created by well-handled questions; the goal of all techniques (Intro).

Empty your cup — Zen lesson: clear your own thoughts to receive the questioner's (Ch 4).

Evasive — Answering a different question than the one asked (Lott; Pedro Martinez) (Ch 1).

Eye Connect — Locking eyes with the questioner until they look back ("the click of engagement"); stronger than "eye contact" (Ch 4, 5).

Fight or Flight — The instinctive stress reaction underlying defensive/evasive (flight) and contentious (fight) behavior (Ch 1, 7).

Forward reference — Answering presented material fresh, without "as I said"; the only reference allowed in Q&A (Ch 5).

Guilty as Charged — A question whose charge is true; handled by the 5-step sequence: Buffer → Agree → "But…" → Evidence → Call to action + benefit (Ch 6).

Head nod (involuntary) — The questioner's automatic assent to a correct Buffer; your accuracy meter (a frown = wrong) (Ch 5).

Key Words (Buffer) — The most advanced Buffer: embed the key word and roll straight into the answer; zero thinking time, maximum sharpness (Ch 5).

Manage the Answer — Meet the issue only head-on; no tangents; ~60-second max (Ch 6).

Paraphrase — Restating the question "alongside" (para) in neutral form — NOT re-phrasing (re = again, carries the negative). Interrogative + Roman Column, voice drops at end (Ch 5).

Point A → Point B — A = audience uninformed/unconvinced; B = convinced and ready to act. Point B is your call to action (Ch 6).

Quid Pro Quo — "If they ask it, you must answer it"; address the Roman Column directly (Ch 6).

Red Flag Issues (Universal) — The handful of recurring concern areas: Management, Competition, Growth, Price/Cost, Contingencies, Timing, Problems, Intellectual Property (Ch 6).

Return to Sender — When you don't understand 100%, hand the floor back: "I'm sorry, I didn't follow; would you mind restating the question?" (Ch 4, 5).

Roman Column — The one or two words at the heart of a question (named for orators' memory-trigger columns); find it before answering. Questions can have a double Roman Column (Ch 4).

Sub-vocalization — Silently naming the key issue under your breath to crystallize the Roman Column (Ch 4).

Topspin — Ending an answer with Point B/WIIFY for a strong, offensive close (tennis metaphor); must be earned by answering first (Ch 6, 7).

Triple Fail-Safe — Three checkpoints before answering: ① grasp the Roman Column (else Return to Sender) ② Buffer + wait for head nod ③ frown → Return to Sender (Ch 5).

Verbalize — Rehearse answers aloud (Buffers, answers, Topspin) like a tennis volley (Ch 5, 8).

Visual Listening — Physical signals of attentiveness: balanced stance, Eye Connect, head nods, voice assent, steady fingers (Ch 4).

WIIFY — "What's In It For You" (pronounced "whiffy"); the audience's reason to act — why they should move to Point B (Ch 6).

Winning Sequence — Question → Buffer → Answer (with evidence) → Topspin (Ch 10).

Worst-Case Scenario — Prep assumption: every question maximally hostile, every group large (Ch 2).

"Wrong Q&A" — Weissman's rename of "Rude Q&A": pre-canning answers before understanding the question (Ch 3).

"You're not listening!" — The fatal audience perception (cousins: "That's not what I asked," "What I'm really asking…") (Ch 3).

"Ready, Fire, Aim!" — Answering before the target (key issue) is in your sights (Ch 3).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — In the Line of Fire

The Winning Sequence (master pattern)

When to use: every challenging question.

How: Question → Buffer (neutralize) → Answer the Roman Column head-on, with evidence → Topspin (Point B / WIIFY).

Trade-offs: Politicians skip the answer (jump to Topspin) → look evasive. Businesspeople skip the Topspin → exert zero influence. Do all four.

Find the Roman Column

When: before answering anything.

How: "Empty your cup"; listen for the 1–2 nouns/verbs that are the essence; sub-vocalize them ("She's worried about cost"). Strip away emotion, misinformation, ramble. Watch for a double column.

Trade-offs: Mistaking the emotional wrapper (e.g., "sexism," "survive") for the column lands you in a danger zone.

Paraphrase Buffer

When: hostile/charged questions; buys thinking time.

How: Interrogative (What/Why/How/Does/Can/Is) + Roman Column, voice drops at end. Strip charged words; fewest words possible. Keep it in the cool zone (don't repeat = guilty; don't reverse = contentious).

Trade-offs: Overuse sounds stilted ("hoot owl"), especially "you"-phrased.

Key Word Buffer (advanced)

When: you already have 100% clarity; non-challenging direct questions; when you want to look razor-sharp.

How: embed the key word and roll straight into the answer ("Our pricing rationale is…").

Trade-offs: zero thinking time — only safe when the Roman Column is crystal clear. (Powell, Schwarzkopf.)

The Power of "You"

When: building a Double Buffer you'd otherwise delete.

How: "Your question is…" not "The question is…"; keeps Eye Connect, reads the head nod, most persuasive word in English.

Triple Fail-Safe

When: every answer, as a guard against rushing.

How: ① Don't retake the floor without the Roman Column → Return to Sender. ② Buffer with the key word; hold Eye Connect until the involuntary head nod. ③ Frown instead of nod → Return to Sender.

Return to Sender

When: you don't understand 100% (not 99.999%), or you get a frown.

How: take responsibility — "I'm sorry, I didn't follow; would you mind restating the question?" Never interpret, speculate, or use the deafness ruse.

Guilty-as-Charged Sequence (5 steps)

When: the charge is true.

How: Buffer → Agree (their words) → "But…" (loud; don't agree too long) → Evidence → Call to action + benefit (Point B + WIIFY).

Trade-offs: In media exchanges, do NOT agree (sound-bite risk) — counter immediately or bury the admission in a subordinate clause before Topspin.

Refute the Inaccurate Question

When: a question contains/implies a falsehood ("When did you stop beating your wife?").

How: skip the Buffer; immediate complete refutation — "No." Then support, then restate the rebuttal. (Powell: "No, of course not… But there is no list.")

Handle Special Question Types

  • Multiple disparate: pick ONE (easiest/hardest/last/surprising), Buffer + answer it, then "You had another question."
  • Statement (non-question): turn into a question via paraphrase.
  • Irrelevant/Tangential: no such thing as irrelevant — Buffer to suppress the snicker, then answer or take offline.
  • Unknown: admit it, promise follow-up, ask for a card (unless central — then you must answer).
  • Confidential/Speculative: give a positive reason (policy/security/legality); don't forecast; still pivot to Topspin.
  • Presented material: answer fresh, forward references only, never "As I said…"; be succinct.

Topspin

When: after a real answer, to close strong.

How: end with Point B (what you want them to do) and/or WIIFY (why they should). Add multiple upward swirls. Counters any "too-anything" charge (Yang to Yin).

Trade-offs: Topspin before answering = evasive (G.W. Bush / Lisa Kee). Never end on a negative (Dukakis).

Manage the Time

When: opening any Q&A.

How: set expectations up front ("time for only a few questions"); count down at the end ("two more… last question"). (Schwarzkopf: 10 questions in 2:48.)

Q&A Cycle Control Moves

Open floor (control time + traffic; open hand, never point; all-names-or-no-names) → Recognize → Yield (mind your body language — no slouch) → Retake (Buffer) → Answer (+Topspin). Repeats per questioner.

Prepare & Verbalize

When: before any mission-critical session.

How: list worst questions → position statement (press-release style) per red-flag issue → enlist colleagues to fire questions → verbalize aloud your Buffers, answers, and a Topspin on each, repeatedly. Treat every Q&A like an IPO road show.

Indistractable: How to Control Your Attention and Choose Your Life

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Indistractable — Cheatsheet

The 4-Part Model (apply IN ORDER — don't skip)

#StepCore moveChapter
1Master internal triggersDeal with discomfort (the root cause)Ch 2
2Make time for tractionTimebox values into a calendarCh 3
3Hack back external triggersRemove cues that don't serve youCh 4
4Prevent distraction with pactsPrecommit to stop yourself slidingCh 5

Two decision rules that resolve most cases

  • Traction or distraction? → "Did this move me toward or away from what I planned?" (You can't call it distraction unless you know what it distracts you from.)
  • The Critical Question (external triggers) → "Is this trigger serving me, or am I serving it?" Serving me = keep. I'm serving it = hack back.

When an urge hits (internal trigger)

  1. Name the discomfort preceding it. 2. Curiosity, not contempt. 3. 10-minute rule — allow it, but wait 10 min. 4. Surf the urge; it passes. → Never suppress (white-bear rebound). After a slip: self-compassion, not shame.

Which pact for which job?

SituationUseBecause
Can add physical frictionEffort pactMakes the bad behavior harder
Short task, removable triggerPrice pactLoss aversion; moves pain to now
Long-term change of selfIdentity pact"I don't" > "I can't"

Price-pact pitfalls: skip if trigger is inescapable, task is long, or you beat yourself up.

Email (TNT = n × t)

  • Reduce n: office hours · delay-send · unsubscribe/black-hole.
  • Reduce t: batch · touch twice · tag by reply-time ("Today"/"This Week"), not topic · answer in blocks.

Smartphone in <1 hour — the 4 R's

Remove unused → Replace (social/YouTube → desktop; wear a watch) → Rearrange (home screen = Primary Tools + Aspirations only) → Reclaim (sound/sight notifications per app; Do Not Disturb).

Meetings & chat tells

  • No agenda + proposed solution → no meeting. Meetings = consensus, not thinking out loud. One laptop per room.
  • Group chat: in/out at scheduled times; only necessary people; not a place to think aloud.

Workplace diagnosis

Chronic distraction/tech-overuse = symptom. Disease = low psychological safety + high job strain (high expectations × low control). Fix: leaders model focus → pilot one small change with one team → open a safe forum.

Kids — the smell test

  • Overuse = symptom of unmet Autonomy / Competence / Relatedness (feed these offline first).
  • Set limits with them, not for them (imposed limits → resentment + cheating).
  • Tech-readiness test: can they use the device's own settings (Do Not Disturb, notifications) to turn off triggers? If not, not ready.
  • Don't be the interrupting external trigger yourself.

Relationships

  • Phubbing → ask sincerely: "I see you're on your phone. Is everything OK?"
  • Protect intimacy with all 4 steps: manage the urge → device-free bedtime (traction) → phones out of bedroom → router/timer shut-off (effort pact).

Identity default

Call yourself "indistractable." It's a strived-for identity, not perfection — "strive" means struggle. You'll still slip; get back on track.

glossary.md

Indistractable — Glossary

Attention residue — The lingering focus on a prior task that makes refocusing after a switch harder (Sophie Leroy) (Ch 4).

Autonomy — One of three psychological nutrients: volition and freedom of control over one's choices (Ch 7).

B = MAT (Fogg Behavior Model) — A behavior occurs only when Motivation, Ability, and a Trigger converge simultaneously (Ch 4).

Burn or burn — A price pact: a $100 bill + lighter beside the calendar; exercise or burn the bill (Ch 5).

Competence — Psychological nutrient: the feeling of mastery, progress, and growth (Ch 7).

Cycle of responsiveness — Off-hours responsiveness trains others to expect it, escalating demands into an always-on norm (Leslie Perlow) (Ch 6).

Distraction — Any action that draws you away from what you planned to do (Ch 1).

Effort pact — A precommitment that makes an unwanted behavior harder to do (kSafe, Forest, Focusmate) (Ch 5).

Effort-reward imbalance — Work condition where little pay/recognition returns for hard effort; predicts depression (Ch 6).

Ego depletion — The largely debunked belief that willpower is a finite fuel that runs out (Ch 2).

External trigger — An environmental cue (ping, ding, person, object) that prompts action (Ch 1).

Hedonic adaptation — The tendency to return to a baseline of satisfaction no matter what happens; one of four factors making satisfaction temporary (Ch 2).

"I don't" vs. "I can't" — Identity framing; "I don't eat meat" resists temptation better than "I can't" (Ch 5).

Identity pact — A precommitment to a self-image ("I'm indistractable") so behavior follows identity (Ch 5).

Indistractable — Striving to do what you say you will do; the defining skill of the 21st century (Ch 1).
