cheatsheet.md

Cheat Sheet — Smart Brevity Decisions

The Core 4 (do these, in order)

#ElementRule
1Muscular tease6 words or fewer, active, provocative-yet-accurate
2Strong first sentence (lede)ONE sentence; something they don't know
3"Why it matters" (Axiom)Bold it; 1–2 sentences of significance; not redundant
4"Go deeper"Optional link to depth

Thresholds & defaults

ThingDefault
Subject line / headline≤6 words
Lede1 sentence
"Why it matters"1–2 sentences
Newsletter item≤200 words
Whole newsletter<1,000 words (>1,200 = a book)
Newsletter items5–10, numbered
Meeting20–25 min (or 5–10 micro)
Meeting agenda3 bullets, max
Slide text<20 words; 1 message
Slide count~5–6 (McKinsey: 2 per 20 you want)
Speech Big Thought≤15 words
TED talk≤18 min
Read speed~265 wpm

If / then

  • Writing anything → picture ONE reader; write the ONE thing first; then stop.
  • Don't know your point? → talk it out loud to someone first, then type that.
  • Point buried? → apply the Sacca rewrite: first 2–3 sentences say it all.
  • 3+ related points/data? → bullets, not a blob.
  • Want a word/figure seen? → bold it (beats italics).
  • Long paragraph? → cap at 2–3 sentences; break it up.
  • Feels curt after cutting? → breathe voice back (the HUMAN check).
  • Lost necessary nuance? → bring it back (the ACCURATE check).

Word tells & smells

KillUse
prevaricate, conundrum, elucidatelie, jam, explain
posit, obfuscate, ubiquitousassume, hide, everywhere
"price point," "core competency"price, skill
could / may / might (fog)planned / feared / expected
passive ("is known to…")active (Who—doing—what)
3-syllable word1-syllable word

Weak framing → Strong Axiom

WeakStrong
"Here's what's important"Why it matters
"A trend we've observed"The big picture
"Let's look at the data"By the numbers
"In conclusion"The bottom line

Axiom menu

Why it matters · The big picture · What's next · Between the lines · The backstory · By the numbers · The bottom line · Reality check · Catch up quick · Zoom in / Zoom out · Go deeper

Four guiding principles (self-check)

  • Authority — Be the expert, or find one.
  • Brevity — Stay short, not shallow.
  • Humanity — Write like you speak.
  • Clarity — Style text for impact.

Tests

  • Tease: Would you read it if you hadn't written it?
  • Lede: If this is the only thing they see, is it what you want to stick?
  • Comprehension: Can a friend spit your point back almost verbatim?
  • Slide: Would someone at 65 mph get it?

Anti-patterns

Length to fake depth · burying the lede · repeating the tease · foggy/passive verbs · big blobs of text · chit-chat past meeting start · reading from slides · one more anecdote · emoji overuse · irrelevant identity descriptors.

glossary.md

Glossary — Smart Brevity

Always be closing — End a presentation by explicitly asking for the outcome you want; it's your final slide (Ch 13).

Audience First — The manifesto's opening move: picture one specific reader and serve their needs, not your ego (Ch 4).

Axiom — A bolded lead-in signpost ("Why it matters," "The big picture") that gives skimmers instant context; the sharpened nut graf (Ch 8).

Axios — Greek for "worthy"; the media company built on Smart Brevity (Ch 3, 8).

Axios HQ — The AI tool that teaches, guides, and scores Smart Brevity writing (Ch 2, 16).

Big Thought — A speech's single, word-for-word memorable point; the spoken lede (Ch 13).

BLUF — "Bottom Line Up Front," the military's version of Smart Brevity; everyone reads it, few read the memo (Ch 12).

Brevity is confidence. Length is fear. — The Axios newsroom maxim (Ch 3).

Continuous partial attention — Linda Stone's term: readers looking at your words while thinking about the next alert (Ch 5).

Core 4 — Smart Brevity's four written parts: muscular tease, strong first sentence, "Why it matters," "Go deeper" (Ch 2).

Elegant efficiency — The cleanest, sharpest, most pleasing way to display something (Ch 9, 14).

5 Big Things — Axios's weekly, in-order-of-importance leadership newsletter, cascaded to every team (Ch 15).

Foggy words — "Could/may/might" and other vague terms that tell the reader nothing; replace with what's actually happening (Ch 10).

Go deeper — Core 4 part 4: an optional link to more depth; signals "I've done the work so you don't have to" (Ch 2, 9).

Golden Rule of Bullets — Split any 3+ related points or data into bullets; nobody wants to stare at a clump (Ch 9).

Hierarchy — Assigning importance to visual/text elements via scale, color, contrast to guide the eye (Ch 9, 14).

Journalese — Words no human would say (posit, obfuscate, ubiquitous); kill them (Ch 10).

Kick-outs — Anything that loses readers; top four: too much text, jargon, choices, long video (Ch 5).

Lede — The strong first sentence (Core 4 part 2); tell me something I don't know (Ch 2, 7).

Literary handcuffs — Imposed structural discipline (e.g., 10 numbered items) that halves word count and frees writer and reader (Ch 11).

Muscular tease — Core 4 part 1: six-or-fewer strong words to yank attention (Ch 2, 6).

Nut graf — Journalism's line telling you why you're reading; Axios pulled it up and bolded it as an Axiom (Ch 3, 8).

1 big thing — The lead newsletter item, signaling the single most important thing; paired with "1 fun thing" at the end (Ch 11).

ONE Big Thing — The one thing you want people to know, in one strong sentence (Ch 7).

Short, not shallow — Cut length without cutting essential facts, nuance, or depth (Ch 1, 2).

Simplify to exaggerate — Fewer words/slides/visuals; destroy anything that distracts from the essential point (Ch 13).

Smart Brevity — A system for creating, sharing, and consuming information: saying more with less (Ch 2).

Smart Brevity count / Score — Read-time estimate shown up top (~265 wpm); Axios HQ's numerical writing score (Ch 11, 16).

Smart Jazz — The Core 4 are guardrails, not unbreakable rules; deviate for the audience (Ch 2).

Strong words — Short, concrete, visible words (one-syllable nouns/verbs) that strike like lightning (Ch 10).

Then stop. — Say your point, then quit; the move that trips everyone up (Ch 4).

Time on text — Ronald Yaros's finding: ~26 seconds spent on a typical piece of content (Ch 5).

Weak words — Abstract or fancy "10-dollar" words; if you wouldn't say it at a bar, kill it (Ch 10).

Why it matters — The most common, effective Axiom; the context (Core 4 part 3) (Ch 2, 8).

You are the chef — Curate the reader's plate; selection is half the "smart" (Ch 11).

patterns.md

Patterns — Smart Brevity Techniques

The Core 4

When to use: Any one-to-many written communication.

How: (1) Muscular tease — 6 words or fewer. (2) One strong first sentence (lede). (3) "Why it matters" context. (4) "Go deeper" option. Fit it on one phone screen.

Trade-offs: Not for every circumstance (Smart Jazz); rigid application can feel curt — add human voice back.

The Muscular Tease

When to use: Subject lines, headlines, tweets, openers.

How: Cap at 6 words; kill funny/ironic/cryptic; write the reason you're writing in ≤10 words; provocative yet accurate; active verbs; read aloud. Test: "Would you read it if you hadn't written it?"

Trade-offs: Provocation must stay accurate; a hot name/brand or emoji boosts opens but can look gimmicky if overused.

The One-Sentence Lede

When to use: The opening line of any message.

How: Boil to your one most important point; skip anecdotes/jokes; one sentence; don't repeat the tease; cut adverbs/weak words. Trick: tell a friend what happened — that's your first sentence.

Trade-offs: Demands you actually know your point first ("Think, then type").

The Axiom ("Why it matters")

When to use: Right after the lede, and as section signposts.

How: Bold "Why it matters:"; 1–2 sentences of significance (what changes, what it signals, larger context); direct, declarative, NOT redundant with the lede. Swap weak framing for strong Axioms.

Trade-offs: A lazy Axiom that restates the lede wastes the slot.

Go Deeper

When to use: The parting line of an item.

How: Type "Go deeper," link to source/video/data. Most won't click — that's fine; it signals rigor and respect.

Trade-offs: Keeps the body short but requires you to have real depth to link to.

The Strong-Word Model

When to use: Sharpening any sentence.

How: One-syllable > two > three; strong = concrete/visible; purge fancy + journalese; kill foggy "could/may/might"; active verbs (Who—doing—what); replace words with one-fewer-syllable versions.

Trade-offs: Over-simplifying can drop needed precision — keep essential nuance.

The Bullet + Bold Format

When to use: Any body text a skimmer will scan.

How: Split 3+ related points into bullets; bold the word/figure/Axiom you most want seen; 2–3 sentences per paragraph, tops; mix bold/bullets/charts/Axioms.

Trade-offs: Overuse of bold dilutes emphasis.

The "1 big thing" Newsletter

When to use: Recurring team/company/group updates.

How: Punchy name; state read time; lead with "1 big thing:"; number 5–10 items in order of importance; ≤200 words each; total <1,000; relevant image; end with "1 fun thing."

Trade-offs: Cadence is a commitment — skipping breaks the habit.

Smart Brevity Email

When to use: Work email.

How: Urgent 6-word subject; news/ask in first sentence; "Why it matters" context; bullets; bold key figures/names; clean visual.

Trade-offs: None if you know your ask; fails if you bury it.

Smart Brevity Meeting

When to use: Any meeting.

How: Confirm you need it; email objective (1 sentence) + agenda (3 bullets) the night before; 20–25 min limit; open with objective, then "Why it matters," then decisions; guide/interrupt tangents; be inclusive; at 2 min left summarize takeaways + owners; send bulleted follow-up.

Trade-offs: Requires a disciplined facilitator; start exactly on time.

Smart Brevity Speech

When to use: Speeches, toasts, talks.

How: Authentic delivery (ditch crutches); short opening story ending in a chuckle; distill ONE Big Thought (≤15 words, word-for-word); announce it ("The one thing I want you to remember…"); verbal "Why it matters"; numbered supporting stats/stories; restate at end; say thank you. Or use Duarte's what is / what could be arc.

Trade-offs: One anecdote max — more kills momentum.

Smart Brevity Presentation

When to use: Slide decks.

How: Write the outcome + 3–5 points; sharpen the ask to ~6 words; one message per slide (3-second billboard); pictures over text; McKinsey rule (for 20 slides you want, use 2); "always be closing" final slide.

Trade-offs: Cutting 90% of slides feels risky but improves recall.

Smart Brevity Social

When to use: Twitter/Instagram/Facebook.

How: One thing per post; match register to platform; pair muscular text with an arresting image; give value rather than ask for a click.

Trade-offs: Platforms ration reach — forces brutal selectivity.

Smart Brevity Visuals

When to use: Art, charts, illustrations.

How: Strong concept → edit out superfluous elements → judge from viewer's perspective; build hierarchy with scale/color/contrast; check legibility and fresh-eyes clarity.

Trade-offs: Good hierarchy is invisible; poor hierarchy distracts.

The Take-It-for-a-Spin Drill

When to use: Converting any update to Smart Brevity (~2 min).

How: Define audience (WHO/WHAT/WHY) → 6-word headline → one-sentence "what's new" → bold "Why it matters:" → build your own Axioms → bullet the data → review (Accurate, Cohesive, Human).

Trade-offs: If the result feels curt, add voice back — the "Human" check.

The Sacca Rewrite

When to use: Any long email you've already written.

How: Write the whole thing, then make the first 2–3 sentences say everything below — often the only part read.

Trade-offs: Front-loading requires you to know your conclusion.

Cheatsheet — Talk Like TED (Decision Rules & Numbers)

The Master Rules

  • When building any talk, start with "What makes my heart sing?" — because you can't inspire others unless you're inspired yourself (Secret 1).
  • When you have a great story but flat delivery, rehearse until it's conversational — because a Ferrari is useless if you can't drive it (Secret 3).
  • When you must persuade, lead with story before data — because you cannot persuade through logic alone; break the wall first (Secret 2).
  • When drafting content, write a ≤140-character headline first — because it forces clarity and the audience needs the one big idea (Secrets 4, 7).
  • When the topic is complex, simplify until a 7th-grader gets it — because simplicity signals mastery and takes courage (Secret 7).
  • When you're tempted to imitate a star speaker, don't — stay in your lane — because audiences spot a phony and won't trust an act (Secret 9).

Hard Numbers & Thresholds

The 9 Secrets (3 Pillars)

EMOTIONAL1 Unleash the Master WithinSpeak on what makes your heart sing
EMOTIONAL2 Master StorytellingAim ~65% pathos; tell stories
EMOTIONAL3 Have a ConversationRehearse until it sounds conversational
NOVEL4 Teach Me Something NewReveal something new / freshly packaged
NOVEL5 Jaw-Dropping MomentsDesign one emotionally charged event
NOVEL6 Lighten UpBe humorous without telling jokes
MEMORABLE7 18-Minute RuleCap at 18 min; rule of three
MEMORABLE8 Multisensory PicturePictures > words; touch >1 sense
MEMORABLE9 Stay in Your LaneBe authentically yourself

The Three Story Types (Secret 2)

  1. Personal stories tied to the theme.
  2. Stories about other people the audience relates to.
  3. Brand/product success or failure stories.

Five Ways to a Jaw-Dropping Moment (Secret 5)

Props/demos · Shocking statistics (in context) · Pictures/images/videos · Memorable sound bites · Personal stories.

Rule: plan the story first, open PowerPoint last.

Five Ways to Be Funny Without a Joke (Secret 6)

Anecdotes/observations · Analogies/metaphors · Quotes · Video · Photos.

  • When you want a laugh, never tell a joke — jokes work only for pro comedians; be humorous instead.
  • When the topic is heavy, use humor + shock + statistics — all three, balanced (Rose George).
  • When opening, don't go for the big laugh — start with light observational humor; bombing early is unrecoverable.

Delivery Fixes (Secret 3)

ProblemQuick fix
Fidgeting / tapping / jinglingMove with purpose; record & review
Standing rigidlyWalk the room; leave camera frame several times / 5 min
Hands in pocketsTake them out; keep gestures in the power sphere
Speaking too slowly / readingInternalize content; match natural conversation
NervesPower pose 2 min + physical warm-up ritual

Tells & Smells (what betrays you) (Secret 3)

Incongruence between words and body = perceived deception (you show the same "tells" as a lying suspect). Truthfulness detection: audio-only 55% · video-only 65% · both 85% · + context 93%. Believe what you're saying, or the body can't fake it.

Message Map (Secret 7)

Headline (≤140 chars) → 3 key messages → stories/stats/examples under each. One page.

Slide Design (Secret 8)

Pictures instead of text · ≤40 words in first 10 slides · kill bullet points · one theme/stat per slide · break data with photos/stories · slides complement (never replace) the narrative · "use visuals to enhance words, not duplicate."

glossary.md

Glossary — Talk Like TED

18-Minute Rule — the hard cap on TED talks; the ideal presentation length: long enough to be serious, short enough to hold attention, and the length of a coffee break so it goes viral (Secret 7).

Affect-induction — humor/laughter as a communication method that captures attention, conveys emotion, and induces similar positive emotions in others to win favor (Secret 6).

Affective Communications Test (ACT) — Howard Friedman's questionnaire measuring how well people transmit feelings to others (charisma); high scorers shift low scorers' moods without a word (Secret 1).

Anaphora — repeating the same opening words across successive clauses/sentences (MLK's "I have a dream"; Bono's "We are going to win because..."); an auditory rhetorical device best delivered without slides (Secret 8).

Brain-to-brain coupling ("sync up") — Uri Hasson's finding that telling a story makes speaker's and listeners' brains fire in the same regions, planting ideas and emotions (Secret 2).

Cognitive backlog — accumulating information that piles up like weights on the listener's mind; the core reason long talks fail and the 18-minute rule works (Paul King) (Secret 7).

Command presence — a military term for presenting yourself as an authority to be respected and followed; begins with dress and carriage (Secret 3).

Congruence — alignment of words, tone, and body language; incongruence signals deception and destroys trust (Secret 3).

Curiosity gap — the painful gap in knowledge that curiosity drives us to fill (Loewenstein/Heath); breaking a pattern grabs attention (Secret 2).

Dopamine — the brain's "save button" (Martha Burns); released by novelty and learning (and emotionally charged events), it tags information for memory (Secrets 4, 5).

Dual-coding theory — Allan Paivio's theory that pictures are encoded both visually and verbally (double-stamped) while words are verbal only, making pictures more memorable (Secret 8).

Eager nonverbal — a persuasive body-language style: animated broad movements, outward-projected hands, forward-leaning posture; best for making an offer more attractive (Fennis & Stel) (Secret 3).

Emotionally charged event (ECS) — the best-processed external stimulus ever measured; a heightened emotional moment that the amygdala tags "Remember This!" (John Medina); the "wow" or "holy smokes" moment (Secret 5).

Emotionally enhanced vividness — Rebecca Todd's finding that how vividly you perceive an event predicts how vividly you'll remember it; like a flashbulb (Secret 5).

Entrepreneurial passion (EP) — Melissa Cardon's definition: "a positive, intense feeling you experience for something profoundly meaningful to you as an individual"; core to self-identity (Secret 1).

Ethos — Aristotle's persuasion via credibility (title, experience, achievements) (Secret 2).

Flashbulb memory — a vivid memory of an emotionally arousing event (e.g., 9/11) vs. forgotten mundane events (Secret 5).

Flynn Effect — the generational rise in IQ scores, attributed to constant mental workouts; TED provides such a workout (Secret 4).

Goldilocks zone — the "not too fast, not too slow" range: ~190 wpm delivery (Secret 3); 18–20 minutes in length (Secret 7).

Holy smokes moment — Gallo's term for the emotionally charged/wow moment when the audience's jaw drops and they "get it" (Secret 5).

Hook — the journalism term for the wow moment/rhetorical device that grabs attention and makes people share (Secret 5).

Logos — Aristotle's persuasion via logic, data, and statistics (Secret 2).

Message map — a one-page visual of your idea: Twitter headline → three key messages → supporting stories/stats/examples (Secret 7).

Mood contagion — the transfer of a leader's positive emotions to the audience, lifting their mood and perceived effectiveness (Bono & Ilies) (Secret 1).

Multimedia principle — retention improves through words plus pictures rather than words alone (Richard Mayer) (Secret 8).

Multitasking myth — the brain is biologically incapable of processing attention-rich inputs (listening + reading a wordy slide) simultaneously (John Medina) (Secret 8).

Neuroplasticity — the brain grows and rewires with repetition; speaking often physically develops the brain's language areas (Secret 1).

Novelty recognition — the hardwired survival instinct that makes the brain seek out what is new and stands out; the single most effective attention-grabber (Secrets 4, 6).

Pathos — Aristotle's persuasion via emotional appeal; delivered through stories (Stevenson's talk was 65% pathos) (Secret 2).

Perceived passion — the audience/investor-detectable trait of genuine enthusiasm; ranked #3 of 13 criteria angels use to fund ventures (Secret 1).

Picture Superiority Effect (PSE) — concepts shown as pictures are recalled far better than words: ~10% recall for words alone vs. ~65% with a picture, three days later (Secret 8).

Power sphere — the zone from the top of your eyes to your outstretched hands to your navel; keep gestures and eye gaze inside it (Secret 3).

Power posing — holding an expansive posture (arms outstretched) ~2 minutes to raise testosterone and lower cortisol; "fake it till you become it" (Amy Cuddy) (Secret 3).

Rule of Three — people reliably remember ~3 chunks of information; structure talks around three key messages (Secret 7).

Sound bite — a short, provocative, repeatable phrase built to be retweeted/reposted ("We will get woolly mammoths back") (Secret 5).

Soft breaks — stories, videos, demos, or extra speakers inserted every ~10 minutes to reset cognitive load in longer talks (Secret 7).

Stay in your lane — Oprah's principle of being the authentic best version of yourself rather than imitating another speaker (Secret 9).

Three A's of Awesome — Neil Pasricha's rule-of-three talk: Attitude, Awareness, Authenticity (Secret 7).

Three Ps — Passion, Practice, Presence — the sequence to genuine, conversational delivery (Secrets 1, 3).

Three types of stories — personal stories, stories about other people, and brand/product success-or-failure stories (Secret 2).

Twitter-friendly headline — the one message you want the audience to remember, in ≤140 characters; Step One of building any talk (Secrets 4, 7).

Willpower/glucose depletion — Baumeister's finding that self-control and attention draw on a finite, glucose-fueled energy; long talks deplete the audience's fuel (Secret 7).

patterns.md

Patterns — Concrete Techniques from Talk Like TED

The "What Makes Your Heart Sing?" Interrogation

When to use: at the very start of building any talk, before content or slides.

How: ask three escalating questions — (1) "What do you do?" (2) "What are you passionate about?" (3) "What is it about this that makes your heart sing?" The third answer, tied to identity and origin story, is the richest. Also ask "What business am I really in?"

Trade-offs: requires honest self-excavation; the true answer may be adjacent to your day job (Mullins → human potential, not prosthetics).

Ethos/Logos/Pathos Content Audit

When to use: reviewing a drafted presentation's balance.

How: categorize every sentence as Ethos (credibility), Logos (data), or Pathos (story/emotion). Benchmark against Stevenson's 10/25/65. If pathos is thin, add stories, anecdotes, personal insight.

Trade-offs: too much pathos with no logos leaves claims unsupported — persuasion needs both head and heart.

Pick One of the Three Story Types

When to use: any pitch or presentation lacking emotional connection.

How: choose a personal story (tied to theme), a story about another person the audience relates to, or a brand success/failure story. For personal stories, make them richly descriptive; favor an unexpected outcome (Ariely's burn unit).

Trade-offs: personal stories require vulnerability; brand stories require you to hunt for them everywhere.

Hero-and-Villain Structure

When to use: framing a product/idea pitch.

How: reveal a challenge (villain) facing the industry; the brand/product (hero) rises to meet it; customers (townspeople) are freed. Ensure the hero saves the day. Tread carefully if the villain is a named competitor.

Trade-offs: can feel formulaic if forced; the villain must be real to the audience.

The Twitter-Friendly Headline

When to use: Step One of crafting any talk.

How: write the single most important message in ≤140 characters; it must convey what the thing is AND what makes it unique. Test: could a listener answer "What did that person talk about?"

Trade-offs: a tagline is not a headline — it must be specific and informative, not clever fluff.

Build a Message Map

When to use: outlining a pitch (15 seconds) or full talk (18 minutes).

How: one page — (1) Twitter headline at top; (2) three supporting key messages; (3) bullet prompts (stories, stats, examples) under each. Optionally three sub-points per message.

Trade-offs: forces you to cut to three; if you have more, group into three categories.

The Three-Story Structure

When to use: as the whole outline for an 18-minute talk.

How: tell three stories of three people/cases that share one theme (Carter's three eco-entrepreneurs). Tie them together with an explicit closing theme.

Trade-offs: needs three genuinely resonant examples; weak third story dilutes.

Deliver a Jaw-Dropping Moment (5 options)

When to use: once per presentation, to create an emotionally charged event.

How: (1) prop/demo (Gates's mosquitoes, Shaw's paint), (2) shocking statistic in context (Stevenson's incarceration numbers), (3) image/video (Raghava's brain-wave art), (4) memorable sound bite ("woolly mammoths back"), (5) personal story (Hrabowski's jail-at-12). Plan the story first; open slide software last.

Trade-offs: props can misfire if under-rehearsed; shock must serve the point, not gratuitous.

Make Statistics Jaw-Drop (Contextualize)

When to use: any data point that is groundbreaking or paramount.

How: never leave data dangling — frame it in a relatable context. iPad Mini "as thin as a pencil, as light as a pad of paper"; strawberries = "10% of ag jobs on 5% of farmland." Brainstorm the framing with a colleague.

Trade-offs: over-framing trivial numbers wastes attention; reserve for the paramount stat.

Be Funny Without Telling a Joke (5 techniques)

When to use: to lower defenses and increase likability, especially on complex/heavy topics.

How: (1) anecdotes/observations/personal stories, (2) analogies/metaphors, (3) quotes (do your homework — off-the-beaten-path, relevant), (4) video (offloads the funny), (5) photos (metaphor for a complex idea). Open with light observational humor, not a big laugh.

Trade-offs: jokes bomb for non-comedians; crass/sexist humor destroys credibility instantly.

Humor + Shock + Statistics Formula

When to use: heavy, uncomfortable, or traumatic topics (Rose George on sanitation).

How: blend all three — humor for a mental break, shock to make them care, statistics for substance. None alone works.

Trade-offs: mistune the blend and you're either flippant or repellent.

Stick to 18 Minutes (with Soft Breaks)

When to use: every presentation; longer ones need modification.

How: cap at 18–20 minutes. If longer is unavoidable, insert a soft break (story, video, demo, or another voice) every ~10 minutes to reset cognitive load.

Trade-offs: "too much information" is the common objection — do the exercise anyway; constraint breeds creativity.

Verbal Highlighting (Rate, Volume, Pitch, Pauses)

When to use: delivery, to emphasize key words.

How: aim ~190 wpm; raise/lower volume, change speed, or set a key word off with a pause. Vary pace by content (Dr. Jill accelerates to 220 wpm acting out chaos; slows for gravity). Get the rate right first — nothing else matters otherwise.

Trade-offs: most people unnaturally slow down when presenting; match natural conversation.

Gesture Within the Power Sphere

When to use: throughout delivery.

How: keep gestures and eye gaze in the zone from eyes → outstretched hands → navel. Use them (hands out of pockets), sparingly, naturally, at key moments. Complex thinkers use complex gestures.

Trade-offs: canned/imitated gestures look like an SNL caricature; hands below the navel read as low-energy.

Power Pose + Physical Warm-Up

When to use: minutes before going on, to manage nerves.

How: hold arms outstretched ~2 minutes where no one sees you (raises testosterone, lowers cortisol). Add a physical ritual (movement, fists) to boost energy.

Trade-offs: overdoing the ritual publicly looks foolish; do it backstage.

Record-and-Review Practice Loop

When to use: refining any presentation.

How: rehearse in front of diverse people; record on phone/camera; watch back for fillers ("um/ah"), distracting habits (fidgeting, hands in pockets, staying rigid), pacing, and eye contact. Leave the camera frame several times to check you're not too rigid.

Trade-offs: time-intensive (Palmer 4 months/105 people; Dr. Jill 200 rehearsals) but it's what makes it look effortless.

Picture Superiority Slide Design

When to use: designing any slide deck.

How: use pictures instead of text; ≤40 words across the first 10 slides; kill bullet points; one theme/statistic per slide; break data runs with stories and photos. Slides complement, never replace, the narrative.

Trade-offs: takes creative effort to find/make images; but text slides are the least memorable channel.

Paint Pictures With Words (No Slides)

When to use: emotional peaks, or when slides would detract.

How: use vivid, concrete, sensory language, metaphors, and analogies — the visual cortex can't tell real from imagined (Shepherd's bike ride; Kramer's Tiffany-box "gift"). Deliver anaphora and emotional climaxes without any slide.

Trade-offs: demands strong writing and delivery; a weak verbal image falls flat.

Multisensory Touch (Props, Demos, Participation)

When to use: to complete the sensory journey, especially for abstract ideas.

How: build in a physical demo (USB-drive transfer race in silence; Krane's feather + blowtorch), a prop (Palmer's milk crate), or audience participation (Gallo's Lush soap giveaway).

Trade-offs: props for pure ideas take imagination; rehearse so they don't feel silly.

Stay in Your Lane / Rehearse to a Friend First

When to use: to ensure authentic delivery.

How: after crafting and rehearsing, let go and speak from the heart; present first to a friend/spouse to let the real self emerge; "hold the space" at vulnerable moments rather than retreating to safe teaching.

Trade-offs: vulnerability feels risky, but audiences distrust the phony; imitation of star speakers fails.

The 4-Hour Workweek

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — The 4-Hour Work Week

Decision rules (if X, do Y, because Z)

  • If you're avoiding a decision "until the timing is right" → run fear-setting now, because the only real answer is fear and inaction is the bigger risk.
  • If a task feels important but isn't moving you toward a goal → eliminate it, because efficiency at the wrong task is worthless (effectiveness > efficiency).
  • If a task keeps expanding → give it a hard, short deadline, because work fills the time allotted (Parkinson).
  • If a recurring task interrupts you → batch it on a schedule, because setup/switching cost is fixed (~45 min to resume).
  • If someone needs your OK for something small → give a written if-then rule + spending limit, because that's an empowerment failure, not real management.
  • If you want a permanent change accepted → propose a small reversible trial (Puppy Dog Close), because people resist permanence but accept "just once."
  • If you're about to delegate → check you can't eliminate or automate it first, because you'd be paying to preserve waste.
  • If you have a product idea → find the market first, then micro-test before manufacturing, because filling demand beats creating it and behavior beats opinion.
  • If cash flow already funds your dreams → stop chasing more customers, because that's W4W.
  • If you feel overwhelmed → take a break and 80/20 both business and life, because lack of time is lack of priorities.

Core formulas & thresholds

ThingRule / number
Relative income$/hr = annual pay ÷ (weeks × hrs/week); this, not $/yr, is wealth
Target Monthly IncomeTMI = (4 dream costs + monthly expenses) × 1.3
Target Daily IncomeTDI = TMI ÷ 30
80/20 review cadenceevery 2–4 weeks, business + personal
Muse product price$50–200 (premium end)
Muse manufacture time≤ 3–4 weeks
Muse market sizemagazine full-page ad < $5,000; ≥ 15,000 readers
Micro-test~$500, ~5 days; 100 narrow terms @ $0.10 > 10 broad @ $1.00
Outsourcer autonomyfix anything under ~$400 without asking
Email frequency1–3×/day → weekly as problems allow
Perfection thresholdgreat for a few things, good enough for the rest (95% = 6 mo; 98% = 20–30 yr)
VA test2–4 weeks, $100–400, ROI in ~10–14 days

DEAL — the sequence (and DELA for employees)

StepWhatKey tools
Definitionrewrite the rules, set the targetNew Rich rules, fear-setting, dreamlining/TMI
Eliminationbuy timeeffectiveness, 80/20, Parkinson, low-info diet, batching
Automationbuy incomeeliminate→automate→delegate, VAs, muse, MBA architecture
Liberationbuy mobilityhourglass remote escape, mini-retirements

Employees implement as DELA: secure location freedom before cutting hours.

The 10 New Rich Rules (fast recall)

1 Retirement = worst-case insurance · 2 Energy is cyclical (mini-retirements) · 3 Less ≠ laziness · 4 Timing is never right · 5 Ask forgiveness, not permission · 6 Emphasize strengths, don't fix weaknesses · 7 Excess → its opposite · 8 Money alone isn't the fix · 9 Relative > absolute income · 10 Kill distress, seek eustress.

Tells & smells (you're in trouble if…)

  • You check email first thing / last thing / constantly → resets the whole day.
  • You're the tollbooth every decision passes through → build rules and route around yourself.
  • You're solving the same problem twice → write an if-then rule.
  • You're making non-urgent things urgent, or blowing up minutiae → W4W relapse.
  • You feel busy but can't name the 20% that matters → skipped your 80/20 review.
  • You're "researching" with no decision pending → just-in-case information; stop.
  • You work where you live/sleep/relax → separate environments.

The Not-to-Do List (9)

1 Don't answer calls from unknown numbers · 2 Don't email first/last thing · 3 No meetings/calls without a clear agenda + end time · 4 Don't let people ramble ("how can I help you?") · 5 Don't check email constantly — batch · 6 Don't over-serve low-profit, high-maintenance customers · 7 Don't work more to fix overwhelm — prioritize · 8 Don't carry a phone 24/7 · 9 Don't expect work to fill a void relationships/activities should.

Refusal scripts

  • Invader at your desk: "I'm right in the middle of something. How can I help you?" (unclear in 30s → "send me a quick email to remind me.")
  • Time limit: "OK, I've got two minutes before a call — what's the situation and how can I help?"
  • Replace "How are you?" with "How can I help you?" — get specific, no stories.

glossary.md

Glossary — The 4-Hour Work Week

80/20 Principle (Pareto's Law) — 80% of outputs come from 20% of inputs; often 90/10 or 95/5. Apply via two questions: which 20% causes 80% of problems (cut) and which produces 80% of results (multiply). (Ch 5)

Absentee management — see Management by Absence. (Ch 11)

Absolute income — income measured in raw dollars per year, ignoring hours worked. Contrast with relative income. (Ch 2)

Batching — grouping similar recurring tasks (email, calls, errands) and doing them on a set schedule to avoid repeated setup/switching cost (up to 45 min to resume interrupted work). (Ch 7)

Bracketing — asking for more than you need in a negotiation so your fallback position is still your real target. (Ch 12)

Comfort challenge — deliberate practice at social discomfort to build the action habit and dissolve fear. (Ch 3)

Cost of inaction — the financial, emotional, and physical price of not acting, measured over 1/5/10 years; usually far larger than the risk of acting. (Ch 3)

Dealmaker — one who treats rules outside science and law as negotiable; "Reality is negotiable" without being unethical. (Ch 1)

DEAL — Definition → Elimination → Automation → Liberation; the New Rich process and the book's structure. (Ch 1)

DELA — the employee's implementation order: read in DEAL order but win Liberation (location freedom) before cutting hours. (Ch 1)

Deferred-life plan — sacrificing your most capable years for freedom "someday"; the book's central target. (Ch 1)

Distress — harmful stress that weakens you (abusive bosses, destructive criticism); to be removed. (Ch 2)

Dreamlining — applying 6- and 12-month timelines to dreams (Have/Be/Do), then pricing them into a Target Monthly Income. (Ch 4)

Drop-shipping — the manufacturer ships directly to your customer, so you hold no inventory and pay a fraction of retail on delayed terms. (Ch 10)

Effectiveness — doing the things that move you toward your goals. Beats efficiency. (Ch 5)

Efficiency — doing a task (important or not) economically; useless unless applied to the right things. (Ch 5)

Eliminate before you delegate — never automate what can be eliminated; never delegate what can be automated. (Ch 8)

Empowerment failure — an interruption caused by someone needing your approval for something small; fixed with written if-then rules. (Ch 7)

Eustress — healthy, growth-producing stress (role models, training, comfort-expanding risk); to be sought. (Ch 2)

Fear-setting — a written exercise defining the worst case, its repairability, and the cost of inaction, to escape paralysis. (Ch 3)

Freedom multiplier — money's practical value multiplied by control of the four W's (what/when/where/whom). (Ch 1)

Geoarbitrage — exploiting global price/wage differences: earn strong currency, spend or hire in weak. (Ch 8, 13)

Hourglass approach — long proof-of-concept → short remote trial → negotiate back up to full-time remote. (Ch 12)

Information product — how-to content (book, DVD, course); the ideal muse: fast to make, high markup, FAQ-able. (Ch 9)

Interruption — anything preventing start-to-finish completion of a critical task; three types: time consumers, empowerment failures, self-generated. (Ch 7)

Just-in-time vs. just-in-case information — pull information only when a task needs it; never hoard "in case." (Ch 6)

License (licensee/licensor) — pay an inventor a royalty (~3–10% wholesale) to sell their product, or invent and let others sell yours. (Ch 9)

Lifestyle Design (LD) — deliberately engineering how and where you spend time rather than accepting the default track. (Ch 1)

Low-information diet — consuming only immediately actionable information; begins with a one-week media fast. (Ch 6)

Management by Absence (MBA) — a self-correcting business architecture that runs without you; be the roadside cop, not the tollbooth. (Ch 11)

Media fast — an abrupt one-week total cutoff of news and non-essential information. (Ch 6)

Mini-retirement — a recurring 1–6+ month relocation/sabbatical distributed throughout life instead of one end-of-life retirement. (Ch 2, 13)

Minimum effective load — doing the least necessary for maximum effect. (Ch 1)

Muse — an automated, low-maintenance business built solely to fund your dreamlines with minimal time. (Ch 9)

New Rich (NR) — those who design a free lifestyle now using time and mobility as currency. (Ch 1)

Nonfinishing (art of) — the skill of quitting boring/unproductive books, tasks, or media mid-stream. (Ch 6)

Parkinson's Law — a task swells in perceived importance/complexity to fill the time allotted; short deadlines force focus. (Ch 5)

Premium positioning — pricing above competitors ($50–200 range) to raise margin, perceived value, and customer quality. (Ch 9)

Puppy Dog Close — winning permanent change by proposing a small, reversible "just try it once" trial. (Ch 7)

Relative income — income per hour of life ($/hr); the true New Rich measure of wealth once absolute income clears your dream threshold. (Ch 2)

Reselling — buying wholesale and reselling; easiest to start, least profitable, fastest to die to price competition. (Ch 9)

Selective ignorance — the trained ability to ignore or redirect irrelevant information and interruptions. (Ch 6)

Target Daily Income (TDI) — TMI ÷ 30; a daily income target. (Ch 4)

Target Monthly Income (TMI) — (four dream costs + monthly expenses) × 1.3; the cash-flow goal your muse must hit. (Ch 4)

Virtual architecture — the interchangeable chain of outsourcers (fulfillment, call center, processor) that runs the muse. (Ch 11)

Virtual assistant (VA) — a remote assistant used as low-risk management training and life outsourcing. (Ch 8)

W4W (work for work's sake) — staying busy to feel productive or avoid hard questions; the book's most-hated acronym. (Ch 1, 5, 13)

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — The 4-Hour Work Week

Fear-Setting (the 7 questions)

When to use: any big, scary decision you keep postponing.

How: in writing — (1) Define the nightmare in detail; rate permanence/probability 1–10. (2) Steps to repair the damage. (3) Benefits of more-probable outcomes (rate 1–10). (4) If fired today, how to regain financial control. (5) What you're putting off out of fear. (6) Cost of inaction over 1/5/10 years. (7) What are you waiting for?

Trade-offs: takes an hour and forces honesty; defuses fear but won't remove real (rare) irreversible risks — those you keep.

Dreamlining → TMI/TDI

When to use: to convert "I want freedom" into a concrete income target.

How: 6- and 12-month timelines × (Have / Be / Do), 5 each; convert "Be" → "Do"; star top 4; TMI = (4 dream costs + monthly expenses) × 1.3; TDI = TMI ÷ 30.

Trade-offs: monthly cash-flow framing makes dreams look affordable, but requires honest expense accounting.

The 80/20 Two-Question Audit

When to use: every 2–4 weeks, on business and personal life.

How: (1) Which 20% of sources cause 80% of problems/unhappiness? → eliminate/fire. (2) Which 20% produce 80% of results/happiness? → double down.

Trade-offs: firing the draining 20% can feel risky; usually the revenue/energy math strongly favors it.

Parkinson's Law (short deadlines)

When to use: any task that expands to fill available time.

How: assign an aggressively short deadline; force execution of essentials only. Pair with 80/20 (limit tasks and shorten time).

Trade-offs: quality is usually equal or better; occasionally too tight — recalibrate, don't abandon.

The Low-Information Diet

When to use: overwhelm, news anxiety, chronic "researching."

How: one-week total media fast (cold turkey) → rebuild only just-in-time sources → ask "will I use this immediately and importantly?" → practice nonfinishing.

Trade-offs: you'll miss some conversations; you lose almost nothing actionable.

Batching + the Batch Cost/Benefit Test

When to use: recurring time-consumer tasks (email, calls, mail, reports).

How: pick a frequency; compute (hours saved × your $/hr) − (cost of problems caused by the delay). If net positive, batch further apart; if negative, step back one frequency (weekly → twice-weekly, not daily).

Trade-offs: slower responses; large gains in deep-work time; risk capped (Ferriss: nothing cost >$300 to fix).

Empowerment via If-Then Rules

When to use: to stop being a decision bottleneck.

How: give outsourcers/co-workers written rules + a spending limit (e.g., "fix anything under $400 without asking"); review monthly and add new rules from their best decisions.

Trade-offs: occasional small losses; huge time freedom and a self-improving system.

The Puppy Dog Close

When to use: overcoming resistance to a permanent change (remote work, no-meeting policy, autonomy).

How: propose a small, reversible "let's just try it once" trial; the return rarely happens.

Trade-offs: slower than demanding the change; far higher success rate.

Eliminate → Automate → Delegate

When to use: before assigning any task to a VA or system.

How: cut the task; if it survives, systematize it; only then delegate what remains. Assign VAs one task at a time (two max), each with a clear deliverable.

Trade-offs: more upfront thinking; prevents paying to preserve worthless work.

Muse Design (product + market)

When to use: building automated income to hit your TMI.

How: (1) niche market first (magazine full-page ad <$5,000; ≥15,000 readers); (2) product meeting 4 criteria — one-sentence benefit, $50–200, ≤3–4 wk to make, FAQ-able; (3) source via resell < license < create (info products ideal); control distribution, hold premium pricing.

Trade-offs: narrow markets cap size but cut competition and cost, and command premium prices.

Micro-Testing (validate before manufacturing)

When to use: before spending on inventory.

How: 1–3 page test site → Google AdWords PPC (~$500, ~5 days, many narrow keywords > few broad) → "temporarily out of stock" page captures purchase intent without charging → read conversion. Or probe on eBay first. Manufacture only if it converts.

Trade-offs: costs ~$500 and a few days; saves months and inventory risk.

Virtual Architecture (Management by Absence)

When to use: after a validated muse, to remove yourself from operations.

How: 3-phase rollout — DIY (build FAQ from real questions) → local fulfillment (net-30) → end-to-end fulfillment + call center + processor that talk to each other. Use replaceable contract companies, not freelancers; check reports weekly/monthly, banks 1st & 15th.

Trade-offs: setup fees and coordination; buys near-total absence and scalability.

The Hourglass Remote-Work Escape (5 steps)

When to use: employees wanting location freedom (DELA).

How: (1) raise your value + get invested-in; (2) prove remote productivity covertly with records; (3) build a business-case bullet list; (4) propose a small revocable trial (bracket: ask 2, accept 1); (5) expand stepwise to full-time; keep a funded willingness to quit as leverage.

Trade-offs: takes ~2 months and nerve; if refused, the job is "beyond repair" — leave.

Cheatsheet — The 48 Laws of Power

Decision rules distilled from Greene's judgment. Use to pick a move fast. (Ethical note: this is descriptive strategy, much of it Machiavellian — read as a lens, not a mandate.)

If you are…Do thisLaw

Master Decision Rules (the meta-logic)

  • Force vs. seduction: if you can make them want it, never coerce it (43 > force). Coercion breeds backlash; seduction breeds loyal pawns.
  • Half-measures rule: with a real enemy, either finish completely (15) or don't strike. A survivor is a future war.
  • Attention dial: too invisible → court attention (6); too common → manufacture absence (16). Manage visibility like a price.
  • Ask framing: every request routes through the other's self-interest (13), never your need or their pity.
  • Peak danger: the moment of victory is the moment of greatest peril — stop (47), stay clean (26), don't get drunk on success.
  • Independence rule: owe no one (40), commit to no side (20), keep no fixed form (48) — freedom is the base of power.

Tells & Smells (recognize the situation)

  • You feel an urge to explain/justify → you're about to violate Law 4. Say less.
  • You're reminding someone they owe you → dead lever; switch to their self-interest (13).
  • You just won an argument and they went quiet-angry → Pyrrhic; you lost (9).
  • You feel safest cutting everyone off → isolation trap (18); the danger is the opposite.
  • A "friend" you elevated seems resentful → Law 2 in motion; envy precedes betrayal.
  • Someone keeps giving you free things/favors → you're being indebted (40) or Trojan-horsed (12).
  • A rival is baiting your temper → they're stirring waters (39); go calm.
  • You're dazzled by someone's spectacle → look at what they're actually doing (37).

glossary.md

Glossary — The 48 Laws of Power

Key terms, coined phrases, and recurring concepts. Chapter references (ChN) point to this skill's thematic chapters, not the book's law numbers.

Air of unpredictability — Deliberate inconsistency in behavior to keep others off-balance and unable to model you (Law 17, Ch8).

Assume formlessness — Keeping no fixed shape, plan, or position so you present no target; being "like water" (Law 48, Ch1).

Bait — A dangled gain used to make an opponent abandon his plan and come to you (Law 8, Ch1).

Boldness — Full, confident commitment to action; it hides deficiencies and eliminates obstacles that hesitation creates (Law 28, Ch6).

Cat's-paw — A disposable intermediary used to do dirty work and absorb blame, keeping your own hands clean (Law 26, Ch6).

Concentrate your forces — Massing energy at your single strongest point or richest source; "intensity defeats extensity" (Law 23, Ch6).

Court / courtier — The circle of power around a ruler; the courtier survives by indirection, flattery, and political dexterity (Law 24, Ch4).

Court attention — Making yourself conspicuous so you're talked about; obscurity is powerlessness (Law 6, Ch3).

Crush totally — Finishing a real enemy completely in body and spirit so no "ember" survives to seek revenge (Law 15, Ch6).

Cultlike following — Devotion won by supplying people a vague-but-promising cause, rituals, and sacrifices (Law 27, Ch7).

Disdain (as revenge) — Refusing to acknowledge a petty problem or thing, denying it existence and appearing superior (Law 36, Ch1).

Effortlessness — Concealing all toil and tricks so accomplishments look like natural, godlike gift (Law 30, Ch4).

Fat cow — The single rich patron or source worth mining deeply rather than scattering effort (Law 23, Ch6).

Formlessness — See Assume formlessness.

Free lunch — Anything offered free; it hides a trick or an indebting obligation and should be despised (Law 40, Ch8).

Infection — Emotional contagion; misfortune and misery spread from the unhappy/unlucky to those near them (Law 10, Ch5).

Interpretation — The book's section, after each historical story, extracting the strategic lesson (structural term).

Judgment — The one-paragraph statement of each law that opens its chapter (structural term).

Keys to Power — The book's how-to section giving tactics for applying each law (structural term).

Mirror Effect — Reflecting others' actions (to confuse enemies) or values (to seduce allies) back at them (Law 44, Ch7).

Never outshine the master — Making superiors feel superior; excess talent inspires their fear and retaliation (Law 1, Ch4).

Observance of the Law — The book's historical example of someone succeeding by following a law (structural term).

Play a sucker — Feigning stupidity so a mark feels superior, relaxes, and drops his guard (Law 21, Ch2).

Pyrrhic victory (of argument) — A won argument that costs you through lasting resentment; hence win by action, not words (Law 9, Ch7).

Re-create yourself — Forging a deliberate public identity and persona rather than accepting society's assigned role (Law 25, Ch3).

Reputation — The cornerstone of power; a story that intimidates and wins for you, and whose cracks invite attack (Law 5, Ch3).

Reversal — The book's closing section for each law noting when the opposite approach applies (structural term).

Scarcity (absence) — Withdrawing to raise your value; "too much circulation makes the price go down" (Law 16, Ch3).

Selective honesty — A single sincere/generous act (a "Trojan horse") used to disarm suspicion and enable manipulation (Law 12, Ch2).

Smoke screen — Bland, expected, or decoy behavior that hides your real intention (Law 3, Ch2).

Spectacle — Striking imagery and grand symbolic gestures that move people and distract from your real aims (Law 37, Ch3).

Strike the shepherd — Removing the single instigator whose influence holds a troublesome group together (Law 42, Ch5).

Surrender tactic — Yielding when weaker to buy time, deny the victor satisfaction, and undermine him from within (Law 22, Ch6).

Sphinxlike — Vague, brief, open-ended speech that seems profound and keeps control; "say less than necessary" (Law 4, Ch1).

Thumbscrew — Each person's exploitable weakness: an insecurity, uncontrollable need, or secret pleasure (Law 33, Ch8).

Timing — Reading the "spirit of the times," waiting out the unripe moment, and striking at fruition (Law 35, Ch1).

Trojan horse — See Selective honesty — a gift or candid gesture that opens the target's guard (Law 12, Ch2).

Wolf in lamb's clothing — A thin-skinned, vengeful person who looks harmless; never offend them (Law 19, Ch5).

patterns.md

Patterns — Recurring Power Techniques

The reusable mechanics that appear across many of the 48 laws. Each is a technique you can deploy, not a single law.

The Decoy / Smoke Screen

When to use: you want to advance a goal without opponents preparing a defense.

How: publicly pursue a plan you don't care about, or adopt bland, expected behavior, while quietly advancing the real objective. Guide observers "far enough down the wrong path."

Trade-offs: requires patience and discipline (Law 4); if exposed, erodes trust. (Laws 3, 14)

The Trojan Horse (Selective Sincerity)

When to use: a target is suspicious and guarded.

How: make one genuine-seeming gift or candid admission — costly enough to seem sincere. It opens a hole in their armor that dozens of manipulations couldn't.

Trade-offs: works because it's rare; overuse trains people to see the pattern. (Law 12)

Control the Options (Choice Architecture)

When to use: you need a decision to go your way without ordering it.

How: pre-select the menu. Offer two-or-more paths that all serve you — lesser-of-two-evils, or a heavy option beside the one you want framed as reasonable. Let them "choose freely."

Trade-offs: if the framing feels manipulative, it backfires; the freedom must feel real. (Law 31)

Appeal to Self-Interest

When to use: asking anyone for help or a favor.

How: find what they gain (visibility, skill, a solved problem of theirs), and lead with it "out of all proportion." Never invoke mercy, pity, or past favors.

Trade-offs: requires knowing the person's motives (Law 19, Law 33). (Law 13)

Find the Thumbscrew

When to use: you need leverage over a specific person.

How: identify their insecurity, uncontrollable need, or secret pleasure — the "gap in the castle wall" — and apply gentle pressure there.

Trade-offs: misreading the weakness, or cornering someone into desperation, backfires. (Laws 33, 19)

The Cat's-Paw (Clean Hands)

When to use: power requires a nasty deed that would stain your reputation.

How: have a disposable intermediary execute it and absorb the blame; you remain the visible paragon of civility. (Classic case: Cesare Borgia and Ramiro.)

Trade-offs: the cat's-paw may gain leverage over you; discard or distance carefully. (Laws 26, 7)

Manufacture Scarcity (Strategic Absence)

When to use: your presence or output is becoming common and undervalued.

How: withdraw at a peak of visibility; let absence raise demand and talk. Return with restored value.

Trade-offs: only works after you've established worth; premature absence = being forgotten. (Laws 16, 6)

Stage a Spectacle

When to use: you need to move a group emotionally or mask your real activity.

How: deploy arresting visuals, symbols, and grand gestures; dazzle so no one examines the substance.

Trade-offs: empty spectacle collapses if reality is later demanded (pair with Law 32's fantasy caution). (Laws 37, 32)

Stir the Waters (Provoke, Stay Calm)

When to use: a rival's judgment is your target.

How: stay calm and objective while needling the chink in their vanity; a rattled opponent overreacts and reveals himself.

Trade-offs: never provoke an opponent stronger than you can manage. (Law 39)

Surrender to Outlast

When to use: you are genuinely weaker and would lose an open fight.

How: yield first, denying the victor the satisfaction of battle; use the bought time to recover and undermine from within.

Trade-offs: surrendering from strength squanders advantage; timing is everything. (Laws 22, 35)

Concentrate Force

When to use: your resources are being spread across many fronts.

How: identify the single decisive point or richest source ("fat cow") and mass everything there. Intensity beats extensity.

Trade-offs: total dependence on one source is fragile if it fails — retain a fallback. (Law 23)

Manufacture Belief (Cult Dynamics)

When to use: you need fervent, self-sustaining devotion, not mere compliance.

How: offer a vague-but-promising cause; emphasize enthusiasm over reason; create rituals; ask for escalating sacrifices that deepen commitment.

Trade-offs: belief is volatile and can turn on its leader; also a defensive pattern — recognize it used on you. (Laws 27, 32)

Convert the Enemy

When to use: staffing a role where loyalty matters.

How: hire/elevate a capable former enemy who has something to prove, rather than a friend prone to envy and entitlement.

Trade-offs: requires accurate judgment of character (Law 19). (Law 2)

Build the Dependence Moat

When to use: securing a durable position.

How: make yourself indispensable — unique knowledge, key relationships, control of a critical system — and never train a replacement; route visible results through yourself (Law 7); owe no one (Law 40).

Trade-offs: extorted (vs. valued) indispensability breeds resentment and eventual replacement. (Laws 11, 7, 40)

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — The Big Book of NLP

Decision-ready rules. Pick the right pattern, apply it the way Vaknin would. Keep beside you while working.

Which pattern for which problem?

The presenting problemReach forChapter
Habit that auto-fires on a cueThe SwishCh 5
Irrational fear / single-event traumaPhobia Cure (V-K dissociation)Ch 8
Two sides of me fighting / inner conflictSix Step Reframe, Parts Negotiation, Visual SquashCh 6
"I can't / I'm a failure" (limiting belief)Belief Chaining, Re-Imprinting, Meta-Model challengeCh 7, Ch 9
Low motivation for a good behaviorGodiva Chocolate, Pleasure InstallationCh 5, Ch 12
Can't access a needed stateAnchoring, Circle of Excellence, State InductionCh 4
Compulsion / cravingCompulsion Blow-Out, Spinning IconsCh 5
Grief, resentment, disproportionate emotionGrief Pattern, Forgiveness, Emotional Pain MgmtCh 8
Procrastination / values conflictHierarchy of Criteria, Excuse Blow-OutCh 7, Ch 8
Problem felt at "who I am"Logical Levels Alignment, Aligned SelfCh 12
Need rapport with a difficult personPacing/Matching, Satir Category rapportCh 3
Need agreement / influence in talkPace–Link–Lead, Double Bind, chunk UPCh 10, Ch 9
Need accurate info / loosen vaguenessMeta-Model challenge, chunk DOWNCh 9
Want to copy someone's excellence2nd/3rd Position ModelingCh 11
Trauma/anxiety needing deeper workReprocessing, Time Line, MatrixingCh 13

Core decision rules

  • Before any change, run an ecology check. Unaddressed secondary gain or system impact silently sabotages the result. (Ch 1, Ch 2)
  • Resistance = lack of rapport. If you meet resistance, stop pushing and rebuild rapport. (Presupposition #16, Ch 3)
  • The meaning of your communication is the response you get — calibrate to the response, not your intention. (Presupposition #12)
  • Change at the highest relevant logical level. A problem felt at Identity won't yield to a Behavior fix; a behavior issue doesn't need an identity overhaul. (Ch 12)
  • Find the positive intention before removing any behavior or belief — removal without it relapses or leaves a void. (Ch 6, Ch 7)
  • Edit the driver submodality, not the content. The charge lives in size/brightness/location/light — find that knob first. (Ch 5, Ch 8)
  • Pace before you lead — match the person's world (3 verifiable facts / their physiology / their values), then move them. (Ch 3, Ch 10)
  • Chunk UP for agreement, DOWN for solutions. Vague is undisputed; specific is actionable. (Ch 9)
  • Phrase suggestions positively — the mind can't process a negation ("non-smoker" cues smoking). (Ch 10, Ch 12)
  • Anchor at the PEAK with a unique, dedicated trigger — peak + purity + uniqueness = the strongest anchor. (Ch 4)
  • Accept and use whatever happens (utilization) — interruptions, resistance, and odd responses are raw material, not derailment. (Ch 1, Ch 10)

The 21 Presuppositions — the decisive ones for change-work

  • #8 Every behavior has utility in some context → look for the gift inside the problem.
  • #12 The meaning of communication is the response you get → own the outcome.
  • #14 There is no failure, only feedback → mine every miss.
  • #15 The most flexible element controls the system → expand your choices.
  • #16 Resistance signals lack of rapport → back up and reconnect.
  • #17 People have the internal resources they need → your job is to direct, not supply.

Meta-Model quick reference (recover the deleted/distorted)

Hear thisViolationAsk
"never / always / everyone"Universal Quantifier"Never? Not once?"
"I can't / I must"Modal Operator"What stops you?" / "What if you did?"
"they / people / it" (vague)Lack of Referential Index"Who, specifically?"
"the relationship / my fear"NominalizationTurn it back into a verb — "relating how?"
"she makes me angry"Cause–Effect"How does what she does cause your anger?"
"I know he doesn't care"Mind Reading"How do you know?"
"It's wrong to…"Lost Performative"According to whom?"

Safety & ethics tells

  • Refer clinical cases (phobia, trauma, addiction, severe grief) to licensed professionals — NLP is not a treatment substitute. (Ch 8, Ch 13)
  • "Poor participant" is often a brain shutdown, not stubbornness — Think Physiology and consider referral. (Ch 13)
  • All communication should increase choice (Presupposition #19) — use Milton patterns to expand options, never to coerce. (Ch 10)
  • Stay the formal authority, one outcome at a time — don't befriend early or work 10 issues at once. (Ch 1)

glossary.md

Glossary — The Big Book of NLP

Key terms with definitions, alphabetical. Chapter references in parentheses.

Alternating bilateral stimulus — Side-to-side eye movement, sound, or touch that triggers the reprocessing state shift (Ch 13).

Anchor — A stimulus conditioned to trigger a particular state; learned, not innate. Firing an anchor activates the state (Ch 4).

Associated — Experiencing from inside your own eyes (1st position) with full felt charge; opposite of dissociated (Ch 5, Ch 8).

Calibration — Linking an observed behavioral cue to a person's internal cognitive/emotional state (Ch 3).

Characterological Adjective (CA) — A single word naming a relationship role; implies its counterpart (victim↔victimizer) (Ch 13).

Chunking up / down — Moving to more abstract/general (up) or more specific/concrete (down) levels; up wins agreement, down enables solutions (Ch 9).

Congruence — Alignment of words, tone, body, and outcomes; root of charisma and effective change (Ch 1, Ch 12).

Conversational (covert) hypnosis — Producing trance through ordinary-seeming talk with no formal induction (Ch 10).

Core state — The centered, expanded peace reached by chaining outcomes inward (Ch 6).

Criteria — Values that drive decisions; ranked in a hierarchy where higher override lower (Ch 7, Ch 11).

Deep structure — The fuller internal experience that words derive from; what the Meta-Model recovers (Ch 9).

Dissociation — Observing yourself from outside (3rd/meta position) with little felt charge (Ch 5, Ch 8).

Double bind — A choice between two options that both fulfill the same presupposition/outcome (Ch 10).

Double dissociation — Two layers of separation (watching yourself watch a movie, from the projection booth); for highly triggering memories (Ch 8).

Downtime — A light internal trance with awareness turned fully inward; uptime is outward awareness informed by inner awareness (Ch 4, Ch 10).

Driver (driving/critical) submodality — The submodality whose change most shifts a state's intensity; the highest-leverage edit point. Find it first (Ch 5, Ch 8).

Ecology / Ecology check — The systemic impact of a change across the whole person/system; verifying no part or life area objects before locking in a change (Ch 1, Ch 2, Ch 6).

Embedded command — A directive inserted and marked out (via tone/tempo/gesture) inside a larger sentence or question (Ch 10).

Evidence procedure — How a person knows an outcome has been achieved (Ch 2, Ch 11).

Extinction — Decay of an anchor from overuse or staleness (Ch 4).

Frame — The boundary on what you consider; "the one who sets the frame controls the action." A reframe changes it (Ch 6, Ch 1).

Imprint / Re-imprinting — A belief installed during a developmental window (imprint); returning to that source to supply missing resources rewrites it (re-imprinting) (Ch 7).

Law of Reversed Effect — The harder one consciously tries, the harder the result becomes; demands indirect suggestion (Ch 10).

Law of Requisite Variety — "Only variety can destroy variety"; more options/positions weaken a rigid belief and increase influence (Ch 7, Ch 1).

Limiting belief — A non-resourceful generalization that blocks goals; treated as loosenable structure, not truth (Ch 7).

Logical Levels — Dilts's hierarchy: Environment, Behavior, Capability, Beliefs/Values, Identity, Spirit/Purpose; higher levels organize lower (Ch 12).

Map vs. territory — Your internal model is never the reality it represents; always improvable (Ch 1).

Matrixing — Strategic case planning across four categories: Meaning, Context, Behavior, Physiology (Ch 13).

Meta-program — A context-dependent, continuum-based tendency in how attention is sorted (toward/away, etc.); never a fixed label (Ch 11).

Meta-position — A dissociated observer stance above a conflict, used to negotiate (Ch 6, Ch 8).

Meta-state — A layered meaning/value stacked on top of another state (Ch 12).

Milton-Model — Artful, deliberately vague language (Meta-Model violations on purpose) to induce trance and bypass conscious resistance; inverse of the Meta-Model (Ch 10).

Modal operator — The word (must/can't/should/could) revealing a mode of necessity, possibility, or impossibility (Ch 9).

Modeling — Extracting another's strategy or state of excellence so it can be reproduced (Ch 11).

Nominalization — A process/verb frozen into a static noun (relationship, fear); fails the "put it in a wheelbarrow" test (Ch 9).

Pacing and leading — Match the person's verifiable experience first (pace), then shift your state to move theirs (lead) (Ch 3, Ch 10).

Part — A largely subconscious cluster of motives/attitudes acting like a sub-personality (Ch 2, Ch 6).

Perceptual positions — 1st (self/associated), 2nd (the other's shoes), 3rd (detached observer/meta) (Ch 6, Ch 8).

Positive intention — The constructive purpose underlying even a harmful behavior; respond to it, not the symptom (Ch 2, Ch 6).

Presupposition — A useful operating belief acted on without proof; the 21 NLP presuppositions are NLP's core beliefs (Ch 1).

Priming — Triggering a state conducive to a way of thinking or acting; broader and vaguer than a command (Ch 10, Ch 13).

Reframe — Changing the frame for a better outcome: content (what it means) or context (where it fits) (Ch 6).

Rep systems (representational systems) — Channels through which experience is coded: Visual, Auditory, Kinesthetic, plus auditory-digital/olfactory-gustatory (Ch 1, Ch 4).

Reprocessing — Re-encoding a poorly stored overwhelming experience so it integrates and symptoms resolve; shared mechanism behind EMDR, EFT, Time Line Therapy, and the NLP phobia cure (Ch 13).

SCORE — Symptom / Cause / Outcome / Resource / Effect; a framework for shaping any problem (Ch 8).

Secondary gain — A hidden benefit a problem behavior delivers that sabotages change until addressed (Ch 1, Ch 2, Ch 6).

Self-sabotage — A negative pattern sustained by a hidden payoff; addressed via its positive intention (Ch 12).

Sensory acuity — Trained ability to notice involuntary micro-changes (skin color, muscle tone, breathing, pupils) (Ch 1, Ch 3).

Somatic / bottom-up — Changing thought by working through body, state, and nervous system rather than cognition (Ch 13).

State — The combined mind-body condition at a given moment; functional or dysfunctional (Ch 4).

Strategy — An ordered sequence (syntax) of internal representations that produces a result; e.g. spelling = visual recall then kinesthetic check (Ch 11).

Submodality — A quality within a sense (visual: size, brightness, color, distance, location, movie-vs-still; auditory: volume, pitch; kinesthetic: location, temperature) (Ch 5).

Surface structure — The spoken words; a compressed, deleted/distorted/generalized output of the deep structure (Ch 9).

Swish — The signature submodality pattern: a big/bright associated trigger image is rapidly swapped for a small/dim dissociated desired-self image (Ch 5).

Thought virus — A toxic, self-propagating belief (Dilts); inoculated against and quarantined (Ch 7).

Time Line Therapy — Processing memory along the timeline via Source Event, Echo Events, and Future Success (Tad James) (Ch 13).

TOTE — Test–Operate–Test–Exit; the feedback loop inside every strategy (Ch 11).

Transderivational search (TDS) — The mind's fuzzy hunt for meaning in vague input; itself produces brief trance (Ch 10).

Trance — A focused, inward, suggestible state; can be light and momentary (Ch 10).

Universal quantifier — Totalizing words (never/always/everyone) signaling over-generalization (Ch 9).

Utilization — Accepting and turning whatever the person presents — even a symptom or resistance — into a resource (Ch 1, Ch 10).

V-K dissociation — Changing a memory's visual viewpoint to break its kinesthetic (felt) charge; engine of the Phobia Cure (Ch 8).

Values hierarchy — Your most important values, ranked, giving higher-level decision direction (Ch 11).

Well-formed (well-defined) outcome — A goal that is positive, specific, self-actionable, context-bound, sensory-rich, and ecological (Ch 2).

patterns.md

Patterns Catalog — The Big Book of NLP

Concrete techniques, when to use them, how, and trade-offs. Grouped by theme. For full steps and worked examples, open the linked chapter.

Outcomes, Feedback & Ecology (Ch 2)

Well-Defined Outcomes

When: Starting any goal or change, before spending resources. How: State it positive → ability-framed → contextualized → in the senses → chunked → resourced → ecology-checked → milestoned → written → tested. Trade-off: Over-specifying can cause analysis paralysis.

Failure Into Feedback

When: A belief makes you feel defeated about a capability or goal. How: Sort the failure's VAK into eye positions, build the goal image up-right, normalize the memories, anchor a positive reference and fire it at the goal. Trade-off: Needs comfort with eye-position/submodality work.

Ecology Check

When: Before committing to any change. How: Dissociate to 3rd position; ask who benefits/is hurt, short- and long-term; use Cartesian questions ("What would happen if you did / didn't?"). Trade-off: Skipping it invites self-sabotage.

Finding Positive Intention / Secondary Gain

When: Self-sabotage or a stalled change. How: Address the part; ask what it wanted to accomplish; recycle answers up to the core value. Trade-off: Relies on accepting the "parts" frame; hidden gains rationalize away easily.

Rapport, Pacing & Mirroring (Ch 3)

Pacing and Matching / Mirroring

When: Building rapport, sales, coaching, modeling. How: Subtly match cadence, predicates, posture, breathing; then test by leading. Trade-off: Obvious imitation breaks rapport and offends.

Satir Category Rapport-Building

When: Pacing a difficult communicator (Blamer, Placater, Computer, Distracter, Leveler). How: Pace each style without triggering its defense, then lead; default to Leveler (congruent, factual) if unsure. Trade-off: Styles are situational, not fixed labels.

When NOT to Mirror

When: Aggression, suffering, or intense-need states. How: Use same-team posture; mirror only general comforting cues. Trade-off: Mirroring distress induces overwhelm.

States & Anchoring (Ch 4)

Anchoring / Self Anchoring

When: You want a resource state on demand. How: Pick a unique trigger, elicit the state strongly, set the anchor at the PEAK, test. Trade-off: Anchors decay if reused or unreinforced.

Collapsing Anchors

When: A situation triggers an unwanted state. How: Anchor the negative and a stronger positive; fire both; release the negative first; test. Trade-off: Needs the positive clearly stronger.

Chaining States / Circle of Excellence

When: A target state is too far to reach in one jump (chaining); or you want a peak state at will (Circle). How: Bridge through intermediate anchored steps; or load a stepped-into spatial circle with the state and future-pace. Trade-off: Tedious; the spatial cue must stay dedicated.

Physiomental State Interruption

When: A stuck/dysfunctional state won't shift. How: Exaggerate its driving submodality to absurdity; test. Trade-off: Fails if you target the wrong submodality.

Submodalities & the Swish (Ch 5)

The Swish

When: An unwanted habit with a clear trigger. How: Big/bright associated trigger image ↔ small/dim dissociated desired-self image; swap fast with a whoosh; repeat 5–7× with break states; test. Trade-off: Needs a real trigger; generalizes only when aimed at a self-image, not a behavior.

Godiva Chocolate

When: Low motivation for a worthwhile behavior. How: Hide a craving image behind the behavior image; open/shrink a hole 3+ times. Trade-off: Requires ecology check; over-talking kills it.

Compulsion Blow-Out / Spinning Icons

When: A compulsion or recurring negative state. How: Overdrive its two strongest submodalities (or orbit negative + antidote icons) to extreme until boring/blended; break state. Trade-off: Refer clinical cases; start with weak states.

Reframing & Parts Work (Ch 6)

Six Step Reframe

When: A habit you "can't stop." How: Signal the part → elicit its positive intention → creative part makes 3 alternatives → part accepts → future-pace + ecology. Trade-off: Needs a cooperative unconscious signal.

Content / Context Reframing

When: A limiting interpretation (content), or a behavior bad only in some settings (context). How: "What else could this mean?" / "Where would this serve you?" Trade-off: Can feel like denial if facts are ignored.

Parts Negotiation / Advanced Visual Squash

When: Two parts at war. How: Elicit each part's outcome and meta-outcome; broker a non-interference treaty (negotiation), or merge a part in each hand after sharing resources (squash). Trade-off: Needs honest meta-outcomes; abstract if parts won't image.

Beliefs & Belief Change (Ch 7)

Re-Imprinting

When: A deeply imprinted childhood belief or symptom. How: Float to the source imprint; give the past self and role models the missing resources; rewrite forward. Trade-off: Heavyweight; overkill for small issues.

Belief Chaining (Basic / Advanced) & Belief Out-Framing

When: Shift a belief from un-resourceful to resourceful. How: Walk spatial steps with reframes; or view the belief from a 3×3 grid (Past/Present/Future × Self/Other/Observer) and gather alternatives. Trade-off: Advanced versions need a partner/guide.

Hierarchy of Criteria

When: Procrastination from a values conflict. How: Tie the stalled behavior to a higher Identity-level criterion. Trade-off: Requires a grasp of logical levels.

Phobias, Trauma & Emotional Healing (Ch 8)

Phobia Cure (Fast Phobia / V-K Dissociation)

When: An irrational fear or single-event trauma. How: Double dissociation; watch a black-and-white movie from the projection booth; then run it backward fast in color, associated; repeat; test. Trade-off: Can re-traumatize — refer clinical cases to professionals.

Change Personal History

When: Recurring button-pushing memories. How: Set an exit cue, chain to the earliest instance, collapse adult-resource anchors onto the memories. Trade-off: Needs flexible real-time adaptation.

SCORE / Dancing SCORE

When: A stuck multi-faceted problem. How: Gather Symptom/Cause/Outcome/Resource/Effect (statically, or spatially with movement); loop effects as feedback; add the missing resource. Trade-off: Analytical; needs space/privacy for the Dancing version.

The Meta-Model: Precision Language (Ch 9)

Meta-Model Challenging

When: Gathering accurate information or loosening a limiting belief. How: Map the words to a sensory representation; spot the deletion/distortion/generalization; ask the recovery question; test back. Trade-off: Over-use feels like interrogation and breaks rapport — use softeners.

De-Nominalizing

When: Someone is stuck/disempowered by a "thing" (a nominalization). How: Find the frozen process; turn the noun back into a verb with an actor in the driver's seat. Trade-off: Dissolves the easy agreement that vague nouns create.

Persuasion by Chunking Up / Down

When: Negotiating (up) vs problem-solving (down). How: Chunk up to vague generalities for agreement; chunk down to specifics to solve. Trade-off: Chunking up is near-hypnotic — wrong for solving.

The Milton-Model & Conversational Hypnosis (Ch 10)

Pace–Link–Lead

When: Inducing light trance in conversation. How: State 3 verifiable facts, join with "and/as," then lead with a suggestion. Trade-off: Needs genuine rapport or feels manipulative.

Embedded Commands / Double Binds

When: Implanting a directive past resistance, or increasing cooperation. How: Mark a short command inside a quote/question with intonation; or offer two choices that both serve the same presupposition. Trade-off: Over-marking becomes obvious; sophisticated listeners spot the non-choice.

Nested Loops

When: Delivering suggestions inside story. How: Open 5 stories, embed the suggestion in #5, close 5→1 in reverse. Trade-off: Requires skill and engaging stories; long.

Strategies, Meta-Programs & Modeling (Ch 11)

Spelling Strategy

When: Poor spelling or rote recall. How: View the word up-left from a calm anchored state; write it from the image; write it backward; loop. Trade-off: Visual-heavy; resists non-visual learners.

Walt Disney Strategy

When: Developing a plan or idea. How: Anchor Dreamer, Realist, and Critic in three separate spots; cycle through them; the Critic asks questions, not attacks. Trade-off: Needs space and discipline to keep states clean.

2nd / 3rd Position Modeling

When: Copying someone's excellence. How: Take 2nd position for the feel, 3rd position for the structure/syntax; extract the strategy and state. Trade-off: Self-report can be inaccurate; needs practiced observation.

Self, Identity & Logical Levels (Ch 12)

Logical Levels Alignment / Co-Alignment

When: Reclaiming direction on a goal (self) or aligning a team. How: Walk the issue through all six levels; build bottom-up carrying each state upward; find overlaps and integrate down. Trade-off: Slow; needs group buy-in for teams.

Loving Yourself / Inner Hero / Assertiveness Installation

When: Low self-worth, acting-out, or passivity. How: See yourself through a loving person's 2nd position and anchor the state; or pace the person's highest identity-level values, then lead; build a state + boundary "force-field." Trade-off: Fails if recognition is artificial; needs a genuinely safe model figure.

Advanced & Newly Introduced Tools (Ch 13)

Reprocessing

When: Trauma, anxiety, or intrusive symptoms. How: Target the memory → state shift via alternating bilateral stimulus → optional cognitive work → body scan / future pace → recovery. Trade-off: Needs training/supervision; refer severe trauma.

Matrixing

When: A complex, multi-issue ("twilight"/subclinical) client. How: Mind-map across Meaning, Context, Behavior, Physiology into actionable items. Trade-off: Requires psychopathology knowledge; slower than single techniques.

Vision Communication Protocol

When: One partner overwhelms the other in relationship talks. How: Single issue → vision → values → steps → one tiny ask, framed in the partner's language. Trade-off: Only for functional relationships; can suppress serious issues if misused.

Smart Eating Pattern

When: Stress eating vs real hunger. How: Felt-sense hunger check → imagine eating → contrast → future-pace. Trade-off: Relies on honest interoception.

The Certainty Illusion: What You Don't Know and Why It Matters

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — The Certainty Illusion

Triage: which illusion is this?

  • Claim leans on research, mechanism, or "studies show" → Science Illusion → run Scienceploitation Detection + Body-of-Evidence Test (ch01–ch05)
  • Claim leans on a virtuous adjective (natural, clean, safe, sustainable, manly) → Goodness Illusion → run Health Halo Deconstruction + separate goal from intervention (ch06–ch10)
