When to use: any big goal with a far deadline.

How: split into near milestones; give each a who and a by when; buffer for the planning fallacy; work backward from the target date.

Debrief / Retrospective

When to use: after a project, on a cadence, or after any error.

How: 1–2 hrs; what went well / badly / to change. Blameless — collective language ("our process failed"), objective timeline. Write down and share learnings.

Delegating a Hard Problem

When to use: growing a report and freeing your own time.

How: confirm you truly believe they can solve it; hand it over; publicly declare them the owner (empowers them); stay "on the boat" coaching — don't walk away.

Put-Yourself-Out-of-a-Job Rule

When to use: continuously, as the team grows.

How: spend your energy only at the intersection of "most important to the org" AND "what you're uniquely best at." Delegate everything a report can do as well or better. Aim to double leadership capacity yearly.

The Would-I-Rehire Test

When to use: a report or manager is persistently struggling.

How: ask "Assume the role were open — would I rehire this person or gamble on someone new?" If no, make the move (help them find a better role or let them go), respectfully and decisively.

Culture-Building Loop

When to use: shaping how your team works.

How: (1) map current vs. aspirational culture; (2) talk about what matters ten times, ten ways; (3) walk the walk; (4) align incentives and address violations; (5) invent traditions that make values concrete.

The Media Training Bible: 101 Things You Absolutely, Positively Need to Know Before Your Next Interview

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — The Media Training Bible (Brad Phillips)

Decision rules

  • Should I do the interview? If the story is about you and runs with or without you → yes (1-for-3 beats 0-for-3). Decline only if irrelevant, off-brand, or zero upside.
  • Reporter calls now? Don't interview on the spot. Get the topic, promise a fast call-back, prep, then call before they've written — not just by deadline.
  • Can't answer this? Never "no comment." Explain why you can't, then give what you can.
  • Tempted to say "off the record"? Don't. Assume everything is on the record, always.
  • Asked a negative/loaded question? Never repeat the loaded word. Reframe positively, then transition to a message.
  • Open-ended "what" question? Use Why + What (lead with why it matters).
  • Any other answer? Lead with the conclusion (start at the end), keep to ≤30 seconds, make each sentence stand alone and on-message.
  • Don't know the answer? Peter Jennings Rule — say what you do know.
  • Print/edited interview? Pause ~3 seconds before answering. Live/hostile? Don't pause long — just let the question finish.

The ATMs (tough-question formula)

Answer (1 word) → Transition → Message (+ supports) → sell (optional)

Time split: 10–20% A+T, 80–90% M+s. Don't use on every answer. Drop the "A" for false-premise and guarantee questions.

Trap-question quick reference

TrapMove
False premiseReject at once: "I don't agree with the premise…" then M
False choice (this/that)"That's like choosing between air and water."
Yes/No (damaging)Reframe with context; don't concede the bad word
Demands a guarantee"Here's what I can guarantee…"
Speculation / hypothetical"I can't speculate, but here's what I can tell you…"
About a competitor"I'll let them speak for themselves, but here's why ours is a hit…"
Indirect attribution ("people say")Dismiss the anonymous claim; return to message
Left fieldPledge to learn more / talk about what you know / zoom out
Don't knowPeter Jennings Rule
ParaphraseReject unless 100% accurate; don't repeat their word

Message thresholds & defaults

  • 3 messages, one sentence each. ≥2 stories + ≥2 statistics + ≥2 sound bites per message (~21 answers).
  • Message ≤ 30 words, ≤ 2 commas, concrete images, spoken aloud to test.
  • Audiences need 7–15 exposures to act. Avg TV quote = 7.3 sec / ~18 words; print quote = 8–20 words.
  • Answers ≤ 30 seconds. Speak 10–15% louder than feels natural.

CUBE A (message checklist)

Consistent · Unburdened (no jargon/abstraction) · Brief (1 sentence) · Ear-worthy (speak it aloud) · Audience-focused (their needs/values)

Statistics: make numbers land

Give context ("122 Fenway Parks") · make it personal ($1,250/family, not $100B) · use ratios ("1 in 3") · avoid bare percentages · give relative distance ("Maine to Miami").

Body language & voice tells

  • Energy: you feel an 8, the room sees a 4 → go bigger. Eye contact: aim ~100% (not the conversational 40–60%).
  • Posture: lean slightly forward, off the chair-back; no crossed legs/arms, no swivel chairs.
  • Voice levers: volume, pace (slow for complex/key points), pitch (avoid upticks), tone, silences, diaphragmatic breathing.
  • Smell test for "off message": if you say "Oh, by the way…" / "Incidentally…" you've strayed.

Attire defaults

Solids in gray/blue/earth tones · high contrast · both sexes wear makeup · shined shoes, long dark socks · avoid stripes/checks, pastels (hard fields), lapel pins, gloss/shimmer, day-of haircut. HD → subtle, smooth, spotless.

The 10 Truths of a Crisis (if you see X, do Y)

  1. You'll suffer first — contain it, don't let it "jump the fire line."
  2. Cast as good/bad guy — show you "get it."
  3. Communicate within the hour — be present in your own coverage.
  4. Media side with victims — right facts + wrong tone = clueless.
  5. Spokesperson choice signals scale — err high, don't always lead with the CEO.
  6. Train receptionists, guards, even spouses — anyone can be the confirming source.
  7. Don't bury bad facts — tear the Band-Aid off; no drip-drip.
  8. Social media first — correct misinformation within ~30 min.
  9. Apologize fully the first time — no "if/then" half-apology; pledge action.
  10. Lawyers can deepen the crisis — weigh reputation against legal payout.

Format fast rules

  • Phone: stand, headset, landline, gesture, listen for typing (slow down/repeat).
  • Radio: prepare for abrupt start, match/exceed host energy, make your own plug.
  • TV: phone off, monitor away, you're always "on" (split screen), stay seated till clear; in a crisis no logos in your background.
  • Edited: never say "as I mentioned earlier," "in conclusion," a date, or the reporter's name.
  • Skype: the one format where you limit gestures (jumpy on low bandwidth).
  • Social media: treat as a nonstop, permanent, on-the-record press conference.

Prep ritual (7 steps)

Worksheets → file cards (trigger words) → interview the reporter → research both sides → small Q&A (≤12) → recorded practice → pick 3 improvement areas. Remember less to perform better.

glossary.md

Glossary — The Media Training Bible

Ambush interview — A reporter showing up unannounced or blindsiding you with an off-topic question mid-interview; win by denying them a defensive "money shot" (Ch 4).

ATMs — Phillips' core system for tough questions: Answer, Transition, Message, sell. Spend 10–20% on A+T, 80–90% on M+s (Ch 4).

Audience focused — The "A" in CUBE A: a message must incorporate the audience's needs and values, not just your points (Ch 2).

Bites interview — The most common TV format; producers use only a few sound bites. Look at the interviewer, not the camera (Ch 5, Ch 6).

Brief — The "B" in CUBE A: one sentence per message; the average TV quote is 7.3 seconds / ~18 words (Ch 2).

Comment without commenting — Declining to answer by explaining why you can't, instead of saying "no comment" (Ch 1).

Consistent — The "C" in CUBE A: repeat the same themes across all platforms; 7–15 exposures move an audience to action (Ch 2).

Crisis — An event, precipitated by a specific incident, that draws critical media attention for a definite period (Ch 7).

CUBE A — The five elements of an effective message: Consistent, Unburdened, Brief, Ear-worthy, Audience focused (Ch 2).

Deskside briefing — A casual one-on-one briefing at a journalist's office; treat everything as quotable (Ch 6).

Diaphragmatic breathing — Breathing from the stomach (not chest) for a fuller, less nasal voice and better breath control (Ch 5).

Ear-worthy — The "E" in CUBE A: write for the ear, not the eye — short, everyday words, contractions; speak it aloud (Ch 2).

Edited interview — Any interview aired/printed in clips; you can restart answers, but avoid "as I mentioned earlier," "in conclusion," dates, and the reporter's name (Ch 6).

Effective frequency — The number of exposures before a message drives action; Phillips' rule is 7–15+ (Ch 2).

File cards — Index cards distilling each message + supports to trigger phrases, so you sound extemporaneous on air (Ch 8).

Head/heart principle — Jordan-Meier's test for crisis spokespersons: deliver the right words in the right (believably caring) way (Ch 7).

IFB (interruptible feedback) — The TV earpiece through which you hear the studio; test it before air (Ch 6).

Jump the fire line — When a specific, limited crisis becomes a referendum on your whole brand's competence (Toyota) (Ch 7).

Live-to-tape — Prerecorded but aired unedited; treat as live, but ask if you can restart on a mistake (Ch 6).

Message — A one-sentence statement marrying one of your key points to one of your audience's needs/values; aim for three (Ch 2).

Message disconnect — When your words and body language contradict; the audience believes the body (Ch 5).

Message support — A story, statistic, or sound bite that reinforces a message (the "three-legged stool"); build ≥2 of each per message (Ch 2).

Money shot — The dramatic, guilty-looking visual a reporter wants in an ambush; deny it by staying calm (Ch 4).

"No comment" — The most damaging phrase in a spokesperson's lexicon; reads as guilt. Never use it or its equivalents (Ch 1).

Off the record — Info that can't be used in any form — but the term is defined inconsistently by journalists; unreliable, so banish it (Ch 1).

On background — Info usable but the source can't be named or quoted (Ch 1).

On the record — The default state of all communication with reporters (Ch 1).

Peter Jennings Rule — When you don't know the answer, tell the public what you do know ("That's unclear, but here's what we know…") (Ch 4).

Phoner — A print or radio interview conducted by phone; stand, use a headset and landline, gesture (Ch 6).

Present in your own coverage — Showing up and speaking so reporters use you as the primary source in a crisis (Ch 7).

Rule of Thirds — A story has three voices (you, opponent, reporter); refusing to comment makes you go "0-for-3." Don't make your opponent's case (Ch 1).

Seven-second stray — A brief off-message moment that becomes the only quote that airs — repeatedly; your message is your "lifeboat" (Ch 4).

Sound bite — A short, memorable/witty phrase expressing a message; usually planned in advance, delivered as if improvised (Ch 2).

Split screen / reaction shot — TV formats where you appear while not speaking; act as if you're always "on" (Ch 6).

Strong language — Declarative words ("here's what we know") replacing hedges ("we think," "we hope") (Ch 3).

Target person — One specific individual you visualize and speak to, representing the whole audience (Ch 3).

Ten Truths of a Crisis — Phillips' crisis framework (Ch 7), e.g. communicate immediately, side with victims, apologize the right way.

Twelve-Year-Old-Nephew Rule — Strip jargon by explaining as you would to a bright 12-year-old (simplify, don't "dumb down") (Ch 3).

Unburdened — The "U" in CUBE A: free of wordiness, jargon, abstractions (≤2 commas, ≤30 words, concrete images) (Ch 2).

Uptick — Rising pitch at the end of statements, making them sound like questions and eroding credibility (Ch 5).

Verbal filler — "Uhhh," "ummm," "like," "you know"; kill with pre-answer pauses and the 30-second-object drill (Ch 5).

Walk and talk — An interview conducted while walking; visually interesting but distracting — slow down or stop to make a key point (Ch 6).

Why + What — Answer open-ended "what" questions by leading with why your work matters, then what you do (Ch 3).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — The Media Training Bible

The ATMs (answering any tough question)

When to use: Off-topic, hostile, or trap questions where you must answer and stay on message.

How: Answer (often one word) → Transition (bridge phrase) → Message (+ supports) → sell (optional call to action). Spend 10–20% on A+T, 80–90% on M+s. Drop the "A" when the transition can serve as the answer (false premise, guarantee).

Trade-offs: Don't use on every answer — overuse reads as canned/evasive.

CUBE A (building a message)

When to use: Drafting or stress-testing your three core messages.

How: Make each message Consistent (repeatable theme), Unburdened (≤2 commas, ≤30 words, no jargon), Brief (one sentence), Ear-worthy (speak it aloud), Audience-focused (their needs/values).

Trade-offs: Frustrating self-editing; the discipline is the point.

The Message-Support Stool (staying on message without repeating)

When to use: Every interview — to answer many questions on-message without sounding repetitive.

How: For each of 3 messages, prepare ≥2 stories, ≥2 statistics, ≥2 sound bites (~21 answers). Pair a support with a message or use it alone.

Trade-offs: Front-loaded prep work; pays off in flexibility.

Why + What

When to use: Open-ended questions ("What does your company do?").

How: Lead with why your work matters (a striking context/stat), then what you do.

Trade-offs: Slightly less direct than a normal lead — reserved for open-enders only.

Start at the End (don't bury the lead)

When to use: Most answers, especially live interviews.

How: Open with your conclusion/most important point → add context → restate the lead.

Trade-offs: Cuts against the chronological storytelling instinct; requires practice.

The Three-Second Pause

When to use: Print and most edited interviews.

How: After a question, stay quiet a few seconds, form the answer, then speak. Kills filler, sharpens focus.

Trade-offs: Skip in live/hostile interviews (long silence reads as evasive) — instead just let the question finish before speaking.

The Peter Jennings Rule (unknown answers)

When to use: Asked something you don't know or shouldn't guess.

How: "That's unclear, but here's what we know…" — give value from what you do know.

Trade-offs: If pressed for the specific fact afterward, it's fine to say you don't know.

Rewrite the Hostile Question

When to use: Aggressive, loaded, or insulting questions.

How: Silently restate the question in neutral terms; answer that. "I disagree with the premise, and am happy to share our accomplishments…"

Trade-offs: Don't repeat the loaded language while doing it.

Trap-Question Playbook

When to use: The ten recurring trap types.

How: False premise → reject immediately, drop the "A." False choice → "that's like choosing between air and water." Yes/No → reframe with context, don't concede the damaging word. Guarantee → "Here's what I can guarantee…" Speculation → "I can't speculate, but here's what I can tell you…" Competition → "I'll let them speak for themselves, but here's why ours is a hit…" Indirect attribution → dismiss the anonymous claim, return to message.

Trade-offs: Zoom-out/general answers can invite more probing follow-ups — practice in advance.

Comment Without Commenting

When to use: Legitimately can't answer (confidential, legal, layoffs, safety).

How: Explain why you can't, then offer what you can. Never say "no comment."

Trade-offs: Comes "perilously close" to no-comment — transition smoothly.

Crisis Response Protocol

When to use: Any breaking crisis.

How: Communicate within the hour ("present in your own coverage"); focus on victims with genuine humanity; get all bad facts out at once (don't drip); apologize fully the first time (no "if/then"); choose the right-level spokesperson (err high); use social media within ~30 min; weigh legal vs. reputational cost.

Trade-offs: Speaking early with incomplete facts feels risky — state what you know, what you're doing, and when you'll update.

Crisis Preparation Drill

When to use: Before any crisis, ideally yearly.

How: Assemble a cross-department team → brainstorm via the 8 categories → reduce to the 5 most likely-and-damaging → write a response per crisis → run staged "real-time" on-camera drills (breaking news → reputation-forming → finger-pointing).

Trade-offs: Time-intensive; "once you hear the thunder, it's too late to build the ark."

Kill Verbal Filler (the 30-second object drill)

When to use: Habitual "uhhh," "ummm," "like," "you know."

How: Shout a random object, talk about it for 30 seconds with pauses but zero filler; record to verify.

Trade-offs: Filler only matters when it distracts — don't over-police the occasional "uh."

The Seven-Step Prep Workflow

When to use: Before every interview (do a "shortcut" version under deadline).

How: (1) Message worksheets → (2) File cards → (3) Interview the reporter → (4) Research both sides → (5) Small Q&A (≤12 Qs) → (6) Recorded practice interview → (7) Pick 3 improvement areas.

Trade-offs: Over-preparation paralyzes — keep the Q&A small; reduce to trigger words.

The Myth of Normal: Trauma, Illness, and Healing in a Toxic Culture

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — The Myth of Normal

Diagnostic questions and decision rules, not a symptom checklist. Not medical, psychiatric, or therapeutic advice.

The four questions that reframe almost anything

Instead of askingAskBecause
What's wrong with you?What happened to you?Trauma is not what happens to you, it's what happens inside you — the wound, not the event
Why the addiction?Why the pain?Addiction is an adaptation to pain, not a disease of choice or a moral failure
What does she have?What process is unfolding, and what sustains it?Disease is a process in a life, not a thing that invades a separate self
How do I get rid of this?What is this for? Why is this here?Everything within us exists for a purpose; it was once protective

Decision rules

  • When a diagnosis explains the symptoms but not the person → ask what was happening in that life in the 2–5 years before onset. The answer is data.
  • When someone is described admiringly as "never angry," "no ego," "always thinking of others," "so easy to care for" → treat that as a coping style, not a virtue. Maté's position: habitual self-suppression and repressed anger are physiologically consequential.
  • When a behavior looks irrational → assume it was once an adaptation. Ask what it solved, and when.
  • When a child's behavior is the problem → look first at the state of the attachment relationship and the adults' capacity to attune, not at the child's will.
  • When "normal" is offered as reassurance → ask normal for whom, and by what standard? Widely shared does not mean healthy. That is the myth.
  • When a cause is attributed to genes → genes load possibilities; environment and experience largely decide expression. Ask what turned it on.
  • When a symptom is being treated and the context is untouched → the intervention is incomplete, however correct the treatment.
  • When self-compassion is absent → do not command it. Notice the absence and get curious about it. Compassion brooks no "should."
  • When healing is discussed → separate it from cure. Healing is a direction, a movement toward wholeness; cure is absence of disease. You can have either without the other. Never promise the second by way of the first.

Tells & smells

If you seeSuspect
"I never get angry" / conflict avoidance as identityRepressed anger, authenticity traded for attachment
Illness onset shortly after a loss, betrayal, or role collapseChronic process made acute by interpersonal stress
"Idiopathic" on the chartNo one asked about the life
A patient apologizing for taking up your timeSelf-suppression pattern, likely lifelong
Compulsive niceness, inability to say noThe childhood adaptation still running
Strong self-condemnation in familiar bodily sensationsThe critic is old and was once protective
A parent describing a toddler's needs as manipulationCulture's toughening script; attunement is being withheld
"You must have brought this on yourself"Victim-blaming — the distortion Maté explicitly rejects

The critical distinctions (get these wrong and you get Maté wrong)

Not thisBut this
You caused your illnessIllness is multifactorial and contextual; responsibility is not blame
Personality causes cancerMaté's position is that emotional repression is a significant contributing factor — a contested claim, not consensus
Blame the parentsParents are themselves shaped by their own trauma and by a culture that undermines parenting
Trauma = the terrible eventTrauma = the internal wound and the adaptation it forced
Big-T Trauma is the only real traumasmall-t trauma — chronic unmet need, absence of attunement — is pervasive and consequential
Acceptance = resignationAcceptance = allowing what is, which is what makes change possible
Healthy anger = ventingHealthy anger flares, defends the boundary, and subsides
Healing = self-improvementHealing = self-retrieval
Disillusionment = lossDisillusionment = gain; the cost of refusing is higher

The authenticity/attachment audit — fast version

Signal appears (tension, anxiety, irritability, regret, depression, fatigue) → ask:

  1. What inner guidance am I defying or avoiding?
  2. What truth am I withholding, and what am I afraid of losing by saying it?
  3. Where, recently, did I abandon myself?
  4. What story made that feel necessary — and where did I learn it?

The chronic pattern matters, not the isolated lapse. Deliberate, chosen sacrifice is not the target; habitual, unwilled selflessness is.

Safety rails

  • Anything that lands as "you did this to yourself" has done harm. Say so plainly and correct it.
  • Never frame Maté's work as a reason to decline, delay, or discontinue medical or psychiatric treatment. His own cases pair conventional treatment with inner work.
  • Contested claims (personality→cancer, ADHD as a stress/attunement phenomenon, psychedelics) are Maté's position and emerging research, not settled science. Attribute them.

glossary.md

Glossary — The Myth of Normal

Acceptance — Allowing that reality is as it is right now; the precondition for change, not resignation or approval. One of the four A's. (Ch 26)

ACEs (Adverse Childhood Experiences) — The ten categories of childhood adversity from the Fellitti/Anda study; dose-dependently associated with adult physical and mental illness. Maté treats them as a floor, not a ceiling — they capture overt harm and miss the absence of attunement. (Ch 1, 9)

Activism / Advocacy — The two additional A's for collective healing: organizing for change, and using privilege to amplify silenced voices. Cannot be individual pursuits. (Ch 33)

Agency — Free, responsible authorship of one's own responses and life. Not control over outcomes, and not blame for what was done to you. (Ch 26)

Anger, healthy — Boundary-defending energy of the moment: it flares, fends off the threat, and subsides. Distinct from rage, resentment, spite, or venting. Both suppressed and amplified anger are toxic. (Ch 26)

Attachment — The drive for proximity and connection with a caregiver; in a child, a survival need that outranks everything else. (Ch 7, 9)

Attachment vs. authenticity — The central developmental trade-off: when a child cannot have both, attachment wins, authenticity is suppressed, and that adaptation becomes the adult pathology. (Ch 7)

Attunement — The caregiver's accurate reading of and resonance with a child's inner state. Its chronic absence is itself traumatic, even where nothing overtly bad happens. (Ch 9)

Authenticity — Fidelity to one's own felt sense, needs, and values; lived rather than conceptual. Cannot be pursued, only embodied. (Ch 7, 26)

Big-T Trauma — Trauma from overt, identifiable catastrophic events: abuse, violence, war, disaster. (Ch 1)

Biopsychosocial — Medicine that treats biological, psychological, and social factors as one inseparable system rather than separate domains. (Ch 2, 3)

Cartesian split — The mind/body separation Maté rejects; the philosophical error underwriting modern medicine's blindness to context. (Ch 2)

Compassionate Inquiry (CI) — Maté's own methodology: open-ended, non-judgmental exploration of the beliefs and behaviors that don't serve us, tracking bodily sensation and familiarity to reach origins. Both a therapist training and a self-reflection practice. (Ch 28, 30)

Compassions, the five — Ordinary human compassion; the compassion of curiosity and understanding (context); of recognition; of truth; of possibility. Non-hierarchical and mutually reinforcing. (Ch 26)

Coping style — Habitual emotional patterns — self-suppression, compulsive niceness, repressed anger, chronic role-taking — that Maté's position links to autoimmune illness and cancer risk. A contested empirical claim, not settled consensus. (Ch 2, 5, 6)

Cure — The absence of disease. Distinct from healing; either can occur without the other. (Ch 25)

Developmental trauma — Trauma arising from the conditions of early development itself — unmet needs, absent attunement, stressed caregivers — rather than from discrete events. (Ch 1, 9)

Disillusionment — Shedding an illusion. Maté treats it as a healing gain rather than a loss, and as the confrontation with denial that makes social change thinkable. (Ch 33)

Epigenetics — The mechanism by which environment and experience switch gene expression on or off; Maté's counter to genetic determinism. (Ch 4, 10)

Foes to friends — The move of turning a distressing inner pattern from enemy into ally by asking what purpose it originally served. (Ch 30)

Healing — A natural movement toward wholeness. A direction, not a destination; closer to self-retrieval than to self-improvement. (Ch 25)

Idiopathic — Medicine's term for a condition of unknown cause; in Maté's reading, often a confession that no one asked about the life. (Ch 6)

Inner critic — The internalized self-accusing voice. Approached not by defeat but by inquiry into what it was once protecting. (Ch 30)

Interpersonal biology — The finding that human physiology is regulated by relationship: nervous systems, immune systems, and hormones are shaped by the people around us. (Ch 3)

Interpersonal neurobiology — Siegel's field describing how relationships physically shape the developing brain. (Ch 3, 9)

Mind-body unity — The premise that emotional, psychological, and social life are inseparable from physiology; therefore the social is always also biological. (Ch 2)

Myth of normal, the — The book's title claim: a toxic culture normalizes conditions that are in fact pathogenic, so widespread does not mean healthy and "normal" is not a standard of health. (Introduction, Ch 19–24)

"Not why the addiction, but why the pain" — Maté's reframe of addiction: the substance or behavior is an adaptation that solved something, so the question is what pain it relieved. (Ch 15, 16)

Peer orientation — Children turning to peers rather than adults for attachment cues, undermining the parenting relationship. (Ch 12, after Gordon Neufeld)

Responsibility vs. blame — Maté's key distinction: responsibility is the capacity to respond now; blame is fault for what happened. He explicitly rejects the "you caused your cancer" reading of his work. (Ch 6, 25, 27)

Rupture and repair — Standard attachment-theory terminology for the cycle of relational break and reconnection: repair, not the absence of rupture, builds security, and unrepaired rupture is where damage accumulates. Maté does not use this exact phrase in this book; Ch 9 makes the same argument as unconditional acceptance holding through correction and momentary anger. He uses rupture separately, in his definition of trauma as a lasting rupture or split within the self. (Ch 9; cf. Ch 1)

Self-compassion — The attitude of non-judgment toward one's own suffering; says simply "I am hurting." Distinct from self-pity, which wraps pain in narrative, and from self-improvement. (Ch 26, 28)

Self-suppression — The habitual, unwilled subordination of one's own needs and feelings to others'. Maté's central pathogenic coping style. (Ch 2, 5, 28)

small-t trauma — Trauma from chronic unmet need and absent attunement rather than overt catastrophe. Pervasive, easily missed, and consequential. (Ch 1)

Sociopathy as strategy — Maté's argument that institutional and corporate structures reward and require the traits that would be pathologized in an individual. (Ch 21)

Toxic culture — The social, economic, and material conditions that systematically frustrate human needs while presenting themselves as normal. (Ch 19–24)

Trauma — Not what happens to you, but what happens inside you as a result — the wound and the adaptations built around it, not the event. (Ch 1)

Wholeness — The state toward which healing moves: recovering the parts of self that were exiled to preserve attachment. (Ch 25, 32)

patterns.md

Patterns & Practices — The Myth of Normal

Maté's actual working methods. These are inquiries, not instructions. None of them is a substitute for medical, psychiatric, or therapeutic care, and none is a self-improvement program — the aim is self-retrieval, not self-betterment.

Compassionate Inquiry (CI)

When to use: whenever a symptom, behavior, or self-judgment resists being argued away — chronic illness, addiction, self-loathing, compulsive people-pleasing. Also as an ongoing self-reflection practice.

How:

  1. Suspend what you already know about yourself. The personality is an expert on itself and that is precisely the problem. Aim to know yourself, not to know about yourself.
  2. Inquire, don't interrogate. An inquiry is open-ended; it starts from the possibility that you haven't yet found the right question.
  3. Bring compassion as an attitude, not a feeling. Feelings come and go; an attitude can be invited in any emotional state. The attitude is inexhaustible non-judgment toward whatever surfaces.
  4. Never issue a "should." Compassion brooks no should, and walled-off parts don't respond to demands. If self-compassion is absent, don't manufacture it — get curious about its absence. Once seen, it softens.
  5. Track the body. Ask where the belief lives as sensation (throat, chest, belly), then ask: is this sensation new, or deeply familiar? The answer is almost always "familiar" — which relocates the material from the present grievance to its origin.
  6. When self-judgment arises, stay curious about its origin without believing its content.

Trade-offs: slow, and it surfaces pain before relief. Done without safety or without genuine non-judgment it becomes another form of self-attack. Maté insists CI participants spend months on their own material before using it with anyone else.

The Self-Inquiry Exercise ("Before the Body Says No")

When to use: as a weekly written practice, especially where chronic self-suppression is suspected. Handwritten, undistracted.

How — six questions, in order:

  1. In my life's important areas, what am I not saying no to? (Where did a "no" want out and a "yes" or a silence came instead?)
  2. How does my inability to say no impact my life?
  3. What bodily signals have I been overlooking? What symptoms have I ignored that could be warning signs?
  4. What is the hidden story behind my inability to say no? (The belief that makes the "no" feel impossible.)
  5. Where did I learn these stories?
  6. Where have I ignored or denied the "yes" that wanted to be said?

Trade-offs: Maté is explicit that this is not about stigmatizing genuine altruism. Deliberate, chosen self-sacrifice — a parent up at night with a sick child — is not the target. The target is habitual, unwilled selflessness that operates without consent. Get current, stay specific, look for chronic patterns rather than lapses. Notice reluctance to do the exercise at all, without judgment — that reluctance is itself data.

The Authenticity Audit

When to use: when tension, anxiety, irritability, regret, depression, or fatigue surfaces. Maté treats these as the signal that authenticity is missing, not as the problem itself.

How — ask:

  • Is there an inner guidance I am defying, resisting, ignoring, or avoiding?
  • Are there truths I'm withholding from expression or even contemplation, out of fear of losing security or belonging?
  • In a recent encounter, is there some way I abandoned myself, my needs, my values?
  • What fears, rationalizations, or familiar narratives kept me from being myself?
  • Do I even know what my own values are?

Trade-offs: authenticity can't be pursued, only embodied — striving toward an idealized authentic self is itself inauthentic. The most direct route is noticing where authenticity isn't, then applying curiosity and gentle skepticism to the limiting beliefs standing in its place. And the cost is real: choosing authenticity may not preserve every attachment. That grief is the adult reversal of the childhood trade, and Maté does not minimize it.

Foes to Friends — Working with the Inner Critic

When to use: self-accusation, self-condemnation, guilt, self-loathing — anything you have been trying to get rid of.

How:

  1. Start from the first principle of compassionate self-inquiry: everything within us exists for a purpose; nothing is there that shouldn't be. However debilitating, it was once functional.
  2. Shift the question from "How do I get rid of this?" to "What is this for? Why is this here?"
  3. Externalize the accusation to make it examinable. Maté's courtroom move: If this were a trial and you were the defendant, what would the prosecution say about you? Then: What's the verdict — because you did those things, that makes you what? This exposes that the person is simultaneously plaintiff, prosecutor, accused, and hanging judge.
  4. Locate the verdict in the body, then ask how familiar the sensation and the self-concept are. Familiarity dates the belief to childhood, where it was protective.
  5. Do not judge yourself for judging — that keeps the wheel of shame turning.

Trade-offs: turning a foe into a friend is not the same as agreeing with it. The aim is that the critic relax and stop hounding, not that it be defeated.

The Five Compassions

When to use: as a diagnostic on the quality of your own regard — for a patient, a person you judge, or yourself. Non-hierarchical; they reinforce one another.

  1. Ordinary human compassion — the ability to be with suffering and to be moved by it. Distinct from pity, which requires unequal roles. Self-compassion says "I am hurting"; self-pity wraps the pain in narrative.
  2. The compassion of curiosity and understanding (the compassion of context) — everything exists for a reason and the reason matters. Seek the why before leaping to the how.
  3. The compassion of recognition — we are all in the same boat. When intense judgment arises, check your own body state; inquire into the judging mind rather than obeying or condemning it.
  4. The compassion of truth — pain is not the enemy; it is information. Shielding people from inevitable hurt is neither kind nor effective. But truth without safety does no healing work, and "I'm just being honest" is not compassion.
  5. The compassion of possibility — there is more to a person than their conditioned personality and their behavior. A present quality, not a someday hope.

The A's of Healing

When to use: as guideposts for the territory, explicitly not as how-to steps. Maté: no one can plot another's course of healing.

AWhat it isWhat it is not
AuthenticityFidelity to one's own felt sense and values; lived, not conceptualPerformed "realness"; an idealized self to strive toward
AgencyFree, responsible authorship of one's own life and responsesControl over outcomes; blame for what happened to you
Healthy AngerBoundary-defending energy of the moment — flares, does its job of fending off threat, subsidesRage, bluster, resentment, spite, venting, or a grievance kept and fed. Both suppressed and amplified anger are toxic
AcceptanceAllowing that reality is as it is right now — the precondition for changeResignation, approval, or ceasing to work for change

Plus two, for collective healing (Ch 33): Activism and Advocacy — socially meaningful syntheses of the first four, adding solidarity and collective thinking. These cannot be individual pursuits.

Trade-offs: each A corresponds to a human need that was likely driven underground early. Welcoming it back is slow and often frightening. Treating the four as a checklist to complete inverts their purpose.

Disillusionment as a Healing Step

When to use: whenever an illusion is protecting you from a truth about your history, your relationships, or your society.

How: treat losing an illusion as a gain, not a loss. Ask which you would rather be — deluded or disillusioned. Expect the ache of loss and the sense of being unmoored first; what follows is the relief of no longer having to hold impossible contradictions together. Disillusionment also confronts denial, which is the main buttress of an unhealthy status quo.

Trade-offs: it does carry a real cost — you may have to relinquish something you valued or a perspective you took refuge in. Maté's point is that the cost of refusing is higher and less visible.

The New Rules of Marketing and PR

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — The New Rules of Marketing and PR

The single decision rule

When making any marketing/PR choice → start with the buyer, not the product, because content that solves the buyer's problem is what drives action. ("You are what you publish.")

Old Rules vs. New Rules

Old RulesNew Rules
Marketing = advertising to the massesReach niche buyers directly with targeted content
Interrupt to grab attentionDeliver content at the moment of need
PR = get media "ink"; measure clipsReach buyers directly; measure revenue/goals
Release only on "big news," to journalistsPublish continuously, for buyers, keyword-rich
One-way spin, "on message"Authenticity, participation, human voice
Agency wins awardsOrganization wins business

Goal vs. "ball" (the soccer test)

Ball (wrong focus)Goal (right focus)
Leads, clips, T-shirtsRevenue growth
Unique visitors, trafficCustomer retention
Google rank for a phraseDonations / members / votes / applications

Rule: traffic and rank matter only if they lead to the real goal.

What to do when...

SituationDo thisBecause
Starting a programRun the 4 steps: goals → personas → words/beliefs → contentEverything else builds on personas
OverwhelmedPick ONE first step (persona research, a few content pages, or read→comment→blog)The Web is iterative; nobody does it all
Writing anythingLead with the buyer's problem in their words, then prove itGobbledygook makes you interchangeable
Negative thread eruptsRespond fast, honestly, in the same forum, in your nameGoing dark reads as guilt
Organic buzz about youPush it along (link, support, contest) — don't fake or distanceHomemade beats slick; astroturf gets exposed
Want a specific reporterRead them first; send one targeted, plain-text pitchBroadcast pitching = spam
Building a siteOrganize by buyer self-selection, not org chartBuyers don't think in your structure
SEMMany specific long-tail phrases + one landing page eachGeneric terms don't convert; homepage can't serve a term

Gobbledygook to ban (substitute plain buyer language)

next generation · flexible · robust · world class · scalable · easy to use · cutting edge · mission critical · market leading · industry standard · best of breed · leading · solutions · "we're excited about…" · unparalleled

Test: swap in a competitor's name — if it still makes sense, rewrite it.

Thought leadership: the one rule

Solve the buyer's problem; never mention your product. Then choose the form buyers consume:

Buyer prefersUse
To read, deepWhitepaper (often gated)
To read, lightE-book (free, no registration)
Regular updatesE-mail newsletter (problem-solving, not pitch)
Live + expertsWebinar
The definitive dataSurvey/research report
Audio (commuters)Podcast (+ companion blog)
VideoVlog / vodcast / YouTube

Free vs. gated content

Choose FREE (no registration) whenChoose GATED when
Goal is reach/awarenessGoal is a contact list / sales leads
E-books, viral contentWhitepapers, B2B lead gen

Trade-off: gating cuts response rates sharply.

News release checklist

☐ Written for buyers, not just press ☐ Sent even without "big news" ☐ Buyer's exact search phrases embedded ☐ An offer that compels response ☐ Links to landing pages ☐ Social tags (Technorati/DIGG/del.icio.us) ☐ Dual-published: wire + permanent site page

Landing page checklist

☐ Short copy, simple graphics ☐ Your brand's tone ☐ Written from prospect's POV ☐ Communication, not advertising ☐ Happy-customer quote ☐ Self-contained (few/no links out) ☐ Clear, easy call to action (offer several) ☐ Ask minimum info (email only if possible) ☐ Follow up fast

Blog on-ramp & ethics

Sequence: monitor → comment → create. Niche + passion + authentic independent voice.

Ethics checks: Transparency · Privacy · Disclosure · Truthfulness · Credit. Gut test: "What would your mother say?"

Tells & smells (old-rules thinking to catch)

  • "We need a Super Bowl ad / an award / the CEO on TV" → not the new rules
  • "Content only works for tech companies" → false (content sells concrete)
  • "Bloggers are geeks in pajamas" → the Rathergate mistake
  • Site organized by product/geography → confuses buyers
  • Media room behind registration / routed through IT → kills the story and speed
  • Optimizing on "travel" or one generic keyword → won't convert
  • Fake viral / stealth YouTube / sock-puppet profiles → community exposes them

Governance defaults

Employee blogging → govern behavior, not the technology (no harassment/secrets/insider-trading/competitor-bashing across all media). If posts must be reviewed → review content, not words (don't gobbledygook it).

glossary.md

Glossary — The New Rules of Marketing and PR

Badge — a graphical image (banner-like or RSS-style) supporters add to their blog/site that links back to your content (Ch 9)

Bait-and-switch (landing page failure) — ranking for a phrase then dumping searchers on a generic homepage; they click away (Ch 20)

Blog (weblog) — a special Web site, usually by one passionate person, posts in reverse-chronological order, tagged into categories, built on easy CMS-like software (Ch 4)

Blogosphere monitoring — using text-mining/blog search (e.g. Technorati) to track and measure what's said about you across millions of blogs (Ch 4)

Browse (vs. search) — one of two ways people use content: being told something you didn't think to ask (Ch 2, 15)

Buyer persona — a representative biography of a distinct buyer type with a specific problem your product solves; the foundation of the plan (Ch 3, 10)

Buyer persona profile — "a short biography of the typical customer, not just a job description but a person description" (Revella): goals, problems, daily activities, media, exact words (Ch 10)

Call to action — the clear next step (buy/donate/subscribe/download) that content funnels buyers toward (Ch 3, 13)

Clip book — old-rules scrapbook of press mentions PR people showed bosses to prove their worth (Ch 1)

Companion blog — the text blog nearly every podcaster runs so search engines index the show and listeners move into the sales process (Ch 18)

Content drives action — the book's thesis: great content brands you a trusted resource and calls people to act (Ch 2, 3)

Convergence of marketing and PR — online, the line between a web page, release, article, and blog post disappears; there's one set of rules (Ch 2)

Direct-to-consumer news release — a release (renamed from "press release") aimed at buyers via search/RSS, not only reporters (Ch 5, 14)

Disintermediation (of the media) — the Web removing the journalist as required middleman between you and buyers (Ch 5)

E-book — a PDF that names a problem and answers it; landscape, graphical, lighter than a whitepaper; best free/no-registration (Ch 11)

Editorial calendar/plan — a scheduled content program (site pages, e-book, blog, releases) per buyer persona (Ch 10, 14)

First-mover advantage — early adopters of a new channel (blog, podcast, Second Life) earn a lasting reputation for innovation (Ch 4, 19)

Gobbledygook — meaningless overused jargon adjectives (next generation, flexible, robust, world class, scalable, cutting edge) that make companies sound identical (Ch 1, 12)

Go dark — not participating during a crisis; reads as "what are they hiding?" (Ch 7)

Journalistic black hole — the fate of untargeted press releases that reach reporters and produce nothing (Ch 1)

Landing page — a targeted page for the phrase/offer a searcher or release-reader clicked; buyer-POV, self-contained, one clear CTA (Ch 13, 14, 20)

Lens / lensmaster — a Squidoo page that filters one person's niche expertise onto a single page pointing to other content; its creator (Ch 9, 19)

List serve — a group email list; members post and messages go out by email (Ch 7)

Long tail (of marketing / of PR) — the shift from a few mass "hits" to countless niches; cultivate many small wins over one blockbuster (Ch 2)

Long tail of search — optimizing for many specific phrases buyers actually search rather than broad generic terms (Ch 20)

Media room (online) — the part of your site built for media but visited by everyone; you control it; free SEO via frequent releases (Ch 15)

Micromarket / micro-campaign — precise messages aimed at a narrow segment at the point of consumption (Ch 2)

News release — see Direct-to-consumer news release; the book's preferred term (Ch 5)

Old Rules (of Marketing / of PR) — the two obsolete rule-sets: interruption advertising and media-gatekeeper PR (Ch 1)

New Rules of Marketing and PR — the unified list: be authentic, participate, publish content buyers want, reach buyers directly (Ch 2)

Pass-along value — content interesting enough that visitors share the link; helped by permanent URLs (Ch 13)

Podcast — audio content connected to an RSS feed; no iPod required (Ch 6, 18)

Podsafe music — music the artist/label has cleared for podcasting (Ch 6)

RSS (Really Simple Syndication) — a subscription format delivering discrete content items to self-selecting niches, bypassing email (Ch 13, 15)

Search (vs. browse) — using content to answer a specific known question (Ch 2, 15)

Search engine advertising — paid text ads (AdWords, Yahoo! Search Marketing) triggered by purchased keywords; placement = bid × click-through rate (Ch 20)

Search engine marketing (SEM) — using search engines to reach buyers directly; the whole book is an SEM program (Ch 20)

Search engine optimization (SEO) — ensuring content is found and highly ranked in natural results (Ch 20)

Site personality — the consistent tone/voice that builds an emotional relationship (Google playful vs. Accenture serious) (Ch 13)

Social media tags — tags (Technorati, DIGG, del.icio.us) that make releases/pages surface in category feeds (Ch 14)

Stealth insertion — sneaking corporate video onto YouTube as if consumer-generated; the community exposes it (Ch 18)

Thought leadership — content that solves buyers' problems without mentioning your product, branding you an expert (Ch 3, 11)

Third-party ink — old-rules coverage earned when a journalist writes about you (Ch 1)

Trackback — a message another blogger sends when they reference your post; like a comment pointing to their post (Ch 17)

TV-industrial complex (Seth Godin) — the old interruption-advertising system (Ch 1)

Vlog / vodcast — video embedded in a blog / a video podcast tied to RSS-iTunes (Ch 18)

Whitepaper — a document that defines a business problem and offers a solution without pitching product; often gated for leads (Ch 11)

Wiki — a site anyone can edit (Wikipedia); red links = unwritten pages inviting expert contribution (Ch 7)

Word-of-blog / word-of-mouse — the online, more-efficient form of word-of-mouth; hundreds of bloggers can reach millions (Ch 2, 21)

You are what you publish — the plan's guiding maxim: your content is your reputation (Ch 2, 10)

patterns.md

Patterns — Techniques & Methods from The New Rules of Marketing and PR

The Four-Step Marketing & PR Plan

When to use: building any New Rules marketing/PR program from scratch (Ch 10).

How: (1) Set organizational goals (revenue, donations, votes, applications — not "balls" like leads/clips/traffic). (2) Identify and profile buyer personas. (3) Learn buyers' exact words and decide what you want each persona to believe. (4) Develop content (editorial calendar per persona in preferred media).

Trade-offs: requires up-front research and interviews; expect old-rules pushback — but eliminates message-debate guessing.

Build a Buyer Persona Profile

When to use: before creating any content.

How: segment buyers; for each, write a named biography (like "NASCAR Dads," "Sam the Athlete") — goals, problems, daily activities, current solutions, trusted media, exact words. Best built by interviewing real people and triangulating with the media they consume; even clip a representative photo.

Trade-offs: time-consuming, but "so much easier to listen before you talk."

Think Like a Publisher

When to use: any content, site, or media-room project.

How: content strategy first, then design/mechanics. Answer: Who are my readers? How do I reach them? What are their problems? How do I inform and entertain? What content compels action?

Trade-offs: fights the agency/IT pull toward design and technology.

The Three Uses of Blogs (Monitor → Comment → Create)

When to use: entering the blog world.

How: (1) Monitor what's said about you/market/products; (2) comment on others' blogs to become known; (3) start your own. Do them in order.

Trade-offs: monitoring is low-risk and wins internal permission before the leap to writing.

Rapid In-Forum Crisis Response

When to use: a negative thread about you gains traction (Ch 7).

How: respond fast and honestly in the same forum, in your own name — acknowledge, apologize, state your plan. Web linking amplifies one good post.

Trade-offs: can't fully reverse a crisis, but "one guy with one post" (B&H) can flip a thread; going dark (Sony) makes it worse.

Direct-to-Consumer News Release Program

When to use: reaching buyers via search/RSS (Ch 5, 14).

How: write for buyers not just journalists; publish continuously ("big news is great, but don't wait"); embed exact buyer search phrases; include an offer + links to landing pages; dual-publish (wire + your own permanent site page); add social tags.

Trade-offs: don't abuse the channel; coexists with media relations.

Keyword-Rich Content + Links (the SEO engine)

When to use: all web content and releases.

How: research the phrases buyers search; embed them naturally; include links (they drive buyers and raise search rankings via inbound links).

Trade-offs: don't let keywords dominate readability.

Thought-Leadership Content

When to use: branding yourself an expert/trusted resource (Ch 11).

How: solve buyers' problems, never mention your product; pick the form buyers consume (whitepaper, e-book, newsletter, webinar, survey report, blog, podcast, video); grabbing title; decide free vs. gated; promote hard; alert bloggers/reporters.

Trade-offs: free = reach but anonymous; gated = fewer downloads but a contact list.

Survey/Research Report

When to use: you own the definitive data buyers crave (Ch 11).

How: run a real, statistically significant survey; publish free; promote via newsletter. (Pragmatic Marketing salary survey.)

Trade-offs: only works if data is genuine and interesting; builds authority + evergreen SEO.

Write for Buyers (kill gobbledygook)

When to use: every piece of writing (Ch 12).

How: start with the buyer's problem in their plain words, then prove it. Run the substitution test — if swapping a competitor's name still makes sense, the copy is worthless. Write like talking to a relative you don't see often.

Trade-offs: plain language stands out precisely because the industry writes in jargon.

Buyer-Centric Site Navigation & Sales-Cycle Content

When to use: building/redesigning a site (Ch 13).

How: organize by buyer self-selection (job/geography/industry/problem), not your org chart. Map content to cycle: educate early → nudge in middle (offer subscriptions) → close late (demos, tools) → continue conversation. Add persona pages incrementally — no full redesign.

Trade-offs: requires knowing personas and the sales process in detail.

RSS to Targeted Niches

When to use: delivering welcome, self-selected updates (Ch 13, 15).

How: syndicate discrete items (releases, posts, product updates) as category/keyword feeds (Netflix genre feeds; Intel product/country feeds).

Trade-offs: bypasses crowded email; underused — a competitive edge.

Build a Buyer-First Online Media Room

When to use: any organization's site (Ch 15).

How: control it with a dedicated CMS (no IT bottleneck); needs analysis first; optimize for search + browse; rich jargon-free media kit with customer case studies; multimedia; post "proprietary" specs; event calendar; journalist calls to action; embrace bloggers.

Trade-offs: fight legal/exec reluctance to post valuable content — but that content earns the story.

The New Rules of Media Relations (targeted pitching)

When to use: you genuinely want a specific outlet (Ch 16).

How: target one reporter; read their work first; reference a specific article; targeted (not cute) subject line; pitch the customer story and big-picture trend, not features; plain-text, no unrequested attachments; follow up promptly. Pitch bloggers like reporters.

Trade-offs: slow and manual, but broadcast pitching is spam and brands you a "bad guy."

Nurture Explosive News Across the Cycle

When to use: you hold news with viral potential (Ch 8).

How: plan a who/when timeline — hint to clients, embargoed advance to select media, let one outlet break it, then feed the blogger + mainstream wave. (Outsell click-fraud.)

Trade-offs: you can't guarantee virality; timing and luck matter.

Push a Viral Event You Didn't Start

When to use: organic buzz erupts about you (Ch 8).

How: link to it, support the creators, add real-world presence, launch an authentic follow-on contest (Mentos). Don't distance yourself (Coca-Cola's mistake) or fake it.

Trade-offs: homemade beats slick; astroturf gets exposed.

Podcast/Video Production

When to use: buyers prefer audio/video (Ch 18).

How: prep and script; record/edit/tag; host + distribute (iTunes); promote + cross-promote; run a companion blog. Human voice, persona-matched length (18–24 min).

Trade-offs: modest hardware/software/editing investment; lets small players out-personalize big ones.

Squidoo Lens / Social-Network Presence

When to use: building a low-cost, authentic niche presence (Ch 19).

How: offline personality or expertise page; target a niche; be a thought leader; lots of links; transparent (no fake profiles); tag and bookmark; participate and lead; experiment.

Trade-offs: communities hate overt pitches and expose fakes; first-movers win.

Long-Tail Search + Landing Pages

When to use: enhancing an already content-rich SEM program (Ch 20).

How: many specific-phrase programs (not generic terms); one buyer-POV landing page per term cluster (short, self-contained, one clear CTA, minimal form, follow up). Choose "ownable" names.

Trade-offs: needs dozens/hundreds of landing pages; never dump paid traffic on the homepage.

Start in Bits and Pieces

When to use: overwhelmed and unsure where to begin (Ch 21).

How: pick one first step — persona research, a few thought-leadership pages, or read/comment/start-a-blog. Experiment; the Web is iterative, delete what fails.

Trade-offs: nobody does all of it — do what works for you.

The Personal MBA: Master the Art of Business

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — The Personal MBA decision rules

One page of Kaufman's judgment: when to do what, and why.

The master diagnostic — Five Parts of Every Business

A struggling business is failing at one of these. Diagnose in order:

  1. Value Creation — does it make something people want? (If no market wants it, nothing else matters — Iron Law.)
  2. Marketing — does the right audience pay Attention?
  3. Sales — do they trust you enough to buy at a price you can support?
  4. Value Delivery — do they get what they expected, repeatably?
  5. Finance — is there enough profit to keep going?

If you can't clearly describe all five for an idea, you don't have a business yet.

Decision rules

When…Do…Because…
Evaluating any ideaScore the market on the Ten Ways firstThe Iron Law: market beats offer every time
You "feel sure" about an ideaList CIAs and Shadow Test themConviction isn't evidence; a preorder is
Gathering feedbackIgnore friends/family; seek paying strangersOnly money is honest feedback
Setting a priceCompute 4 methods, price on Value ComparisonValue-to-buyer is almost always the highest support
A price feels "too high to charge"Raise it and support itAll prices are arbitrary (Pricing Uncertainty Principle)
Prospect hesitatesAdd Risk Reversal + a Damaging AdmissionShifting risk and admitting flaws both build Trust
Want more revenuePull one of the Four Methods; start with ReactivationLapsed customers are the cheapest to sell
Deciding marketing spendCap it at AAC (marketing slice of LTV)Spend more and each customer loses money
Improving anythingRun WIGWAM, maximize Iteration VelocityMore at-bats beats one big bet
A system underperformsFind the one Constraint, fix only thatOptimizing non-constraints yields nothing
OptimizingAttack the Critical Few (20%); stop at the 85% SolutionDiminishing Returns make the last 15% costly
Tempted to act when unsureConsider Cessation (do nothing)Absence Blindness makes "do nothing" feel wrong when it's right
Designing a new complex systemStart simple, evolve itGall's Law: complex-from-scratch never works
Behavior won't changeChange the Environment, not the willpowerGuiding Structure beats discipline
DelegatingGive Commander's Intent, not step-by-stepPeople adapt to Change only if they know why

Numbers & thresholds Kaufman commits to

  • Team size: 3–8 people (Communication Overhead grows fast past that).
  • Dunbar's number: ~150 — beyond it, minds treat people as statistics (Cognitive Scope Limitation).
  • Decide at 40–70% of available information; less is reckless, more is paralysis.
  • Loss Aversion ≈ 2×: losses feel about twice as strong as equal gains.
  • Pareto: ~20% of inputs → ~80% of outputs (often more extreme).
  • 85% Solution: stop optimizing where added effort exceeds returns.
  • Personal R&D: reinvest ~5% of monthly income in your own learning.
  • Attention span: ~30 min before even motivated minds need Novelty.
  • MITs: 2–3 per day, chosen before the day starts.

Quality & value formulas

  • Quality = Performance − Expectations (manage both; never over-promise).
  • Perceived Value = better End Result + less customer effort.
  • Profit Margin = (revenue − cost) ÷ cost; Value Capture too high → customers flee.
  • Sufficiency = the profit point where continuing is worth it ("ramen profitable").

Tells & smells (recognize the trap fast)

  • Measuring an easy proxy (lines of code, hours logged) → you'll reward the wrong behavior.
  • A correlation cited as a reason to act → demand the full cause-effect chain first.
  • "We'll just add more automation" → recall the Paradox of Automation: you need better humans, not fewer.
  • Optimizing a metric while the system gets fragile → you're trading Resilience for Throughput.
  • Defending a choice by past investment → that's a Sunk Cost; ignore it.
  • Blaming a person's character for a failure → likely Attribution Error; check circumstances.
  • Tightly coupled system "running fine" → Normal Accidents: failure is when, not if. Build a Fail-safe now.

glossary.md

Glossary — The Personal MBA

Key terms with one-line definitions and the chapter that introduces them.

Absence Blindness — We can't perceive what isn't there, so prevention and "doing nothing" go unrewarded; beat it with checklists (Ch 7).

Accumulation — Small helpful or harmful inputs compound over time into huge results (Ch 5).

Addressability — How easily you can reach people who might want your offer (Ch 3).

Akrasia / Conflict — Two control systems fighting over the same perception (work vs. rest = procrastination) (Ch 7, Ch 8).

Allowable Acquisition Cost (AAC) — The maximum you can spend to acquire a new customer; the marketing slice of Lifetime Value (Ch 6).

Amortization — Spreading the cost of a large resource investment across its useful life (Ch 6).

Amplification — A small change to a scalable system produces a huge result (Ch 5).

Analytical Honesty — Measuring data dispassionately, resisting the pull to make things look better (Ch 11).

Association — The mind links co-occurring things even when illogical (Coke = happiness) (Ch 7).

Attention — The scarce, rationed resource every offer competes for (Ch 3).

Attribution Error — When others fail we blame their character; when we fail we blame circumstances (Ch 9).

Authority — People comply with authority figures even against their own judgment (Milgram) (Ch 9).

Autocatalysis — A self-reinforcing loop whose output feeds the next cycle (network effects) (Ch 10).

Barrier to Competition — Every Value Stream improvement makes you harder to replicate (Ch 5).

Barriers to Purchase — The five standard objections blocking a sale: too expensive, won't work, won't work for me, can wait, too hard (Ch 4).

Breakeven — The point where cumulative revenue exceeds cumulative expenses (Ch 6).

Buffer — A third party (agent, broker) empowered to negotiate for you (Ch 4).

Bundling / Unbundling — Combine offers to raise perceived value, or split one into many to open new sales (Ch 2).

Bystander Apathy — More people who could act means fewer who actually act (Ch 9).

Call-to-Action (CTA) — Directing a prospect to one single, obvious next action (Ch 3).

Caveman Syndrome — We run demanding modern life on survival-tuned biology (Ch 7).

Cessation — Intentionally stopping something counterproductive; often the better move (Ch 12).

Checklist — An externalized, predefined SOP for a specific task (Ch 12).

Clanning — Humans automatically form in-groups and out-groups (Ch 9).

Cognitive Scope Limitation — Past ~150 people (Dunbar's number) we treat people as statistics (Ch 7).

Cognitive Switching Penalty — Every attention shift forces the brain to reload context — a Friction cost (Ch 8).

Commander's Intent — Tell people why a task matters, not just how, so they adapt when circumstances change (Ch 9).

Common Ground — The overlap between your options and the prospect's; a precondition for a deal (Ch 4).

Communication Overhead — Time spent communicating instead of producing; grows with team size — keep teams 3–8 (Ch 9).

Comparative Advantage — Capitalize on your strengths; specialize and trade rather than do everything (Ch 8, Ch 9).

Constraint (Theory of Constraints) — One critical input limits the whole system; fix it and Throughput rises (Ch 10).

Context — Related measurements used to interpret data; numbers in isolation say little (Ch 11).

Contrast — We judge by comparison to what's present, not what's absent (pricing camouflage) (Ch 7).

Convergence and Divergence — Group members grow alike; rival groups grow apart (Ch 9).

Core Human Drives — Five drives shaping buying: Acquire, Bond, Learn, Defend, Feel (Ch 2).

Correlation and Causation — Moving together (correlation) is not a repeatable cause-effect chain (causation) (Ch 11).

Counterparty Risk — The risk that a partner won't deliver, damaging your Reputation (Ch 5, Ch 10).

Critical Few (Pareto / 80-20) — ~20% of inputs produce ~80% of outputs (Ch 12).

Critically Important Assumptions (CIAs) — Facts that must be true for the offer to succeed (Ch 2).

Damaging Admission — Volunteering a real drawback, which counterintuitively raises Trust (Ch 4).

Deconstruction — Break a system into the smallest subsystems, understand each, rebuild (Ch 11).

Decision — Committing to one path by cutting off others; decide at 40–70% of information (Ch 8).

Desire — The visceral wanting marketing connects to; you can't manufacture it, only tap it (Ch 3).

Diminishing Returns — Past a point, more of a good thing is detrimental (the "85% Solution") (Ch 12).

Distribution Channel — How value reaches the user: direct (control, capped) or intermediary (reach, less control) (Ch 5).

Duplication — Reliably reproducing something of value; near-free for information (Ch 5).

Economically Valuable Skills — Only skills tied to the Five Parts get paid (Ch 2).

Education-Based Selling — Make prospects better-informed customers; builds Trust and willingness to pay (Ch 4).

End Result — The experience/emotion the prospect wants ("holes, not drills") (Ch 3).

Energy Cycles — Circadian and ~90-min ultradian rhythms; maximize peaks, rest on downswings (Ch 8).

Environment / Guiding Structure — The structure around you is the biggest determinant of behavior (Ch 7, Ch 10).

Expectation Effect — Quality = Performance − Expectations (Ch 5).

Experimental Mindset — Constant experimentation as the only reliable way to learn (Ch 12).

Externalization — Converting internal thoughts into written/spoken form to reprocess them (Ch 8).

Fail-safe — A backup built before it's needed, kept separate from the system it protects (Ch 12).

Feedback — Real-prospect signal sought via open questions; a preorder is the strongest (Ch 2).

Feedback Loop — When a system's output becomes the next cycle's input (Ch 10).

Five Parts of Every Business — Value Creation → Marketing → Sales → Value Delivery → Finance (Ch 1, Ch 2).

Five-Fold Why / How — Repeated "why" to find what you truly want; repeated "how" to reach action (Ch 8).

Fixed vs Variable Costs — Fixed are incurred regardless of output; variable scale with output (Ch 6).

Flow / Stock / Slack — Movements of resources (flows), pools that accumulate (stocks), and how much sits there (slack) (Ch 10).

Force Multiplier — A tool that multiplies force, thought, or attention; the only good use of debt (Ch 5).

Four Methods to Increase Revenue — More customers, bigger transactions, more frequency, higher prices (Ch 6).

Four Pricing Methods — Replacement Cost, Market Comparison, Discounted Cash Flow/NPV, Value Comparison (Ch 4).

Framing — Emphasizing some details, de-emphasizing others; inevitable, not lying (Ch 3).

Free — Giving genuine value away to win Attention fast (Ch 3).

Friction — Any force that removes energy from a system over time (Ch 12).

Gall's Law — Every working complex system evolved from a working simple one (Ch 10).

Garbage In, Garbage Out — Bad input always yields useless output (Ch 11).

Golden Trifecta — Treat everyone with appreciation, courtesy, and respect (Ch 9).

Habits — Regular supportive actions; install one at a time via triggers (Ch 8).

Hierarchy of Funding — Financing ladder from cheapest/most-control to costliest/least-control (Ch 6).

Hook — A single phrase conveying the offer's primary benefit ("1,000 songs in your pocket") (Ch 3).

Humanization — Using data to tell a real person's story, often via personas (Ch 11).

Importance — Everyone craves feeling Important; listening makes it happen (Ch 9).

Inhibition — The forebrain's ability to override instinct ("free won't"); fueled by Willpower (Ch 7).

Internal Controls — Standard procedures keeping finances accurate and protected (Ch 6).

Interdependence — Reliance of one system on others; tightly vs. loosely coupled (Ch 10).

Iron Law of the Market — Market size and quality cap every business (Ch 2).

Iteration Cycle (WIGWAM) — Watch, Ideate, Guess, Which?, Act, Measure (Ch 2).

Iteration Velocity — Speed through cycles; more at-bats beats one big bet (Ch 2).

Key Performance Indicator (KPI) — The few measurements of a system's critical parts (Ch 11).

Leverage — Borrowed money that magnifies gains and losses alike (Ch 6).

Lifetime Value — Total value of a customer over the whole relationship (Ch 6).

Locus of Control — Separate what you can control/influence from what you can't (Ch 8).

Loss Aversion — Losses feel ~2× as strong as equivalent gains (Ch 7).

Management — Coordinating a group toward a Goal amid Change and Uncertainty (Ch 9).

Mean / Median / Mode / Midrange — Four measures of typicality (Ch 11).

Mental Simulation — Imagining an action's result before acting; needs a "point B" Goal (Ch 7).

Middle Path — The shifting balance between too little and too much (Ch 12).

Minimum Economically Viable Offer (MEVO) — The smallest offer that produces an actual sale (Ch 2).

Monoidealism — The flow state of focusing all attention on one thing (Ch 8).

Most Important Tasks (MITs) — The 2–3 critical tasks that drive your results (Ch 8).

Motivation — An emotion linking feeling to action; "move away" beats "move toward" by default (Ch 7).

Narrative — A story (often Hero's Journey) that makes the customer the hero (Ch 3).

Next Action — The next concrete physical step to move a project forward (Ch 8).

Next Best Alternative — What each party does with no deal; power lies with who can walk away (Ch 4).

Normal Accidents — In tightly coupled systems, failure is "when," not "if" (Ch 10).

Norms — Historical measurements used as Context for current ones (Ch 11).

Novelty — New sensory data is required to hold Attention (Ch 7).

Onion Brain — Hindbrain (survival) → midbrain (emotion) → forebrain (logic) (Ch 7).

Option Orientation — When something goes wrong, focus on options, not the problem (Ch 9).

Overhead — Minimum ongoing resources to keep operating regardless of sales (Ch 6).

Paradox of Automation — The more efficient the automation, the more crucial its human operators (Ch 12).

Pattern Matching — The brain auto-learns cause-effect patterns; experts hold better ones (Ch 7).

Perceived Value — Better End Result + less user effort = higher value and price (Ch 2).

Perceptual Control — People act like thermostats: act only when a perception drifts out of range (Ch 7).

Permission — Asking to follow up after giving Free value; a reusable asset (Ch 3).

Personal R&D — Earmark ~5% of income for your own learning and tools (Ch 8).

Planning Fallacy — People underestimate completion times; plan anyway for the Mental Simulation (Ch 9).

Point of Market Entry — The moment someone crosses the interest threshold (Ch 3).

Power — The ability to influence others' actions: influence or compulsion (Ch 9).

Predictability — Customers want to know what to expect; deliver it the same way every time (Ch 5).

Pricing Power — Ability to raise prices over time without losing too many customers (Ch 6).

Pricing Uncertainty Principle — All prices are arbitrary but must be supported (Ch 4).

Priming — Programming your Pattern Matching to flag relevant information (Ch 8).

Probable Purchaser — The specific person perfectly suited to your offer (Ch 3).

Profit / Profit Margin — Bringing in more than you spend; the gap as a percentage (Ch 6).

Prototype — An early tangible representation made to gather feedback (Ch 2).

Proxy — Measuring a closely correlated stand-in for what you care about (Ch 11).

Purchasing Power — Sum of all liquid assets you can deploy (Ch 6).

Qualification — Deciding if a prospect is a good customer before they buy (Ch 3).

Ratio — Comparing two measurements by dividing one by the other (Ch 11).

Reactivation — Getting lapsed customers to buy again — cheapest revenue source (Ch 4).

Receptivity — How open someone is to your message (what + when) (Ch 3).

Reference Level — The set point/range that defines "under control" (Ch 7).

Refactoring — Improving a system's efficiency without changing its output (Ch 12).

Referrals — Transferring "known and liked" trust to a stranger (Ch 9).

Reinterpretation — Rewriting the meaning of past events to change future simulations (Ch 7).

Remarkability — Designing an offer literally worth remarking on (Purple Cow) (Ch 3).

Reorganization — Random trial-and-error when a Reference Level is violated but the fix is unknown (Ch 7).

Reputation — What people generally think of your offer; "branding" demystified (Ch 3).

Resilience — Toughness/flexibility to handle an uncertain world (Ch 12).

Risk Reversal — Shifting transaction risk from buyer to seller via a guarantee (Ch 4).

Return on Investment (ROI) — Value created per unit of time/resources invested (Ch 6).

Safety — Communication requires both parties feel safe; threatened people stonewall (Ch 9).

Sampling — Using a small random share of output as a proxy for the whole (Ch 11).

Scale — Ability to reliably Duplicate/Multiply as volume rises (Ch 5).

Scarcity — Limited quantity/time triggers Loss Aversion; fake scarcity backfires (Ch 7).

Scenario Planning — Constructing hypotheticals and simulating your response (Ch 12).

Second-Order Effects — Consequences have consequences, sometimes opposite to intent (Ch 10).

Segmentation — Splitting data into subgroups to reveal hidden relationships (Ch 11).

Selection Test — The environmental constraint deciding which systems survive (Ch 10).

Shadow Testing — Selling an offer before it exists (transparently) to test CIAs (Ch 2).

Social Proof — Learning how to act by watching others, especially when ambiguous (Ch 9).

Social Signals — Tangible indicators of an intangible quality (a Rolex's message) (Ch 9).

Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) — A predefined process for a recurring task (Ch 12).

States of Being — Present-experience qualities used as decision criteria, not goals (Ch 8).

Stress and Recovery — Run near, not at, 100%, with guilt-free rest (Ch 8).

Stress Testing — Simulating extremes to find a system's breaking point (Ch 12).

Sufficiency — The profit point that makes continuing worthwhile ("ramen profitable") (Ch 6).

Sunk Cost — Unrecoverable past investment that should not drive forward decisions (Ch 6).

Systemization — Making a process explicit, repeatable, and externalized (Ch 5).

Ten Ways to Evaluate a Market — Score a market 0–10 on ten dimensions before entering (Ch 2).

Threat Lockdown — Perceived threat triggers fight/flee/freeze, killing productive work (Ch 7).

Three Dimensions of Negotiation — Setup, Structure, Discussion (two happen before you sit down) (Ch 4).

Three Universal Currencies — Negotiations trade in resources, time, and flexibility (Ch 4).

Throughput — The rate at which a system reaches its goal (Ch 5, Ch 10).

Transaction — An exchange of value; the defining moment of every business (Ch 4).

Trust — Belief you'll deliver what you promise; no Trust, no Transaction (Ch 4).

Twelve Standard Forms of Value — Product, Service, Shared Resource, Subscription, Resale, Lease, Agency, Audience Aggregation, Loan, Option, Insurance, Capital (Ch 2).

Uncertainty — Unknown unknowns (black swans); distinct from plannable Risk (Ch 10).

Value Capture — Retaining a share of value created per transaction; too much and customers flee (Ch 6).

Value Stream — Every step from Value Creation through delivery to the customer (Ch 5).

Value-Based Selling — Reinforcing the Reasons Why the offer is valuable to this buyer (Ch 4).

Visualization — Helping prospects imagine life after accepting your offer (Ch 3).

Willpower Depletion — Willpower runs on glucose and depletes with use (Ch 7).

patterns.md

Patterns — Techniques & Procedures from The Personal MBA

Concrete, repeatable methods you can run. Each: when to use, how, trade-offs.

Test an Idea Before Building It (Shadow Testing + MEVO)

When to use: You have a business idea and want evidence of real demand before investing.

How:

  1. List your Critically Important Assumptions (CIAs) — the facts that must be true for it to work.
  2. Build a Prototype / Minimum Economically Viable Offer (MEVO): the smallest thing that can produce an actual sale (landing page, one-pager, mockup).
  3. Shadow Test: transparently offer it for sale (or take preorders) before it fully exists.
  4. Treat a preorder/payment as the only feedback that counts; refund if you can't deliver.

Trade-offs: Must stay transparent (don't take money you can't honor). Friends/family feedback is noise — only paying strangers validate.

Evaluate a Market Before Entering (Ten Ways + Iron Law)

When to use: Choosing among business or product ideas.

How: Score the market 0–10 on each: Urgency, Market Size, Pricing Potential, Cost of Customer Acquisition, Cost of Value Delivery, Uniqueness of Offer, Speed to Market, Up-Front Investment, Upsell Potential, Evergreen Potential. Sum and compare. Remember the Iron Law of the Market: a great offer to a market that doesn't want it still fails.

Trade-offs: Scores are estimates, not facts — use to compare options, not to predict revenue. A low total is a strong stop signal; a high total is not a guarantee.

Run an Improvement Loop (The Iteration Cycle — WIGWAM)

When to use: Improving any offer, process, or skill.

How: Watch what's happening → Ideate options → Guess which will help most → Which? (choose) → Act → Measure → repeat. Optimize for Iteration Velocity (cycles per unit of time/money).

Trade-offs: Favors many small bets over one big bet; needs honest measurement or it degenerates into noise.

Support a Price (Four Pricing Methods)

When to use: Setting or defending a price.

How: Compute all four as inputs — Replacement Cost (what to rebuild it), Market Comparison (what similar things sell for), Discounted Cash Flow/NPV (value of future cash it produces), Value Comparison (worth to this buyer). Use the first three as a floor/baseline; price on Value Comparison because it's almost always highest.

Trade-offs: Value pricing requires understanding the buyer's Reasons Why; without that you fall back to commodity (market) pricing.

Close More Sales (Trust + Risk Reversal + Damaging Admission)

When to use: Prospects hesitate at the buying moment.

How: Dissolve the five Barriers to Purchase (too expensive, won't work, won't work for me, can wait, too hard). Build Trust via Education-Based Selling; volunteer a real drawback (Damaging Admission) to raise credibility; apply Risk Reversal (strong guarantee) so the buyer, not the seller, is protected.

Trade-offs: Risk Reversal can attract abusers; price in the refund/return rate. Works only when you can actually deliver.

Grow Revenue (Four Methods)

When to use: You want more money from an existing business.

How: There are only four levers — (1) increase the number of customers, (2) increase average transaction size, (3) increase transaction frequency per customer, (4) raise prices. Pick the lever with least Friction first; Reactivation of lapsed customers is usually cheapest.

Trade-offs: Discounting to add customers can shrink margin; raising prices tests Pricing Power and may lose price-sensitive buyers.

Size Customer Acquisition Spend (Lifetime Value vs AAC)

When to use: Deciding how much to spend on marketing/acquisition.

How: Estimate Lifetime Value (total profit per customer over the relationship). Your Allowable Acquisition Cost (AAC) is the marketing share of that — spend up to AAC to win a customer and still profit.

Trade-offs: Overestimating LTV (ignoring churn) leads to overspending; revisit as real retention data arrives.

Find What You Actually Want (Five-Fold Why / Five-Fold How)

When to use: Goal-setting, or stuck on motivation.

How: Ask "why do I want this?" ~5 times to reach the core desire (a State of Being). Then ask "how can I get this?" ~5 times to descend to a concrete Next Action you can take now.

Trade-offs: Surfacing a deeper want can reveal your stated goal is the wrong one — useful but unsettling.
