cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — The Unspoken Rules

Decision rules and tells to keep beside you. The judgment, not the vocabulary.

The master test: the Three Cs

Before any move, ask: does this show competence, commitment, AND compatibility? Each fails two ways:

CUndershoot (reads as…)Overshoot (reads as…)Aim
Competenceclueless, sloppy, slowknow-it-all, makes others look baddo it fully, accurately, promptly
Commitmentapathetic, clock-watcherdoormat, burning out, fakepresent and eager, with boundaries
Compatibilitycold, hard to be aroundposer, sucking up, inauthenticcomfortable to work with, still yourself

Managers judge the perceived version of your work, not just the actual output. Make progress visible.

Should I act / ask / push? (curiosity vs. entitlement)

  • Imagine getting a flat "no." Honest reaction "just thought I'd ask" → ask, it's curiosity. Reaction "outrageous!" → don't, it's entitlement.
  • Worst case is almost always a "no," not danger. Fear is of judgment, not safety → give it a shot.
  • Got an unearned edge? Be less entitled. Habitually wait for permission? Be more.

Is this a good question to ask? (three circles)

  • I already know it → don't ask.
  • I could figure it out (Google, the wiki, 5 min) → figure it out, don't ask.
  • Only learnable by asking → ask — and show your homework: "Here's what I know, here's what I don't."

New here — which mode am I in?

  • Learner mode (new): expected to ask. Always have a good question ready; "Any questions?" is a yes-question.
  • Leader mode (established): expected to know and contribute. Don't ask what you should already own.

How urgent / important is this task?

  • Urgency = proximity + scrutiny + anxiety + time-sensitivity.
  • Importance = centrality + scrutiny + criticality.
  • Triage: urgent+important → do now · important not urgent → schedule · urgent not important → timebox/delegate · neither → delete.
  • Force-rank ties. Default: under-promise, over-deliver; no surprises.

Receiving a task — clarify before you start

  1. What / How / By When — get all three up front.
  2. RACI — who's Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed?
  3. Work backward from the deadline; ask for interim check-ins.
  4. Repeat it back to catch misunderstandings.
  5. Stuck? Propose A or B + a recommendation, never an open "what do you think?"

Before you hit Send (digital signals)

Typos? · Caught up on the thread? · Right time? · Tone matches intent? · OK if this gets forwarded?

  • Match the room: email-first vs. IM-first; monochronic (time = blocks, be prompt) vs. polychronic (time = fluid).
  • You're judged on impact, not intent — over-clarify in writing.

Appearance: how much to conform

  • Mirror coworkers at your level; unsure → default more formal.
  • Sort each element: Sacred (protect) · Negotiable (weigh by situation) · Indifferent (give away freely).
  • Tactic: bend — conform first, reveal your authentic self once trust is built.

Reading a new team (tells)

  • Power ≠ title. Watch who decisions route through → the influencer: Gatekeeper / Veteran / Expert / Socialite / Adviser.
  • Friendly ≠ loyal to you. Note first loyalties before confiding.
  • Swimlane rigid? → ask permission first. Loose? → act, then inform. In doubt → ask.
  • Don't overshoot your zone of commitment — it reads as threatening.

Decoding feedback (two axes)

VerbalNonverbal
IndirectSubtle hints (softened)Behavior changes (avoidance, micromanaging)
DirectUncensored comments (blunt)Blunt actions (work redone/reassigned/rejected)
  • Separate substance (what they mean) from delivery (how they said it). Ask the root cause.
  • Remember negativity bias — one criticism outweighs three compliments; don't spiral.
  • Ask: "What should I start / stop / keep doing?" Apply fast, report back (coachability = commitment).

Something's wrong — fix it / live with it / leave it

  1. Diagnose root cause: is it People / Position / Place? (Use the "Why?" exercise.)
  2. Strip emotion with 10-10-10: best in 10 minutes / 10 months / 10 years?
  3. Choose the path of least regret, not the fastest relief.
  4. Leaning toward leaving? Run the ten-question leave-it test — more "yes" = more sense to go. Protect your last impression.

Positioning for promotion

  • Nine-box: aim top-right = do today's job well AND show you can do the next one / lead.
  • Claim an unoccupied swimlane — what can I do / fix / bridge / know / share that no one owns?
  • Contribution counts only if noticed AND reported, and better (not merely different), on a mission-critical problem.
  • Asking for a raise: data + one-page summary + a specific number + appreciation.

Build relationships (when you know no one)

  • Answer bids (small connection requests) — don't let them drop.
  • Can't relate? Fall back to EAR: Engage, Ask, Repeat. Use "Yes, and…"
  • First move by audience: casual chat (nearby) / double opt-in intro (warm) / customized cold email (stranger).
  • Be an energy giver, not a complainer. Relationships compound — start early.

glossary.md

Glossary — The Unspoken Rules

Accountable — the person whose reputation is on the line for a deliverable; only one per task (Ch 8).

Ask-for-permission vs. beg-for-forgiveness spectrum — how rigid a team's swimlanes are; rigid → clear it first, loose → act then inform (Ch 10).

Authentic — true to who you are, as opposed to the average of your coworkers (Ch 6).

Bare-minimum rule — outcomes scale with the initiative you put in; doing only what's asked caps your results (Ch 2).

Bid — a small request for connection (a comment, question, gesture); relationships are built by noticing and answering bids (Gottman) (Ch 11).

Big picture / the eight blanks — understanding how your org and role fit the whole; the senior-leader mindset that turns a workhorse into a thought partner (Ch 3).

Blunt actions — direct + nonverbal feedback: reassigning, redoing, or rejecting your work (Ch 13).

Behavior changes — indirect + nonverbal feedback: avoidance, micromanaging, going quiet (Ch 13).

Boomerang employee — someone who leaves an organization and later returns, often at the same level (Ch 14).

Call to action — the specific response a message asks for; every message should make the next step obvious (Ch 8).

Coachability — visibly applying feedback; reading as coachable signals commitment (Ch 13).

Cold email — outreach to a stranger, customized enough that it can't be mistaken for spam (Ch 11).

Comfort zones — the topics and behaviors a given person treats as appropriate vs. taboo (Ch 10).

Commitment — being fully present and eager to help the team hit its goals; one of the Three Cs (Ch 1).

Compatibility — making others comfortable and glad to be around you, without seeming inauthentic; one of the Three Cs (Ch 1).

Competence — doing your job fully, accurately, and promptly without micromanagement or making others look bad; one of the Three Cs (Ch 1).

Curiosity vs. entitlement test — imagine getting a "no"; if your honest reaction is "just thought I'd ask," the ask is curiosity, not entitlement (Ch 2).

CYA ("cover yourself") — because digital messages are permanent and forwardable, communicate so a forwarded copy never hurts you (Ch 7).

Double opt-in intro — connecting two people only after both have agreed to be connected (Ch 11).

EAR (Engage, Ask, Repeat) — conversation fallback: engage, ask a question, repeat; default to questions when you can't relate (Ch 11).

Eight blanks — see Big picture: the gaps you fill to understand how everything fits (Ch 3).

Eisenhower Matrix (adapted) — triage by urgency × importance: do / schedule / timebox-or-delegate / delete (Ch 9).

Energy givers vs. energy vampires — people who add energy to a room vs. those who drain it with complaints; be the former (Ch 11).

External narrative — the audience-tailored version of your story that proves the Three Cs; lead with this, not the internal "me, me, me" version (Ch 5).

Feedback ranges — feedback mapped on two axes, verbal↔nonverbal and direct↔indirect (Ch 13).

Fire drill — a sudden, urgent demand that disrupts planned work (Ch 9).

First loyalties — who someone is loyal to first; friendly toward you ≠ on your side (Ch 10).

Fix it / live with it / leave it — the three responses to any bad situation (Ch 14).

Gatekeepers / Veterans / Experts / Socialites / Advisers — the five informal-influencer types who hold power beyond their title (Ch 10).

Good question — one you genuinely can't answer on your own; only learnable by asking (Ch 3).

Hero of your own journey — others are too busy with themselves to scrutinize you, so act (Ch 2).

Hero's journey (Past, Present, Future) — frame your story as origin → present → goal in about two minutes (Ch 5).

High-context vs. low-context — cultures/people who communicate through the unspoken vs. at face value (Ch 13).

IC (individual contributor) — someone who does the work directly rather than managing others (Ch 15).

Importance (three factors) — centrality, scrutiny, criticality: how much a task matters (Ch 9).

Indifferent zone — appearance/identity elements you can abandon without any felt loss (Ch 6).

Influencer — someone with leverage to sway decisions without formal authority (Ch 10).

Intent vs. impact — what you mean vs. how you come across; close the gap, especially in writing/remote work (Ch 7, Ch 13).

Internal narrative — your private "why I do this" story; build it first, but rarely lead with it (Ch 5).

Learner mode vs. leader mode — the two expectation states: new → expected to ask questions; established → expected to know and contribute (Ch 4, Ch 12).

"Let's give this a shot" — the mindset of trying things you might fail at but might succeed at (Ch 2).

Mental fridge — a stocked set of talking-point "ingredients" you can pull from to answer unexpected questions (Ch 5).

Mirroring — inferring the unspoken norm from coworkers at your level and matching it (Ch 6).

Monochronic vs. polychronic — cultures that treat time as fixed blocks vs. fluid and flexible (Ch 7).

Nine-box matrix — performance × potential grid; aim for the top-right box to position for promotion (Ch 15).

Negativity bias — criticism registers more strongly than praise; weight feedback accordingly (Ch 13).

Nonpromotable tasks / office housework — note-taking, lunch orders, event-planning: work that rarely advances a career and disproportionately falls on women and people of color (Ch 9, Ch 11).

Ownership — treating a task as if your reputation depends on it, including knowing when to ask for help (Ch 8).

Path of least regret — choose the option best for the long term, not the one that relieves discomfort fastest (Ch 14).

Pattern of behavior — your "whenever… always…" reputation; managed by being predictable (Ch 9).

People / Position / Place — the three root sources of a conflict; diagnose which before acting (Ch 14).

Perceived vs. actual — managers judge the perceived version of your work (visible progress, confidence), not just the actual output (Ch 1).

Performance vs. potential — effectiveness in your current job vs. ability to do the next one / lead (Ch 15).

Pre-day-one research (15 strategies) — a ~45-minute prep routine to "see the big picture" before any role, call, or meeting (Ch 3).

Preread / prework — materials circulated before a meeting; mining them yields your one comment + one question (Ch 12).

Promotable tasks — visible, valued work that advances your career; seek these over office housework (Ch 9).

Puddle (locality) — the scope of a problem: small, medium, or large; sets how far you must go to escape it (Ch 14).

RACI — Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed: clarify roles on any task (Ch 8).

Reject / embrace / bend the rules — three stances when your appearance doesn't "fit" the norm (Ch 6).

Sacred / negotiable / indifferent zones — three concentric circles for sorting which identity elements to protect, weigh, or give up (Ch 6).

Seen and heard / seen but not heard / neither — the three roles you can hold in a meeting; calibrate by size, attendees, topic (Ch 12).

Skip manager — your boss's boss (Ch 10).

Swimlane — what a person owns and when, regardless of their title (Ch 10, Ch 15).

Subtle hints — indirect + verbal feedback: softened, diluted messages (Ch 13).

Ten-ten-ten (10-10-10) — strip emotion from a decision by asking how each option feels in 10 minutes / 10 months / 10 years (Ch 14).

Three Cs — competence, commitment, compatibility; the book's central lens, needed all at once (Ch 1).

Three circles of question quality — what you know / what's figure-out-able / what's only learnable by asking; ask only from the outer circle (Ch 3).

Thought partner vs. workhorse — perceived as someone who grasps the big picture vs. someone who just executes (Ch 3).

Transferable skills — capabilities from a past role bridged explicitly to the new one (Ch 5).

Trade-off triangle (people/position/place) — you rarely get all three good at once; know which you're trading (Ch 14).

Uncensored comments — direct + verbal feedback: blunt, unsoftened criticism (Ch 13).

Undershooting vs. overshooting — each C fails in two directions: too little (clueless/apathetic) or too much (overbearing/poser) (Ch 1, Ch 5).

Unoccupied swimlane — an unclaimed but valuable need you can own to show potential (Ch 15).

Uptalking — rising intonation at the end of statements that undercuts perceived confidence (Ch 5).

Voluntelling — a higher-up framing an assigned task as if it were optional (Ch 4).

Virtuous circle — early relationships and opportunities compound into more of both (Ch 11).

What / how / by when — the three things to clarify the moment you receive any task (Ch 8).

"Why?" exercise — repeatedly asking "why is this happening?" to drill from symptom to root cause (Ch 9, Ch 14).

Zone of commitment — the scope you're authorized to act within; overshooting it reads as threatening (Ch 10).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — The Unspoken Rules

Concrete, repeatable methods from the book. Each: when to use, how, trade-offs.

The Three Cs

When: As a diagnostic lens on any workplace move, message, or decision.

How: Before acting, check that you're showing all three at once — Competence (do the job fully/accurately/promptly), Commitment (be present and eager for the team's goals), Compatibility (make others comfortable). For each, avoid undershooting (too little → clueless/apathetic) and overshooting (too much → overbearing/poser).

Trade-offs: Optimizing one C can dent another (e.g. over-asserting competence can hurt compatibility); balance, don't maximize.

"Let's Give This a Shot" + Curiosity vs. Entitlement Test

When: Facing an opportunity you might fail at, or unsure whether to ask for something.

How: Ask "what's the worst that can happen?" (usually a "no"). Then run the entitlement test: imagine the "no" — proceed only if your honest reaction is "just thought I'd ask," not outrage. Then act and let others say no.

Trade-offs: Some people need to be less entitled (got an unearned edge), some more (habitually wait for permission). Calibrate to which you are.

Pre-Day-One Research (15 strategies)

When: Before any new role, first call, big meeting, or interview.

How: ~45 min of higher-priority moves — skim Wikipedia/company About + News, recent Google news, memorize key faces, LinkedIn the people CC'd, confirm dress code + logistics (arrive 15 min early), set a Google Alert, accept intro chats — plus lower-priority depth (competitors, Glassdoor/Reddit, "anyone else I should speak with?"). Goal: see the big picture and fill "the eight blanks."

Trade-offs: Time-box it; research is prep, not a substitute for showing up and asking good questions.

Three Circles of Question Quality + "Do — and Show — Your Homework"

When: Before asking anything as a newcomer.

How: Sort the question — inner circle (you already know) / middle (figure-out-able → don't ask) / outer (only learnable by asking → ask). When you ask, narrate your work: "Here's what I know, here's what I don't" or "Here's my question and why I'm asking."

Trade-offs: Asking good questions early earns credit that buys leeway for naive questions later.

Twelve "Yes!" Onboarding Questions + Find Your Job

When: Starting a role, especially with weak onboarding.

How: Self-check you can answer "Yes!" to all twelve (paperwork, reporting lines, role expectations, check-in cadence, intros, priorities, tools/access, routine…). Where the answer is "no," ask the scripted question. If given tasks but no real role: observe & take notes, ask & learn, volunteer for work.

Trade-offs: Think like an owner — the gaps are yours to close even when no one hands you a map.

Tell Your Story: Internal vs. External Narrative (5 steps) + Mental Fridge

When: Any "tell me about yourself / why are you here" moment.

How: Build the internal narrative (your real why), then the external one (audience-tailored, proves the Three Cs), add structure (Past/Present/Future hero's journey), finesse style (no uptalking/overshooting), and practice. Stock a "mental fridge" of talking-point ingredients to answer the unexpected.

Trade-offs: Lead external, not internal — the "me, me, me" version reads as self-absorbed.

Manage Appearance: Mirror, then Reject/Embrace/Bend + Sacred/Negotiable/Indifferent

When: Deciding how much to conform your look/identity to a workplace.

How: Infer the unspoken norm by mirroring coworkers at your level (default more formal when unsure). Choose to reject, embrace, or bend (conform first, reveal authentic self after building trust). Sort each element into sacred (protect), negotiable (weigh), indifferent (give away freely).

Trade-offs: Over-adapting wastes energy on things coworkers never noticed; protect what's sacred.

Send the Right Signals: Five Questions Before Send + Intent vs. Impact

When: Before sending any message; calibrating remote/written presence.

How: Before send, check — typos? caught up on the thread? right time? tone matches intent? OK if forwarded? Match the team's email-first vs. IM-first culture, and its monochronic (time = blocks) vs. polychronic (time = fluid) rhythm.

Trade-offs: You're judged on impact, not intent; permanent digital signals mean over-clarify rather than assume.

Take Ownership: What/How/By When + RACI + Give Others Something to React To

When: The moment you receive any task.

How: Clarify what, how, by when immediately; map RACI (who's Responsible/Accountable/Consulted/Informed); work backward from the deadline with interim check-ins. For non-urgent questions: search first, bundle them, escalate one rung with context. When stuck, propose option A/B with a recommendation instead of asking an open "what do you think?"

Trade-offs: Repeating the task back feels redundant but catches costly misunderstandings early.

Manage Workload: Urgency × Importance Triage

When: Too much to do; deciding order.

How: Score urgency by four factors (proximity, scrutiny, anxiety, time-sensitivity) and importance by three (centrality, scrutiny, criticality). Triage on the adapted Eisenhower Matrix: do / schedule / timebox-or-delegate / delete. Preempt predictable patterns (Friday updates, post-holiday clearing, templates) and report problems at root cause via the "Why?" exercise.

Trade-offs: Seek promotable work over office housework; under-promise and over-deliver to avoid surprises.

Read between the People (5 steps) + Five Influencer Types

When: Joining any new team.

How: Map (1) the chain of command, (2) the influencers, (3) swimlanes, (4) loyalties, (5) comfort zones — by observing behavior and language, not titles. Spot the five influencer types (Gatekeepers, Veterans, Experts, Socialites, Advisers) by who decisions route through. Gauge swimlane rigidity on the ask-permission ↔ beg-forgiveness spectrum.

Trade-offs: Friendly ≠ loyal; don't mistake an early ally's warmth for first loyalty.

Spark Relationships: Spark → Play → Sustain + Bids + EAR

When: Building a network from zero.

How: Respond to others' bids for connection; keep conversation flowing with EAR (Engage, Ask, Repeat) and "Yes, and…"; tailor the first move to the audience (casual chat / double opt-in intro / customized cold email); sustain ties over time. Be an energy giver.

Trade-offs: Relationships compound (virtuous circle) — small early investment pays outsized later returns.

Master Meetings: Seven Questions + Three Roles + One Comment + One Question

When: Before, during, and after any meeting.

How: Run the seven prep/participation/follow-up questions, scaling depth to the meeting's importance. Calibrate your role — seen and heard / seen but not heard / neither — by size, attendees, and topic. With prep time, mine the preread for one thoughtful comment + one thoughtful question (what's missing/confusing/wrong/unexpected).

Trade-offs: Every meeting has a hidden goal and two unspoken duties — to learn and to represent your team.

Manage Feedback: The Feedback Ranges + Intent Behind Impact + Feedback Meeting

When: Receiving or soliciting feedback.

How: Locate the feedback on two axes (verbal↔nonverbal, direct↔indirect) → subtle hints / uncensored comments / behavior changes / blunt actions. Separate substance (what they mean) from delivery (how they said it). In a feedback meeting, ask "what should I start / stop / keep doing?", apply fast, and report back.

Trade-offs: Negativity bias makes criticism sting; coachability (visibly applying it) is itself a signal of commitment.

Resolve Conflicts: Fix it / Live with it / Leave it

When: Any persistently bad work situation.

How: Diagnose root cause via People / Position / Place (and the "Why?" exercise). Strip emotion with 10-10-10 (how does each option feel in 10 min / 10 months / 10 years). Then fix it tactfully, live with it, or leave graciously — choosing the path of least regret. Use the leave-it ten-question test when weighing quitting.

Trade-offs: The people/position/place trade-off triangle means you rarely fix all three; your last impression matters as much as your first.

Show Your Potential: Nine-Box + Unoccupied Swimlane + Ask-for-It

When: Positioning for a raise or promotion.

How: Aim for the top-right of the performance × potential nine-box (do your job well and show you can do the next one). Claim an unoccupied swimlane via the five questions (what can I do / fix / bridge / know / share?). Prioritize contributions that are noticed and reported, and that are better (not just different). To ask for a raise: bring data, a one-pager, a specific number, and appreciation.

Trade-offs: Different-but-unnoticed work doesn't count; aim for better-and-visible on a mission-critical problem.

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Think Faster, Talk Smarter

The method in one line

Calm · Unlock · Redefine · Listen · Structure · Focus — manage your state, lower the bar, reframe, listen, pick a structure, then trim. Aim to be great, not perfect.

Pick a structure (the core decision)

The moment is…Use this structure
Anything general (answer, update, reaction)What? / So What? / Now What?
Stating an opinion / a crisp answerPREP (Point–Reason–Example–Point)
Persuading / pitching / proposingProblem / Solution / Benefit
Reporting change / a status updatePast / Present / Future
Toast, tribute, introductionWHAT: Why here → How connected → Anecdote → Thank
Answering a question / interviewADD: Answer → Detail an example → Describe the value
Giving feedback4 I's: Information → Impact → Invitation → Implications
ApologizingAAA: Acknowledge → Appreciate → Amends

Rule: choose the structure first, then fill it. You assemble in the moment; the structure did the thinking.

In-the-moment rules

  • Nervous? → it's a conversation, not a performance. Exhale long, greet the anxiety, use your mantra. Channel it — don't fight it.
  • Freezing / over-thinking? → dare to be dull. Get merely-okay words out; fluency beats flawless.
  • Feel "put on the spot"? → relabel threat → opportunity before you speak.
  • Asked a question? → pause and listen (pace & space); buffer by paraphrasing to buy time; then answer what was actually asked.
  • Rambling? → run it through the Focus filters: Precision → Relevance → Accessibility → Concision. Cut the rest.
  • Don't know the answer? → say so honestly + how you'll find out. Credibility > bluffing.

Focus filters (trim any answer)

Precision (exact words) · Relevance (only what this audience needs) · Accessibility (plain, relatable, no jargon) · Concision (fewest words). When in doubt, cut.

Small talk

  • Favor support responses (ask more, build on theirs) over shift responses (redirect to yourself).
  • Match self-disclosure levels; don't put your partner on the spot; treat it as a shared game, not a test.

Apology that works — AAA (Ch 12)

Acknowledge the specific offense and own it (no "if," no "but") → Appreciate the impact, especially the emotional one → Amends: state what you'll do or change. Avoid "sorry you felt that way" — it deepens the breach.

Feedback that lands — the 4 I's (Ch 11)

Information (specific, unemotional observation) → Impact ("I feel/think…") → Invitation (a request, ideally a question) → Implications (consequences of changing or not).

Tells you're in perfectionism/anxiety mode

Scripting every word · replaying the "spotlight" (overestimating how much others notice) · long runway before answering · fillers ("um") from held breath · fixating on being right. → breathe, dare to be dull, pick a structure.

Prep that pays off (do it cold)

Rehearse What/So What/Now What, PREP, and Problem/Solution/Benefit until automatic; pre-list your likely Q&A questions. Structures only help in the moment if you don't have to think about them.

glossary.md

Glossary — Think Faster, Talk Smarter

AAA — the apology structure: Acknowledge (the specific offense, owned) → Appreciate (its impact, esp. emotional) → Amends (what you'll do/change) (Ch 12).

ADD — the Q&A answer structure: Answer (one declarative sentence) → Detail an example (concrete evidence) → Describe the value (relevance to the asker). Order is flexible; all three should appear (Ch 10).

Accessibility — one of the four Focus filters: make ideas easy to grasp — plain language, relatable framing, no jargon (Ch 6).

Back-pocket question — a ready-made question you pose yourself ("A question I often get is…") to break the ice when no one asks in Q&A (Ch 10).

The 4 I's — the feedback structure: Information (specific, unemotional observation) → Impact ("I feel/think…") → Invitation (a request, ideally phrased as a question) → Implications (consequences of changing or not) (Ch 11).

Anxiety Beast — Abrahams' name for speaking anxiety; managed (not eliminated) by addressing both symptoms and sources (Ch 1).

Buffering — in Q&A, briefly restating or bridging from a question to buy thinking time and ensure you answer what was actually asked (Ch 10).

Concision — one of the four Focus filters: say it in as few words as needed; less is more (Ch 6).

Dare to be Dull — the Unlock mantra: give yourself permission to be merely adequate; lowering the bar frees you to speak fluently (Ch 2).

Focus (the F-word) — the sixth step: streamline what you say through Precision, Relevance, Accessibility, Concision (Ch 6).

Greeting your anxiety — acknowledging nervousness ("hello, anxiety") instead of fighting it, which reduces its grip (Ch 1).

Growth mindset — seeing spontaneous-speaking ability as improvable through practice; part of Redefining the situation (Ch 3).

Inner critic — the self-monitoring voice that drives perfectionism and freezing; quieted in the Unlock step (Ch 2).

Maximize Mediocrity — the aim of the Unlock step: accept "good enough" in the moment so you can actually perform (Ch 2).

Opportunity, not threat — the core Redefine reframe: treat being put on the spot as a chance, changing your physiology and performance (Ch 3).

Pace and space — giving yourself time and room (pausing, listening) before responding, rather than rushing (Ch 4).

PREP — a spontaneous structure: Point, Reason, Example, Point; for clear opinions and answers (Ch 5).

Precision — one of the four Focus filters: choose exact, concrete words that convey your meaning (Ch 6).

Problem–Solution–Benefit — the persuasion/pitch structure: name the problem, present the solution, spell out the benefit (Ch 5, 9).

Past–Present–Future — a structure for narrating change, updates, and transitions (Ch 5).

Relevance — one of the four Focus filters: include only what matters to this audience (Ch 6).

Shift vs. Support response — in conversation, a "shift" turns attention to yourself; a "support" response keeps focus on the other person — favor support (Ch 7).

Six-Step Method — Calm, Unlock, Redefine, Listen, Structure, Focus: the book's core methodology for spontaneous speaking (Part I).

Spontaneous speaking — unplanned, in-the-moment communication (questions, small talk, toasts, feedback); the book's whole subject.

Structure — a simple reusable story spine (not a script) that organizes thoughts on the fly; the fifth step (Ch 5).

WHAT formula — for toasts/tributes/introductions: Why are we here → How are you connected → Anecdotes/learnings → Thank (Ch 8).

What? So What? Now What? — the most versatile spontaneous structure: what it is → why it matters → what to do next (Ch 5).

patterns.md

Patterns & Structures — Think Faster, Talk Smarter

Structures are the heart of the method: rehearse them cold, and in the moment you only fill in the blanks.

What? / So What? / Now What?

When to use: the universal default — answers, updates, reactions, feedback, most on-the-spot moments.

How: What = describe the thing/idea/situation. So What = why it matters to this audience. Now What = the implication, next step, or ask.

Trade-offs: so flexible it can feel generic; sharpen with a concrete example in the "What."

PREP (Point, Reason, Example, Point)

When to use: stating an opinion or giving a crisp answer under pressure.

How: Point (your position) → Reason (why) → Example (evidence/story) → Point (restate).

Trade-offs: best for single clear claims; less suited to complex multi-part answers.

Problem / Solution / Benefit

When to use: persuading, pitching, proposing, selling an idea (Ch 9).

How: Problem (the pain, made concrete) → Solution (your proposal) → Benefit (what the listener gains).

Trade-offs: weak if the "problem" isn't one the audience feels — establish the problem first.

Past / Present / Future

When to use: status updates, narrating change, transitions, career/story questions.

How: where we were → where we are → where we're going.

Trade-offs: chronological, so it can drag — compress past/present, dwell on future.

The WHAT formula (toasts, tributes, introductions — Ch 8)

When to use: weddings, launches, panels, farewells, introducing a speaker.

How: Why are we here (the occasion) → How are you connected to the honoree → Anecdotes or learnings (one vivid story) → Thank (close with gratitude). Keep it about them.

Trade-offs: brevity matters — one anecdote, not three.

ADD — the Q&A answer structure (Ch 10)

When to use: fielding questions after a talk, in interviews, in meetings, tough questions from a boss.

How: A — Answer the actual question in one clear declarative sentence (no preamble) → D — Detail an example (a few sentences of concrete evidence) → D — Describe the value (relevance/benefit to the asker; for a negative question, use this step to state your remedy/plan). Order is flexible but keep all three. Prep likely + toughest questions in advance; keep a back-pocket question; wait five seconds before closing; answer honestly ("I don't know — I'll follow up by Friday").

Trade-offs: don't over-elaborate the example; don't bluff.

Anxiety-Management Toolkit (Calm — Ch 1)

When to use: before/at the moment of being put on the spot.

How: reframe as a conversation, not a performance; greet the anxiety; take slow exhale-heavy breaths (belly breathing) to lower arousal; use a grounding mantra; hold objects / cool your hands to manage physical symptoms; stay present-focused.

Trade-offs: aim to channel moderate anxiety (it sharpens you), not erase it.

Dare to be Dull (Unlock — Ch 2)

When to use: when perfectionism is making you freeze or over-prepare.

How: deliberately lower the bar — permit a merely-okay response; quiet the inner critic; get the first words out. Fluency beats flawlessness.

Trade-offs: not license to be careless — it's a starter to break the freeze.

Redefine the Situation (Redefine — Ch 3)

When to use: the instant you feel "put on the spot."

How: relabel threat → opportunity, test → conversation, verdict → practice. The label you assign changes your physiology and behavior.

Trade-offs: takes rehearsal to make the reframe automatic under stress.

Listen with Pace and Space (Listen — Ch 4)

When to use: before responding to any question or comment.

How: pause; listen to what's said and unsaid and to your own intuition; give yourself space rather than rushing to fill silence. Then respond to what's actually needed.

Trade-offs: silence feels longer to you than to them — tolerate it.

Focus Filters (Focus — Ch 6)

When to use: to tighten any spontaneous response.

How: run it through Precision (exact words) → Relevance (only what this audience needs) → Accessibility (plain, relatable) → Concision (fewest words). Cut the rest.

Trade-offs: over-editing in real time can stall you — apply lightly, favor concision.

Support (not Shift) responses (Small talk — Ch 7)

When to use: conversations, networking, small talk.

How: when someone shares, respond with a support move (ask more, build on it) rather than a shift move (redirect to your own story). Seek comparable self-disclosure; don't put your partner on the spot.

Trade-offs: too much support with no sharing feels like an interview — balance.

The 4 I's — the feedback structure (Ch 11)

When to use: giving feedback in the moment — to a report, peer, boss, student, or child.

How: Information (specific, verifiable observation, emotion stripped out; scope what you're not discussing) → Impact (the effect on you, first-person: "I feel/think…", which lowers defensiveness) → Invitation (a specific request, ideally a question — "How can we…?" — or a declarative for urgency) → Implications (positive/negative consequences of adopting or rejecting the change).

Trade-offs: skipping Impact makes it feel like an attack; skipping Invitation makes it a lecture, not a collaboration.

AAA — the apology structure (Ch 12)

When to use: after you've caused offense or dropped the ball ("emergency roadside assistance" for a relationship).

How: Acknowledge the specific offending behavior and own it (no justifying/minimizing) → Appreciate the impact on others, especially the emotional consequences (don't "put it in perspective") → Amends — state specifically what you'll do, stop doing, or how your thinking will change.

Trade-offs: a defensive or conditional apology ("sorry you felt that way," "I'm sorry, but…") worsens the breach.

Think Like a Rocket Scientist

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Think Like a Rocket Scientist

Decision rules and tells for reasoning under uncertainty, generating ideas, testing them, and learning from outcomes.

If / Then decision rules

If you're…Then…
Paralyzed by a scary leapName the worst and best case in writing; turn unknown unknowns into known unknowns
Justifying something only with "we've always done it this way"You've found an invisible rule — question it; the best way to expose a rule is to violate it
Copying a competitor's playbookStop — you're in a "smartness contest with everyone who came before"; reason from first principles or invert
Stuck on HOW to solve itQuestion the WHAT — reframe the problem; ask "What problem is this tactic here to solve?"
In love with your first solutionBreed multiple conflicting hypotheses; you're probably solving the wrong problem
BrainstormingDiverge first (be the fly, "What could we do?"), converge second (be the bee) — never reverse the order
Aiming for 10% improvementAim 10x instead — force a new approach, not an incremental tweak
Starting an audacious projectDo the monkey first (hardest part); set kill metrics now, while clearheaded
About to trust a test that "passed"Test to fail — hunt the breaking point; exaggerate the flaw you found
Feeling the dopamine of being proven rightTry to prove yourself wrong — every "no" carries more information than a "yes"
On a winning streakAssume you're slightly behind; run a postmortem on the success
About to act on a big decisionRun a premortem — assume it failed, list why, assign probabilities
Relying on a safety net (redundancy, deadline extension, ABS)Pretend it isn't there (risk homeostasis)

Idea generation (separate from judgment)

  • Generate before you evaluate. Idea generation and idea evaluation are different modes — don't let "we've tried that / no budget / won't be approved" kill ideas before generation finishes.
  • Be the fly, not the bee: flutter freely first; the bee dies bumping the light.
  • Ask "What would a science-fiction solution look like?" and "What could we do?" (not "should").
  • Compare apples and oranges — collect diverse inputs, then connect them.
  • Get bored on purpose — the answer arrives when you walk away.

Tells of the certainty trap (Ch 1)

  • You're "looking for keys under the street lamp" — choosing the familiar/safe because that's where the light is.
  • You're forcing a definite conclusion onto genuinely ambiguous evidence.
  • You feel a story clicking into place (narrative fills the vacuum of understanding).
  • You're ignoring the anomaly that doesn't fit ("That's funny…" is the entrance to discovery — don't discard it).
  • Antidote: say "I don't know"; be "uncomfortably uncertain over comfortably wrong."

Tells of the success trap (Ch 9)

  • "We got away with it last time, so we can lower the standard a bit" (normalization of deviance).
  • A recurring flaw has quietly become an "acceptable risk."
  • You're calling something "routine"; you've stopped running postmortems.
  • Near misses feel like wins — you treat "no harm" as "no foul."
  • Dissenters are being branded downers; the burden has shifted to prove danger rather than prove safety.
  • Antidote: stay in "Day 1"; treat yourself as a permanent work in progress; fix the cause behind the cause.

Testing (test as you fly)

  • Make the test mirror flight; then fly as you tested. Any gap can be catastrophic.
  • Test the assembled system, not just the parts ("understand the 'and'"); retest the whole after any change.
  • Observe behavior, don't self-report — put the iPhone in their hands; watch people grimace.
  • Diversify testing instruments and calibration targets — never rely on one.

Failure (learn fast, not fail fast)

  • Ask both "What went wrong?" and "What went right?" — keep the good inputs (Amazon's Fire → other tech; failed angina drug → Viagra).
  • Judge inputs, not outputs — avoid "resulting" (a good decision can produce a bad outcome).
  • Reward excellent failures, punish mediocre successes.
  • Leaders advertise their own failures to build psychological safety.
  • A single failure ≠ final defeat; breakthroughs are evolutionary ("solve one problem, then the next").

The three stages (map)

StageMoveCore principles
LaunchIgnite thinkingDance with uncertainty · first principles · a mind at play · moonshots
AcceleratePropel ideasReframe the question · prove yourself wrong · test as you fly
AchieveLearn from outcomesIntelligent failure · guard against the success trap

glossary.md

Glossary — Think Like a Rocket Scientist

Antelopes vs. mice — Go after the big prize, not the sure small one; a lion burns more energy catching a mouse than it yields, while an antelope feeds it for days (Ch 4).

Backcasting — Starting from an imagined future and working backward to the steps, letting vision drive resources instead of forecasting forward from current resources (Ch 4).

Beginner's mind (shoshin) — Approaching a problem as an outsider with no stake in the status quo; "in the beginner's mind there are many possibilities; in the expert's mind there are few" (Ch 3).

Breaking point (test to fail) — Designing tests for the worst case to find where a thing breaks, before reality breaks it; exaggerate a flaw rather than dismiss it as an outlier (Ch 7).

Certainty fetish / certainty trap — The compulsion to make ambiguous things appear definite, leading us to "look for keys under the street lamp" (Ch 1).

Combinatory play — Recombining ideas from unrelated fields ("compare apples and oranges"); "to create is to recombine" (Ch 3).

Confirmation bias — Overvaluing evidence that confirms our beliefs and undervaluing what contradicts them; coined by Peter Wason (Ch 6).

Connoisseur of uncertainty — Someone exhilarated rather than frightened at the edge of the known; they "dance" in the dark room (Ch 1).

Convergent thinking (the bee) — Narrowing to the seemingly obvious solution; useful for evaluation but deadly if used first (the bees die bumping the light) (Ch 4).

Dance with uncertainty — Treating the unknown as friend not foe; "first chaos, then breakthrough" (Ch 1).

Divergent thinking (the fly) — Free, open-ended idea generation without judging constraints; the flies find the exit by fluttering (Ch 4).

Einstellung effect — A fixed mental set: once a familiar solution is known, we stop seeing better alternatives (Ch 5).

Falsifiability — A hypothesis has value only if it can be proven wrong (Popper); separates science from pseudoscience (Ch 6).

Family of hypotheses — Generating multiple, ideally conflicting, working hypotheses so you can't fall in love with one (Ch 6).

First-principles thinking — Stripping a problem to its irreducible fundamentals and reasoning up from there, instead of by analogy (Ch 2).

Flip-flopping (as a virtue) — Changing your mind when the facts change; "I'd rather be right than consistent" (Ch 6).

Frankenstein's monster / Frankenstate — Individually benign components turning catastrophic in combination; why you must test the assembled system ("understand the 'and'") (Ch 7).

Functional fixedness — A mental block against using an object in a new way (Duncker's candle-box problem); dissolved by seeing form over function (Ch 5).

How fascinating! — A curiosity ritual that strips the drama out of a failure and creates emotional distance (Ch 8).

Intelligent failure — A failure from exploring the edges and solving unsolved problems; an investment and teacher, unlike sloppy failure (Ch 8).

Inputs over outputs — Judging decisions by their quality, not by outcomes you don't fully control; avoids "resulting" (Ch 8).

Invisible rules — Habits that have rigidified into rules without anyone deciding they should ("tie the cat to the pole") (Ch 2).

Inversion ("What if we did the reverse?") — Flipping a question or best practice on its head; "invert, always invert" (Ch 5).

It remains Day 1 — Treating every success as a fresh start; "Day 2 is stasis… followed by decline" (Bezos) (Epilogue).

Kill metrics — Predefined go/no-go criteria set while clearheaded, so you can quit a moonshot before sunk cost distorts judgment (Ch 4).

Kill-the-company / red teaming — Playing the antagonist trying to destroy you, then switching back to defend the weak points (Ch 2).

Learn fast, not fail fast — The goal is the lesson, not the crash; celebrate the learning, never failure itself (Ch 8).

Margins of safety — Building stronger/thicker than the minimum required, sized to the stakes and the irreversibility of the decision (Ch 1).

Medici effect — The creative explosion when people from different disciplines are combined (Ch 3).

Monkey first — Tackling the hardest, riskiest part of a project before the easy "pedestal" work (Ch 4).

Moonshot (10x not 10%) — An audacious goal so big the status quo has to go, forcing first-principles solutions (Ch 4).

Near miss — An incident that could have been a hit; masquerades as success because luck held, and breeds complacency rather than urgency (Ch 9).

Normalization of deviance — Repeated success with a known flaw turning an anomaly into an "acceptable risk" (O-rings, foam-shedding) (Ch 9).

Occam's razor — Given two hypotheses that explain the data equally well, prefer the simpler — a guiding principle, not an absolute rule ("seek simplicity and distrust it") (Ch 2).

Observer effect — Being watched changes behavior; mitigate with double-blind tests and real-world observation (Ch 7).

Path dependence — What we've done before shapes what we do next (the shuttle's engine width traced to Roman roads) (Ch 2).

Permanent work in progress — Never declaring a project or yourself finished or "routine"; train like you're #2 (Ch 9).

Premortem — Before acting, assuming the project failed and working backward to why; the inverse of backcasting; assign probabilities (Ch 9).

Problem finding (reframe the question) — Searching for a better question instead of a better answer; "a problem well defined is a problem half solved" (Ch 5).

Psychological safety — A climate where "no one will be punished or humiliated for errors, questions, or requests for help" (Edmondson) (Ch 8).

Redundancy — A backup that prevents a single point of failure from killing the mission; must be independent to work ("fail without failing") (Ch 1).

Resulting — Equating the quality of a decision with the quality of its outcome (Annie Duke) (Ch 8, Ch 9).

Risk homeostasis (the unsafety of safety) — Safety measures offset by riskier behavior; "pretend the crosswalk isn't marked" (Ch 9).

Risking your significance — Abandoning the identity story that constrains you (Steve Martin quitting stand-up at his peak) (Ch 2).

Steel man — Articulating the strongest version of an opposing argument before rejecting it; the opposite of a straw man (Ch 6).

Strategy vs. tactics — Strategy is the objective; tactics are the actions serving it — "What problem is this tactic here to solve?" (Ch 5).

Success is a lousy teacher — Success seduces smart people into thinking they can't lose; a wolf in sheep's clothing (Ch 9).

Test as you fly, fly as you test — Making tests mirror real "flight" conditions, then operating as you tested (Ch 7).

Thought experiment (Gedankenexperiment) — Running a fictional scenario in "the laboratory of the mind" to disprove or illuminate (Ch 3).

Two-way vs. one-way doors — Reversible vs. irreversible decisions; keep the door two-way when you can (Ch 1).

Unknown knowns — Self-delusion: thinking we know what we know but don't; the land of false confidence (Ch 1).

Working hypothesis — A testable, disposable work-in-progress belief, held "for the sake of the facts" — the opposite of an opinion (Ch 6).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Think Like a Rocket Scientist

Concrete, reusable methods Varol draws from rocket science for work and life.

Name Your Fear (Worst-Case / Best-Case on Paper)

When to use: Before a scary, paralyzing leap into the unknown.

How: In writing, ask "What's the worst that can happen, and how likely given what I know?" AND "What's the best that can happen?" Turn unknown unknowns into known unknowns.

Trade-offs: The naming defangs fear (usually worse than the fact), but forces you to confront things you'd rather not see. Pair with redundancies and margins of safety for irreversible one-way decisions.

First-Principles Teardown

When to use: A high-leverage problem where the conventional answer is expensive, stuck, or inherited without reason.

How: Break the thing to its fundamental components/physics ("What is a rocket made of?"), find the true cost/constraint of those fundamentals, then rebuild up from there instead of copying a template.

Trade-offs: Effortful; deploy where it matters most, not on every daily decision. Reason by analogy for the trivial.

Question Your Assumptions ("What if this weren't true?")

When to use: To expose invisible rules governing your work or life.

How: Spend a day questioning each commitment, budget line, and process: "Why am I doing it this way? Can I get rid of this or replace it?" The best way to expose a rule is to violate it. Be suspicious when you list multiple reasons to keep something.

Trade-offs: Not everything should be questioned constantly — routines free you from decision fatigue.

Kill-the-Company / Red Teaming

When to use: To surface blind spots invisible from the inside; before a big strategic bet.

How: Play the competitor trying to put you out of business; generate the attacks; then switch back and defend the weak points. Personal version: "Why is this employer justified in not hiring me?"

Trade-offs: Emotionally uncomfortable; requires genuinely inhabiting the adversary rather than humblebragging.

Thought Experiments ("What if?")

When to use: Testing an idea, disproving an assumption, or finding a path before any physical experiment.

How: Construct a fictional world where things work differently, run it in imagination, follow the logic to its extreme to surface contradictions. The word experiment lowers the stakes — if it fails, nothing bad happens.

Trade-offs: The goal is to ignite inquiry, not to be immediately right; some experiments lead nowhere but still shake you off autopilot.

Deliberate Boredom / Incubation

When to use: When a hard problem won't yield to direct effort.

How: Schedule distraction-free unstructured time — walks, showers, a "Think Week," a daydreaming chair. Switch the brain from focused to diffuse mode and let the subconscious connect ideas.

Trade-offs: Feels unproductive and underwhelming in an instant-gratification culture; creativity arrives as a whisper, not a bang.

Combinatory Play (Compare Apples and Oranges)

When to use: A creative jam or the need for a genuinely novel solution.

How: Collect diverse inputs across disciplines, then connect the dissimilar. Ask "What other industry has faced this before?" Recruit cognitively diverse people (the Medici effect); cycle between solitude and collaboration.

Trade-offs: The fit is rarely perfect, but the act of comparing sparks new lines of thought.

Moonshot Framing (10x not 10%)

When to use: When you want a breakthrough, not a marginal gain.

How: Set a goal so large the status quo can't reach it (eliminate all accidents, not improve safety). The bigness forces first-principles solutions and clears the crowded center where competitors chase mice.

Trade-offs: Requires tolerating a portfolio where most bets fail; must be paired with pragmatic execution.

Diverge Then Converge (Fly, Then Bee)

When to use: Any idea-generation problem.

How: First be a "fly" — generate wildly, "This could be done if…," ask "What could you do?" and "What would a science-fiction solution look like?" Only then switch to the "bee": rapid evaluation, kill metrics, business plans. Never let judgment kill ideas before generation finishes.

Trade-offs: Order matters — converging first ("we've tried that, no budget") strangles originality.

Backcasting & Monkey First

When to use: Planning toward an audacious goal.

How: Work backward from the imagined future (or happy customer — Amazon's pre-written press release) to the steps. Then tackle the hardest, riskiest part first (train the monkey before building the pedestal) and set kill metrics up front.

Trade-offs: Don't treat the plan as a bible ("detailed dreams blind you to new means"); the pedestal is satisfying busywork that postpones the real risk.

Reframe the Question (Strategy vs. Tactics, Function vs. Form, Inversion)

When to use: When stuck, or before committing to solve any problem.

How: Spend more time in problem definition. Ask "What problem is this tactic here to solve?" to find the strategy. Describe tools function-free to defeat functional fixedness. Ask "What if I did the reverse?" to beat stronger competitors.

Trade-offs: Feels slower than jumping to answers, but the framing of the question determines the answer.

Prove Yourself Wrong (Falsification)

When to use: Testing any belief before you commit.

How: Hold working hypotheses, not opinions (change your vocabulary). Breed multiple conflicting hypotheses. Generate cases that would break your rule (like the 2-4-6 game), not confirm it. Ask "What's missing? What fact would change my mind?" Seek dissent and steel-man opponents.

Trade-offs: Self-falsification is genuinely unpleasant (no dopamine hit), but every "no" carries more information than a "yes."

Test as You Fly, Fly as You Test

When to use: Before any launch, speech, interview, or high-stakes performance.

How: Recreate real conditions (jittery, in an unfamiliar room, with a stranger throwing curveballs). Test to fail — hunt the breaking point and exaggerate flaws. Test the assembled system, not just parts. Observe real behavior instead of self-reports; diversify testing instruments and calibration targets.

Trade-offs: Harder and less comfortable than a friendly dress rehearsal, but any gap between test and flight can be catastrophic.

Celebrate Intelligent Failure & Near-Miss Reporting

When to use: Building a team that must take risks and surface problems.

How: Reward excellent failures, punish mediocre successes. Leaders advertise their own failures repeatedly to build psychological safety. Focus on inputs, not outputs. Keep a "black box" and a "Flight Rules" catalog so lessons endure. Mine near misses — frequent, cheap, predictive.

Trade-offs: Requires distinguishing intelligent from sloppy failure; hold people accountable for failing to learn, not for failing.

Guard Against the Success Trap

When to use: After success and hot streaks.

How: Treat everything as a permanent work in progress; drop "routine." Run postmortems after wins ("What went wrong with this success? What role did luck play?"). Run premortems before acting (assume failure, list causes, assign probabilities). Fix the cause behind the cause. Distrust the safety net (risk homeostasis) and protect dissent.

Trade-offs: Wanting less uninterrupted success feels irrational, but regularity signals hidden fragility.

Thinking in Bets: Making Smarter Decisions When You Don't Have All the Facts
