cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Thinking in Bets

Decision rules and tells to keep beside you while deciding, learning, and communicating under uncertainty.

Core reflexes

  • Bad outcome? Ask first: bad decision or bad luck? Judge the bet given what was knowable, not the roll. (Avoid resulting.)
  • A non-0%/100% prediction can't be "wrong" from one result. A 2% event happening doesn't refute "2%." Judge calibration over many bets.
  • Replace "Am I sure?" with "How sure?" State a % or a range; update in small increments, never a right↔wrong flip.
  • Nearly nothing is 0% or 100%. If you're saying "always/never/certain," you're probably miscalibrated.
  • You're already guessing whenever you decide. So make the probabilities explicit — a wide range beats no estimate.

Tells → what's happening → countermove

If you notice…You're probably…Do this
Grading a decision by how it turned outResultingReconstruct what was knowable; judge the bet, not the result
Crediting your wins to skill, blaming losses on luckSelf-serving bias / fielding errorAsk "would this repeat?"; take the other's perspective
"So unlucky," "I always get screwed"Motivated outcome fieldingField into luck and skill buckets; look for a controllable
Dismissing an idea because of who said itShooting the message (universalism fail)Judge the claim on merit; imagine a source you respect
"I knew it all along," "it was bound to happen"Hindsight biasRebuild the tree; the outcome was one branch of many
"Worst day ever," reacting to the last half hourTicker watching / zoom lens / tiltRun 10-10-10; take the long view; step away
Everyone in the room agrees with youEcho chamber / confirmatory driftSeek dissent; add someone who disagrees
The detail you want to leave outCommunism fail (spinning a narrative)Share it — hesitation is the signal it matters

CUDOS checklist (rules of engagement for a truthseeking group)

  • Communism — is all the data on the table? "More is more."
  • Universalism — am I judging the idea, not the messenger?
  • Disinterestedness — did I hide the outcome and my own opinion so I don't infect them?
  • Organized Skepticism — am I asking "why might this not be true?" civilly?

Are you on tilt? (don't decide if yes)

Verbal tells: "Seriously? Again?", swearing, "why do I bother." Physical tells: flushed cheeks, racing heart, fast breathing.

→ Precommit to walk away, take ten breaths, sleep on it. Ask: "Will this matter in the long run?"

Which time-travel tool?

SituationTool
Hot, in-the-moment choice10-10-10
Map the path to a goalBackcasting (positive space)
Stress-test a plan before committingPremortem (negative space) — pair with backcast; the two sum to 100%
Predictable future temptationUlysses contract (raise or lower a barrier)
Choosing among uncertain futuresScenario planning + expected value
Catch yourself veering liveDecision swear jar

Talking to people who haven't opted in

  1. Express uncertainty first ("I'm not sure, but…").
  2. Lead with assent, then "and" — never "but."
  3. Ask permission: "Want to vent, or looking for advice?"
  4. Focus on the future: "What could you do so it turns out better next time?"

Life is poker, not chess — and it's one long game. Take satisfaction in making good bets; outcomes will vary. Calibrate a little better each time.

glossary.md

Glossary — Thinking in Bets

10-10-10 — A decision routine (Suzy Welch): weigh the consequences of each option in 10 minutes, 10 months, and 10 years to recruit future-self and defuse in-the-moment emotion (Ch 6).

Accountability — A willingness or obligation to answer to others for our beliefs and actions; a bet is a form of accountability that makes us hypervigilant about our confidence (Ch 4).

All decisions are bets — Every choice commits resources to one uncertain future while foreclosing others; "not betting" is itself a bet (Intro, Ch 2).

Backcasting — Imagining you've already achieved a goal ("We Achieved Our Goal!") and working backward to identify how you got there; reveals the positive path (Ch 6).

Belief-formation flaw — We don't hear→vet→believe; we hear→believe→(maybe) vet. Default is to believe what we hear (Gilbert) (Ch 2).

Bet — A decision about an uncertain future that risks resources on one outcome; the book's core reframe (Intro, Ch 2).

Blind-spot bias — Spotting bias in others but not ourselves; larger the smarter/more numerate we are. A group helps fill in our blind spots (Ch 2, Ch 4).

Calibration — Holding beliefs as probabilities and updating in small increments toward accuracy, instead of flipping between right and wrong (Ch 1, Ch 2).

Confirmatory thought — One-sided reasoning that rationalizes a held view; amplifies bias and breeds groupthink (Ch 4).

CUDOS — Merton's four norms for a truthseeking group: Communism, Universalism, Disinterestedness, Organized Skepticism (Ch 5).

Communism (Mertonian) — Data belong to the group; share everything, "more is more" (Ch 5).

Decision-interrupt — The stop-and-think moment a precommitment creates when you consider breaking it (Ch 6).

Decision quality ≠ outcome quality — A good process can yield a bad result (bad luck) and vice versa; judge the bet, not the roll (Intro, Ch 1).

Decision swear jar — A precommitment to flag words/thoughts signaling irrationality ("I'm sure," "so unlucky," "wrong"), triggering reflection (Ch 6).

Devil's advocate — An assigned role to argue against a position, raising alternative hypotheses (from the Church's canonization process) (Ch 5).

Disinterestedness (Mertonian) — Vigilance against conflicts of interest; use outcome/belief blindness so evaluators aren't infected (Ch 5).

Dissent Channel / red team — Institutional mechanisms (State Dept., CIA) that protect and reward dissenting views (Ch 4, Ch 5).

Echo chamber — A homogeneous group that repeats and confirms its own views; the natural drift of confirmatory thought (Ch 4).

Expected value — Probability-weighted worth of an option (a $50k grant at 70% beats a $200k grant at 10%) (Ch 6).

Exploratory thought — Even-handed consideration of alternative viewpoints; moves a group toward accuracy (Tetlock & Lerner) (Ch 4).

Fielding outcomes — Deciding whether a result came from skill (your decisions) or luck (outside your control); the mechanism of learning (Ch 3).

Hindsight bias — After an outcome, seeing it as inevitable ("I should have known"); the chainsaw that lops off unrealized branches of the tree (Ch 1, Ch 6).

Learning loop — Outcomes → field into luck/skill → update beliefs → better bets; fielding errors sever it (Ch 3).

"Lettermanning" — Offering a truthseeking challenge to someone who hasn't agreed to it, so it lands as an attack (Ch 4).

Loss limit — A preset stop-loss enforced by accountability to a group; a check against chasing losses while irrational (Ch 4, Ch 6).

Luck — The influence on outcomes of things outside our control (others' actions, weather, genes, hidden cards) (Intro, Ch 3).

Mental contrasting — Oettingen's finding that imagining obstacles (not just success) makes goals more achievable; basis of the premortem (Ch 6).

Mental time travel — Recruiting past- and future-selves as decision buddies to engage deliberative mind (Ch 6).

Motivated reasoning — Processing information to protect existing beliefs — seeking confirmation, discrediting the rest (Ch 2).

Organized skepticism (Mertonian) — Engaging dissent through civil discussion; asking "why might this not be true?" (Ch 5).

Outcome blindness — Presenting a decision up to the decision point, omitting the result, so it's judged on process not outcome (Ch 5).

Path dependence — Emotional response driven by the recent path, not the overall result (win $100 and feel sad, lose $100 and feel happy) (Ch 6).

Poker vs. chess — A model of decision environments: chess = perfect info, little luck; poker = hidden info, real luck (Ch 1).

Premortem — Imagining you've failed ("We Failed to Reach Our Goal") and listing why; reveals the negative space (Klein, Oettingen) (Ch 6).

Rashomon Effect — Different people give drastically different accounts of the same event; no one version is complete (Ch 5).

Reconnaissance / scenario planning — Mapping the range of possible futures of a decision and assigning probabilities (Ch 6).

Redefining "wrong" — A non-0%/100% prediction can't be proven wrong by a single outcome; judge calibration over many bets (Ch 1).

Resulting — Judging a decision's quality by its outcome; the core error to avoid (Ch 1).

Self-serving bias — Fielding wins into the skill bucket and losses into the luck bucket to protect self-image (Ch 3).

SnackWell's Phenomenon — Consuming more of something with less of a "bad" ingredient; a case of how hard it is to work backward from outcome to cause (Ch 3).

Temporal discounting — Overvaluing a reward now versus a bigger reward later (Night Jerry vs. Morning Jerry) (Ch 6).

"They saw a game" effect — Prior beliefs change how we experience the same event (Ch 2).

Tilt — Emotionally unhinged decision-making caused by recent outcomes; the limbic system shuts down the prefrontal cortex (Ch 6).

Truthseeking pod / buddy system — A small chartered group that helps you fight bias and field outcomes honestly (Ch 4).

Truthseeking charter — The explicit agreement for a productive group: accuracy, accountability, openness to diverse views (Ch 4).

Truthseeker — Someone who wants to know what's true regardless of whether it flatters existing beliefs (Intro).

Ticker watching — Reacting to moment-by-moment fluctuations instead of the long-term trend (Ch 6).

Ulysses contract — A precommitment by past-self to bind present-self against a predictable irrational impulse (Odysseus at the mast) (Ch 6).

Universalism (Mertonian) — "Don't shoot the message": judge a claim on its merits regardless of its source (Ch 5).

"Wanna bet?" — A challenge (real or imagined) that triggers vetting of a belief (Ch 2, Ch 3).

"Yes, and" — The improv rule for offering dissent: accept the construct, then add ("and" not "but") (Ch 5).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Thinking in Bets

Concrete, reusable practices Duke endorses for making smarter decisions under uncertainty.

The "Wanna Bet?" Self-Challenge

When to use: Whenever you catch yourself stating something as certain.

How: Imagine a credible person says "Wanna bet?" Then run the vetting questions — How do I know this? How good is my source? What am I missing? What are the plausible alternatives? Why might I be wrong? — before committing to the belief.

Trade-offs: Slows down snap judgments; the payoff is beliefs calibrated closer to the truth and fewer over-confident bets.

Express Confidence as a Percentage or Range

When to use: Any belief or prediction you state to yourself or others.

How: Replace "I'm sure" with a number ("I'm 60%") or a range ("Elvis died between 40 and 47"). Update in small increments as evidence arrives rather than flipping right↔wrong.

Trade-offs: Feels less authoritative, but it's more credible and invites others to add information and dissent.

Field Outcomes into Luck vs. Skill

When to use: Any result you want to learn from.

How: Ask "Would the same decision predictably produce this result again?" If yes → skill; if it hinged on things you couldn't control → luck (most outcomes are a blend). Treat the fielding itself as a bet, and use perspective-taking ("What if this had happened to someone else?") to reach the truthful middle.

Trade-offs: Fights self-serving bias, which credits wins to skill and blames losses on luck; requires honesty that stings.

Build a Truthseeking Pod with a CUDOS Charter

When to use: To sustain truthseeking that willpower alone can't; habits hard to change.

How: Recruit as few as three people (two to disagree, one to referee) who opt into a modified social contract. Charter it on accuracy (reward objectivity over confirmation), accountability (members answer for beliefs, with advance notice), and diversity (actively seek dissent). Operationalize Merton's CUDOS: Communism (share all data), Universalism (judge ideas independent of source), Disinterestedness (outcome/belief blindness), Organized Skepticism (civil dissent).

Trade-offs: Requires discipline against the natural drift toward clones and echo chambers; must be freely chosen, never imposed.

Communicate for Feedback (Don't Lead with Your Conclusion)

When to use: Seeking honest input on a decision, inside or outside your group.

How: Describe the situation up to the decision point and omit the outcome and your own opinion ("It doesn't matter how it turned out"). Optionally omit the source too, so the group isn't biased for or against the messenger. Ask specific questions inviting reasons you might be wrong.

Trade-offs: Resisting the urge to reveal "how it ends" is hard, but it prevents infecting listeners with resulting and confirmation.

Truthseek Gently Outside Your Group

When to use: With people (kids, coworkers, friends) who haven't agreed to the charter.

How: (1) Express your own uncertainty first; (2) lead with assent — state specific points of agreement, then add with "and," never "but"; (3) ask permission ("Do you want to vent, or are you looking for advice?"); (4) focus on the future ("What might you do so things turn out better going forward?").

Trade-offs: Slower and less direct, but avoids the defensiveness that shuts down the conversation (see Letterman/Conrad).

Run 10-10-10

When to use: In-the-moment decisions where emotion is running high (tired, on tilt, a bad break).

How: Ask the consequences of each option in 10 minutes, 10 months, and 10 years — or the past-frame ("How would I feel today if I'd decided this 10 minutes / months / years ago?"). Draw on past experiences to engage deliberative mind.

Trade-offs: Won't make you perfectly rational, but keeps momentary events in proportion.

Backcast (Then Premortem)

When to use: Planning toward a goal or committing to a strategy.

How: Backcast — imagine you've already succeeded ("We Achieved Our Goal!") and work backward to list the decisions and events that got you there. Then run a premortem — imagine you've failed ("We Failed to Reach Our Goal") and list every reason why. The positive and negative space must add to 100%.

Trade-offs: The premortem feels pessimistic in the moment, but negative visualization (mental contrasting) makes goals more achievable and shrinks over-optimism to realistic size.

Scenario Planning / Reconnaissance of the Future

When to use: Before any consequential bet; budgeting, sales pipelines, strategy.

How: List the possible futures of a decision, then assign probabilities to each — even wide ranges (20%–80%) beat not guessing. Use expected value (probability × payoff) to prioritize. Memorialize the tree so you don't rewrite it with hindsight.

Trade-offs: People resist guessing probabilities, but you're already guessing whenever you decide; making it explicit reduces resulting and hindsight bias.

Set a Ulysses Contract

When to use: Wherever you can predict a future irrational impulse.

How: Have past-you bind present-you. Raise barriers (throw out junk food, ride-share to the bar, preset settlement floor, home-buying budget) or lower them (carry healthy snacks, automatic retirement allocation). Even a soft, tamper-able version creates a decision-interrupt — a stop-and-think moment.

Trade-offs: Rarely 100% tamper-proof, but the interrupt prompts deliberative thought and reduces reactive decisions.

Keep a Decision Swear Jar

When to use: To catch yourself veering from truthseeking in real time.

How: Predefine words/thoughts that signal irrationality — illusion of certainty ("I know," "always," "0%/100%"), irrational fielding ("so unlucky"), universalism violations ("idiot," "typical ___"), zoom-in language ("worst day ever"), motivated reasoning ("everyone agrees"), and especially the word "wrong." When you catch one, stop and reflect.

Trade-offs: Your list is personal and never complete, but each catch is a decision-interrupt back toward calibration.

Thinking, Fast and Slow

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Thinking, Fast and Slow

Decision rules and tells you'd want beside you while judging, forecasting, or choosing.

Bias → Tell → Countermove

If you notice…You're probably in…Do this
A story feels complete and obviousWYSIATI / illusion of validityAsk "what's missing?"; check evidence quality, not just coherence
A vivid case drives your risk estimateAvailability heuristicLook up the actual base rate / frequency
A number was mentioned before you estimatedAnchoringEstimate independently first; argue the anchor is wrong
A description matches a stereotypeRepresentativeness / base-rate neglectStart from the base rate, adjust by evidence's real validity
Extreme result → confident causal storyRegression fallacyExpect regression to the mean; no cause needed
"This time/we are different"Planning fallacy / competition neglectTake the outside view (reference class)
Confident expert in a noisy fieldIllusion of skillApply the two-condition test (below)
One good trait colors the whole judgmentHalo effectScore independent traits separately
You're holding a loser to avoid selling at a lossSunk cost / disposition effectAsk "would I buy this today?"
Choice flips when rewordedFraming effectRestate in the opposite frame + common units

Should I trust this intuition? (Expert-intuition test)

  1. Is the environment regular/predictable (valid cues exist)? → if No, don't trust it.
  2. Was there prolonged practice with rapid, clear feedback? → if No, don't trust it.
  3. Both Yes → trust the intuition. (High validity: anesthesiology, chess, firefighting. Low: stock picking, long-term political forecasting.)

Subjective confidence ≠ accuracy. Certainty is a feeling, not evidence.

Prospect theory in one screen

  • Value is over changes from a reference point, not final wealth.
  • Loss aversion: losses hurt ~1.5–2.5× more than equal gains delight.
  • Diminishing sensitivity: $0→$100 feels bigger than $900→$1000.
  • Decision weights ≠ probabilities: rare events overweighted; near-certain events underweighted.

Fourfold pattern (risk attitudes)

GainsLosses
High probability (certainty effect)Risk-averse — take the sure thing (accept unfavorable settlement)Risk-seeking — gamble to avoid sure loss (reject favorable settlement, "go to court")
Low probability (possibility effect)Risk-seeking — buy lottery ticketsRisk-averse — buy insurance

Forecasting rules of thumb

  • Regress predictions to the mean by (1 − correlation): weak evidence → stay near baseline.
  • Equal-weight formulas beat holistic judgment in low-validity settings; consistency > cleverness.
  • Reference-class base rate first, case details second.
  • Run a premortem before locking a big decision.

Two selves — decision defaults

  • Experiencing self feels moments; remembering self keeps score via peak-end + duration neglect.
  • Memory over-rewards good endings and ignores duration → don't confuse a good story with a good life.
  • Focusing illusion: "Nothing in life is as important as you think it is while you are thinking about it." Discount how much any single change (income, climate, new car) will shift lasting well-being.

System 1 vs System 2 (fast reference)

System 1System 2
SpeedFast, automaticSlow, effortful
FeelEffortless, always onCostly, lazy, depletable
JobImpressions, intuitions, patternsChecking, computing, self-control
Failure modeBiases, WYSIATIEndorses System 1 without checking

System 2 is the lazy controller: it usually ratifies System 1. Deliberate friction (slow down, ask for base rates, reframe) is the only reliable fix.

glossary.md

Glossary — Thinking, Fast and Slow

Affect heuristic — Letting likes and dislikes determine beliefs about risks and benefits; emotion substitutes for analysis (Ch 9, Ch 13).

Affective forecasting — Predicting how future events will make you feel; usually distorted by the focusing illusion (Ch 38).

Anchoring effect — A number you consider before estimating pulls your estimate toward it, even when arbitrary (Ch 11).

Anchoring index — The ratio measuring how much an anchor moves estimates; ~55% is common (Ch 11).

Associative activation — One idea automatically triggering a cascade of linked ideas, emotions, and bodily responses (Ch 4).

Availability cascade — A self-sustaining chain where media coverage of a minor risk breeds public fear that breeds more coverage (Ch 13).

Availability heuristic — Judging frequency or probability by how easily examples come to mind (Ch 12, Ch 13).

Base rate — The prior probability of an outcome in the population, before individuating evidence (Ch 14, Ch 16).

Base-rate neglect — Ignoring statistical base rates in favor of a representative description (Ch 14, Ch 16).

Bernoulli's error — Modeling utility as a function of wealth states rather than changes relative to a reference point (Ch 25, Ch 26).

Broad framing — Evaluating decisions as part of a portfolio of many similar choices rather than one at a time (Ch 31, Ch 34).

Certainty effect — Overweighting outcomes that move from very likely to certain; drives the fourfold pattern (Ch 29).

Cognitive ease — A pleasant state of low mental strain signaling that things are familiar, true, and safe; opposite of cognitive strain (Ch 5).

Competition neglect — Ignoring rivals' plans when forecasting your own success ("this town is big enough only for us") (Ch 24).

Conjunction fallacy — Judging a specific conjunction (Linda is a feminist bank teller) as more probable than one of its parts (Ch 15).

Decision weights — The psychological weights the mind assigns to outcomes, differing from their objective probabilities (Ch 29, Ch 30).

Denominator neglect — Focusing on the numerator (13 winning marbles) and ignoring the denominator, so vivid frequencies beat probabilities (Ch 30).

Diminishing sensitivity — Each additional unit of gain or loss feels smaller as you move away from the reference point (Ch 26).

Disposition effect — Selling winners and holding losers to avoid closing a mental account at a loss (Ch 32).

Duration neglect — When evaluating an experience, ignoring how long it lasted (Ch 35).

Ego depletion — Reduced self-control and effort after prior mental exertion (Ch 3).

Endowment effect — Valuing something more merely because you own it; selling price exceeds buying price (Ch 27).

Experiencing self — The self that lives in the present moment and feels each experience as it happens (Ch 35, Ch 37).

Expert intuition — Reliable pattern recognition, valid only in high-validity, regular environments with prolonged practice and rapid feedback (Ch 22).

Focusing illusion — "Nothing in life is as important as you think it is while you are thinking about it"; attention inflates the felt weight of any factor (Ch 38).

Fourfold pattern — The signature pattern of risk attitudes across gains/losses × high/low probability (Ch 29).

Framing effect — Logically equivalent descriptions (survival vs. mortality, 90% fat-free vs. 10% fat) producing different choices (Ch 34).

Halo effect — Letting one salient trait (or first impression) color your evaluation of everything else about a person (Ch 7, Ch 19).

Hindsight bias — After an event, believing you knew it would happen; the "I-knew-it-all-along" effect (Ch 19).

Illusion of validity — Unjustified confidence in a judgment that fits a coherent story, despite poor predictive accuracy (Ch 20).

Intensity matching — Translating a value on one scale (crime severity) onto another (loudness, dollars) automatically (Ch 8, Ch 9).

Law of small numbers — Overtrusting small samples and seeing patterns in what is really sampling noise (Ch 10).

Loss aversion — Losses loom larger than equivalent gains, by a factor of roughly 1.5–2.5 (Ch 26, Ch 28).

Mental accounting — Keeping money and outcomes in separate psychological accounts that shouldn't be treated separately (Ch 32).

Mere exposure effect — Repeated exposure to a stimulus increasing liking for it (Ch 5).

Mood/coherence (WYSIATI) — "What You See Is All There Is": building confident stories from available evidence while ignoring what's missing (Ch 7, Ch 19–20).

Narrative fallacy — Constructing simple, coherent stories of the past that overweight skill and intention and hide the role of luck (Ch 19).

Norm theory — System 1 maintains a model of what's normal; deviations trigger surprise and a search for causes (Ch 6).

Outside view — Forecasting by using the statistics of a reference class of similar cases, instead of the details of your own case (Ch 23).

Peak-end rule — Retrospective evaluation of an episode is dominated by its most intense moment and its ending (Ch 35).

Planning fallacy — Plans and forecasts that are unrealistically close to best-case scenarios (Ch 23).

Possibility effect — Overweighting a change from impossible to merely possible (0% → 5%) far more than a proportional change in the middle (Ch 29, Ch 30).

Priming — Exposure to one idea unconsciously influencing thoughts and actions related to it (Ch 4).

Prospect theory — Kahneman & Tversky's descriptive theory of choice: value defined over gains/losses from a reference point, with loss aversion, diminishing sensitivity, and nonlinear decision weights (Ch 26).

Regression to the mean — Extreme observations tend to be followed by more average ones, purely statistically (Ch 17).

Regression fallacy — Inventing a causal story for what is only regression to the mean (praise/punishment "working") (Ch 17).

Remembering self — The self that keeps score, tells the story, and makes decisions based on memories, not moments (Ch 35, Ch 36).

Representativeness — Judging probability by similarity to a stereotype or prototype, ignoring base rates and sample size (Ch 14, Ch 15).

Reference point — The status quo or expectation against which outcomes are coded as gains or losses (Ch 26).

Risk policy — A standing rule to treat repeated small risks broadly ("always take the favorable gamble"), reducing narrow-framing errors (Ch 31).

Substitution — Answering an easier heuristic question in place of the hard target question, without noticing (Ch 9).

Sunk-cost fallacy — Continuing a failing endeavor because of resources already invested (Ch 32).

System 1 — Fast, automatic, effortless, associative, intuitive thinking; always on (Ch 1).

System 2 — Slow, effortful, deliberate, rule-governed thinking; lazy and capacity-limited (Ch 1, Ch 3).

Theory-induced blindness — Once you accept a theory, its flaws become nearly impossible to see (Ch 25, Ch 26).

U-index — The fraction of time a person spends in an unpleasant emotional state (Ch 37).

Utility (experienced vs. decision) — Experienced utility is the pleasure/pain actually felt; decision utility is the weight given to an outcome when choosing (Ch 25, Ch 37).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Thinking, Fast and Slow

Concrete, reusable methods Kahneman endorses for making better judgments and decisions.

Take the Outside View (Reference-Class Forecasting)

When to use: Any plan, estimate, or forecast (project timelines, budgets, success odds).

How:

  1. Identify a reference class of past, similar cases.
  2. Get the distribution of actual outcomes for that class (the base rate).
  3. Use that base rate as your anchor.
  4. Adjust for your specific case only with information that has proven predictive value.

Trade-offs: Feels impersonal and can be resisted ("we're different"); requires real reference data. Counters the planning fallacy and optimism bias.

Run a Premortem

When to use: Before committing to a major decision the group is converging on.

How: Assemble the people who know about the decision. Say: "Imagine it's a year from now and this plan has failed disastrously. Write the history of that failure." Legitimizing dissent surfaces risks that groupthink and the illusion of validity suppress.

Trade-offs: Doesn't stop bad decisions outright; it widens the search for problems and tempers overconfidence.

Decompose an Intuitive Prediction (Regress Toward the Mean)

When to use: Predicting an outcome (GPA, sales, performance) from an impression or single indicator.

How:

  1. Start from the baseline (the average outcome / base rate).
  2. Make your intuitive prediction from the evidence.
  3. Estimate the correlation between your evidence and the outcome.
  4. Move from baseline toward your intuitive prediction by that fraction (e.g. correlation 0.3 → move 30% of the way).

Trade-offs: Deliberately sacrifices vivid, extreme predictions for calibrated moderate ones; feels less satisfying but is more accurate.

Adopt Broad Framing & Risk Policies

When to use: Repeated, small, independent risky decisions (investments, insurance, deadlines).

How: Decide a standing rule you'll apply to the whole class ("never buy extended warranties"; "always take the favorable gamble if I can afford the loss") rather than agonizing over each instance in isolation.

Trade-offs: Reduces loss-averse, narrow-framing errors and emotional churn; requires discipline to hold the policy when a single loss stings.

Use Algorithms / Simple Formulas Over Clinical Judgment

When to use: Repeated predictions in low-validity, noisy environments (hiring, admissions, loan approval, medical triage).

How: Select 2–6 predictive, independent attributes; score each on a standard scale; sum with equal weights. Trust the total over a holistic gut feel. (Apgar score is the archetype.)

Trade-offs: Experts resist ceding judgment; formulas beat them mainly because they're consistent, not smarter.

Structure Interviews to Beat the Halo Effect

When to use: Evaluating candidates or options where a first impression contaminates the rest.

How: Predefine 4–6 independent traits. Score each trait separately, one at a time, across all candidates before forming an overall view. Sum the scores; give the formula its due weight.

Trade-offs: Slower and less "intuitive"; sharply improves validity.

Reframe to Neutralize Framing Effects

When to use: Any consequential choice stated in one frame (losses vs gains, survival vs mortality, monthly vs annual cost).

How: Restate the same facts in the opposite frame and in a common unit; decide only if your choice survives both framings. Adopt "Econ" defaults where possible.

Trade-offs: Effortful System 2 work; most people won't do it unaided — so design defaults for others (nudges).

Trust Expert Intuition Only Under Two Conditions

When to use: Deciding whether to believe a confident expert (or yourself).

How: Ask (1) Is the environment regular and predictable enough to contain valid cues? (2) Did the expert have prolonged practice with rapid, unambiguous feedback? Both yes → trust it. Otherwise treat the confidence as an illusion of validity.

Trade-offs: Confidence and subjective certainty are not evidence of skill; long experience in an irregular world (e.g. stock picking) breeds skill-less confidence.

Guard Against WYSIATI

When to use: Whenever a story feels coherent and conclusion feels obvious.

How: Ask "What would I need to know that I don't?" and "What's the quality and quantity of the evidence?" Deliberately seek disconfirming data and the base rate.

Trade-offs: Coherence is seductive; this friction is the price of calibration.

Design for the Peak-End & Duration Neglect

When to use: Designing experiences (service, care, events) or reasoning about your own well-being.

How: Improve the most intense moment and, especially, the ending; don't assume adding pleasant-but-milder time at the end helps memory. For your own choices, ask whether you're optimizing the experiencing self or the remembering self.

Trade-offs: What memory rewards (a good ending) and what the experiencing self lives through can diverge.

Trust Me, I'm Lying: Confessions of a Media Manipulator

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Trust Me, I'm Lying

The one rule that explains everything

Advertisement × Traffic = Revenue → "traffic by any means." When a blog's behavior confuses you, ask: what did their business need? The answer predicts the coverage.

Decode a blog post (tells & smells)

You see…It really means…
"According to a tipster"Someone (like a manipulator) tricked the blogger
"We're hearing reports"Random tweets / message-board posts
"Leaked" / "official documents"An email; docs likely fake or fabricated
"BREAKING" / "developing"Published before facts confirmed
"Updated"Pasted at the bottom; story not reworked
"EXCLUSIVE"A favorable-coverage deal, or a stolen/multi-given story
"Sources tell us"Unvetted, uncorroborated, attention-hungry
"Said in a press release"Probably just spam email
"According to a report by"Summarizer exaggerating with poor comprehension
"We've reached out for comment"Emailed 2 minutes before hitting publish at 4 a.m.
Headline ends in "?"Answer is "No, of course not" — a lie with cover
"which means / will result in"Blogger has zero expertise, no consequences

Virality decision rule

When you need something to spread, engineer for VALENCE. Rank emotions:

  1. Anger (strongest — ≈ 3 hrs as NYT front-page lead)
  2. Awe / excitement / titillation / laughter (arousing = shareable)
  3. Positive (≈ 1.2 hrs) — decent
  • Avoid: sadness (low-arousal, kills sharing) and reasonableness/complexity (the unshareable middle).
  • Rule of thumb: "Things must be negative but not too negative." Despair/pity → inaction; anger/fear → spread.

Trading up the chain (the play)

Level 1 (small, high-trust, understaffed blog) → get 3–4 links → Level 2 (legacy-media blogs, look legit) → soft sell → Level 3 (national). Don't pitch the big reporter; seed what they read. A cluster of links = a "trend piece."

Which tactic fits the goal?

GoalTactic
Coverage without cashIndirect bribe: free stuff, access, paid tweets (#1)
Publish without verificationFake leak / press release / Wikipedia / HARO (#2)
Go viralCrank valence, lead with anger (#3)
Click-driven coverageFeed rhetorical questions → question headline (#4)
News from nothingManufacture urgency, fake multi-exclusive (#9)
Turn critics into distributorsMake them irrationally angry; underdog cloak
Extract a payoutImplicit shakedown / leak an intention-to-sue letter
Deflect a serious claimEncourage snark

If you are the target (defense)

  • The post is already live. A response = a buried "update." Corrections backfire (backfire effect) — they entrench the false belief.
  • Don't fight snark — reason and appeals to humanity are used against you (jujitsu). "Nothing you can say."
  • Speaking validates / silence leaves it standing — the iterative trap has no clean exit.
  • Ask: "What do I plan to do with this information?" Usually: nothing → it's distraction.

Red flags a story is manufactured

  • Appears simultaneously across many sites with near-identical wording → link-economy propagation.
  • "May" on site 1 → "is" on site 2 → "has" on site 3.
  • Question-mark headline; CAPS tags (EXCLUSIVE, UNPRECEDENTED); no named/verified source.
  • A short, conveniently edited clip prefit to one group's biases (doctored-clip play).
  • A pseudo-event: press release, launch, "leak," award show, banned ad, contrite post-scandal interview.

Structural truths to remember

  • One-off distribution forces sensationalism; subscription enables nuance. RSS died on purpose.
  • A blog isn't small if its readers are media elite. Influence = who reads, not how many.
  • Blogs are built to be sold, so short-term traffic desperation is maximal — and desperation is the manipulator's best asset.
  • "If the news is important it will find me" is false — what finds you rose by slickness, titillation, and polarity, not value.
  • Skepticism is not enough to defend yourself; the reliable markers of authority are gone.

glossary.md

Glossary — Trust Me, I'm Lying

Abandoned shells — Words like exclusive, sources, leaked, developing that keep their old aura of authority while emptied of meaning; George W.S. Trow's term ("in the age of no-authority, these are the authorities") (Ch 25).

Advertising as content — Turning ads into "news" by leaking them to blogs or getting them "banned," gaining free coverage companies normally pay for (Ch 21).

Agenda manufacturing — Blogs creating candidates, celebrities, or controversies (to fill infinite space/profit) that mass media then legitimizes (Ch 2).

Backfire effect — Nyhan & Reifler: a correction makes readers believe the original falsehood more strongly and confidently by reintroducing the claim (Ch 20).

Blog (broad definition) — All online publishing — Twitter to newspaper sites to group blogs — anything subject to the same attention incentives (Ch 2).

Blog Con — Blogs are built not to be profitable but to be sold to a larger buyer for a multiple of traffic; scoops and marquee bloggers inflate the exit (Ch 4).

Cognitive dissonance / rigidity — The mind's refusal to abandon an accepted premise; the conclusion persists even after its supporting facts are removed (Ch 20).

Coverage about coverage — Worthless meta-filler ("how the story broke") that borrows relevance from real news (Ch 21).

Degradation ceremony — Ritualized public destruction that expels a target from the group; works by reframing known facts, not new evidence (Ch 23).

Delegation of trust — Old-media habit of building on another outlet's facts, valid only when all share high verification standards (Ch 17).

Douchebag insult — Dismissing someone entirely without reasons or work, depriving them of being taken seriously (Ch 22).

Experience technology — A medium (the web) that earns more trust the more it's used — a trust the culture abuses (Ch 16, 24).

Feeding the monster — The controlling metaphor: new media is a cute monster you feed for attention until it grows dangerous and turns on you (Ch 1).

Fiat over culture — The influence gained by mastering the rules that govern blogs (Ch 2).

Frovocation — Jack Shafer's portmanteau: manufactured "faux provocation" / online controversy (Ch 3).

Genetically modified entertainment — Content engineered around search terms, tested titles, and calibrated length to maximize dependence (Ch 16).

HARO (Help a Reporter Out) — Service connecting "self-interested sources" to reporters; manufactures self-promotion disguised as research (Ch 6).

Illusion of control — The manipulator's fatal belief he can feed the monster without being devoured (Ch 1).

Indirect bribe — Feeding the levers a blogger is paid on (traffic, speed, access, free product) instead of paying cash (Ch 5).

Iterative journalism (process/beta journalism) — Publish first, verify later; sold as a "learning process" but really a profit model (each correction = another post) (Ch 19).

Laurel leaf illusion — A credibility marker (festival laurels, an html link) that survives after its underlying scarcity/meaning is gone (Ch 25).

Lead steer — Michael Sitrick: the one Level-1 site that starts the media stampede (Ch 3).

Link economy — Recursive trading of traffic/links between blogs; links look like citations but rarely are (Ch 17).

"May becomes is becomes has" — How speculation hardens into asserted fact as a story climbs the linked chain (Ch 13, 17).

Narcotizing dysfunction — Lazarsfeld & Merton: mistaking media busyness for knowledge; consuming as a substitute for action (Ch 16).

One-Off Problem — When news is sold story-by-story, publishers must create/sensationalize news to sell each unit anew (yellow press then, blogs now) (Ch 9).

Pageview compensation — Paying writers by traffic (Gawker's "big board"), making every post a conflict of interest (Ch 5).

Pseudo-event — Daniel Boorstin: anything staged solely to attract media attention (press release, launch, "leak," award show) (Ch 24).

Pseudo-exclusive — Nick Denton: "take ownership of a story even if it isn't a strict exclusive" — pretend you have a scoop (Ch 4).

Pseudo-metrics — Faked traffic/comments/coverage signals that trick blogs into treating you as newsworthy (Ch 11).

Snark — Cheap, unanswerable, click-friendly mockery; a defense mechanism of the weak that annihilates without effort ("cultural vandalism") (Ch 22).

Specious present — The window in which news has "news interest"; once read it becomes fact, so it can never truly be iterative (Ch 19, 20).

Stacking — Reverse-chronological "new stuff at the top"; makes the time stamp an expiration date, forcing short, constant posts (Ch 12).

Substance words — Weasel-word signals ("developing," "sources") that lend flimsy stories borrowed status (Ch 25).

Suppression by transmission — Misinforming the public not by omission but by what the sharing filter selects to spread (dead Detroit photos) (Ch 7).

Three-level media chain — Level 1 (small blogs) → Level 2 (legacy-media blogs) → Level 3 (national); the pathway of trading up (Ch 3).

Trading up the chain — Plant a story with a small low-standards blog and let it climb to major outlets "until the unreal becomes real" (Ch 1, 3).

Traffic by any means — The single dictum ruling every publisher decision; Advertisement × Traffic = Revenue (Ch 4).

Unreality — The netherworld where fake and real build on each other and can't be told apart — the cumulative endpoint of the system (Ch 24).

Valence — The intensity of positive or negative emotion; both extremes drive sharing, the moderate middle doesn't (Ch 7).

Warnock's Dilemma — Publishers can't tell whether silence means satisfaction or apathy, so they fear silence and chase any feedback (Ch 11).

Yellow press — 1830s–1900s sensational street-sold papers (Day, Bennett, Pulitzer, Hearst) whose incentives blogs recreate (Ch 9).

patterns.md

Patterns — Manipulation Tactics & Defenses

Book One = manipulation tactics. Book Two = the critique and how to read defensively. Each technique is a "pathetic vulnerability in our media system."

Trading Up the Chain

When to use: Inject a narrative into mass culture with no money, credentials, or connections.

How: Seed a fabricated/exaggerated story at Level 1 (small, high-trust, understaffed blogs) → gather 3–4 links → present the cluster to Level 2 (legacy-media blogs) as a "trend" → soft-sell Level 3 (national) by targeting what their reporters read, plus anonymous multi-address tips ("How have you not covered this?").

Trade-offs: Once started, it "takes on a life of its own" and can't be controlled; the same machinery causes riots and deaths, not just publicity.

The Indirect Bribe (Tactic #1)

When to use: Buy a blogger's coverage without cash.

How: Feed the levers their pay depends on — free product (rarely disclosed), affiliate commissions, exclusives, set visits, access, paid tweets, or invested-early influence in a rising blogger.

Trade-offs: Builds sources you can direct, but ties you into the same conflicted economy; the blogger knows and doesn't care.

Tell Them What They Want to Hear (Tactic #2)

When to use: Get a message published without verification.

How: Fabricate a "leaked" internal document and email it as an anonymous insider; put out press releases for everything (SEO'd, auto-syndicated to finance sites); edit Wikipedia framing then cite it; use HARO to become a quoted "expert" and bootstrap upward.

Trade-offs: The same unverified-source pipeline can end careers (or your own) with one anonymous tip.

Give Them What Spreads (Tactic #3)

When to use: Make content go viral.

How: Engineer for valence — crank anger first, then awe/excitement/titillation; strip out sadness and complexity. Make the ad itself the story via provocation.

Trade-offs: What spreads is systematically false to reality; provocation invites blowback and pulled ads (a "slap on the wrist" the author deems worth it).

Help Them Trick Their Readers (Tactic #4)

When to use: Get click-driven coverage.

How: Feed rhetorical/loaded questions and leave issues open; the blogger converts them into question-mark headlines (a lie with legal cover — answer is always "no"). Avoid giving them anything final, useful, or reasonable.

Trade-offs: Escalation cycle — each headline must out-inflame the last; occasional exposure, but low consequences.

Make It All About the Headline (Tactic #6)

When to use: Win the "Pick Me!" fight for a one-off story.

How: Pre-write the headline (or hint at options) in your email/release so the blogger steals it; make it extreme, literal, SEO-friendly ("Google doesn't laugh").

Trade-offs: Truth is irrelevant to the headline's job; the reader gets the buyer's remorse.

Kill 'Em With Pageview Kindness (Tactic #7)

When to use: Hijack a metric-driven newsroom.

How: Give bloggers content that moves them toward pageview quotas; fake the pseudo-metrics — buy traffic (StumbleUpon/Outbrain), post to your own social channels, leave fake positive/negative comments to simulate a "hot debate" (exploiting Warnock's Dilemma).

Trade-offs: "The beast bites back" — once a site sees traffic in you, it won't stop and will fabricate scandal to keep the topic alive.

Use the Technology Against Itself (Tactic #8)

When to use: Exploit the format's structural constraints.

How: Meet bloggers on-format (short, skim-friendly, spoon-fed into itty-bitty bites); fill their pre-shaped story with your terms. They cut expertise, so they can't check you.

Trade-offs: Blame the format, not the writer — but the same constraints distort everything, including in your favor and against you.

Just Make Stuff Up (Tactic #9)

When to use: Create news from nothing.

How: Manufacture urgency (fake ~20-min "exclusive," given to multiple blogs; arbitrary deadlines). Rely on the self-feeding two-blog hustle where each site reifies the other's speculation up the chain.

Trade-offs: Runs with or without you; you can't reason or litigate a "kook" out of an invented angle.

Weaponize the Backlash (Book Two)

When to use: Turn critics into distributors.

How: Make critics irrationally angry ("Bring It On" / "Blow Me" releases) so they spread your message everywhere; assume the persecuted-underdog cloak so exposure only re-famous-es you.

Trade-offs: Ethically corrosive; produces real collateral-damage victims (Sherrod, ACORN, Assange).

The Implicit Shakedown / Illusion of a Lawsuit (Book Two)

When to use: Extract a payout or force behavior.

How: Veiled threats ("it'd be a pity if…"); leak a lawyer's intention-to-sue letter (not a real suit) to gossip blogs.

Trade-offs: Starts an arms race; frictionless enough that "it was almost difficult not to do so."

Encourage Snark to Deflect (Book Two)

When to use: Change the nature of coverage away from a serious untrue claim.

How: Make the easiest story the mocking one — file a countersuit stuffed with hilarious trivia, email it with jokes hinting "make fun of this."

Trade-offs: Works for untrue facts as well as true ones, but "impossible to truly control" — snark burns everyone eventually.

DEFENSIVE PATTERNS (how to read / protect against the above)

Decode the Substance Words

When to use: Reading any blog post.

How: Translate "abandoned shells" — tipster = someone tricked the blogger; leaked = an email, likely fake; BREAKING = unconfirmed; Updated = pasted at the bottom, not reworked; EXCLUSIVE = a coverage arrangement or stolen story; reached out for comment = emailed two minutes before publishing.

Trade-offs: Skepticism alone "is not even enough to be a starting point" — the reliable markers are gone.

Refuse the Published-First Trap

When to use: You're the subject of an iterative story.

How: Understand the post is already live; a response becomes a buried "update" that won't change minds (corrections backfire). Don't over-respond to snark (jujitsu — energy used against you). Ask "what do I plan to do with this information?"

Trade-offs: Speaking validates the story; silence leaves it standing — an impossible position by design.

Change the Incentives

When to use: Fixing the system, not a single story.

How: Move from one-off/pageviews to subscription/paywall (NYT/Ochs → "more than twenty must-read articles a month"); demand quality over quantity as a reader; hold publishers to "Is this information true?"

Trade-offs: There is no tidy "solution" — the word itself takes the broken assumptions for granted.

Until the End of Time: Mind, Matter, and Our Search for Meaning in an Evolving Universe

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Until the End of Time

The Cosmic-Era Timeline (Empire State Building: floor n = 10^n years after the bang)

FloorYearsWhat ends / what happens
1–910–10⁹Particles, atoms, stars, planets, life, mind. We are on floor ~10.
1010¹⁰Present epoch. Sun dies ~5 Gyr; Milky Way + Andromeda → Milkomeda
1110¹¹Distant galaxies pass the cosmic horizon; the observable sky empties
12–1410¹²–10¹⁴Era of red dwarfs; last star formation ends; traditional life/mind window closes
15–2010¹⁵–10²⁰Burnt-out stars and wandering planets; solar systems unbind via gravitational waves
~34+>10³⁴Proton decay (if grand unification holds) dissolves complex matter
38–6810³⁸–10⁶⁸Black hole era; stellar-mass holes evaporate by floor 68
10210¹⁰²Largest supermassive holes finish evaporating — top of the building
102–359—Estimated window for Higgs vacuum decay
10^6810^(10⁶⁸)Boltzmann brains become likely (unwritable exponent)

Rule: predict this timeline in broad strokes only. Structure, not specifics.

Entropy vs. Local Order — Decision Rules

If you see…Then…Because
Order appearing spontaneouslyFind the energy flow and the waste sinkEntropic two-step: local decrease requires larger export
No identifiable sinkYour accounting is wrong, not the second lawTotal entropy never decreases
Entropy apparently vanishingLook for the hidden ledger entryBekenstein: it went into horizon area
A low-entropy configurationSuspect an organizing influence, not luckLow entropy = rare = special
An entropy-raising change that isn't happeningLook for a missing catalystEntropic hurdles block accessible states
A system that must keep runningAsk how it purges waste heatYou are a steam engine; erasure, not thought, costs entropy
Gravity involvedExpect self-sustaining orderNegative heat capacity: losing heat makes it hotter
A far-future structure proposedCheck the sink still exists at that eraExpanding, cooling space eventually offers none

Threshold: entropy = number of configurations that "pretty much look the same." Long/short, likely/unlikely have no absolute meaning — always state the comparison scale.

Which Level of Explanation Applies Here?

The question is about…Answer at this levelDo NOT
What will happen next, physicallyParticles and fieldsInvoke purpose or will
Why this structure is possible at allEntropy + energy flowClaim it explains which structure
Why this variant persistedSelection (incl. molecular Darwinism)Assume adaptation before ruling out byproduct
What a person is doing and whyInstinct, memory, perception, social expectationSay "it's just particles" — the insight isn't there
What a work of art meansStory, myth, artistic truthDemand propositional verification
Whether something mattersCreated meaning, inside mindsLook for it in the laws — it isn't there

Test: layers must be consistent with those below, never replaceable by them. If your explanation dismisses a level, you've lost information; if it exempts a level from physics, you've lost the constraint.

Fast Tells

  • "It's all just particles" → eliminativism smuggled in as reductionism.
  • "This trait evolved because it does X" → run the byproduct check first.
  • "It feels wonderful" → proximate explanation only; the ultimate one is still owed.
  • "That's too unlikely to matter" → over an open horizon, compute waiting time instead.
  • "The theory implies I can't trust my evidence" → the model is incomplete (Boltzmann brains).
  • "Coincidence, therefore significance" → pattern-detection outrunning analysis (the tarantula).
  • "My legacy will endure" → symbolic immortality is real but bounded by the era of minds.
  • "Do you believe X?" → reframe as calibrated confidence; then name literal vs. metaphorical register.
  • Existential dread about the far future dismissed as silly → no principled basis for the dismissal (Scheffler, Wolf); the timescale intuition is parochial, not the worry.

Meaning — the closing rules

  1. The universe does not exist as an arena for life and mind; it will not hug you.
  2. Value and meaning are created inside subjective worlds, not found in the laws.
  3. Invented ≠ arbitrary: evolved predispositions + group feedback loops constrain what emerges.
  4. Finitude generates the calculus of value. Unlimited do-overs would drain choices of consequence.
  5. Species continuity, not personal continuity, is what secures the sense that things matter.
  6. Equations have no intrinsic worth — "their worth derives from the minds they inhabit." Same for every artifact.
  7. Look inward. "That is the noble direction to look."

glossary.md

Glossary — Until the End of Time

Adaptation vs. byproduct (spandrel) — Whether a trait was selected for its own effects or came bundled free with something else that was selected for (Ch 6, 7, 8).

Aperiodic crystal — Schrödinger's prescient term for the information-bearing molecule of heredity (Ch 4).

ATP — The strained-spring molecule synthesized by membrane turbines that ferries energy through the cell (Ch 4).

Attention schema — Graziano's proposal that consciousness is the brain's radically simplified model of its own attention (Ch 5).

Belief calculus — The mixed reasoning-plus-emotion-plus-authority process by which beliefs actually form, mostly below awareness (Ch 7).

Big bounce / cyclic cosmology — Steinhardt–Turok–Ijjas alternative in which expansion dilutes entropy enough for cycles of hundreds of billions of years to repeat (Ch 10).

Big crunch — Collapse following a tunneling of dark energy to a negative value (Ch 10).

Big rip — Scenario where dark energy strengthens until repulsive gravity tears apart galaxies, stars, molecules, and atoms (Ch 9).

Black hole evaporation — Slow shrinkage via Hawking radiation, once a hole's temperature exceeds the ambient temperature of space (Ch 10).

Boltzmann brain — A free-floating mind assembled by a rare spontaneous entropy drop, complete with false memories (Ch 10).

"Cheesecake for the mind" — Pinker's claim that the arts are adaptively useless confections pressing pleasure buttons evolved for other purposes (Ch 8).

CMB (afterglow of creation) — The big bang's residual heat, now 2.7 K, with hot/cold spots differing by ~1 part in 100,000 (Ch 3).

Cosmic horizon — Boundary beyond which objects recede faster than light; it glows at a tiny constant temperature (Ch 9, 10).

Costly signaling — Extravagant, hard-to-fake investment that certifies commitment or quality (Ch 7, 8).

Dark energy — Uniformly spread energy whose gravity is repulsive, driving accelerated expansion (Ch 9).

Denial of death — Becker's thesis that mortality awareness drives literal and symbolic immortality systems (Ch 1, 7, 8).

Dissipative adaptation — England's proposal that driven particle collections spontaneously reconfigure to absorb and dissipate energy more efficiently (Ch 4).

Dissipative structures — Prigogine's configurations that spontaneously order under sustained energy flow (Ch 4).

Eliminativism — The position that consciousness is an illusion; idealism is its mirror (Ch 5).

Emergence — The appearance of genuinely new descriptive levels — entropy, life, mind — from coordinated simple constituents (Ch 5).

Empire State Building timeline — Cosmic time mapped onto floors, where floor n = 10^n years since the big bang (Ch 9, 10, 11).

Entropic two-step — Any process in which a system's entropy decreases because it exports a more than compensating increase to its environment (Ch 2, 3, 4, 9).

Entropy — A count of how many microscopic rearrangements yield the same macroscopic configuration; high = common, low = special (Ch 2, 3).

Erasure cost — Computation can be heat-free, but erasing memory necessarily produces waste heat — new thoughts, not thoughts per se, cost entropy (Ch 9).

Event horizon — A black hole's boundary of no return, radius proportional to mass (Ch 10).

Fitness indicator — A display whose expense certifies the quality it advertises (Ch 8).

FOXP2 — Gene implicated in speech and grammar; identical in Neanderthals (Ch 6).

Free will vs. human freedom — Volitional intercession in physical law (rejected) vs. an emancipated range of response (affirmed) (Ch 5, 11).

Hard problem of consciousness — Chalmers' question of why physical processing is accompanied by subjective experience at all (Ch 5).

Hawking radiation — Particles emitted at a horizon when quantum-fluctuation pairs are split, causing the hole to lose mass (Ch 10).

Higgs field — Space-filling field (value 246) giving particles mass; possibly metastable (Ch 10).

Hyperactive agency detection — Evolved bias toward over-attributing agency; cheap false positives beat costly false negatives (Ch 6, 7).

Inflaton field — The "cosmic fuel" whose uniform energy produces repulsive gravity (Ch 3).

Integrated information theory (IIT) — Tononi and Koch's proposal that consciousness is highly integrated, highly differentiated information, quantified by ф (Ch 5).

Macrostate — The set of microscopic configurations sharing the same macroscopic properties; entropy counts its members (Ch 2).

Meaning as created, not found — Greene's conclusion that value and purpose are invented inside subjective worlds, constrained but not dictated by evolved predispositions (Ch 11).

Milkomeda — The merged Milky Way–Andromeda galaxy (Ch 9).

Minimally counterintuitive concept — An idea violating one or two intuitive expectations, making it memorable and transmissible (Ch 6, 7).

Molecular Darwinism — Natural selection operating on replicating molecules before life exists (Ch 1, 4).

Monomyth — Campbell's template: call, perilous adventure, return transformed (Ch 6).

Multiverse — If space is infinite, a patchwork of ~90-billion-light-year regions in which every history recurs infinitely often (Ch 10).

Negative entropy — Schrödinger's term for the low-entropy structure organisms ingest to hold their own entropy down (Ch 4).

Nested stories (reductionism without eliminativism) — Multiple level-specific accounts of one reality; consistency across levels is required, replacement is not possible (Ch 1, 4, 5).

Past hypothesis — The postulate that the universe began in an extraordinarily low-entropy state (Ch 2, 3).

Panpsychism / proto-consciousness — Chalmers' revival of an irreducible primitive subjective quality in matter (Ch 5).

Physicalism — The view that conscious experience will be fully explained by physical properties and existing physical law (Ch 5).

Proton decay — Predicted disintegration of protons; not yet observed, lower bound ~10^34 years (Ch 9).

Proximate vs. ultimate explanation — "It feels wonderful" answers the immediate impetus only, not the evolutionary origin (Ch 8).

Qualia — The subjective felt characters of experience (Ch 5).

Redox reaction — Electron transfer; life's universal slow burn, staged in small steps (Ch 4).

Repulsive gravity — Outward-pushing gravity arising when energy is spread uniformly rather than clumped (Ch 3, 9).

RNA world — Hypothesis exploiting RNA's dual role as software and hardware to bypass the origin-of-life chicken-and-egg (Ch 4).

Sacred, the — The status conferred on certain stories and rules that elevates them above all others (Ch 7).

Scheffler's afterlife scenario — Thought experiment removing descendants rather than yourself, isolating what anchors value (Ch 11).

Second law of thermodynamics — Total entropy of a system plus its environment overwhelmingly likely to increase (Ch 2, 3).

SPONCH — Sulfur, phosphorus, oxygen, nitrogen, carbon, hydrogen — the atoms dominating all known life (Ch 4).

Story as flight simulator — Oatley's refinement of Pinker: fiction as safe, cheap rehearsal that refines intuition (Ch 6).

Sublime, the — Experience so enveloping it feels like stepping beyond time (Ch 8).

Substrate independence of mind — Treating life and mind as processes rather than as cells and brains (Ch 9).

Symbolic immortality — Rank's displacement of the urge for eternity onto self-authored works (Ch 1, 8).

Terror management theory — Mortality salience covertly amplifies defense of one's cultural worldview (Ch 7).

Theory of mind — Attribution of beliefs, desires, and intentions to other agents and to oneself (Ch 5, 6, 7).

Universal grammar — Chomsky's innate neurobiological language primer (Ch 6).

Vacuum decay — Higgs tunneling to a new value, spreading near light speed and rewriting physics inside the bubble (Ch 10).

Worm at the core — James's term for tamped-down awareness of one's own ending underlying ordinary delight (Ch 1).

patterns.md

Patterns — Reasoning Moves from Until the End of Time

Greene offers explanatory methods, not procedures. Each pattern below is a reasoning move: a way of setting up a question so the physics, biology, or philosophy can answer it.

Entropic Two-Step Reasoning

When to use: Any time order appears where the second law seems to forbid it — a star forming, a cell metabolizing, a brain thinking, a civilization building.

How: (1) Identify the local entropy decrease (the structure that got built). (2) Find the energy flow that paid for it. (3) Locate the waste sink — where the more-than-compensating entropy was dumped (heat, radiation, excreta, expanding space). (4) Confirm the total went up. If you cannot name the sink, your accounting is wrong, not the second law.

Trade-offs: Powerful and universal, but it explains permission, not cause — knowing a structure is entropically affordable does not tell you why this structure rather than another. Pair it with a selection argument. Also: it only works if a sink actually exists; in the far future (Ch 9) or inside a black hole (Ch 10) the sink is the binding constraint.

Choosing a Level of Description (Nested Stories)

When to use: When someone claims one level of explanation is the real one — "it's all just particles," or conversely "you can't reduce this."

How: (1) Identify which layer the question actually lives on (particle, chemical, biological, neural, mental, cultural). (2) Answer in that layer's own vocabulary and grammar. (3) Check the answer is consistent with the layers beneath, not replaceable by them. (4) Keep the linkages explicit — Cervantes's neurons and Don Quixote's yearning are connected but not interchangeable.

Trade-offs: This is reductionism without eliminativism, and it costs you a unified theory of everything-that-matters. The discipline is refusing both moves: no dismissing a higher story as "just" lower-level activity, and no exempting a higher story from physical constraint.

Evaluating an Adaptationist vs. Byproduct Claim

When to use: Any assertion that a human behavior — storytelling, art, music, religion — "evolved because it does X."

How: (1) State the proposed adaptive benefit precisely. (2) Ask the byproduct question first: could this be a package-deal consequence of something else already selected for (theory of mind, agency detection, pattern sensitivity, pleasure circuits)? (3) Apply the "just so" story test — does the account make any prediction that could fail? (4) Separate proximate from ultimate explanation: "we do it because it feels wonderful" answers only the immediate impetus. (5) Accept that the debate may stay open, and check whether your downstream conclusion actually depends on which side wins.

Trade-offs: Byproduct explanations are cheap to generate and hard to falsify, so the test cuts both ways. Greene's own practice in Ch 11 is instructive: he leaves the origin question unresolved and rests his conclusion on the observed function — a longing to be part of something larger — which holds under either account.

Reasoning About Far-Future Timescales

When to use: Any claim about the fate of stars, life, mind, or civilization beyond a few million years.

How: (1) Convert everything to the Empire State timeline — floor n = 10^n years. (2) Predict in broad strokes, not fine detail: commit to structural claims (stars burn out, protons may decay, black holes evaporate), refuse detail-level extrapolation of technology or civilization. (3) Replace "likely vs. unlikely" with waiting time vs. horizon — over unbounded time, probability × duration is what matters, so no nonzero-probability process may be discarded. (4) Ask the thinker question for any proposed future mind: can it still expel the waste heat that new thought requires?

Trade-offs: The method's honesty is its limitation — it yields a skeleton, not a scenario. It also resurrects self-undermining conclusions (Boltzmann brains); treat self-undermining as evidence the model is incomplete rather than as a result to accept.

Testing What Anchors Value (The Doomsday Move)

When to use: When you need to know whether a commitment rests on personal continuation or on humanity's continuation.

How: (1) Imagine a terminal prognosis for yourself; note the reaction (typically: heightened intensity, significance conferred on ordinary moments). (2) Now use Scheffler's variant — thirty days after your natural death, everyone remaining is obliterated — which excises your own premature mortality. (3) Re-ask activity by activity: would I still do the research, finish the book, send the kids to school? (4) Whatever survives step 3 is intrinsically motivated; whatever collapses was resting on descendants.

Trade-offs: Responses genuinely differ (Frankfurt thinks art and science survive; Greene thinks they don't), so the exercise reveals your own structure of value rather than a universal fact. Use imminence only as artificial urgency to catalyze an authentic response — the intuition then transfers to the far future, since long and short have no absolute meaning.

Calibrating Belief Instead of Declaring It

When to use: Contested claims where "do you believe X?" invites tribal rather than evidential answers.

How: Replace the yes/no with "what is my calibrated confidence, given the evidence, and what would update it?" Then check the register: a claim read literally and contradicting established science is simply false; the same claim read as poetry, symbol, archive, or community practice remains inside rational discourse — a belief in the value of the content rather than its veridicality.

Trade-offs: The register move can be used dishonestly, to retreat from a falsified literal claim while keeping its rhetorical force. Name which register you are in before arguing.

Diagnosing Low Entropy as Evidence

When to use: On encountering any strikingly ordered configuration — biological, cosmological, or social.

How: Treat low entropy as evidence of an organizing influence, not of luck; then find the influence (gravity, selection, an engineer, an energy gradient). Where entropy appears simply to vanish, look for the ledger entry (Bekenstein's answer to Wheeler: it went into horizon area).

Trade-offs: A statistical fluke is possible and, given enough time or enough regions, eventually mandatory — see the past hypothesis and the multiverse. The pattern tells you where to look first, not what you will find.

What Got You Here Won't Get You There: How Successful People Become Even More Successful

3 markdown files

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Decision Rules & Diagnostics

Decision Rules

  • When you're about to correct someone's idea, do nothing, because you'll improve the idea 5% and cut their commitment 50% (fallacy of added value, #2).
  • When you're about to speak, run the four gates first — will this help our customers / our company / the person I'm talking to / the person I'm talking about? — because if it fails all four, being right is worthless.
  • When the question is "is it true?", switch to "is it worth it?", because roughly half of what you were going to say is accurate and still not worth the damage.
  • When you're diagnosing a problem in yourself, don't — get feedback, because self-diagnosers see cancer where a professional sees a muscle pull.
  • When a behavior seems tied to your success, ask "because of or in spite of?", because the superstition trap is what keeps successful people from changing.
  • When you want to change more than one thing, pick one, because one gun, one bullet; multiple simultaneous changes is a personality makeover, not improvement.
  • When you can't decide whether to be nicer or stop being a jerk, stop being a jerk, because omission is cheap and commission requires filling an entire box.
  • When you apologize, stop talking, because every added word converts the apology into a defense.
  • When you've improved but no one has noticed, advertise harder, because you must get 100% better to earn 10% credit; you're in the dumb phase.
  • When someone gives you feedback or a suggestion, say only "thank you", because it's the one response that cannot be argued with or escalated.
  • When you want ideas without defensiveness, ask for two future suggestions (feedforward), not a critique, because people accept ideas about the future and reject verdicts on the past.
  • When you're deciding whether to keep coaching someone, stop if they don't think they have a problem, they're in the wrong job, or they think everyone else is the problem. Test: "if we shut down today — surprised, sad, or relieved?"
  • When you're 70 and being corrected for the ten-thousandth time, let it go — and grant the same to others.

Tells & Smells (a habit is firing)

  • You start a sentence with "No," "But," or "However" — you've already said "I'm right, you're wrong."
