Answer: Gavage: Ads didn't ship what people asked for, so products were forced down partners' throats and then advertisers'; when partners reported no difference, the response was to push harder. Fog: cultish product development can't be seen from inside; nobody from Sheryl to line PMs called bullshit; a VP kept a magnum of champagne with a Post-it targeting "10% revenue from Sponsored Stories" by end-2011, never approached.

Q11.6 [SA] What is "Only Good News" and what happened in March 2012?

Answer: Zuck outsourced monetization to Sheryl; her conference room was the appellate court for product disputes. In March 2012 she declared the Like-buying party over: no one will pay ten million for Likes anymore (Burberry, Ford, Starbucks, BMW had bought Likes that were at best a license to spam feeds).

Q11.7 [Own words] Why are Ads and Growth "yin-yang" and anticorrelated?

Answer: Ads turns users into money; Growth turns money into users; they sat in opposing wings. "What makes a user use the product does not necessarily make money, and the reverse is also true." Growth held Facebook's only real marketers (retargeting near-registrants on ad exchanges before Ads knew exchanges existed, three-decimal conversion stats, Skinnerian reminder-email cadences, carrier deals, a Risk-board map of countries yet to "tip").

Q11.8 [SA] Do the "running out of humans" arithmetic.

Answer: ~3B internet users minus ~600M in China and most of Russia, minus a 25% never-join haircut gives about 1.8B addressable. At 1.44B (Q1 2015) and ~13% growth, roughly a year of growth was left; hence Internet.org and solar drones to create connectivity, rich-market ad revenue subsidizing it: "money follows eyeballs, even if slowly."

Q11.9 [Scenario] Your team proposes selling the logout page to brands for a few hundred thousand dollars. A growth team objects but cannot quantify the harm. How should the decision be made, and what happened at Facebook?

Answer: This is LOX (Logout Experience): the most common webpage on the world's shared computers and the primary on-ramp for new users in developing countries. Growth couldn't quantify the usage cost, so outrage and personal sway decided it: LOX ran only where Facebook had already won (the US), not where rivals like Orkut were "still warm" (Brazil). Lesson: usage first, money when usage is safe; anti-pattern: springing a cross-team trade-off without a way to quantify it and selling the on-ramp for a quarter's revenue.

Q11.10 [Scenario] A VP presents a plan whose success needs partners and brands both to change behavior, and a metric no one can measure. What do you apply?

Answer: Count the miracles (Sponsored Stories needed two) and ask for lift against the best available alternative rather than your own baseline. Treat a plan nobody measures as a religion ("the Shroud of Turin must not be carbon-dated"). Listen when partners say it isn't working. FMC (Feb 2012) shows the mood: "never let the facts get in the way of a good story," and Paul Adams's Grouped thesis was contradicted by Facebook's own research.

Chapter 12: The Great Awakening, Barbarians at the Gates, IPA > IPO, IPO Reevaluation, Flash Boys

Q12.1 [Own words] What does "advertising is name-calling" mean?

Answer: Every channel is a different "name" for the same nervous primate: direct mail uses a postal address, mobile a quasi-immutable device ID, the web a cookie. Each key carries behavioral data and they differ in longevity (address > device > cookie), which is why mobile privacy is harder. The platform war among Facebook, Google, Amazon and Apple is over who controls the joins between names; everything else is "a parasitic sideshow."

Q12.2 [SA] Who is the "real Big Brother" in this chapter?

Answer: Data brokers (Acxiom, Experian, Epsilon, Merkle, Neustar) who have tracked consumer America since the 1960s, ingest retailers' CRM data and sell segments no citizen can inspect. Nielsen's PRIZM segments ("Beltway Boomers") are a predictive zodiac: "You consume; therefore, you are."

Q12.3 [SA] Give direct mail's numbers and why they matter.

Answer: ~$17B in postage, a $50B+ industry (roughly a Google, three internets or three Facebooks of money), at ~$1,000 CPMs vs. ~$1 online, so online can be a thousand times less effective and still break even. It is a $50B pile waiting to move online once identity translates.

Q12.4 [SA] How does data on-boarding work?

Answer: Firms (Datalogix, Neustar, LiveRamp) place invisible pixels where name/email meets a browser (newsletters, dating sites, second-tier social networks), drop or read a cookie and store the join in hashed form ("privacy theater" if everyone uses the same hash); the join is resold constantly. Facebook and Google out-on-board everyone because they have more data and see you constantly: Custom Audiences match rates up to ~90%.

Q12.5 [SA] How did Facebook "learn" about this, and what was the Experian anecdote?

Answer: By "mooching" information from potential acquirees and partners (Turn, MediaMath, BlueKai, Acxiom, Epsilon) in meetings of dubious good faith; they explained their plumbing while privately incredulous. Experian sent a junior team bearing a box of bakery cookies to a meeting about cookies: anti-pattern, sending the B team to the join of the century.

Q12.6 [Worked example] How was FBX sold internally (March 13, 2012)?

Answer: Find the single hour KX, Hegeman, Boland, Rabkin and a dozen engineers are free; physically round them up five minutes before; let an outsider with market credibility (Zach Coelius of Triggit, a poker player who read the author's aces) hold the room for an hour on real-time programmatic buying; sell the gee-whiz real-time decisioning to engineers and whiteboard the business case; end in a rare lovefest; follow up within days with a written product and business case tied to the post-IPO quarters. Result: approval by a leadership that had never heard of retargeting, and three engineers.

Q12.7 [SA] Describe the FBX build.

Answer: Five weeks to ship by June 15 (to book Q3 and Q4 revenue), three engineers (a "brogrammer," a recruit poached from Adchemy, a reviewer nothing passed without), a parallel ads system with separate data stores, real-time global bidding hundreds of thousands of times per second, dynamic creative, separate stats, monitoring tools, partner on-boarding docs and tests, and a sales spiel; bought with a promise of $100M in 2012 revenue. First successful FBX bid June 15 via TellApart.

Q12.8 [MC] Why did FBX lose money in Europe? (a) language; (b) taxes; (c) 120 ms bid window versus ~60 ms practical one-way latency from North Carolina to Amsterdam (about 23 ms at light speed); (d) no advertisers.

Answer: (c). A third of an eye-blink must include network latency; European requests timed out: "the Flash Boys of media."

Q12.9 [Own words] What was the "unforgivable sin" of FBX?

Answer: FBX bids fed into Facebook's own auction, making Facebook "merely one more DSP"; outside bidders, who knew you'd just shopped for a handbag, bid higher than Facebook's data and won. Equality with outsiders was a feature to the author and a bug to management; incumbents prefer monopoly pricing power and asymmetry, the Goldman CDS lesson forgotten.

Q12.10 [Scenario] A newspaper headline says a company's IPO "popped 30% on day one" and calls it a triumph. How do you read it, and what were Facebook's numbers?

Answer: Use "who gets the pop?": the syndicate underprices, hypes to deep pockets and engineers the pop; an orderly open never moves 20-30% for an ordinary stock, so a pop means founders and employees were skinned and bankers' clients made fortunes. Facebook opened ~$42, closed ~$38.37, paid ~1% in fees instead of up to 7% and raised a mountain of money with minimal dilution: "the most successful tech IPO in financial history," whatever Fortune and Forbes said. Also recall the wealth inflections: below fuck-you money only the indifference threshold moves; the author's package (75,000 shares over four years, $175K salary, 5,000 shares cashed up front) was ~$971K/year at the IPO price, ~$550K after tax.

Chapter 13: Full Frontal Facebook, Microsoft Shrugged, Ad Majorem, Adiós Facebook

Q13.1 [SA] What does "great powers and temporary allies" mean for Facebook?

Answer: Facebook has no partners, only existential rivals (Amazon, Google, once Apple, mirrors of Zuck) and convenient alliances; negotiations with peers are arms-control treaties with red-lined contracts and mutual suspicion. Twitter didn't register ("a clown car that drove into a gold mine").

Q13.2 [SA] What did the Google Plus numbers reveal?

Answer: Google Plus claimed 400M registered/100M active by counting anyone who clicked a Plus button. Inside Facebook, panic gave way to the recognition of Enron-style accounting; Larry Page's ultimatum reoriented all of Google, including Search, around social; Vic Gundotra became the internal Emmanuel Goldstein.

Q13.3 [Own words] Explain "do something vs. be someone."

Answer: Via Col. Boyd: one road is impact, truth to your vision and management's scorn; the other is plum products, facile praise and forgettable work. With children's tuition riding on unvested stock, the author chose the first: "double down and dig in."

Q13.4 [SA] Define incrementality with the CA vs. FBX comparison.

Answer: Revenue that would not otherwise have landed on the platform. Custom Audiences' dashboard dollars came largely from existing "Facebook" budget lines (discount by half); FBX competed for budgets earmarked for Google's AdX, so it was 100% incremental, but needed new creative and explicit reallocation from burned retailers before Q4. Advertisers budget by channel, not technique.

Q13.5 [SA] Why does the ad server matter and how do Google and Facebook differ?

Answer: Nobody in the chain trusts anyone; the ad server is the source of truth that counts delivery, frequency and geography and defines the units of marketing value. Google counts clicks only ("clicks trump impressions") because search exploits existing intent; Facebook must manufacture desire, so it worships viewthroughs (the billboard vs. the turn-off) and wants credit for Likes, shares and comments, hence its own yardstick. Containers: IAB/MMA standard units are the intermodal containers of media, which Google Search, Facebook and Twitter refuse.

Q13.6 [Worked example] Tell the Atlas arithmetic and moral.

Answer: Microsoft's creaky ad server (ran only on certain Internet Explorer versions; 20% share; thousands of publishers) was bought for roughly the $0.1B left after Microsoft wrote down $6.1B of its $6.2B aQuantive purchase: "Facebook's biggest ad tech acquisition to date was Microsoft's accounting rounding error." Boland and ex-Microsoft colleagues engineered it; "it's not what you pay, it's what they cost you": two-plus years of delays.

Q13.7 [SA] What happened on April 12, 2013?

Answer: In "Only Good News," Boz recommended to Sheryl: no identity matching and no mobile on FBX. Sheryl: "if that's what you think... that's what we'll do." Gokul fled the room; FBX was on life support. The decision was for the closed stack (Custom Audiences plus Atlas) over the open one. Earlier, LiveBoz (April 4) had produced a pissing match: Boland said CA was way ahead, the author said only if you count non-incremental dollars.

Q13.8 [Own words] Why are middle managers "what they are"?

Answer: Negative selection: the ambitious leave, the rest master managing up, acting visibly on feedback, championing reports, allying with sales, routing around incompetence and banking the logo on the business card. Boz was dispatched to end Ads' Lord-of-the-Flies anarchy and reconfigured Ads along one axis, from "Boz likes you" to "fired."

Q13.9 [SA] Give the exit playbook.

Answer: Don't quit before the vest; take vacation over the vesting date so you can't be fired; clear your desk over the weekend; secure-erase personal files (you don't need to be at fault to be sued); expect a severance-for-non-disparagement offer ($30,000 for a year of silence) and decline to sign on the spot; keep the badge and unwiped phone "at home." April 16: Miss HR's script, the kegerator wheeled out, Gokul's "Remember the non-solicit! (seriously)."

Q13.10 [Scenario] You've bet your career on an internal product that makes money, but the leadership narrative has already chosen a different path. What does the chapter say?

Answer: Anti-pattern: betting a career on winning an internal argument with money when the narrative is fixed. "Money talks... only if what it said was part of the bigger, accepted narrative." "The Spartans lost at Thermopylae": a movie reference in reply to a resource plea means no support. Also the data-portability argument: closed plan would brick over the opening FBX created; the Fidelity analogy shows lock-in only works if your identity data is so superior that advertisers accept inferior tooling, otherwise it's "Sponsored Stories Part II."

Chapter 14: Pandemonium Lost, Epilogue

Q14.1 [Own words] What is the "outsider's blog post as insider's mouthpiece"?

Answer: Executives in an acquisition can't explain strategy publicly (FTC, secrecy) but can retweet a perceptive outsider. The Medium post on Twitter-MoPub, written during eight weeks immobilized by a plantar fascia rupture, was circulated by the deal's principals and reopened a door slammed two years earlier. Twitter bought MoPub (~$350M deal) to build the exchange Facebook had refused.

Q14.2 [SA] What is "show enough skin for a second date"?

Answer: In the reconciliation meeting the author gave Twitter the full whiteboard (data flows, cross-device de-duplication, leakage-safe targeting): "if in doubt, show more." An advisory offer followed within days: a thousand shares a quarter (~$160K/year), no badge, no email.

Q14.3 [Own words] Why did mobile save Facebook?

Answer: Structural reasons, retrospective. (1) Data: mobile browsers block third-party cookies, apps silo data, Apple polices device IDs and developers hoard; so where desktop had a mature data marketplace that made Facebook's data marginal, mobile was data-starved and even age/gender was a godsend ("in the land of the mobile data blind, the one-eyed Facebook man was king"). (2) Inventory: mobile's savvy monetizers (games, commerce) charged users directly, leaving ad exchanges with tiny bars, interstitials and Grindr, so Facebook's stylish in-feed units with single-digit-percent clickthroughs had no competition. Q2 2013: mobile actives up 50%+, mobile revenue roughly doubled.

Q14.4 [SA] What is the "success generator"/ten dice idea?

Answer: Try ten things on hunches and mythology; seven fail and are forgotten, two do OK, one becomes transformational for reasons discovered afterward; the press writes the narrative fallacy; you're crowned a genius and roll again until the dealer sweeps your chips. Use "which of the ten dice came up?" to discount any founder's retrospective genius.

Q14.5 [SA] What happened to FBX?

Answer: ~$500M in new revenue by early 2014, all incremental, second only to News Feed ads, built by a handful and now costing nothing: a "perpetual motion machine of cash" and Facebook's window into programmatic competitors (like Goldman watching order flow). Kept alive because too profitable to kill, starved of identity and mobile. The author predicts Facebook will eventually run a full exchange; even Goldman moved CDS clearing to ICE in 2013.

Q14.6 [SA] Name Facebook's buy-your-way-out moves.

Answer: Instagram (2012, $1B, a weekend, a growth curve like early Facebook's; Dorsey outmaneuvered) and WhatsApp (2014, $19B, phone number as identity). Someday a founder as proud as Zuck will refuse, and Facebook will have to build, "a far riskier proposition."

Q14.7 [T/F] Google Plus ultimately beat Facebook.

Answer: False. Vic Gundotra left in April 2014 and Google Plus was demoted to a "platform," "an army... advancing in reverse"; Facebook's lockdown had won.

Q14.8 [Worked example] Explain why the desktop thesis didn't transfer to mobile.

Answer: On desktop, Facebook's data lost to first-party and broker data because browsers leak cookies to everyone (Chorizo and FBX findings were correct there). On mobile, the same data (age, gender, interests) became scarce and valuable because nothing leaks. Same asset, different market structure, opposite outcome, so mobile News Feed ads (championed by Fidji Simo) made the numbers, not identity joins.

Q14.9 [Scenario] You were ejected from a company and a rival offers advisory work. Which pattern applies and what are its limits?

Answer: The grudge job and the Land of the Stateless Machines: working for Twitter against Facebook's interests while employed by Facebook's biggest partner (Nanigans), building buying tools to move spend from Facebook back to Google. The notes call it "just shy" of corporate treason, "which was how Silicon Valley worked." Caveat: he was under NDA from Facebook; it is a description, not an endorsement.

Q14.10 [Scenario] You received restricted stock at $38 that is taxed as income, a lockout expires near $20 and you are ejected two years in. What does the epilogue say about this outcome versus the AdGrok engineers'?

Answer: Compensation form, tax timing, lockouts and tenure, not talent, decided who got rich: Twitter's options, a post-lockout price above $50 and four-plus years of vesting made the AdGrok engineers rich, while Facebook's restricted stock left the author with little ("paying taxes on money I hadn't made," the dot-com bankruptcies' plight in miniature). Afterward he sold everything and outfitted Ayala, a forty-foot cutter, to sail around the world alone.

Cumulative Final Exam (20 questions)

F1 [SA] State the book's one-line judgment of ad tech and the three rules that follow from it.

Answer: "Ad tech is finance for attention; incumbents keep markets inefficient; count miracles, price per head, vest before you leave." (Ch 1, 2, 7, 10)

F2 [Own words] Link Goldman's refusal to move CDS onto exchanges to Facebook's treatment of FBX.

Answer: Both incumbents preferred owning a small market with information asymmetry and price-making power to competing in a larger transparent one. Facebook's FBX showed outside data beating its own in its own auction, so it chose the closed stack (Custom Audiences, Atlas). Irony: Goldman itself moved CDS clearing to ICE in 2013, and the author predicts Facebook will eventually run a full exchange. (Ch 1, 12, 13, 14)

F3 [MC] Which of these is a "two-miracle" idea in the notes? (a) Airbnb; (b) Sponsored Stories; (c) a laundromat; (d) Google.

Answer: (b) (and AdGrok's first plan, which needed five). Airbnb and Google are single-miracle (user behavior; technical); a laundromat is zero. (Ch 2, 11)

F4 [SA] What is the difference between a cap and a valuation, and what is $100K at a $3M cap?

Answer: The cap is a maximum conversion valuation, "an input to a hypothetical calculation"; $100K at a $3M cap = 3.3% regardless of the A price. (Ch 4)

F5 [SA] Name a giant's two weak points and the specific tactic used against Adchemy.

Answer: Investors and prospective partners. PG threatened to blacklist Adchemy's VCs (August, Mayfield) from YC deal flow; Sam Altman got Microsoft BD to call the litigation "problematic" for the Bing deal. (Ch 5)

F6 [Scenario] A founder wants to be "fair" and split equity three ways, and is also tempted to hide a dire cash forecast from the team and investors. Evaluate both choices using the book.

Answer: Equal splits produce paralysis and factions: have a leader (51%+ or a true mind-meld). On the forecast: Martínez hid the Death Clock from cofounders and investors and "cooked the books," and the lie held. The notes' later rule is to lie to investors and acquirers if you must but never deceive cofounders (he himself deceived his cofounders for two weeks in the acquisition and calls the optimal line "a step too far out on the prick spectrum"). So the notes themselves are inconsistent or at least morally ambivalent ("morality... is an expensive hobby"); a good answer names that tension and the firewall logic (keep the crisis out of the team's headspace). (Ch 3, 4, 5, 7)

F7 [SA] What are the tells listed in the quick-tells section?

Answer: "Stealth" or an NDA before the pitch means loser; a counterpart calling back within the hour means weak hand; "six months" of dashboard revenue that merely reallocates budget means not incremental; an empty parking lot on Sunday means not at war; a first-ever reminder of your one-on-one means HR is waiting; champagne with a revenue Post-it signals a cult in progress. (Ch 2, 7, 8, 11, 13)

F8 [Own words] Compare how a bluff worked in Ch 6 and how a verification failure mattered in Ch 9.

Answer: The Google bluff worked because the counterpart couldn't verify it ("Everybody in tech feared Google"). In Ch 9 the Irish audit assurance from a senior engineer couldn't be trusted, so the PM verified it himself on production Christmas Eve. Common principle: whether claims can be checked decides who wins; verify what you vouched for, bluff only where the target has no back channel. (Ch 6, 9)

F9 [SA] Summarize the compensation rules: vesting, offers, and wealth thresholds.

Answer: Four-year vesting with 25% at one year; halve any big-company offer (you'll leave in two years) and halve again for stock vs. options; acqui-hire headlines are mostly signing bonuses and vesting for founders; founders own nothing until they vest; two inflection points matter, fuck-you money and fuck-the-world money. (Ch 7, 10, 12)

F10 [SA] Name the Facebook cultural mechanisms: blue tape, memento mori, onboarding, posters, Faceversaries.

Answer: Blue tape = bold experiment, fast failure, prune, encode the lesson as a macro; Sun logos = memento mori; onboarding as citizenship oath with posters as commandments; Faceversaries celebrate start dates and "Facebook deaths" mourn departures. Zuck's mission culture is compared to a revolutionary regime ("People's Republic of Facebook"). (Ch 8, 10)

F11 [Own words] Why is Facebook's social data both "inert" and later "scarce and valuable"?

Answer: On desktop a mature data marketplace and cookies leaked everywhere, so Facebook's data was marginal (Chorizo's "one measly sausage," the noisy bar). On mobile, third-party cookies are blocked, apps are siloed and Apple polices device IDs, so even age and gender were valuable. Market structure decides the value of a dataset. (Ch 8, 9, 14)

F12 [MC] Which metric does the book say to use when judging a new ad product? (a) dashboard revenue; (b) clickthrough lift vs. your baseline; (c) incremental dollars and lift vs. the best outside alternative; (d) number of partners.

Answer: (c). Ch 11 gives the lift rule (40-60% on a 20x deficit is piddly-boo) and Ch 13 gives the incrementality rule (CA discounted by half; FBX 100% incremental).

F13 [SA] What are the two traits founders need and which can be learned?

Answer: Monomaniacal focus (cannot be taught) and endurance of endless shit (can be: cross an ocean, join the Marines). Enemies help. (Ch 5)

F14 [Scenario] You are a product manager at a large company and an engineer says your idea is impossible. Which concepts apply?

Answer: Be technical enough to detect bullshit (lazy "impossible"), be the tiebreaker, build a dashboard you know to the decimal, and verify anything you personally vouched for even in production. Remember power is borrowed from engineers' trust and from the company's name. (Ch 8, 9)

F15 [Own words] Synthesize what the Twitter acqui-hire (Ch 6-7) and Facebook's FBX decision (Ch 12-13) both teach about speed and tempo.

Answer: Tempo reveals hands: Twitter called back within the hour (weak, a "call station"), and an acquirer's speed is a function of the fire you've lit under it. FBX was built in five weeks to book Q3 and Q4 revenue (a fiscal-calendar deadline), yet the notes say light speed and management could still beat it. A counterpart's behavior tells you more than its words, and deadlines (a fiscal calendar, a no-shop) shape leverage. (Ch 6, 7, 12, 13)

F16 [SA] Why does Martínez say acquirers don't care about the founder/investor split, and how did this play out for investors?

Answer: Acquirers price people (per-head), so the split is the founders' choice from their own wallet. Twitter's default term sheet gave investors ~$1M of ~$10M instead of the ~$2M pro rata; Sacca's rage followed. (Ch 7)

F17 [T/F] The book argues that the open FBX would have been the right strategy because mobile News Feed ads were inevitable.

Answer: False. The epilogue says the 2013 debate was moot: neither FBX nor Custom Audiences saved Facebook; mobile News Feed ads did, for structural reasons nobody argued about at the time. Being right about the technology was not the same as being right about what would save the quarter. FBX nevertheless grew to ~$500M. (Ch 13, 14)

F18 [Own words] Compare "Open Graph/Sponsored Stories" and "FBX" as strategies using the miracle count and incrementality.

Answer: Sponsored Stories needed two miracles and rested on cognitive dissonance and unmeasurable brand Likes; FBX needed one idea (adopt the industry standard, outside data), was built in five weeks, and produced fully incremental revenue. (Ch 11, 12, 13)

F19 [SA] List five numbers from the book and what each shows.

Answer: E.g., Google $70B (auction); $100K at $3M cap = 3.3%; 120 ms bid window with ~60 ms NC-Amsterdam one way; direct mail ~$1,000 CPM vs. ~$1 online; IPO opened ~$42/closed ~$38.37 with ~1% fees; FBX ~$500M by early 2014; Atlas for ~$0.1B of a $6.2B write-down. (Ch 3, 4, 12, 13, 14)

F20 [Scenario, synthesis] Design a one-paragraph playbook for a founder who (a) joins YC, (b) faces an incumbent's lawsuit, (c) raises seed money, (d) gets acquired, using at least five concepts from different chapters.

Answer: Count the miracles and have a leader (Ch 2-3); launch via content marketing with servers ready (Ch 3); groom a lead, negotiate the cap and ask "do you have decision-making power?" (Ch 4); if sued, firewall the team, get a first-tier firm to take mispriced equity and hit the giant's investors and partners via your network (Ch 4-5); stalk each counterpart, create an auction before the no-shop and read tempo (Ch 6-7); price per head, demand a replicating portfolio, resign before you sign, and know you own nothing until you vest (Ch 7, 10).

End of quiz. Source: the martinez-chaos-monkeys skill's chapter notes, not the book's own wording.

Arguments & Evidence

Chaos Monkeys: Arguments and Evidence

Book: Chaos Monkeys: Obscene Fortune and Random Failure in Silicon Valley by Antonio García Martínez (about 500 pages; events 2007-2016).

Source note. This file reflects the martinez-chaos-monkeys skill's chapter notes (SKILL.md, glossary, patterns, cheatsheet and the 14 chapter files), not the book's own wording. It uses only that material: no outside facts, numbers, quotes or stories were added, and where the notes are silent this file is silent. Quotes are quotes as recorded in the notes. The notes group the book's 46 sections (three parts plus prologue and epilogue) into 14 chapters; "Ch" below means the notes' chapter. Ad-tech specifics (CPMs, cookies, match rates) are period data and have changed since.

Time estimates in Part 1 are my own planning estimates, not from the notes. The companion file is martinez-chaos-monkeys-quiz.md.

PART 1 - How to read this book fast without missing anything

1.1 What the book is, in one paragraph

A memoir of an ex-Goldman quant turned startup founder (AdGrok), Y Combinator alumnus, acqui-hire negotiator and Facebook ads product manager. Its through-line: ad tech is finance for attention; incumbents keep markets inefficient; startups are experiments with other people's money in which team, leverage and timing matter more than ideas; and Facebook's monetization was shaped less by foresight than by structural luck (mobile). Three parts: Part One (Goldman, Adchemy, the YC decision), Part Two (YC, fund-raising, the lawsuit, the acquisition dance), Part Three (Facebook).

  1. Ch 2 (diagnostics and the miracle count): the cheapest high-yield chapter.
  2. Ch 1 only for the framework (price on perception, incumbents, first-party data).
  3. Then straight through in order, because Parts Two and Three are one continuous narrative (AdGrok's lawsuit leads to Twitter/Facebook, which leads to the FBX war).

PART 2 - Chapter by chapter

Chapter 1: Prologue, The Undertakers of Capitalism, The Human Attention Exchange

Central argument

Wall Street and ad tech are the same business, putting a price on human perception, and both are being taken over by machines. Martínez opens with the April 2012 Zuck meeting that green-lit retargeting, then rewinds to his Goldman Sachs quant days to establish the book's lens: markets are run by whoever makes prices, inefficiency is profitable to incumbents, and quants and engineers are enablers rather than stars.

Full stories

The April 13, 2012 Zuck meeting. Facebook's IPO was imminent and revenue was plateauing; Open Graph and Sponsored Stories were a market failure. Martínez and colleagues brought three proposals to Zuckerberg: using Like-button browsing data (Zuck said no) and two ways to join external data (retargeting got a yes: "yes to retargeting, but no to using social plugins"). Beforehand, Sheryl acted as gatekeeper, holding pre-meetings to shape the message for Zuck: the "Supreme Court of Sheryl." Martínez's observation is that such decisions are "made on gut feel, the residue of whatever historical politics were in play, and the ability to cater persuasive messages to people either busy, impatient, or uninterested." The meeting sets the stage for the outside-data pivot of Chapters 12-13. The chapter also paints Facebook's geography: proximity to Zuck as status, the Aquarium, HACK in the courtyard, and Ads kept "at arm's length... like sweaty underwear."

Goldman Sachs and SLK. Martínez's Goldman years frame everything. Goldman's acquired broker SLK went from hundreds of traders and two programmers (2000) to two traders and twenty quants with fast machines (2007). Via Andreessen, the generalization: two future job types, people who tell computers what to do and people told by computers what to do. Finance saw it first; ad tech (real-time bidding), then Uber, Airbnb and Instacart follow. Goldman's ecology: partners as feudal lords (Elisha Wiesel), traders as chainsaw jugglers, sales as "complete tools," quants as "eunuchs at the orgy" who get knee calluses. Goldman could compute risk across desks "to five decimals" and never lost its cool.

Why Goldman wouldn't move CDS to exchanges. With few players, total information asymmetry and price-making power, transparency only invited competition. "Goldman felt more comfortable owning a small market than merely participating in a larger one," a pattern Martínez says he saw again at Facebook. Also: a CDS is unlike car insurance because anyone can buy or write protection on someone else's "car," including the thief.

The trading-floor gambling and the ID lottery (worked example). The White Castle burger contest, push-up over/unders and the Friday ID-in-a-sack lottery. With a $2,000 pot and ten IDs left, fair value is $200 each; options on IDs traded above fair value, and the premium rose as fewer remained (irrational overbidding for large, likelier payouts, plus Friday cash pressure) until a memo banned betting. Lesson: markets deviate from fair value in predictable, exploitable directions when payouts are large and participants have outside pressures.

The bonus number and Scott Weinstein. The bonus number was your entire worth; the "roach-motel collar" tied people in. Scott Weinstein, who prized security, was fired after twenty years: "the best advice... that I ignored to my extreme peril."

The DUI gambit. Over the limit at 0.91, Martínez offered the officer a taxi under observation instead of a station blood test, reframing the encounter from castigation to haggling. Lesson: "if you want to be a startup entrepreneur, get used to negotiating from positions of weakness."

Adchemy and the throwaway RTB engine. A NYT item, a whim CV, a Mustang and a Zeitgeist Bloody Mary led him to Adchemy, betting that tech would be "the last man standing." At Adchemy he built a throwaway RTB engine to feed the CEO's pitch; it later made him "light-years ahead" of Facebook's product team. Anti-pattern: building tech to support a CEO's bullshit, but keep the knowledge.

Evidence

  • SLK headcount (Goldman, 2000 vs. 2007): hundreds of traders and two programmers vs. two traders and twenty quants. Proves the computers-replace-decision-makers thesis; caveat: a single firm illustration.
  • Facebook's data barely moved monetization: a year of ingesting posts, check-ins, Likes and friends did little (the evidence for "Facebook data isn't that valuable"; formalized by Project Chorizo in Ch 8).
  • Programmatic buying (Right Media, 2007): shifted power from publishers to advertisers with first-party data, e.g., Amazon's purchase data beats "35-year-old male in Ohio."
  • The ID lottery: observed premiums above the $200 fair value; proves predictable mispricing under large payouts. Caveat: a floor anecdote, not a controlled study.
  • Cheatsheet numbers: Goldman average pay 2005 $521K; grad stipend $19K.

Key terms

Price on perception; derivative; CDS; SLK lesson; RTB (a stock exchange for attention: every page load emits a sell order for one share of your brain); direct response vs. brand; first-party data; programmatic buying; "every new medium imitates the last" (radio read books; TV filmed quiz shows; internet ads copied 1836 newspaper boxes; websites are still called "publishers"); Only Good News/"Supreme Court of Sheryl."

So what

When you meet any "data" business, ask what it really sells and who makes the price. Prefer first-party purchase data to demographics. Expect incumbents to resist transparency. Negotiate by reframing the encounter, not by pleading.

Chapter 2: Knowing How to Swim, Abandoning the Shipwreck

Central argument

How to diagnose a doomed startup from the inside, why you should leave it, and how to get into Y Combinator. Adchemy showed every terminal symptom; the three-person team applied to YC with a five-miracle idea, won a ten-minute interrogation on team quality, and escaped Adchemy through harassment, retention bribes and an immigration threat, arriving at the book's cynical fourteen-line creed.

Full stories

Adchemy's decay. The author's former employer displayed all four signs: a lone surviving founder (the Team page purged like a Stalin photo); ~$6M/month of lead-gen revenue unrelated to the product (a trust fund that "makes a drug addict's spiral more long lasting"); a rotating set of beta-customer logos every quarter; and loyal employees despite mistreatment. Murthy broke the author's finger with a baseball and mocked him for months; staff still bought stock and lost savings. Adchemy's later end (2014): after $130M+ raised, a fire-sale "acquisition," and employees who had bought stock lost savings: "Their Stockholm syndrome lasted to the very end."

The team. Matthew McEachen (MRM, Adchemy's employee #11 and author of half its codebase, family man, "the silverback"), Argyris Zymnis (Stanford AI lab, Greek, non-citizen) and the author (words and bets). The team's first idea, linking a bar code to a local ad, needed five miracles. Their product pivoted until it ended as "Plan J."

The YC application (March 1-29, 2010). Procrastinating by reading PG essays, the author noticed "Deadline March 3," handed Argyris the printout (the "gateway drug": PG's "How to Start a Startup") and spent two days at Peet's writing the application ("the Goldman Sachs of advertising"; the Craigslist man-in-the-middle hack as the answer to "what non-computer system have you hacked?"). The boys built a demo. They took the last interview slot on the last day (be first or last on any list). The interview was ten minutes, four partners firing overlapping questions ("How do you join the online click to the physical person?" "So how do you get paid again?"), a countdown clock, Jessica silent, no demo reached; an alum trashed the idea afterward. Over beer at the Rose & Crown, PG called with the acceptance; the author blundered by saying "I should probably ask him first," the WRONG ANSWER, because commitment should be decided before the offer. MRM was convinced by phone, packaged as provisional, and the acceptance came by voicemail. Pattern: apply late and fast, sell the team, pre-commit.

YC people. PG's twice-yearly boot camp (small money, ship in three months, Demo Day); Jessica Livingston (Founders at Work, "a startup anarchist's cookbook"), Robert Morris ("He's never wrong"), Trevor Blackwell (Anybots' landlord).

Leaving Adchemy. McEachen said goodbye to Murthy, who didn't look up or shake his hand; the author admits he was doing the same thing: "he was merely trading Murthy for me" ("every Jobs has his Wozniak"). Retention pressure came as equity, fear and legal threats. Adchemy's immigrant executives threatened to report their former employee to ICE for planning to work on an F-2, "former slaves turned slave owners"; the author blurted his legal workaround to the party that wanted to hurt him (an anti-pattern). The truth ("we have no products, no clients") made them a threat; expect quarantine.

British Trader and Zoë. An ex-Deutsche Bank derivatives trader met on Match; pregnant after weeks; Zoë born March 2010 during YC applications: "life is what happens when you're making other plans."

Evidence

  • Adchemy lead-gen revenue ~$6M/month, with no product clients: shows a cash cow masking product failure.
  • Murthy and the baseball: the Stockholm-syndrome anecdote; staff still bought stock.
  • Adchemy's outcome (2014): $130M+ raised, fire-sale acquisition, employee losses. Caveat: this is the notes' retrospective in Ch 5.
  • PG's endorsement of the "X of Y" tagline ("the Goldman Sachs of advertising"): now cliché.
  • YC interview: no demo reached; yet accepted: evidence that YC judges team quality, using the idea as a probe.

Key terms

Four signs of a doomed startup; miracle count; pivot ("a panicked sprint"); rage equation ((society's valuation of you - your self-valuation) x ego); X of Y tagline; H-1B peonage; stealth/NDA as a loser tattoo; "Writing as engineered deception" (language exists "to better deceive, not inform"); the fourteen-line creed; "Every Jobs has his Wozniak."

The creed (paraphrase): investors have more money than time; employees more time than money; entrepreneurs are the seductive go-betweens; startups are experiments with other people's money; marketing is like sex, only losers pay; culture is what goes without saying; no rules, only laws; success forgives all sins; people who leak to you leak about you; meritocracy is propaganda; greed and vanity are the twin engines; most managers survive via inertia and politics; lawsuits are expensive feints; capitalism is an amoral farce in which everyone is complicit.

So what

Before joining or investing, check who left, where the money really comes from, whether logos become contracts and whether loyalty is earned or induced. Count miracles before any pitch, investment or job offer. Decide commitments among cofounders before the offer arrives. Treat retention pressure as confirmation to leave.

Chapter 3: War Face, Like Marriage, Speed Is a Feature, D-Day

Central argument

Inside YC: weekly dinners, partner access, the "YC mafia" network, prestige and Demo Day. Google's keyword auction prints money while the SMB last mile is a graveyard. Equal-equity founder teams fail ("Have a leader!"). Content marketing manufactured AdGrok's existence. The book's title comes from Netflix's chaos monkey as a metaphor for entrepreneurs who pull the plug on whole industries.

Full stories

YC dinners. Marissa Mayer arrived with a Google handler and shook; Reid Hoffman "thundered like an emperor," the best speaker.

The GrokPad and the GrokBar. A Mountain View one-bedroom with Home Depot door desks, near Red Rock Coffee and Fenwick & West ("an entity we would, sadly, come to know well"). The GrokBar was a browser bar (ripped from the DiggBar) showing, on each page of an online store, which Google keywords drive sales and at what cost. The pitch: AdWords is an undammed river of money; take a fraction.

The three founders. MRM can fix anything (Leatherman on a street sign), designs well, inflates his own centrality, chases shiny bugs and is emotionally fragile; Argyris is a renaissance hacker, pugnacious "emotional IED," works on whatever he likes; the author supplies words, bets and the unwanted peacemaker role. Equal thirds produced decision paralysis and rotating two-against-one factions. PG diagnosed the leadership gap in ten minutes of a walk. About six of thirty batch companies had disputed leadership and crumbled or had coups. AdGrok's eventual undoing was the founders' natures, not an enemy. Geoff Ralston: "people don't really change, they just become better actors."

Prototype Day and the rehearsal. The author tripped over the projector cord, delivered five seconds of demo, "a complete fucking fiasco" - then AdGrok took second place in the Demo Day rehearsal vote. The T-shirt arms race: AdGrok wore logo shirts at rehearsal; by Demo Day every team had rush-ordered its own. Rapportive's polished Prototype Day pitch dismayed him, yet two years later both companies had the same acqui-hire exit: "This too shall pass."

The New York post (full worked example). Trigger: Ron Conway and PG praised New York's startup scene at dinner. Thesis: New York's economy is monopolies of information (banks, agents, rental brokers) that go unchallenged, while San Francisco builds Craigslist and makes the pimp obsolete. Two nights writing; a Tuesday 9 a.m. post to Hacker News (Monday too groggy, Thursday drifting, Friday for burying news); friends upvote; #1 within minutes; a Scoble tweet; the single-server blog melts; MRM clones the blog across new AWS machines; traffic jumps from about a dozen views/day to 50,000; Business Insider and 20/20 call. The Goldman post was held in reserve for Monday's attention decay. The result: thousands of sign-ups and a viral post every 3-4 weeks. Principles: media attention is like sex, only good and better; pick the biggest nerve; seed upvotes; reply to fans; egg on trolls; double down when it works; have servers ready.

Demo Day. About 30 companies, 2.5 minutes each, three salvos in descending investor importance, two rehearsals (batch, then alumni), no actual demos (investors care about the business), hours of "nut-to-butt" networking; the running-of-the-bulls waiting feeling.

Chaos monkey. Netflix's tool randomly kills servers to test resilience; entrepreneurs are "society's chaos monkeys" (Uber vs. medallions, Airbnb vs. hotels, Tinder vs. dating), fed by VC "bananas." Whether society survives them, and at what human cost, is society's problem, not the zoo's.

Evidence

  • Google makes $70B via auctions on every query. Mechanism: bid x estimated click probability. Words are the products: insurance, loans, mortgage, lawyer; "mesothelioma" at ~$90/click.
  • ROAS = revenue / cost - 1, e.g., "nevada cheap divorce": 47%.
  • SMB graveyard: Clickable ($32M), Lexity ($6M), Trada ($19M) all died; SMBs pay $50-100/month and cancel fast.
  • YC batch leadership failures: ~6 of 30 companies had disputed leadership.
  • Blog traffic: from ~a dozen views/day to 50,000; #1 on Hacker News. Caveat: a single viral event, but repeated every 3-4 weeks.
  • YC's network: ~80% of the consumer/infrastructure stack can be rebuilt from YC companies, with discounts and preferential adoption.

Key terms

What YC sells; ROAS; SMB trap; last-mile thesis; Have a leader; Vulcan mind-meld; chaos monkey; Demo Day; This too shall pass; "Not every problem has an engineering solution. That doesn't mean you can't sell one."

So what

Use YC's network as customers and logos. Search advertising rewards intent at its apex. Avoid Mom-and-Pop unless you partner with or build on someone who owns them. Appoint one leader (51%+ or genuine mind-meld) before you start. Launch with provocation, timing and doubling-down, with scalable servers; at Demo Day pitch the business.

Chapter 4: A Conclave of Angels, Hill of Sand, Widening Gyre, ¡No Pasarán!

Central argument

A field manual for seed fund-raising (angels vs. micro-VCs, convertible notes and caps, dilution, VC hierarchy and the "do you have decision-making power?" test) interrupted by Adchemy's personal trade-secret lawsuit at peak post-Demo Day momentum. AdGrok survived by lying in a spreadsheet, halving its cap and getting Fenwick & West to defend it for mispriced equity. Thesis: startups are founded on forgotten crimes; "there are no real rules, only laws"; success forgives all sins.

Full stories

Russ Siegelman, the angel. Ex-Microsoft/MSN and ex-Kleiner, investing his own money, he wants 2-4x, wants it back if the company is imploding, does haphazard due diligence through friends, and is committed. The author groomed Russ weeks before Demo Day even though he arrived late and lost to the first meeting ("he almost wrote us off"). Had they not groomed him, "we'd have lost... our lead investor." At a $4M cap Russ's headshake was a tell that he'd do it if pushed: the author's self-described skill.

Chris Sacca, the micro-VC. A $20-40M fund ("a fund of bosses"), needing outsized outliers and supplying a gold-plated name that makes weak-kneed investors follow; he said "I'm in!" in half an hour.

Sand Hill Road and Sequoia. The road "starts in a shopping mall and ends at a particle accelerator," with the Rosewood's cougar nights between; Sequoia's lobby is a "mini-Louvre" of tombstones (Apple, Google, Airbnb) with model-caliber receptionists; VC offices are "absolutely still." The engineers broke the codebase a minute before the Sequoia pitch (hence "fund-raise alone"). Sequoia passed citing "white space" with a competing investment (Kenshoo): "a truth that is also a polite lie," but stayed prompt and offered intros: "it's the incompetent and insecure who are generally the assholes." At Charles River, Bill Tai asked "would you sell for $50M?" and the author smirked; the wrong answer cost the deal, and the question "would prove prescient."

Ben Narasin (TriplePoint) and Ace & Company. Narasin: sockless Top-Siders, the rumpled $50,000 emergency check from a Schwab account at a Turkish-Mexican tapas bar, wallet photos ("this is who you're working for"); MRM asked "what about my kids?" Ace & Company: a Swiss family fund, an Egyptian telecoms fortune, a wire from Zug: "a little red never made money less green." The round: four investors, ~$500K at a $2M cap.

The suit (Sept 10, 2010). Wilson Sonsini filed for trade-secret misappropriation, breach of contract and loyalty, and injunctive relief personally against all three founders and the company, with ~$2,000 in AdGrok's bank. Apocalypse planning: MRM would quit, Argyris would flee to Greece, the author would blog every filing to shame Adchemy; the unspoken fear was that Murthy would rehire the boys. None happened; MRM, the family man, bet everything: "the actual daredevil."

Fenwick and the Undertaker. Rodger Cole, Fenwick's litigator with a "frigid demeanor." The Fenwick deal: $250K in fees fronted as a loan for a small equity slice plus options; if AdGrok died, nothing repaid; if it won, buy back the equity at the seed price with no prepayment penalty: "a one-in-a-million lottery ticket to win $250,000... for $250,000." Cash-only solo lawyers at $400/hour cost more than $700/hour partners who take equity ("cash is the poor man's credit"). The French-mathematician gambit: tell lawyers the investors are in and would they take equity; tell investors legal costs are minimal because lawyers take equity; let the engineers code.

The Death Clock. A cash-burn spreadsheet including Fenwick's estimate (~$500K to trial, ~$1.5M total over 18 months, ~$20K/month); every version crashed into the ground. He hid it from cofounders and investors and "cooked the books" - lower legal costs, an impossible launch date, an "unconscionable" growth rate. Russ stayed, but cut the cap from $4M to $2M and required $200K more from others; about 22% was sold (a future Series A problem: "worrying about cholesterol while dying of cancer").

Murthy's kindness that armed his enemies. Murthy's one kindness, the Ted Wang intro (framed as a tribute to the late Rajeev Motwani), led Wang to fight out of outrage at the bullying of a startup. "If you're going to be a sociopath, do it properly." Sun Tzu: leave your opponent a way out; Murthy didn't, so even the skittish fought.

Forgotten crimes. Gates cloned Kildall's QDOS and kept the copyright; Jobs pocketed the Atari bonus and paid Wozniak $350; Zuckerberg ran with the idea he was hired to build. Balzac: "The secret of great fortunes without apparent cause is a forgotten crime." The Valley is reactionary about its image. Also the Silicon Valley network is fluid: unlike Wall Street's birth-and-prep-school pipeline, anyone who makes superficial friends and publishes a few thought pieces can join the elite and fall out as fast. Kiteboarding and the MaiTai camp are the VC elite's club, entered via social capital and "thought leadership."

Evidence

  • Cap math (worked): $100K note, no cap: Series A at $10M gives 1%; at $100M gives 0.1%. With a $3M cap: 3.3% regardless. Founders' side: $4M discussed, $2M closed, ~22% sold for ~$500K (roughly double typical seed dilution).
  • YC 2010 cap benchmarks: $3-4M middle; $6M good; ~$8M stellar (Hipmunk). Dilution as cheesecake: every round sells a slice.
  • Legal costs: ~$500K to trial; ~$1.5M total over 18 months; ~$20K/month; ~$800/hr is also quoted in the cheatsheet; $400 vs. $700/hr in the chapter (see conflicts in Part 3(f)).
  • Monday partner meeting: four to five hours; yeses that night, nos drift or never arrive.
  • The suit's timing: ~$2,000 in the bank when sued.

Key terms

Angel vs. micro-VC; convertible note; cap; dilution; Death Clock; decision-making power; mispriced option; forgotten crime; French-mathematician gambit; groom your lead; fund-raise alone.

So what

Negotiate the cap, not a "valuation." Groom a lead before Demo Day and talk cap on the third date. Ask any VC "Do you have decision-making power?" and route around hedgers. Disclose a lawsuit only when pens hover, price it into terms, and get a first-tier firm to take mispriced equity.

Chapter 5: The Dog Shit Sandwich, Victory, Launching!

Central argument

How a broke three-person startup beat a $130M-funded incumbent's lawsuit by finding the giant's two weak points, investors and prospective partners, and applying leverage through the YC network. Then the sobering aftermath: the two traits founders actually need, a PR-only launch, and the Trough of Despair that kills 90%+ of startups that survive everything else.

Full stories

The leak and the search for a connector. An Adchemy employee's drinks-fueled disclosure revealed a $50M-scale Bing deal with Microsoft: Murthy's "last business bet." A LinkedIn search for a Microsoft connector landed on Sam Altman, who had come to AdGrok through Angel Day (a YC mini-Demo Day where elite investors vote on whom to mentor; AdGrok drew Jeff Clavier and Altman in Friday-afternoon sessions the cofounders were too scared to repeat).

PG's response (knife to balls, October 2010). Week 1: leak and LinkedIn search. Week 2: PG's email thread with Murthy; a Saturday summons to Old Palo Alto; PG's plan to anathematize Adchemy's VCs (John Johnston of August; Yogen Dalal of Mayfield) by disinviting them from Demo Day and steering founders elsewhere. PG had gone to Wilson Sonsini on a bicycle and emailed Murthy first. "To have influence in the world, you need to be willing and able to reward your friends and punish your enemies." YC blacklists investors who cross its companies regardless of fund size. PG's instruction: "Come alone... keep them out of it." The author didn't tell the boys about the plan in case it failed. Week 3: Altman ("Manson Lamps"; PG: "parachute him into an island full of cannibals... he'd be the king") called from the 280: Microsoft BD had told Adchemy litigation was "problematic" for the deal, "the decapitated horse's head in Murthy's bed." Meanwhile the Undertaker offered audited code and began hostile depositions, and Dalal was seen in a "strained conversation" dressing down Murthy at Mayfield. Late October: Adchemy unilaterally offered to dismiss; settled February 2011. Victory paperwork: token reaffirmations, an encrypted zip of the codebase kept by Fenwick that nobody would open, and a last taunting email to Murthy.

Adchemy's end (2014). After $130M+ raised, a fire-sale acquisition; employees who had bought stock lost savings.

British Trader, December 2010. The household "run to the beat of Pimm's cups... and the Queen's speech"; "You sure don't smile like that when you see me anymore"; move-out in December 2010; a second pregnancy from "that relationship coda"; the author's suspicion of being "snookered into fatherhood" and his verdict: "we're all either subjects or objects of one or another conspiracy"; "the heir and the spare."

The launch (March 7, 2011). A PR agency ("like losers, we paid for it"), Internet Retailer and Direct Marketing News interviews, a small wave of sign-ups, rotating support chats. Tech press covers births, deaths, weddings and bloody accidents (funding rounds, collapses, acquisitions, scandals); a launch is a PR event under embargo, timed Monday for echo, even on your child's first birthday ("the startup won"). The chapter ends with the pivot to Twitter via a blog fan (@jess): never ignore people who can write really big checks.

Evidence

  • Adchemy funding: $130M+ raised and beaten by a company with ~$2,000 in the bank (Ch 4): evidence that leverage matters more than resources.
  • Timeline: leak to dismissal offer in about three weeks; formally settled February 2011.
  • Trough of Despair (the YC whiteboard curve): launch spike, crash, long flatline, slight rise, dip ("misconfigured analytics code"), steady climb to acquisition; kills 90%+ of startups that survived founder fights, shipping and fund-raising.
  • Deal flow context (2010): angel glut, $20-40M micro-funds, YC, AWS, Rails and "shovel" startups like Parse; pro-rata rights meant later-round access depended on being in early. YC thus controlled "the water sluice."
  • Founder traits claim: an assertion with a personal example (watching his daughter grow up "through a Skype window"), not a study.

Key terms

Two weak points; deal flow; reward friends/punish enemies; firewall; two-hop node; Trough of Despair; product-market fit; positive run rate ("getting the wings on mid-fall"); monomaniacal focus; endurance of endless shit.

So what

Map who the aggressor needs (investors, partners). Activate loyal power brokers. Keep existential crises out of the team's headspace. Don't believe the launch spike; plan the trough. Founder fairy tales (Drew Houston on the cover) are post-hoc narratives.

Chapter 6: Dates @Twitter, Acquisition Chicken, Getting Liked, Getting Poked

Central argument

A due-diligence and negotiation manual disguised as a courtship story: stalk everyone before every meeting, always be ready to demo, treat acquisition interest as mutual seduction, run two channels (formal email, clandestine phone), cultivate insiders, create an auction before a no-shop lands, bluff with the name everyone fears (Google), and understand why your VC's home-run-only economics will push you to reject a good-enough offer.

Full stories

@jess and the first lunch (March 17). Jessica Verrilli, Twitter's one-woman corp dev (Stanford lacrosse, Lake Washington gentry, a blog fan), initiated contact. At lunch Adam Bain (ex-Fox, "the adult in the room keeping an eye on the register") asked "what are you working on?" and the author had no laptop; MRM's hosted demo, runnable from any machine, saved the day (always be closing).

The ten days in March. 17th: lunch, impromptu demo on Bain's laptop. 22nd: team lunch; Kevin Weil ("Maybe you should join us... like in acquiring you"); PG says ignore, Sacca reactivates. 23rd: Bain's monetization pitch. 25th: NDA arrives; Orrick engaged; Deep Tweet opens. 27th: Deep Tweet: "create an auction"; doors beaten at Google (silence), Microsoft (remote pitch), Facebook ("in play"). 29th: Twitter's verbal "$5 million thing" for three hires plus IP and YC bling; Facebook meeting confirmed. 30th: Facebook pitch, the Google bluff, the garage call, three emails. April 1: Facebook interview day.

Twitter in 2011. About 400 employees, de minimis revenue, two-stage security with disappearing-ink badges, Restoration Hardware aesthetics (Sara Morishige), Lady Gaga visiting. Deep Tweet (Epicenter Café's back door to Twitter) said board meetings were dysfunctional with entourages, Ev and Biz were checked out, and there was no product leadership. Twitter's Ads lieutenants (Weil, Roetter, Bain, Verrilli) became Product, Engineering, COO and Corp Dev by 2015. Kevin Thau, Alex Roetter (AdSense founding engineer) also featured.

Orrick and the lawyers. After a Kinko's-faxed incorporation, get a first-rate corporate firm (Orrick, via Mixer Labs' founders); the best firms give "the first dose free" and play the long game; pay in something other than money if you must. "Trust, but verify - and keep a loaded shotgun under your bed."

Sacca's reappearance. Silent for months, then calling at all hours once Twitter, where he was a major holder who had reportedly helped JPMorgan buy 10% at $21/share, was in play: "a man who only ever talked his book." His email: "No fucking way should you engage on this offer."

Facebook, March 30. HACK on the doors, the real-time friending globe, the signed Facebook Wall; KX Jin ("like Wisconsin"), Amin Zoufonoun (corp-dev chief in his first week), Ambar Pansari, Nipun Mathur. When Amin asked who else was bidding, the author gestured at the Google keywords on screen and said "we want to be part of the future, not the past." It worked because Amin was three days out of Google with no back channel there: "Everybody in tech feared Google." Also "fake it till you make it": Sacca told Twitter another offer existed (false), "a truth that hadn't quite birthed itself."

The parking-garage board call. Russ and Sacca on speakerphones; the founders in MRM's Honda; Twitter paused pending "more cash." The author's three emails: grovel to Sacca, decline Jess, accept Facebook's interview request - and chose not to tell Sacca about Facebook. Anti-pattern: wimping out on the call so the VC plays bad cop invited Sacca's angry texts.

Facebook interview day (April 1). Alon Amit, Rohit Dhawan (then BMW talk), Jared Morgenstern (design a music app; explain shake-to-pair), Justin Shaffer (VC-style interrogation), Gokul. Campbell's soup from a microkitchen; someone coding in a toilet stall; buckets of disposable toothbrushes: "They had my attention." The cofounders hated the "fascist vibe." The five PM archetypes: designer, analyst (Fermi estimate: planes in the sky), old-timer, culture ("FoZ" arrogance), domain boss (Gokul: "What's the first thing you would change?" "a conversion-tracking system"; an ads system without one "is like a car without even rear or side windows").

SoMa. The eight-by-eight-block "playing field of global technology" between First and Eighth, King and Market, where Twitter destabilizes regions, Airbnb roils Barcelona rents and Uber gets bricks through windshields in Paris.

Evidence

  • Acqui-hire price range: $0.5-2M per engineer in four-year vesting equity (2011); Twitter's $5M for three hires was "way too cheap" vs. a pre-lawsuit $4M cap and YC seeds above $5M.
  • No-shop: typically 60 days and enforceable.
  • Sacca's stake: reportedly helped JPMorgan buy 10% of Twitter at $21/share (a reported claim in the notes).
  • Fund structure: funds are fire-and-forget, not compounding, so VCs need 10x (as stated in Ch 6; Ch 4 says 100x outliers; see Part 3(f)); angels take 2x.
  • Interview speed: Facebook interviews within 48 hours of the pitch.

Key terms

Stalking; always be closing; dragoman; Deep Tweet; no-shop; in play; fiduciary duty ("moral license to screw someone"); acquisition as self-seduction; cultural fit; lifestyle business (VC sneer); fake it till you make it.

So what

Stalk every counterpart and interviewer; keep a demo that runs on any laptop; read phone calls as yes and emails as no; create the auction before the no-shop; bluff only where the counterpart can't verify; don't let a buyer-invested investor run your process; negotiate each head as a separate job.

Chapter 7: The Various Futures of the Forking Paths, Retweets, The Dotted Line, Endgame

Central argument

The anatomy of a hybrid acqui-hire: Facebook rejected the engineers but wanted the CEO; Twitter returned at ~$10M; the CEO lied to his cofounders for two weeks, helped them win Twitter's interviews, then walked to Facebook at the term-sheet meeting - and Twitter still called back within an hour with $5M+ for the two engineers. The post-mortem: acquirers buy people at a target price per head; founders own nothing until they vest; "AdGrok was simply a long, stressful job interview"; the optimal play would have required deceiving cofounders.

Full stories

April 5: the split. Twitter offered ~$10M. Amin's call said Facebook was "mixed" on Argyris and Matt (MRM a definite no; "cultural fit"), but "we want you." British Trader advised: don't tell the boys. Facebook is "legalized crack": CityVille hit 100M users in a month; a Florida mother shook her baby to death over FarmVille notifications - "products that cause mothers to murder their infants in order to use them more... simply cannot fail." (The domino set: his Cuban grandmother's five smuggled pounds, now unused because his mother plays FarmVille.)

The Whereoscope template (Mick Johnson). Shop to Twitter, Zynga, Google, Facebook; force bidders who each want part into the same room; accept a Frankenstein of cash, dual vesting and an investor side-deal. Skulduggery is the non-meritocrat's tool: "anyone who claims the Valley is meritocratic... has profited vastly from it via nonmeritocratic means."

Technical due diligence and the engine dying. Twitter inspected the stack, possibly line by line; AWS and off-the-shelf components let anyone fake a product, so they check scaling competence. At the South Park picnic table (where Twitter itself was conceived), the confrontation about waning commitment led to the realization: no shipping for a month post-launch, MRM checked out, the mind-meld gone. "The dev team is the engine of a tech company. If they were done, then we were dead in the water."

The Twitter interview day (April 13). Half the interviewers came from the DabbleDB acquisition; second-order stress ("if I didn't do well, they'd suffer"). A Twitter engineer's selling point, that nobody works past six - breakfast and lunch only - sealed the choice against Twitter. The Getaround race: a Tesla Roadster vs. Matt Tillman's Mini to Stinson Beach, a wrong-side-of-the-road pass through Muir Beach, a depleted battery, then a Porsche on Lombard: "he didn't get to that Porsche by turning down all-in challenges."

The desengaño (April 14-18). Jess's "Call" promised a term sheet; the CEO confessed the lie to the boys before the reckoning and presented his departure as a fait accompli to avoid mutiny. April 15: term sheets from both. April 16: Sacca's last call - fury at the investor-light term sheet, then at the Facebook news ("You're going to fuck up this entire deal!") - and a hang-up; they'd never speak again. Facebook's replicating-portfolio offer (~$32/share pre-IPO; ~$2.3M, about a 25% AdGrok stake after the split) accepted verbally.

April 18: walkout and callback. At noon at Twitter, Satya Patel (new head of product): "So you're telling us you're bailing on the deal?" The team walked out unescorted; the boys "would have kicked me to death." At 2:00 p.m. Twitter called MRM with $5M+ for the two engineers; 2:45 a lawyer said accept now and resign first; the 3:07 Caltrain; the resignation email went out as corp dev opened the door - "unemployed for all of five minutes." The scanning frenzy was "like the last few minutes inside the safe room of the American embassy in Tehran." The deal remained "a minor Silicon Valley oddity."

The master play he didn't make. Negotiate both offers in secret, front-load Twitter with single-trigger acceleration or up-front cash, accept, quit day one, walk to Facebook (Twitter too embarrassed to sue). Impossible without deceiving cofounders: "a step too far out on the prick spectrum." "Morality... is an expensive hobby."

Evidence

  • Price figures: Twitter ~$10M -> $5M+ for two engineers; investors received ~$1M of ~$10M vs. ~$2M pro rata under Twitter's default term sheet.
  • Facebook replicating portfolio: ~$32/share pre-IPO -> ~$2.3M, ~25% of AdGrok stake.
  • Speed of Twitter's callback: within about two hours of the noon announcement per the day-by-day (the notes also say "within an hour" of the walkout): evidence of a weak hand.
  • Headline vs. reality: "sold for $X million" may be 10% company price and 90% signing bonuses and vesting for founders.
  • Vesting: founders' 20-40% stakes vest like employees'; ten months in, "nobody at AdGrok actually owned anything."

Key terms

Legalized crack; Whereoscope template; Land of the Stateless Machines (Californians hold no grudges and reward no generosity; the sunny "Hi!" means "I don't care"; "hippies with a capitalization table and a vesting schedule"); desengaño; consideration; replicating portfolio; call station; resign before you sign; corp dev = HR with a fatter checkbook; single-trigger acceleration.

So what

Treat an acqui-hire as N separate job offers wrapped together. Know who bears the cost of the investor split (you). Sequence disclosures so each party learns your move when it can no longer stop it, but notice the notes treat deceiving cofounders as the line. Get employment counsel; accept the same day; resign before you sign.

Chapter 8: Boot Camp, Product Masseur, Google Delenda Est, Leaping Headlong

Central argument

Facebook's onboarding is a citizenship oath, producing true believers who work fourteen-hour days for a zealot's mission. The product manager's real job is "shit umbrella" internally and warlord externally. Two early revelations: per-impression monetization was "utter dog shit," and Project Chorizo proved that no Facebook user data improved ad performance.

Full stories

Boot camp and the oath. Chris Cox's vision: Facebook as "the New York Times of You," the personal newspaper. Pedram: leave your old culture behind. Chamath Palihapitiya (Growth chief, poker host): "just fucking do it," "we're not here to fuck around," and the Mercedes-across-from-BMW story. HR's secrecy and discretion parables: Zuck's all-hands "Please resign" email to a leaker; "the Sec" fires anyone who looks at profiles without cause; one ask, no means no; an obscenity waiver; "call them out... go on with your day." Engineering boot camp: six weeks of bug-fixing in a home-brewed PHP stack (because that's what Zuck knew); first act: change the Like button's text to an obscenity on a dev server. Posters (MAKE AN IMPACT, DONE IS BETTER THAN PERFECT, FORTUNE FAVORS THE BOLD) on every wall and monitor; the blue T-shirt as uniform. Martínez: "corporate fascism was intoxicating" and he was seduced too. Cultural rituals: Faceversaries (start dates celebrated like baptisms) and Facebook "deaths" (departures mourned with a photo of a worn badge and an epitaph; ex-employee secret groups as purgatory). The Chris Putnam story: a kid whose virus deleted user data was hired, not prosecuted.

The hashtag decision (week one). A dozen engineers and PMMs deadlocked on replacing keyword targeting with topic "super-keywords." The new PM kept keywords (20% of revenue), denoted topics with "#" (users already read #Golf as an abstract concept; drafting off Twitter, with gallows humor), made no UI redesign, launched fast, then had marketing push partners toward "#Action Movies." Kitten (topic extraction mapping "Tiger... birdie... US Open" to Golf/Tiger Woods/US Open) launched August 1, 2011 without a hitch: "earned my spurs." Hundreds of thousands of advertisers adopted hashtagged segments.

Lockdown (June 2011). Google Plus launched ad-free, subsidized by AdWords. The neon Lockdown sign; Zuck's impromptu speech (zero-sum, raise the quality bar, Cato's "Carthage must be destroyed"); weekend cafés and families; posters printed by the Analog Research Laboratory; a defected Google Plus PM briefed leadership on launch day. Reconnaissance: Google's engineering lot empty on a Sunday, Facebook's full. Google's instant counteroffer policy for anyone with a Facebook offer led to a rush to interview at Facebook for leverage.

Project Chorizo. Systematic tests fed every user action (posts, messages, links, check-ins) into topic targeting. Nothing improved advertiser performance: "A mile-long trainful of meat cows... one measly sausage." It tested his faith in Facebook's data primacy.

Ads org (2011). About 30 engineers, one designer, ~a dozen products and six PMs under Gokul (the "product masseur"); PMMs under Brian Boland; sales under David Fischer, downstream; weekly PM meetings like YC dinners; monthly all-PM meetings run by Cox with his whip-clap. Two buildings (California Avenue and Page Mill); Pong and Ping rooms; the Aquarium. Nobody on Ads had worked in ad tech; pre-2012 Ads monetized whatever user-facing products Zuck shipped, "a house out of parts selected at random from a Home Depot." "Any culture able to shut itself off from the outside world goes insane in its own unique way." Caveat: by early 2013 the company "would get very smart, very fast."

Evidence

  • Average CPM: the dashboard's big yellow number was bottom-of-the-barrel; usage was "up there with heroin"; 2011 clickthrough ~0.05% (Ch 11 numbers).
  • Keyword revenue: 20% of revenue could not be migrated abruptly (the basis for the layering decision).
  • Kitten: shipped in two months; hundreds of thousands of advertisers adopted.
  • Chorizo: null result across all tested user actions.
  • Lockdown reconnaissance: parking-lot occupancy as commitment signal (anecdotal).
  • Mobile app: made money on volume despite a 90-second latency.

Key terms

Personal newspaper; Ellis Island onboarding; shit umbrella/pirate captain; data per pixel; tiebreaker; bias for launching; you make what you measure; Chorizo; Kitten; Lockdown/Carthago delenda est; Faceversary; "Sturmabteilung/Blueshirts."

So what

Be the tiebreaker, layer new on old, launch fast, own a dashboard to the decimal, and be technical enough to catch BS. Treat onboarding as conversion. Watch for insularity. Don't mistake usage for monetization.

Chapter 9: One Shot, One Kill, Twice Bitten, Ads Five-Oh, The Narcissism of Privacy

Central argument

Why Facebook's data was so hard to monetize (the noisy bar), why scale sets a $100M bar on any new ads idea, how ads were tested on slices of humanity, how the Irish audit ended with a Christmas Eve SQL command on a live production database - and Martínez's contrarian privacy thesis: what embarrasses you is commercially worthless, advertisers want your purchases and browsing, and Facebook doesn't sell your data, it buys it.

Full stories

Ads Review and Quality. The ads police: two engineers plus ops in Austin and Bangalore; MOSI negative-feedback rereviews; fuzzy image matching against bit-level tweaks; "free iPad" scam models; a dreaded assignment the author schemed out of.

Sheryl's quarterly ops meeting (PC Load Letter). Her skill at running big egos; a kitten-as-porn-placeholder demo that ended with "if there were women on that team, they'd never choose those photos"; the author's slide: ads reviewed up and to the right, human hours flat. Anti-pattern: demoing to executives with placeholders you haven't thought about.

Scalps@Facebook. The internal trophy group of predators caught with law enforcement; Facebook stays quiet about safety work because publicizing it would scare parents; users treat a social utility "on par with running water" as a toy.

Testing on users. Users as poker chips; New Zealand ("Aotearoa... roughly translated means 'Facebook test set'") as the sandbox; ads tests dosed rich-market tranches like drug trials; engineers horse-traded test populations the size of countries when experimentation was capped. The PM was a portfolio manager: "we were all making it up as we went along."

Christmas Eve 2011. The Irish audit was settled with a discontinuation deadline that day. Ireland (tax incentives made Dublin the EU base; 4.5M people "wouldn't even fill a Facebook test set"; the Dublin office as "Noah's ark of the EU"). The most authoritative ads engineer assured him all was in order (the anti-pattern in the notes is believing an engineer's "we're not doing that" without checking the tables, and the assurance turned out wrong); a "paranoid itch" led him to open a terminal into production; Hong Ge, the best-dressed man at Facebook, asked to watch; an UPDATE TABLE SET on the live targeting tables behind ~$2B in spend; a real-time dashboard check; then a beer. "All the responsibility, none of the power." Lesson: verify the thing you personally vouched for, even on a holiday.

The 2011 data-policy referendum. Zuck's 2009 pledge that policy changes would be voted on, with a 30% participation threshold (~300M people). 90% of voters opposed the new policy Facebook needed, but almost nobody voted, so the result was "taken under advisement." Without the new policy, the products of 2012-13 would have been impossible.

Personal thread. Noah Pelayo was born September 2011; the father's marimbero lesson ("they can come after your family"); child support as "paying my way out of fatherhood" to avoid the dependency of a bourgeois lifestyle: "only the man who needed nothing was truly free"; the $700/month sailboat in Redwood City. Facebook ads late 2011: small right-rail units; ads in News Feed "sacrilegious"; outside data "heretical"; Gokul's product roulette assigned PMs to orphaned teams.

Evidence

  • Revenue bar: ~5% of revenue (~$100M/year then); failed ideas: political-district targeting, a Hispanic cluster, travel-intender geodata.
  • Referendum: 30% threshold (~300M), 90% of voters opposed, almost nobody voted.
  • Production update: ~$2B in spend behind the targeting tables.
  • Ads review slide: ads reviewed up and to the right; human hours flat.
  • 49ers-jersey anecdote: explained by game weekend and broad campaign rather than advanced image recognition; a reminder that "aha!" stories are weak evidence.
  • Chorizo (Ch 8) supports the noisy-bar claim.

Key terms

Noisy bar; $100M bar; PM as portfolio manager; unit of account; telephone exchange; ad blocking as theft; privacy as Iran's nukes; embarrassing != valuable; "a black hole of data that can never leave"; MOSI; Scalps@Facebook.

So what

Kill ideas that can't reach ~5% of revenue; prefer platform-wide, programmatic changes. Use technical depth as a lie detector. Verify what you vouched for. Treat "Facebook is showing me X" as a category error: the advertiser addressed you. Don't publicize wins when the frame will backfire.

Chapter 10: Are We Savages or What?, O Death, Barbaric Yawn, Going Public

Central argument

Four vignettes on Facebook's culture as it prepared to go public: the mob looting of the old California Avenue office and the failed "make art" experiment (corrected with blue tape and turned into a code-review macro); the Sun logos as corporate memento mori and the little red book; the startup-to-big-company deceleration and the vesting math that makes acqui-hire offers worth a quarter of their headline; and the IPO announcement in a revival tent, where Martínez compares Facebook's mission cult to his Cuban cousins' revolution and dissects the haves and have-mores.

Full stories

The move-out riot (Dec 2011) and the art experiment. Zuck announced employees would decorate the new campus: unlimited spray cans, any wall. By evening: stick figures, thought-bubble jokes, a child dragging a red line down a hallway, an unfinished Superman mural, one algorithmic unicorn. Day 2: still going. Weekend: Zuck's message - I trusted you to make art and you vandalized the place. Monday: blue tape on everything to be removed. Same week: an engineer made "bluetape" a code-review macro meaning "remove this for sanity." With thirty minutes to vacate the old office, staff stripped artwork and conference-room plaques; the one Ads admin bellowed in vain; the author pried the SPAIN plaque off with a rigging knife and mounted it on his sailboat. David Choe, the muralist, was commissioned (again) to decorate the new campus, arguably to remedy the DIY fiasco.

Sun's logos and the red book. Sun logos were deliberately left on doors and on the back of the Facebook sign as reminders that complacency (Sun ignored Linux on commodity hardware) leads to extinction. The red book, Facebook Was Not Originally Created to Be a Company, holds lore (the fax-button prank), values ("the quick shall inherit the earth"; make money to build services) and the exhortation that if Facebook doesn't build what kills it, someone else will; posters: OUR WORK IS NEVER OVER, THIS JOURNEY 1% FINISHED, WHAT WOULD YOU DO IF YOU WEREN'T AFRAID? Its closing warning: the internet grants irrelevant things no ruins; they simply disappear.

The campus and the shuttles. The Menlo Park campus: an artificial spit in tidal marsh; a six-mile bike commute past quarries and algae; undersized bathrooms with cyclists' shorts airing inside out. Shuttle buses: unmarked white charters vs. Muni; protesters smashing windows; Google "spies" boarding the wrong bus and being reported on the Facebook Commute group; Googlers older and nerdier, Facebookers younger and edgier. PM daily life: three free meals, six to twelve scheduled meetings plus impromptu ones, a calendar fought over like no-man's-land, and "Poopin'!" as the penalty for an unlocked laptop.

Ads happy hours and the utility closet. Friday Q&A with Zuck, kegs, the Ads "cool kids" (Rabkin, Fidji Simo, Boland); Mike Fox's product marketing crew; the Shady Lady bar in Building 10 (Thunderbird in the fridge); the author's utility-closet fumble with "PMMess": "even on the extracurricular front, Facebook was no racetrack." Bonnie Brown's Google memoir offered the image of one employee checking movie times beside another booking a weekend in Belize.

Track racing to commuting. After a startup, a big company feels like crawling at 80 mph. Facebook was an autobahn (fast lane by Zuck's permission only), Apple/Google the 101 at rush hour, Oracle a Delhi intersection. The itch to leave starts within months. The author ran a countdown clock to his first vest.

The IPO tent (Feb 1, 2012). An email from Zuck (email meant serious; "the Sec will come get you"); the filing was announced with a warning about public ridicule and "stay focused on our mission"; the author watched a Harvard old-timer browse $2.4M Diamond Heights listings during the speech. Martínez compares Facebook to his Cuban cousins' revolution: "Welcome to the People's Republic of Facebook."

Haves and have-mores.
