The Certainty Illusion. Definition: the more we seek certainty the harder it is to find, because valued guideposts attract distortion. When to use: when a source offers unusually clean, confident, fast clarity on a contested topic; ask who profits from my feeling certain. Common mistake: treating high trust as safety, or treating the whole problem as downstream lies.

The Three Illusions. Definition: Science (appearance replaces science), Goodness (a messaging strategy making a choice feel right), Opinion (reviews/rankings/polls faked, biased or manufactured). When: triage which guidepost a claim leans on. Mistake: applying the wrong toolkit (e.g., checking a halo word for peer review).

Scienceploitation. Definition: using scientific verbiage and hot research topics to sell unproven products and agendas. When: any claim leaning on scientific vocabulary. Mistake: debating the jargon rather than asking for a body of evidence; assuming training protects you. (Note: produces false positives on genuinely novel legitimate work; resolve with the range-of-sources test.)

The quantum test. Definition: if quantum explains a health product, stop evaluating. When: consumer health. Mistake: exporting it to physics contexts.

The science-y/scary dyad. Definition: jargon plus fear. When: scare claims that stick (gluten, GMOs, vaccines, fluoride, 5G, per the notes). Mistake: answering with accurate but boring facts alone.

The Sagan standard. Definition: extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, scaled to improbability, onus on the claimant. When: contrarian or "they don't want you to know" claims. Mistake: using it as a licence to dismiss; it will slow acceptance of the rare valid revolution, which Caulfield accepts.

The Galileo gambit. Definition: answering evidence with a persecution narrative. When: someone invokes persecution. Mistake: arguing it on its own terms; expecting it to persuade the claimant (its value is protecting the audience).

The humility fix / inventory. Definition: default intellectual humility; list positions revised and live grey areas. When: before defending a position. Mistake: gaming the self-report; an empty list is the finding.

The hype pipeline. Definition: exaggeration at every stage: excitement, grants, publication, press release, media. When: tracing a breakthrough headline. Mistake: blaming individuals instead of incentives; reading only abstracts.

Red-flag audit. Definition: publisher, affiliation, acceptance interval, ethics review, methods, author's regulatory history, retraction status, citation pattern. When: one paper is waved at you. Mistake: spending the effort on claims that don't matter; relying on a journal name.

Single study syndrome rule / body-of-evidence test. Definition: never rest on one study; refuse it, name your bias, check venue and retraction, find consensus via aggregators. When: any extraordinary, contrarian or personally flattering claim. Mistake: hunting primary papers yourself; forgetting that you underestimate consensus.

Zombie science. Definition: retracted or discredited findings that keep circulating. When: citing or sharing research. Mistake: assuming retraction status will reach you passively.

Health halo and the Devious Dozen. Definition: a word that creates an impression of health that the evidence does not support. When: any label. Mistake: reading the list as "these are bad," when the point is the implied certainty.

Motte-and-bailey. Definition: defend a weak claim by retreating to a truism. When: you find yourself apparently arguing against something obviously good. Mistake: getting cast as the villain instead of restating the original claim.

Substitution risk. Definition: swapping a well-studied ingredient for a poorly studied one is information loss. When: "free-from" claims. Mistake: assuming "natural alternative" means gentler.

White hat bias / goodness bias. Definition: distortion of research for perceived righteous ends. When: noble topics. Mistake: assuming only industry money biases research.

Separate the goal from the intervention. Definition: isolate the goal, ask if argued or assumed, what evidence supports this intervention, whether insecurity was manufactured. When: pitches riding safety, sustainability, masculinity. Mistake: overcorrecting into debating the goal's moral worth.

The Starbird emotional-signal check. Definition: political self-righteousness is the cue to slow down. When: before sharing charged content. Mistake: checking only the source and skipping your own emotion.

Certainty grift and documentary audit. Definition: selling false certainty about goal and path, usually through a good story. When: a compelling documentary or pitch. Mistake: rejecting narrative entirely.

Opinion economy toolkit (Goldilocks zone, accuracy test, knowledge asymmetry, assume-you-can't-detect). When: any rating-driven decision. Mistake: trying to sharpen your fake-detection filter.

Review escape plan and four poll questions. When: purchases, professionals, quoted percentages. Mistake: using a single expert outlet (experts can be incentivized) or treating an open internet poll as data.

The Certainty Six and Fundamental Fix. When: standing checklist and advocacy. Mistake: using the Six as an audit; it is deliberately low-effort and will not catch sophisticated fraud.

(b) The big ideas (numbered)

  1. Trust is a risk indicator, not a safety indicator. The signals worth faking are those we trust most; distortion follows value. Ch 0, Ch 11-12, cheatsheet.
  2. This is a knowledge production crisis, not just misinformation. Upstream incentives (publish-or-perish, hype, predatory journals) keep making raw material. Defend science as process, not institution. Ch 0, 3, 4, 14.
  3. Jargon works through opacity. Science-y language persuades regardless of education; demand a plain-language mechanism. Ch 1, 2.
  4. Certainty is inversely related to knowledge. The most confident know least; conspiracy believers overestimate agreement; humility is protective. Ch 2.
  5. Hype is built into the pipeline. From NIH grants (+1,400%) to press releases, hype is an incentive emission; media attention correlates with poorer replication. Ch 3.
  6. Publication is an address, not a credential. Predatory, hijacked and agenda journals produce real-looking papers that reach guidelines and policy. Ch 4.
  7. Never rest on one study. The load-bearing habit of Part I; retractions rarely register (5.4%) and zombies thrive. Ch 5, 14.
  8. Halos sell a feeling of having decided well. The Devious Dozen deliver certainty shortcuts that change behaviour, not a verified benefit. Ch 6, 7.
  9. A noble goal is a risk factor for weak evidence. White hat bias warps research, coverage and even ethics judgments. Ch 8, 9.
  10. Ideology and insecurity are amplifiers. Wrapping claims in identity (masculinity, politics) makes them travel further; emotional reactions are the cue to pause. Ch 9.
  11. A good story beats good data, even for experts. Anecdotes and production quality create felt certainty; the 2.7% gap is where it is sold. Ch 10.
  12. Reviews are a market in perceived authenticity. Crowd wisdom needs independence; herding, incentives and fakes break it (25-30% unreliable). Ch 11.
  13. Ratings fail where they matter most. 57% agreement with experts, no resale relationship, no relationship to clinical outcomes; you cannot detect fakes. Ch 12.
  14. Substitute sources; don't sharpen filters. Independent comparative experts, four poll questions, and awareness that aggregates are populations. Ch 13.
  15. Cheap habits beat heroic vigilance. The accuracy pause, body-of-evidence check and Certainty Six, plus systemic fixes (quality over quantity, visible retractions, replication). Ch 14.

(c) Wisdom, memorable lines and heuristics (only quotes present in the notes)

  • "Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence." (Carl Sagan; Sagan standard, Ch 2)
  • "Science that can't be understood is bad science." (Gordon Pennycook, Ch 2)
  • "Extreme opponents know the least, but think they know the most." (2019 anti-GMO study, Ch 2)
  • Sagan's rebuttal to the Galileo gambit: they also laughed at Bozo the Clown. (Ch 2)
  • "Whenever some piece of content makes me feel politically self-righteous, like I'm about to spike a political football, that's when I know I need to be extra careful about sharing." (Kate Starbird, Ch 9)
  • "Human mind is a story processor, not a logic processor." (Jonathan Haidt, Ch 10)
  • "The salience of an anecdote can turn a molehill into a mountain." (Jonathan Jarry, Ch 10)
  • "While science searches for broad patterns... storytelling celebrates the particulars of a single experience." (Michael Dahlstrom, Ch 10)
  • "Sound survey research should be a mirror measuring public opinion, not a force shaping it." (Frank Graves, Ch 13)
  • "People seem far more willing to accept lower-quality data and call it conclusive when it fits with what they perceive to be righteous ends." (David Allison, Ch 8)
  • "Distortion of research-based information in the service of what may be perceived as righteous ends." (Allison and Cope, white hat bias, Ch 8)
  • "It has created monsters." (journalist on the Spanish prolific-publisher system, Ch 14)
  • "Yeah, it is." (Caulfield's concession, Ch 0)
  • "Be open to the wonder, but not closed to the facts." (Ch 8 calibration point)
  • "Consensus often isn't sexy." (Jonathan Jarry, Ch 14)
  • "A five-year-old could expose this in one click." (Daube, Ch 4)
  • "Telling new stories about the same old products." (Perry Romanowski on clean beauty, Ch 7)
  • Heuristics: if a science-y claim sounds too good to be true it is; substitute "evil-spirits-free" for "toxin-free"; "if you are a fan, you are a fan"; ask "what is the pattern?" not "is this item good or bad?" (Ted Kyle); the Sagan ratio over a binary.

(d) Anti-patterns to avoid

  • Becoming a cynical disbeliever of everything (skepticism is a filter, not an off switch).
  • Answering "why should we trust you?" with more studies instead of conceding the incentive problem.
  • Treating misinformation as the whole problem and ignoring upstream production.
  • Assuming your own research beats the noise (81%/96% online).
  • Treating opacity as depth; debating jargon on its own terms; assuming education protects you.
  • Believing economic-impact projections and trusting grant rank as a quality signal.
  • Reading only the abstract; treating animal data as human-relevant.
  • Treating a journal name as a signal; trusting reputable databases implicitly; rewarding quantity over quality.
  • Citing without checking retraction status; false balance in media; letting a case study carry causal weight.
  • Treating a halo word as a decision terminus; reading "organic" or "local" as a sustainability guarantee.
  • Confusing lawsuit outcomes with scientific findings; reading "natural alternative" as "gentler."
  • Grading evidence by the virtue of its goal; amplifying observational findings with causal language.
  • Accepting a real trend as proof of a fabricated cause; trusting the physique as evidence.
  • Assuming subject-matter training protects you from documentaries; mistaking emotional certainty for evidentiary certainty.
  • Treating volume of reviews as a fix; reading a balanced-sounding review as authentic; using ratings to pick a physician.
  • Trying to filter signal from review noise; treating an open internet poll as data; letting an aggregate score gate your experience.
  • Sharing before checking accuracy; chasing the contrarian hammer; treating any single dramatic study as overturning a field; hunting for "the one trustworthy reviewer."

(e) If you remember only ten things

  1. Trust level is a risk indicator, not a safety indicator.
  2. Pause and ask "is this accurate?" before you share (the highest-return habit).
  3. Never rest on one study; ask for the body of evidence and the consensus via aggregators.
  4. Publication is an address, not a credential; check venue, acceptance time and who cites it.
  5. Quantum on a health product means stop; always demand a plain-language mechanism.
  6. Halo words (the Devious Dozen) sell a feeling, not a benefit; read the ingredient list.
  7. A noble goal is a reason for more scrutiny; separate the goal from the intervention.
  8. Stories and documentaries manufacture certainty; ask about the base rate and the body of evidence.
  9. Star ratings are not evidence (57% agreement; 25-30% unreliable; you cannot detect fakes); use comparative experts.
  10. Be humble, keep a list of positions you have changed, and like what you like.

(f) Open questions and limits the notes flag

  • Consensus lags on emerging topics: psychedelics for mental health, probiotics and parabens are listed as "in flux"; seek independent expert advice rather than letting a single study or confident podcaster settle it.
  • The Certainty Six is a filter, not an audit: it will not catch sophisticated fraud; it targets the ~90% of everyday claims.
  • False positives on novel science: scienceploitation detection can flag legitimately novel work; resolve with the range-of-sources test (which introduces lag by design).
  • Caulfield's self-reflexivity: he acknowledges his own work sits inside distorting incentives, and the literature about polluted literature may itself be polluted.
  • Observational limits: the masculinity-health literature is largely observational and cannot establish causation; the talc literature is uncertain (the book does not claim no link); paraben science is equivocal rather than proven safe.
  • Tension in health messaging: leaning on masculine norms may help reluctant men seek care while reinforcing harmful norms.
  • Expert reviewers can also be incentivized, so single-source reliance reintroduces the problem; expert comparatives do not exist for every category and do not apply to purely subjective goods.
  • Regulatory fixes are doubtful: Caulfield sees the opinion ecosystem as terminally broken and worsening with AI-generated content; incentives align against clean-up (analogy: regulating the stock market). The notes offer no complete solution for reviews beyond personal habits.
  • Systemic reforms are slow: Oransky calls the scale of the literature's pollution "generational." Nothing in the notes says how quickly funding and retraction reform will arrive.
  • Skepticism about hype vs support for science: the notes insist on investing in science generally while discounting specific promises; they do not give a formula for how much funding is right.
  • Where the notes are silent: details of the Eben Byers/Radithor story, the Hungarian-apple client's follow-up, the exact method of the apple taste experiment, and methodology of several cited studies are not in the notes and are not supplied here.

End of file. Next step: take the quiz in certainty-illusion-quiz.md.

The Essential Psycho-Cybernetics: The Science of Success

2 markdown files

Quiz

Quiz Book: The Essential Psycho-Cybernetics (Maxwell Maltz)

Source note. This quiz reflects the skill's chapter notes for "The Essential Psycho-Cybernetics: The Science of Success" (SKILL.md, glossary, patterns, cheatsheet and all 24 chapter files), not the book's own wording. Quotations are quotations as recorded in those notes. Where the notes are silent, the quiz is silent.

How to use this quiz

  • The notes cover an omnibus of five volumes in 24 chapter files. Because there are 24, chapters are grouped in pairs (12 sections). Each section has 10 questions: short answer (SA), true/false (T/F), multiple choice (MC), "explain in your own words" (OW), story/evidence recall (ST), and at least two scenario/application questions (SC).
  • Cover the answers: answers sit in an "Answers" block after each question set. Say or write your answer first, then check.
  • Score yourself: 2 points for a correct answer with the reason, 1 for the right idea with a gap, 0 otherwise. 80%+ in a section means move on; below 60% means re-read that chapter's notes.
  • Finish with the 20-question cumulative final exam at the end (answers included).
  • A caution about numbering: "Goal Builder", "Book One...Five" and "Ch" numbers refer to the notes' sequential chapter files (Ch 1-24), not to each volume's original numbering.

Section 1 - Ch 1-2: Overcoming Frustration; Winging Away and the Road to Self-Respect

Q1 (SA). What does "Psycho-Cybernetics" mean, where does the word come from, and what is the one-sentence definition used in these notes?

Q2 (T/F). "Frustration is an event that happens to you; you break it by changing your circumstances." True or false?

Q3 (MC). Which of these is not one of the Twelve Faces of Frustration?

(a) You wear a mask. (b) You retire from life. (c) You work too few hours. (d) You consider yourself a loser.

Q4 (OW). Explain the "consent" principle in your own words and why it is called the leverage point.

Q5 (ST). Tell the story of the seventeen-year-old with the cleft lip. What did he shout on the table, what did he cry two weeks later, and what question does Maltz turn on the reader?

Q6 (ST). What is the concentration-camp survivor image, and what is "tattooed" in the reader's case? Also: what did the woman who said the book "didn't do anything for me" do wrong?

Q7 (SA). Walk through Maltz's literal "operation on the face of your mind" (the mirror operation) in order. What are the "prune wrinkles"? Then tell the treasure story against himself and its point.

Q8 (SA). How does Maltz reinterpret "conscience," and what does he tell you to say instead of "I can't live with my conscience"? What does Mañana, Incorporated tell you to postpone and not postpone?

Q9 (SC). A project lead keeps saying, "Once the reorganization is over and things calm down, I'll finally set my goals and fix my work habits. Meanwhile I'm furious at the colleague who undermined me." Which concept applies, and what should she postpone versus do today?

Q10 (SC). A salesman misses a quota, blames his regional manager loudly, and then privately feels worthless. A coach asks which Maltz idea explains why scapegoating ends up hurting him, and what to do instead. Answer as the coach.

Answers - Section 1

A1. Psycho = mind; cybernetics from the Greek kybernetes, "helmsman." Definition: steering your mind toward a productive, useful, worthwhile, predetermined goal. The ship image: the engine always runs; the question is who has the wheel and where the port is. (Ch 1, Ch 11)

A2. False. Frustration is a habit of self-relation, broken by changing your opinion of yourself. Maltz's example: happiness is not conditional on "Sally leaving you $30,000"; there are no "ifs" to happiness. (Ch 1)

A3. (c). The twelve faces include: not true to yourself; imagination used destructively (no goal); can't relax; aim is unhappiness; frustration as habit/self-hypnosis; not accepting weaknesses; no compassion; wearing a mask; repeating mistakes; retiring from life; considering yourself a loser; not accepting yourself (living in fantasy). Working "too few hours" is not on the list. (Ch 1)

A4. "No one can make you feel frustrated without your consent." Frustration requires your signature, and the same goes for unhappiness and loneliness, so the point of control is inside you. Because you grant consent, you can withhold it. (Ch 1, Ch 3)

A5. As an intern Maltz delivered a baby with a cleft lip; the father fainted and Maltz felt responsible, which pushed him toward plastic surgery. Later, in Latin America, a terrified seventeen-year-old shouted "I'm going to die!" on the table. Two weeks after the repair Maltz handed him a mirror; he stared at a face he had never seen and cried, "I'm going to live!" Maltz asks the reader: Are you going to live? Do you carry an emotional disfigurement no surgeon can operate on? Answer: "be your own plastic surgeon" with belief and compassion for yourself. (Ch 1)

A6. A survivor came to have the tattooed number removed from her arm to begin a new life; Maltz asks whether you have tattooed numbers on your mental arms that only you can remove. The woman who found the book useless had only read it; Psycho-Cybernetics is "positive doing," a practice, not a reading. (Ch 1)

A7. (1) Identify the scar: a specific blunder, hatred or bigotry. (2) Scrub in: go to a mirror alone. (3) Excise: refuse aloud to play games with yourself ("You're my friend. I like you."). (4) Close: forgive yourself for that specific item. (5) Post-op check: the "prune wrinkles" on the face of your mind are gone; Maltz says you are old at three or one hundred and three if you keep the negative feelings. Treasure story: a rumor said a million dollars was hidden on the eighteenth floor of his building; on a moonlit night he found his butler on the terrace in a white coat with pick and shovel hacking at the rock garden. Point: everyone digs outside for treasure buried in the self-image. (Ch 2)

A8. He rejects Shakespeare's "conscience doth make cowards of us all": we make cowards of our conscience. Conscience is your opinion of yourself, audible after a blunder. Restate "I can't live with my conscience" as "I can't live with myself," then treat it as a fixable self-image problem. Postpone only the resentment ("wait till tomorrow, I'll give vent to my anger tomorrow"); never postpone the goal. (Ch 2)

A9. The Tomorrow Illusion / Mañana, Incorporated. Reverse the deferral: do the constructive thing (set goals, fix habits) today, and postpone only the destructive feeling (the anger). Frustration is the thief of time; deferral gives negative feeling a permanent lease. (Ch 2; cheatsheet: members never get dividends)

A10. Scapegoating: refusing to blame yourself for a blunder and hunting for someone to hold responsible, "which ends with you attacking your own self-image" (Ch 1). Fix: restate the problem as an outcome to correct, stop chronic self-criticism first (Ch 2: once you stop criticizing yourself you stop criticizing others), and set a goal within your capabilities for tomorrow. Also run the Twelve Faces scan and name the one face you are wearing. (Ch 1-2)

Section 2 - Ch 3-4: Happiness and Crises; On To Success!

Q1 (T/F). "Per Maltz, happiness is a reward that arrives once conditions improve, so you should wait for it." True or false? Give the correct view.

Q2 (T/F). An eighty-two-year-old attended Maltz's Monterey workshop because he was winding down for retirement. True or false?

Q3 (MC). In Ch 3 the "Seven Key Characteristics of Frustration" are Fear, ___, ___, Loneliness, Uncertainty, Resentment, Emptiness. The two blanks, versus the later F-A-I-L-U-R-E acronym, are:

(a) Aggressiveness/Insecurity in Ch 3, Anger/Inferiority in the final acronym. (b) Anger/Inferiority in Ch 3, Aggressiveness/Insecurity later. (c) Anxiety/Isolation in both. (d) Apathy/Ignorance in both.

Q4 (SA). What are the "wonderful computer" and the "decompression chamber"?

Q5 (ST). What happened with the ringing telephone at a lecture, and what principle does it illustrate?

Q6 (SA). Spell out S-U-C-C-E-S-S and give one clause of Maltz's gloss for each letter.

Q7 (OW). Explain "you cannot be a success unless you are a success to yourself," using the house-and-lawn analogy.

Q8 (SA). State the Four Principles of Relaxation and the four operating conditions for the servo-mechanism.

Q9 (SC). A product manager sets a goal to run daily, skips it one Tuesday, and concludes, "I'm a failure; this never works for me." Which Ch 4 ideas apply, and what should she do Wednesday?

Q10 (SC). An account executive loses one big pitch and then says: "I'm unlucky. Clients are cruel. I'll avoid pitching for a while." Using Face 9 and Face 11 from the Twelve Faces of Success, diagnose the thinking and prescribe the corrective.

Answers - Section 2

A1. False. Happiness is a habit installed deliberately (like brushing teeth), not a conditional reward; "I'll be happy if X" is the trap. Install it with a fixed trigger (the mirror on waking): think of yourself kindly, smile, resolve to do your best today, accept the escape clause ("if you fail, you fail... the next day, you try all over again"), hold a "meeting with your self-image," guard your climate, and spend the free eight hours on activities you enjoy. (Ch 3)

A2. False. He said, "I'm eighty-two, and I'm practicing to be ninety." The story supports the anti-retirement theme: never retire from life. (Ch 4)

A3. (a). Ch 3 lists Fear, Aggressiveness, Insecurity, Loneliness, Uncertainty, Resentment, Emptiness; Ch 24 gives F-A-I-L-U-R-E with Anger and Inferiority. The notes treat these as the same roster; use "Anger/Inferiority" for the acronym. (Ch 3, Ch 24)

A4. The wonderful computer is the goal-striving mechanism in the mid-brain, smaller than a hazelnut and beyond any committee of scientists to build; it diagnoses your health, not your disease. The decompression chamber is a designated room in your mind where, under frustration, you regroup, reassert identity and give yourself another chance; build it before you need it. (Ch 3)

A5. At a lecture a telephone kept ringing and annoying Maltz; he simply took the receiver off the hook. Lesson: don't make a mountain out of a molehill; remove the small aggravation before it recruits you into a large one. (Ch 3)

A6. Sense of direction (a realistic goal within your limitations); Understanding (a mistake doesn't make you a failure; communicate with yourself first); Courage (take chances, start toward another goal after a failure, act creatively); Compassion (first for yourself, then others; your capacity to forgive); Esteem (appreciate your worth; no one will give you self-respect); Self-acceptance (don't imitate: "second fiddle to someone else's image"); Self-confidence (calculated risks and recalled past successes; not conceit). (Ch 4)

A7. Success is a growing self-image, not accumulated results. You mow the lawn, paint the house and trim the shrubbery, then let weeds grow over the self-image. "You will not be a success if you make a million dollars but leave your self-image impoverished." (Ch 4)

A8. Relaxation: (a) forgive others, (b) forgive yourself, (c) see yourself at your best, (d) keep up with yourself (compare only with your own past). Servo-mechanism conditions: (a) one thing, one thought, one goal at a time; (b) live in the present; (c) use anxiety creatively to reach the goal; (d) if a situation defies solution, sleep on it, not with it. (Ch 4)

A9. "If you set a goal and fail one day, this is no failure at all." Reset the goal for the next day and the day after; Face 9 (live through mistakes) and the "escape clause" from Ch 3 (the next day you try all over again). Wednesday: try again, hold the same goal. An athlete cannot win every day; reaching most goals makes you "a champion in the art of living." (Ch 4, Ch 3)

A10. Face 9 (live through your mistakes): a blunder's only legitimate function is to stimulate you to rise above it. The pitch-loser draws four illegitimate conclusions (unlucky, people cruel, evade people, evade commitment), all of which deposit you in "a pit of despair and hatred"; note they are conclusions about the world from one data point about yourself. Corrective, Face 11 (consider yourself a winner): deliberately call on the confidence of past successes. The failure loop is self-sealing; the Success Cycle is the same loop with the sign flipped. (Ch 4)

Section 3 - Ch 5-6: Self-Respect, Understanding, Sincerity; Uncertainty, Resentment, Emptiness

Q1 (SA). Why is self-respect "a lifetime job, not a state," and how does it stay replenished?

Q2 (SA). What specific "understanding" does Maltz mean in Goal Builder 2, and what are the steps of that exercise?

Q3 (T/F). "Sincerity is the capacity to be nice; confidence is optional." True or false?

Q4 (MC). Maltz's "tell" that your self-respect is low, visible in how you admire others, is: (a) boredom (b) envy (c) anger (d) fatigue.

Q5 (OW). Explain "living hopefully with anxiety" and its three-part method.

Q6 (ST). Describe the circling-airplane image and what it says about a life with no sense of direction.

Q7 (SA). List the Five Ways to Vanquish Emptiness.

Q8 (SA). Walk through Goal Builder 5 (Overcoming Resentment), including what the written audit is meant to prove. Then give the four tests in Goal Builder 6.

Q9 (SC). A VP, anxious about a rumored reorganization, reads it as proof she is not valued, and spends the weekend rehearsing grievances. Which Ch 6 concepts apply and what are the steps?

Q10 (SC). An employee with a "secure" job says he feels empty: lots of activity, no sense of why. A friend suggests a bigger house. Which Maltz diagnosis applies, and what is the minimal intervention?

Answers - Section 3

A1. "When you feel self-respect, you still seek more, and when you find more, you keep your momentum alive and give your self-respect to others." Source it internally and spend it outward; sharing keeps it replenishing. It is like savings built week after week, more basic than money, and like a plant you keep watering as long as it lives. (Ch 5, Ch 10)

A2. The understanding that you have the right to live happily, pleasurably and with self-respect. Exercise: walk a familiar street; ask of each person passing, "Does he believe he has the right to be happy?"; accept that often you cannot tell; notice the clear cases at both ends (slouchers who avert their eyes vs. people who walk erect without swaggering); go home; write UNDERSTANDING on the mirror in erasable pencil or lipstick; say "Do I have rights? Yes. Yes, I do."; erase the word but keep the feeling. (Ch 5)

A3. False. Sincerity is the capacity to face reality without evasion, so it requires confidence ("enough belief in yourself"). Without confidence it collapses into evasion or brutality. (Ch 5)

A4. (b) Envy. If you downgrade yourself you can still admire others "but your respect will be tainted with envy," and others sense it. (Ch 5; Ch 21 repeats this for friendship)

A5. You don't eliminate uncertainty; you stop personalizing it. Method: (1) don't take uncertainties personally (the world is uncertain for everyone); (2) accept anxiety as creative while choosing and dead weight after; (3) translate theory into action, moving toward the objective with wisdom and determination in spite of uncertainty. "When you reach for a goal, you bend uncertainty to your will." (Ch 6)

A6. A plane leaves New York, whisks over Philadelphia, circles back, jets to Chicago, drifts toward Canada, circles back and never lands. Absurd, yet it is what a person with no sense of direction does with a life ("An airplane with no sense of direction is a horrifying thing to contemplate"). (Ch 6)

A7. (1) Stop sleepwalking (sleep eight hours soundly; when awake, stay awake and concentrate); (2) resign from Mañana Incorporated (members never get dividends); (3) renew your sense of direction (set goals daily, don't downgrade them); (4) enrich your self-image; (5) orient outward and give your self-respect away. (Ch 6)

A8. Write today's worries; then last week's; last month's; a year ago's if recalled. Check each: Was it realistic? Did it make sense? Maltz predicts many, "perhaps most," were unrealistic, and the result is evidence of your overreaction rate to apply to today's fears. Then mirror: write OVERCOME RESENTMENT and say you will reduce your anxieties and set constructive goals. Goal Builder 6 (NO EMPTINESS; "Time is my treasure"): write a goal and test it: Is it your goal? Does it mean something to you? Can you achieve it? Do you have at least a fighting chance? (Ch 6)

A9. She is taking uncertainty personally and nursing grievances in fantasy (the "torture of resentment in fantasy": physiological cost, no resolution). Intervene at the anxiety layer: run the written anxiety audit; spend anxiety before decisions; set a goal and move toward it (a goal converts an open-ended threat into a bounded problem). Resentment is downstream of unmanaged anxiety. (Ch 6)

A10. Emptiness (the E of F-A-I-L-U-R-E): "twentieth-century emptiness" is affluence with no direction, activity without purpose. The cure is directional, not emotional: set a daily goal (however small) that passes the four tests, concentrate fully on what he does, and give involvement/self-respect outward. A bigger house won't help because the empty person "lacks goals." (Ch 6; cheatsheet: write one goal, however small)

Section 4 - Ch 7-8: Opportunity and Forgiveness; Mirror Watchers and Prison Walls

Q1 (SA). What makes forgiveness "active" in Maltz's treatment, and which wrongs does it include?

Q2 (T/F). "Maltz says mumbling 'I forgive him' wipes the slate clean." True or false?

Q3 (OW). Explain "each day is D-day."

Q4 (ST). What is the Philadelphia cab driver story and what lesson did Maltz draw?

Q5 (SA). Give the steps of Goal Builder 8 (Forgiveness), including the torture-scene turn and the arrow.

Q6 (MC). In Creative Mirror Watching, the calibrating question is: (a) "Am I as good as the other people in the room?" (b) "Do you feel this hostile when a friend walks into your home?" (c) "What would a stranger say about me?" (d) "How much do I weigh?"

Q7 (SA). Name the three misuses of the mirror that the notes warn about, and what "creative" means.

Q8 (ST). Describe the prison caricature exercise (Goal Builder 10) and its purpose. What fairness footnote does Maltz add about real inmates?

Q9 (SC). A founder is about to pitch and mentally rehearses the investor's cold stare, the stumbling answer and the silence after. Which Ch 8 anti-pattern is this, and why is it dangerous?

Q10 (SC). After losing a promotion, a manager tells herself, "Opportunity is for other people; I'm realistic," and begins avoiding stretch assignments. Which Ch 7 ideas apply and what four moves does Maltz give for moving toward opportunity?

Answers - Section 4

A1. It is a daily, all-out operation, not a word: forgive others for their faults, imperfections, wrongs done to you, and wrongs you only imagine they did, then forgive yourself for lifetime mistakes and human flaws. "No half effort, no tentative stumble — a real thrust, all-out." (Ch 7)

A2. False. "Is forgiveness a magical word...abracadabra?" No. Passive forgiveness ("lie down to take a catnap") returns you to "the passive void" and half-living. (Ch 7)

A3. A framing device: the war against the invisible enemy (negative feelings) for the invisible goal (self-respect) using invisible, peaceful weapons (ideas, feelings, images), "bloodless, constructive, and without casualties," fought against self-depreciation, not people. (Ch 7)

A4. A Philadelphia cab driver told Maltz his ex-wife had phoned at 3 a.m., the first contact in twenty years since the divorce, only to say hello. Maltz pocketed his prepared notes and spoke off the cuff: what you refuse to cancel does not decay, it waits. (Ch 7)

A5. Mirror; draw an arrow and say "From forgiveness to self-respect" (self-respect depends on forgiving yourself). Diagnose honestly whether you cannot stop self-condemnation. Imagine a torture scene ("So, you won't talk, eh?"), notice your recoil, then turn it: "What about your own cruel self-torture? Is this not equally horrifying?" Erase the arrow, write FORGIVENESS, say "I will try to forgive myself. I will try to forgive others. We are all human and imperfect." The next step is self-respect; the sequence is one-directional. (Ch 7)

A6. (b). Step to the mirror, look in honesty, walk away and notice the critical torrent; ask whether you'd be this hostile to a friend; return, picture a specific good friend, write FRIEND, and say you will look at yourself with kind eyes. (Ch 8)

A7. Narcissism (admiring the surface), superficial apathy, and critical self-destruction/prosecution (cataloguing flaws; the most common). "Creative" means looking behind the face to "the mature, dynamic, and compassionate person you want to become." (Ch 8)

A8. Sit in a quiet place and imagine you are a convicted criminal playing the heavy: shaking bars, beating your plate to stir a riot, snarling, attacking the kindly warden. The overdrawn picture makes you feel how ludicrous it is to obsess over guilt and deny yourself self-respect. Footnote: many inmates Maltz met in penitentiaries have constructive attitudes, want another chance and "deserve our compassion. Self-respect is their right too"; the Hollywood criminal is a distortion, which is why it works as a mirror for yours. (Ch 8)

A9. Cooking up failure: pre-rehearsing the bad outcome in vivid detail is mental rehearsal running in reverse and "works just as well," programming the servo-mechanism with exactly what you dread. Catch it and rehearse the intended outcome instead. (Ch 8; Ch 14, Ch 17)

A10. Ch 7: opportunity is only visible to someone whose self-image hasn't ruled them out; "pre-emptive withdrawal disguised as realism" closes the door. Four moves: (1) refuse to renounce your self-image whatever happens; (2) keep past successes in imagination ready for the screen of your mind; (3) hold faith when you lose and stand up to crises with calm; (4) don't decide in advance opportunity is for the other guy. (Ch 7)

Section 5 - Ch 9-10: Tranquility and the Active Life; Integrity, Survival, Goal Builders

Q1 (SA). Spell out TRANQUILITY (the Daily Dozen for Tranquility).

Q2 (T/F). "Tranquility is won by withdrawing from stress." True or false?

Q3 (OW). Explain why Maltz schedules relaxation after a go at your goals.

Q4 (ST). Retell Maltz's French Resistance analogy and its lesson about "resistance."

Q5 (SA). What is the Retirement Mechanism and name at least five paired alternatives. What is the note about unnamed items?

Q6 (SA). Describe the Goal Builder program: structure, sequence and common shape.

Q7 (ST). Retell the Goal Builder 14 (Survival) caricature, including the numbers.

Q8 (SA). What are the five steps of "survival with self-respect," and why do past successes serve a "dual purpose"?

Q9 (SC). A newly retired executive says, "I've earned it; I'll just coast; it's the generation gap, anyway." Which ideas apply?

Q10 (SC). A junior engineer is terrified before presenting to 300 people and plans to "fight the nerves" and tell himself he won't fail. Using Goal Builder 14, what does Maltz say to do instead?

Answers - Section 5

A1. Tension, Resistance, Arrogant aggressiveness, Negation as a way of life, Quandary, Unbelief, Inferiority, Life of loneliness, Laissez-faire, Irritation, Trepidation, Yesterday Incorporated. (Ch 9)

A2. False. Tranquility is active, won by combat against twelve named forces; passivity renders us helpless and ties us up in tension. (Ch 9)

A3. Relaxation is the reward on the far side of goal-directed action. People try to relax instead of pursuing goals, which fails because unpursued goals are themselves a tension source. Tension drill: think of something constructive, get off your back, fight off worries as expected, live in the world; "after a good go at your goals, you are ready for your trip to the good land — tranquility." (Ch 9)

A4. The French Resistance dynamiting a munitions train bound for the front was a good thing; but "when you sabotage your worthwhile daily goals...in resistance of your legitimate satisfactions, that is not so good." Same skill, wrong target: check which side you're sabotaging. (Ch 9)

A5. Ten components of withdrawal from life, each with an alternative: Retreat to Return, Eviction to Conviction, Tendency to withdraw to Courage to Act, then Imaginative Power, Reaffirmation, Responsibility, Mañana to Today, Ennui to Emancipation, No direction to Goal Orientation, Traitor to Friend. In the notes the first labels for the 4th-6th alternatives are given only as parentheticals (loss of imagination, self-negation, abdication); do not treat them as Maltz's wording. "No police come in the middle of the night"; you do it to yourself. (Ch 9, Ch 22)

A6. Fourteen weeks, one goal builder per week, six days of application then one day of rest. Sequence: Self-Respect, Understanding, Sincerity, Defeating Uncertainty, Overcoming Resentment, Getting Rid of Emptiness, Opportunity, Forgiveness, Creative Mirror Watching, Tearing Down Prison Walls, Tranquility, No Retirement Clock, Integrity, Survival. Shape: seeing component, mirror (write the word in erasable pencil or lipstick), spoken first-person sentence, erase (keep the feeling). Progression: constructive thinking to imaging to action. (Ch 10)

A7. You must deliver a speech; workmen enlarged the stadium to hold 125,000 if it doesn't rain; you can't recognize yourself in the mirror, forget your name, pray for rain, brush your teeth with soap and wash your face with toothpaste, check that you have a shoe on each foot, and your terror peaks at 250,000 eyes. Maltz breaks frame: it's a caricature, "I am a veteran lecturer, and this picture scares me, too." Overshooting the simulation lets you right-size the real problem. (Ch 10)

A8. (1) Accept the fear, nervousness and panic; (2) accept yourself regardless of the audience; (3) stop expecting yourself to fail; (4) bring images of past successes to mind; (5) do your best. Past successes displace nervousness now and, if you do fail, "make acceptance of this failure easier." (Ch 10)

A9. Retiring from a job is optional; retiring from life/self-image is self-inflicted and a mechanism of Retreat, Eviction, Mañana, Ennui, Traitor; the generation gap is a communication failure, not a reason to retire from the young. Anti-retirement protocol: a goal every day, however small (Goal Builder 12: "I must not resort to killing time"). (Ch 9, Ch 22)

A10. Don't fight the nervousness; say aloud: "I will accept my fear. And my nervousness. And my panic"; accept yourself no matter what the crowd thinks; stop expecting yourself to fail; recall past successes; do your best. The intervention is on the expectation, not the symptom. (Ch 10, Ch 21)

Section 6 - Ch 11-12: Psycho-Cybernetics Defined and the 21 Days; The Self-Image as Ceiling

Q1 (SA). What is the "21-day rule" and why is it significant to the book's claims?

Q2 (T/F). "In Book Three, Maltz tells you to argue the theory fully before trying it." True or false?

Q3 (OW). What is "Divine Discontent" and what practical reading does it give to chronic restlessness?

Q4 (ST). Retell the two ocean liners and explain what they isolate.

Q5 (SA). Define the self-image and state its relation to behavior, feelings and abilities.

Q6 (MC). Maltz says positive thinking that is incompatible with the self-image: (a) works slowly (b) works if repeated enough (c) absolutely will not work (d) works only at night.

Q7 (ST). What are the elephant and the pike stories and what do they show?

Q8 (SA). Explain the effectiveness range / comfort zone, including why success can feel destabilizing and why performance reverts.

Q9 (SC). A manager performs superbly in rehearsals and badly in front of the board, and her company sends her to another skills course. What does Ch 12 say, and what are the steps of the diagnostic?

Q10 (SC). A new hire says, "I tried affirmations for a month and they felt like lying; they did nothing." Which Ch 12 principle explains it, and what does the notes' decision rule say to do first?

Answers - Section 6

A1. "For a person to experience a noticeable change in a mental picture, a minimum of twenty-one consecutive days must elapse." It makes the book falsifiable: "No amount of debate...can give you proof...if you follow them for twenty-one days, you will be able to judge the outcome for yourself." Mark off consecutive days; don't evaluate before day 21. (Ch 11)

A2. False. "Avoid debating": debate substitutes for the trial that settles the question. Also "Confusion is helpful": disorientation means the old picture is loosening. (Ch 11)

A3. Man is teleological, motivated toward an ultimate meaning; when not moving that way he gets negative feedback, which Maltz calls Divine Discontent. Chronic discontent is data about direction, not a character defect. (Ch 11)

A4. One liner, fully crewed and with a goal, reaches port 9,999 times out of 10,000; the other, with no crew and no goal, engines running, runs aground before clearing the harbor. Same engine, same sea; the difference is entirely the goal and the helmsman. (Ch 11)

A5. "The overall average of the various attitudes we hold towards our capabilities in a multitude of areas." Behavior, feelings and abilities are always consistent with it; it is the ceiling on the effectiveness with which you can use your true potential. It is area-specific. (Ch 12)

A6. (c). "When it is compatible with a person's self-image, positive thinking does undoubtedly function, but when it is incompatible with the self-image, it absolutely will not work." Fix the self-image first. (Ch 12)

A7. An elephant chained as a calf to a stake it couldn't pull out stays put as an adult who could uproot a tree: the chain is gone, the picture remains. A pike separated from minnows by glass batters itself until it stops; remove the glass and it starves surrounded by food. Both show a self-image built from former conditions; check whether the glass is still there. (Ch 12)

A8. Your self-image in a given area sits on a scale surrounded by an effectiveness range; you perform effectively only inside it, and performance outside produces tension, which the mechanism resolves by pulling you back. So an unusually good result feels uncomfortable and reverts; tension is a boundary marker, not a verdict. Raise the ceiling by revising the picture; this releases existing ability. (Ch 12)

A9. Locate the self-image, not the skill. Steps: (1) find the area-specific picture ("I'm not good in front of people"); (2) predict the band; (3) read the tension as a boundary marker; (4) don't start with skill training (wasted-effort trap); (5) repaint the picture with the Method, ten minutes a day for 21 days; (6) expect release, not acquisition ("the elephant does not get stronger"). (Ch 12)

A10. Positive thinking incompatible with the self-image will not work at all; "as long as you hold any negative view of yourself, you will find it out of the question to think in positive terms." The decision rule: if affirmations feel like lying, do The Method before the recitation. (Ch 12; cheatsheet)

Section 7 - Ch 13-14: The Quiet Place and Relaxation; Goals, Synthetic Experience, The Method

Q1 (SA). What are the construction rules for the Quiet Place and how long does it take to enter it?

Q2 (T/F). "Maltz advises telling a trusted friend where your quiet place is so they can help." True or false?

Q3 (ST). Who was Truman in this chapter and what was his "foxhole"? Who is Marcus Aurelius cited for?

Q4 (OW). Explain "It is not outside events...but your own response."

Q5 (SA). State the Method step by step, including the three essentials.

Q6 (OW). Why does Maltz say you must be a participant, not an onlooker, and what's the "think from vs. think about" distinction?

Q7 (SA). Why can synthetic experience work, and what three things does successful affirming require?

Q8 (MC). Which is not one of Maltz's nine affirmation rules? (a) use the present tense (b) set a deadline (c) be personal, positive and non-comparative (d) avoid "able to" and "can".

Q9 (SC). A sales leader plans to "build a calm place" for the first time mid-meltdown during a failed negotiation, and wants to tell her team where it is. Evaluate.

Q10 (SC). An aspiring speaker rehearses by imagining himself on stage seen from the back row, then goes away dissatisfied. Another writes: "I am going to be better than my rival at presenting by next March." Diagnose both.

Answers - Section 7

A1. Construct it in imagination (plan, paint, furnish to your taste; beach house, cloud, deep in the earth, distant planet; the constraint is that you feel at home). Rules: completely isolated from the outside world and nobody else knows where it is. Entry is instant, "the same instant it takes to picture the Golden Gate Bridge." Enter at least once a day and immediately on agitation. (Ch 13)

A2. False. Shared, it becomes a topic; private, it stays a refuge. (Ch 13)

A3. Harry Truman described "a foxhole in my mind where I allow nothing to bother me," and retreated into it whenever anything bothered him, used mid-presidency, which shows the technique scales to high stakes. Marcus Aurelius: men seek retreats in the country but "it is in your power, whenever you shall choose to retire into yourself." (Ch 13)

A4. Your state is set by how you respond, not by events; that is why a technique like the quiet place or daily recitation can work at all. (Ch 13)

A5. Ten minutes daily, alone, eyes closed, body still. Choose one situation; build it in all five senses and environmental detail; be inside as participant; imagine yourself successful (past actions irrelevant); shift to the feeling ("Begin by knowing you have arrived"); mark the day; 21 consecutive days. Essentials: (1) strong desire; (2) immobility induced at will ("the greater energies of the mind are available only when the body is still and the door to the senses is closed"); (3) the felt experience of having achieved it, daily for 21 days. (Ch 14)

A6. "Not as an onlooker (objectively), but as a participant (subjectively). We actually must be there." A goal you think of is a possibility; a goal you think from is "overpoweringly real." Watching from outside gives a pleasant picture and no change. (Ch 14)

A7. The nervous system cannot distinguish a real experience from a vividly imagined one, so you can manufacture success experience before you have any. Affirming requires Desire, Information, Repetition. "Nothing succeeds like success." (Ch 14)

A8. (b). The nine rules: personal (I/me/my); positive; present tense; not progressive ("I am going to"); not comparative; avoid "able to"/"can"; balanced; realistic (no absolutes); no time limits ("Time limits are deadly; they create tension"). (Ch 14)

A9. Useless if first built mid-crisis: build it in calm, in detail, once. Telling her team converts it from refuge to topic. Truman used his foxhole mid-presidency, but it was built and ready. (Ch 13; patterns: trade-offs)

A10. The first is an onlooker (most common execution error): switch to participant. The second violates rules: progressive ("going to"), comparative ("better than"), and a time limit (by next March), all creating tension that jams the mechanism. Deadlines belong on written plans (Ch 15), not affirmations. (Ch 14)

Section 8 - Ch 15-16: Negative Feedback and the Plan of Action; Happiness and Exercises

Q1 (SA). State Maltz's line about negative feedback and the three-step reflex.

Q2 (T/F). "To use negative feedback, you should give the warning light your undivided attention." True or false?

Q3 (SA). List the three prohibitions for being effective with others and name the diagnosis behind inhibition.

Q4 (SA). Give the five parts of Your Own Plan of Action and say where a deadline belongs.

Q5 (OW). Explain the tennis-player/golfer analogy.

Q6 (SA). What is the Personal Balance Sheet and the six-area life review?

Q7 (OW). Define happiness per Dr. Schindler as quoted, and say why Maltz calls it a by-product and "present or nowhere."

Q8 (SA). Describe the Mirror Magic practice and the traffic-light drill.

Q9 (SC). A founder's proposal is rejected. He stews for days, reviews it repeatedly and tells himself he isn't cut out for this. Rewrite his response in servo-mechanism terms.

Q10 (SC). A colleague is inhibited at meetings, constantly calculating how she lands and hurt by what she thinks people think. Which concept explains it and what is the remedy? Also, what would "Just For Today" ask of her?

Answers - Section 8

A1. "Negative feedback is never a STOP sign"; its concern is to alter and adjust direction, not halt it. Three steps: be aware of the negative; evaluate it (the outcome) as unwanted and unacceptable; correct at once. Repeat until it becomes an automatic reflex stored as data. (Ch 15)

A2. False. "An occasional glance at the negative indicators is all that is required"; concentrate on the positive. Nobody gets upset at a dashboard light; the upset is an optional, expensive addition. (Ch 15)

A3. (1) Avoid trying too hard at the conscious level to impress; (2) avoid doing or saying anything for its effect on them; (3) avoid thinking about what they think or feel about you. Inhibition = excessive negative feedback, including hurt by "what he thinks they think" (a loop with no external input). (Ch 15)

A4. (1) Crystallize your thinking; (2) written plan and deadline; (3) real desire ("Is it really worth it to me?"); (4) self-confidence from past successes; (5) determination. Deadlines belong on plans, never on affirmations. (Ch 15)

A5. A tennis player doesn't consciously attend the net; a golfer, the traps and water; a bowler, the channels; a pole-vaulter, the bar. They concentrate on objectives. Hazards exist but aren't where attention goes. (Ch 15)

A6. A self-audit across Know-how, Energy, Time, Imagination, People, Research and Development, Leadership, Intellectual Efficiency, Ambition, Responsibility, Conviction of Success; plus a life review of Social, Mental, Family Life, Spiritual, Physical, Financial. (Ch 15)

A7. "A state of mind in which our thinking is pleasant a good share of the time." Mechanically, contentment improves health, efficiency, brain competence, memory and sensory sharpness. It's a by-product of goals ("No one is really ever alive unless he is striving for a series of goals") and must be experienced now. Also: perpetual happiness is nonsense; there are gray days. (Ch 16)

A8. Six-day drills attached to existing events: morning breathing then mirror question "Am I a friend to myself?"; garbage disposal (emptying the wastebaskets while discarding mental garbage); closing the door (symbolically closing it on the past mistake). Traffic light: a red light is your fear of failure holding you back; expect green; then move forward "with the confidence of past successes." (Ch 16)

A9. Failure reading: verdict, repeated review, attention pinned to the warning light. Servo reading: (1) aware, the light is on; (2) evaluate the outcome as unwanted, no commentary on worth; (3) correct at once; (4) return attention to the objective; (5) repeat until automatic. "Our future...[is] not decided by constantly turning over and reviewing the past." (Ch 15)

A10. Excessive negative feedback / over-monitoring. Remedy: the three prohibitions, not more self-scrutiny. "Just For Today": live through the next twelve hours; equal in TIME; refuse to worry about what might happen ("I am going to spend my time making things happen"). Also mark off 21 days of the daily recitation. (Ch 15-16)

Section 9 - Ch 17-18: The Starring Role and Origin Story; Relaxation and Winning Habits

Q1 (ST). Tell the story of the woman with the cheek scar. Include what she said, what Maltz discovered, and what would have cured her.

Q2 (SA). What does Maltz's "theater of the mind" cast you as?

Q3 (T/F). "The subconscious is a second mind that sometimes works against you." True or false?

Q4 (OW). Explain why "worry is mental rehearsal running backwards."

Q5 (SA). What does the "as if" model say, and how do you distinguish it from a mask?

Q6 (SA). Give the two roadblocks to relaxation and Maltz's key line about compassion and love.

Q7 (ST). Retell the tense millionaire scene and the exercise Maltz sets.

Q8 (SA). What are the three winning habits? How are habits born?

Q9 (SC). A founder keeps getting promoted but says, "It looks better, but I don't feel better," after the title upgrade. Which origin-story concept applies?

Q10 (SC). A manager works 14-hour days "to get ahead," paces, drums on the table at dinner, and cannot rest. Using Ch 18, what questions and exercises does Maltz offer?

Answers - Section 9

A1. A woman in her mid-twenties had a deep indented scar on her left cheek from a car accident. Maltz removed it perfectly, handed her a mirror, and got an uncertain response. "I really don't see any improvement." Shown "before" photos: "It looks better, but I don't feel better." The real scar was an unhappy romance that had ended two years earlier, months before the accident. A strengthening of her self-image would have cured her, but she "had to see it and want to make things better"; she had rejected herself and future happiness. Lesson: not all scars can be seen. (Ch 17)

A2. "You are the producer, director, writer, actor or actress, hero, or villain...the film technician up in the booth and the audience." No external critic is in the room. (Ch 17)

A3. False. The subconscious is "not a 'mind' but a goal-striving servomechanism"; we have one mind operating an automatic, goal-oriented machine. It's impersonal: fed success goals it's a success mechanism, fed negative aims a failure mechanism. The main goal-image is the self-image. (Ch 17)

A4. Worry is a state of mind before the event: you are seeing what can happen to you. Same mechanism as rehearsal, opposite content. "If you can worry, you can visualize." (Ch 17)

A5. The method actor playing a king thinks as if he were the king and projects it into reality: "Act the way you want to be (in your imagination), and you'll be the way you act." The mask conceals a self-image you consider indefensible; "as if" rehearses one you intend to inhabit. Strain = mask. (Ch 17; patterns)

A6. (1) Accept your limitations; (2) learn the healing power of forgiveness (stop holding grudges against others and yourself). "You cannot have peace of mind while you hate. Compassion and love are parents of relaxation." (Ch 18)

A7. A rich man comes home to a mahogany dining room he doesn't notice; paces, bangs the table, gobbles food "as if his hands were two shovels hurling it down a hole"; hurls himself in a living-room chair, throws down the paper, lights and drops a cigar, flicks the TV, grabs his hat and goes for a walk. "He can't find himself...cannot relax...has forgotten who he is." Asked who he is: "I'm Mr. X." Exercise: close-up on the forehead lines, fists and stiffness, see him (not just think), then run the beach scene and work the two roadblocks. (Ch 18)

A8. (1) Do the practice exercises regularly like washing your hands; (2) understand the importance of your mind (sustaining a single mental picture); (3) realize the power of your self-image. Habits are learned responses that became automatic and can be discarded and rebuilt. (Ch 18)

A9. The surgery lesson: fixing the outside doesn't fix the inside; the operative image is the self-image, and "not all our scars can be seen." Tell: "I don't feel better" after the external problem is fixed. (Ch 17; cheatsheet)

A10. Accept limitations: stop and ask "what am I accomplishing at this pace?" and "Would you rather drive yourself into a heart attack or relax with your human limitations?" Don't mask tension; "What price material success? Is it worth hypertension?" See the millionaire in your mind; forgive; the Franklin line (taking rest is a deeper capacity than taking cities). (Ch 18)

Section 10 - Ch 19-20: Seven Rules and Emotional Scars; Masks, Sex and Accepting Weakness

Q1 (SA). List the Seven Rules for Happy Living.

Q2 (SA). List the Four Miracle Drugs.

Q3 (T/F). "Maltz says to feel resentment for no more than a day, never longer." Correct this.

Q4 (ST). Retell the unfair-firing case and the intervention.

Q5 (OW). Explain the "ointment of kindness" and the "vicious cycle" of emotional scars.

Q6 (MC). What gives you "a floor to stand on"? (a) perfection (b) accepting your weakness (c) ignoring mistakes (d) wearing a mask.

Q7 (OW). Why does Maltz say self-punishment buys nothing?

Q8 (SA). Walk through the Be Yourself exercise and the role of item 5.

Q9 (SC). An employee dismissed after a harsh boss's criticism now refuses to ask anyone for favors and snaps at family. Which Ch 19 ideas apply and what steps?

Q10 (SC). An engineer is mocking himself as "not a numbers person" and playing the confident expert at work; at home he has no one he can be honest with. Which Ch 20 concepts apply and what is the diagnostic?

Answers - Section 10

A1. (1) Get the happiness habit; (2) declare war on negative feelings; (3) strengthen your self-image; (4) learn how to laugh (a real belly laugh; part of your success mechanism); (5) dig out your buried treasures; (6) help others; (7) seek activities that make you happy ("An active life is a happy life if you're doing what's right for you"). (Ch 19)

A2. (1) Accept your limitations (a stretched rubber band breaks); (2) forget your mistakes; (3) forgive others (they're human); (4) see yourself at your best and feed your success mechanism. (Ch 19)

A3. False. A "few days" of bitterness after an unfair blow is understandable, even desirable ("better to cleanse your system than to let inner hate eat away at you"). What is forbidden is letting it permanently dominate your thoughts. The notes give no "one day" limit. (Ch 19; cheatsheet: older than a few days = disease)

A4. You are in your late twenties, with three or four unsuitable jobs, hired by a large publishing company as assistant personnel director. The director was skeptical (bank clerical background) and impatient; you needed three or four months; he watched from day one; you made mistakes, got nervous, made more; he told you you weren't suitable. Since then, an emotional scar. Intervention: (1) widen the field; (2) forgive by considering the fear driving him (courage to hire, fear of responsibility), without deciding he was right; (3) forgive on grounds of symmetry ("you're not always fair yourself"); (4) remove the scar and redirect to positive goals. (Ch 19)

A5. Emotional scars are invisible but can cause stomach, heart, dizziness and insomnia, and "bring on a vicious cycle of negative feelings, which never ends until you resolve to heal the wound." Apply kind thinking gently on the hurting areas ("rub gently till it no longer hurts"); don't wait for others to see the scar. (Ch 19)

A6. (b). Accepting weakness gives a floor: "You turn a crisis into an opportunity, not an opportunity into a crisis." (Ch 20)

A7. "If you punish yourself for your mistakes, what do you gain?" No answer exists. Be kind to yourself instead. (Ch 20)

A8. List words describing yourself; words you think others use; words you would like to describe you. The gap between (1) and (2) is the mask; between (1) and (3) is working material. Write a biography of the person you want others to see. Item 5: list every reason it would be impossible, plus the people/circumstances in your way; most are expired conditions (the pike's glass). Then accept genuine limits (the floor), discard expired ones, stop punishing yourself. (Ch 20)

A9. Resentment radiates outward and returns (the "wounded man" hostile to sister, postman, cat); "Don't hold a grudge against yourself." Steps: allow a few days of bitterness; widen the field; forgive by imagining the boss's fear; forgive on symmetry; redirect to goals; "meet life halfway." (Ch 19)

A10. The mask (Face 8 / Unmasking), "not a numbers person" (area-specific self-image), and "a good friend will like you for yourself." Run the Be Yourself diagnostic; accept the weakness to get the floor; stop self-punishment. Imitation is "playing second fiddle." (Ch 20)

Section 11 - Ch 21-22: Individuality, Pressure and Friends; Peace of Mind and Living Fully

Q1 (SA). What is the "secret of winning under pressure," and what must accompany it?

Q2 (SA). Give the crisis protocol steps as they appear in Ch 21.

Q3 (ST). Tell the Bing Crosby story and its moral.

Q4 (ST). Tell the Whistler story and its moral.

Q5 (SA). List the Five Rules for Winning Friends.

Q6 (SA). What are the pleasant room and daily vacation, and why daily?

Q7 (T/F). "At twelve, the anger delay should leave you calm." Correct.

Q8 (SA). Walk through the Delay Your Response scene, including the numbers.

Q9 (SC). A founder gives a keynote with an actress-style stage fright. Using Ch 21, what do you do and what don't you do?

Q10 (SC). A 66-year-old consultant says, "I'm retired now; I'm winding down my ambitions." Apply Ch 22 and cite Maltz's own routine.

Answers - Section 11

A1. Calm people aren't those with fewer problems: "their self-image holds up." Also adaptability: "Sometimes, to succeed, you must change your plans." Ask "is my picture of myself holding?" (Ch 21)

A2. Set your goals; believe in them; bring back your triumphs; don't be afraid to be nervous; recognize your power in a crisis. The stage-fright worked example runs set goal, believe, bring back triumphs, permit the nervousness, go. (Ch 21)

A3. Live radio broadcast, ten seconds to air, Crosby drops his script; everyone panics but Bing, who bent down, picked up the first page, cocked his hat and came in exactly on cue. The scarce thing wasn't competence but an intact self-image. (Ch 21)

A4. In 1854 Cadet Whistler at West Point began on silicon, "Silicon is a gas"; told "That will do," and was discharged weeks later. Later, famous as a painter: "If silicon had been a gas, I would have been a general." Point: adaptation; the plan changed, the man didn't stop. (Ch 21)

A5. (1) Be a friend to yourself; (2) reach out to people; (3) imagine you're the other person; (4) accept their individuality; (5) try to meet their needs (talk to people, not at; listen). (Ch 21)

A6. The pleasant room: rebuild a favorite childhood room in your mind to recuperate and work: accept insecurities, re-picture cherished memories, set goals. The daily vacation: the length of the workweek has limited bearing on relaxing (Maltz's contrast: 60-80 hours in his youth, now 35-40 plus two weeks, still tense), so take a meaningful vacation every day; tension accrues daily. (Ch 22)

A7. False. "By the time you get to 12, you may still be irritated, but your rage will be more subdued." Success is control of action, not absence of feeling. (Ch 22)

A8. Tight budget (over-reaction domain identified in advance); quiet evening, pipe, income-tax-savings headline, ten-year-old's excellent report card; wife mentions worn linoleum and blurred TV (irritated but not thrown); then the $180 dentist bill: anger builds beyond check. Count slowly to twelve; actions back under control; return to visualizing pleasant enterprises after the bills are paid. (Ch 22)

A9. Goal on the performance, believe in it, recall triumphs in sensory detail, permit the nervousness, go. Don't reassure, don't tell her to calm down, don't attack the nervousness. Intervene on the expectation, not the symptom. (Ch 21)

A10. Retiring from a job is optional; retiring from your self-image is self-inflicted ("No police come in the middle of the night"). Keep a goal every day; Maltz past sixty alternated days of surgical practice and days of writing. "You're as young as you feel." (Ch 22)

Section 12 - Ch 23-24: Daily Dozen and Rave Notices; Thoughts To Live By

Q1 (SA). List the twelve items of the Daily Dozen.

Q2 (OW). What does "stoking the fires" mean for That Winning Feeling, and who is quoted?

Q3 (OW). Explain the grudge test in item 3.

Q4 (SA). State F-A-I-L-U-R-E and S-U-C-C-E-S-S as they appear in Ch 24.

Q5 (SA). State the therapeutic forgiveness formula and why we resist it.

Q6 (SA). List the Five Roadblocks of Frustration with cures.

Q7 (ST). Retell the hurdler who became a salesman.

Q8 (ST). What are Maltz's own organic-chemistry failure and Casals's quote?

Q9 (SC). A VP feels nervous about a decision she already made last Monday and is still agonizing. Apply the roadblocks.

Q10 (SC). A founder carries a five-year grudge against a former partner and says, "Forgiving would mean he was right." Apply Ch 24 and Ch 23 item 3.

Answers - Section 12

A1. Truth, Imagination, Relaxation, That Winning Feeling, Good Habits, The Aim of Happiness, Unmasking, Compassion, Accepting Your Weakness, Living with Your Mistakes, Being Yourself, Never Retiring. (Ch 23; Ch 4 has a near-identical Twelve Faces of Success list.)

A2. The winning feeling is maintained, not attained once: "As long as you keep stoking the fires of this feeling, you are rich. You feed your automatic success mechanism." Emerson: "Self-trust is the first secret of success." (Ch 23)

A3. Before renewing a years-old grudge, ask whether you're blaming someone "for an inconsiderate act that you, in your own imperfection, might have committed." (Ch 23)

A4. F-A-I-L-U-R-E: Fear, Anger, Inferiority, Loneliness, Uncertainty, Resentment, Emptiness. S-U-C-C-E-S-S: Sense of direction, Understanding, Courage, Compassion, Esteem, Self-acceptance, Self-confidence. (Ch 24)

A5. "The only difficulty is to secure your own willingness to...cancel out the debt with no reservations." We resist because "as long as we condemn another, we can feel superior to him." Endpoint: the debt itself is not valid; "there is and was nothing for us to forgive." Surgical model: no partial, tentative or halfway measures. (Ch 24)

A6. (1) Worrying after the decision: express anxiety before deciding, then call on past successes; (2) worrying about yesterday and tomorrow: think only of today ("Every day is a complete lifetime"); (3) too many things at once: "Don't fight relaxation. Join it"; (4) wrestling problems around the clock: sleep on it, not with it; (5) refusing to relax: sit in a room of your mind to cut the circuit of distress. (Ch 24)

A7. A college hurdle champion became a mediocre insurance salesman; fear of not being a perfect salesman distorted his self-image; one rejection frustrated him. At a reunion, slightly drunk, he borrowed sneakers to jump hurdles and broke his leg. A month in a cast gave him time to recall he had become a champion through practice and overcoming failures, with confidence, skill understanding, courage, self-respect, self-acceptance and direction. "Why couldn't he jump the hurdles of his job?" He practiced in his mind how to approach a customer; within a year he was a top salesman. "Failure teaches success." (Ch 24)

A8. As a premed at Columbia he failed organic chemistry and feared he'd never be a doctor; he took it over the summer and passed with an A: "I rose above failure because I had a goal, a goal important to me." Casals at ninety-three: "Every day I am reborn, every day is a new lifetime for me." (Ch 24)

A9. Roadblock 1: worry after the decision is "this extra fifty pounds of worry...all day." Stop; call on past successes; if you call on past failures you "create immediate frustration." Sleep on it, not with it. (Ch 24)

A10. Therapeutic forgiveness: his price of keeping the grudge is feeling superior; name the payoff, then cancel the debt with no reservations; the debt itself isn't valid. Item 3 test: might you have committed such an act in your own imperfection? Ch 19: considering what fear drove them is not agreeing they were right. (Ch 24, 23, 19)

FINAL EXAM - 20 Questions (Cumulative)

  1. (SA) Give Maltz's definition of Psycho-Cybernetics and the origin of "cybernetics."
  2. (SA) What is the master framework and what is its relation to behavior, feelings and abilities?
  3. (T/F) Improving your self-image requires first improving your skills.
  4. (MC) The correct treatment of a mistake is: (a) stop, it's a STOP sign; (b) aware, evaluate the outcome as unwanted, correct at once; (c) review it for a week; (d) ignore it.
  5. (SA) What did the "failure" patients in plastic surgery teach Maltz? Cite the quotation.
  6. (SA) What is the Method (steps and numbers)?
  7. (OW) Why is worry "the technique running backwards"?
  8. (SA) What are the Four Principles of Relaxation and the two roadblocks to relaxation? Reconcile with the "Easy does it" idea.
  9. (SA) Give the F-A-I-L-U-R-E and S-U-C-C-E-S-S acronyms, and flag the wording discrepancy in the notes.
  10. (OW) Explain therapeutic forgiveness and why it is hard.
  11. (SA) Name the five roadblocks of frustration and one cure each.
  12. (SA) What are the numbers 21, 10, 12, 6/1, 60/20, 125,000/250,000, 9,999, $180?
  13. (SC) Cross-chapter: a speaker facing 300 people uses Ch 10, Ch 14 and Ch 21. Combine into one plan.
  14. (SC) Cross-chapter: affirmations feel like lying. Which chapters explain and what's the sequence?
  15. (SC) A leader reads a failed launch as proof of incompetence and rehearses it nightly. Which concepts from Ch 8, 15, 17 apply?
  16. (OW) Compare the Tomorrow Illusion (Ch 2/6) with Yesterday Incorporated (Ch 9) and the Yesterday Tomorrow Complex (Ch 6/24).
  17. (OW) How do the Goal Builders (Ch 10), Mirror Magic (Ch 16) and Daily Dozen (Ch 23) relate?
  18. (SC) Someone says "I was born unhappy." Which chapters respond, and how?
  19. (OW) Name a tension within Maltz's notes: e.g., relaxation as precondition (Ch 18) vs. reward after effort (Ch 9); and "past performance is irrelevant" (Ch 14) vs. "bring back your triumphs" (Ch 21). How do you reconcile?
  20. (OW) If you could keep only three ideas, which and why? (Judged on coherence.)

Final Exam Answers

1. Steering your mind to a productive, useful, worthwhile, predetermined goal; kybernetes = helmsman (Ch 11).

2. The self-image; behavior, feelings and abilities are always consistent with it; it is the ceiling on the effectiveness with which you can use your potential, bounded by an effectiveness range (Ch 12).

3. False. "It is not necessary actually to improve yourself"; repainting the mind-picture releases talents you already possess (Ch 12).

4. (b). Aware, evaluate, correct at once; then glance at negatives, concentrate on positives (Ch 15).

5. That the operative image is inside, not on, the face: "as a plastic surgeon, my 'failures' really taught me the vast importance of a person's self-image." The cheek-scar woman: "It looks better, but I don't feel better" (Ch 17).

6. Ten minutes daily, alone, eyes closed, body still; one situation in full sensory detail; inside it as participant; ignore the past; feel already being that person; 21 consecutive days, then judge (Ch 14).

7. Worry is imagination before the event; if you can worry you can visualize; only the content is wrong. Same for "cooking up failure" (Ch 8, 17).

8. Forgive others, forgive yourself, see yourself at your best, keep up with yourself (Ch 4). Roadblocks: refusing limitations and holding grudges (Ch 18). Easy does it: strain jams the mechanism; compassion and love are parents of relaxation.

9. Fear, Anger, Inferiority, Loneliness, Uncertainty, Resentment, Emptiness / Sense of direction, Understanding, Courage, Compassion, Esteem, Self-acceptance, Self-confidence. Ch 3 words them Aggressiveness and Insecurity for the second letters A and I (Ch 3, 24).

10. Cancel the debt with no reservations, seeing the debt itself was never valid. Hard because condemning lets us feel superior; surgery-style, no halfway measures (Ch 24).

11. Worry after decision (express anxiety before); yesterday/tomorrow (today only); too many things (one at a time); problems 24/7 (sleep on it); refusing to relax (room of the mind) (Ch 24).

12. 21 consecutive days minimum (Ch 11); 10 minutes daily Method (Ch 14); count to 12 (Ch 22); six days on, one off (Ch 10); 60% yesterday/20% tomorrow (Ch 6, 24); 125,000 seats/250,000 eyes (Ch 10); 9,999 of 10,000 arrivals (Ch 11); $180 dentist bill (Ch 22). Also 1,440 minutes in a day (Ch 24).

13. Goal Builder 14: accept fear/nervousness/panic and stop expecting to fail; crisis protocol: goal, belief, triumphs, permit nervousness, go; the Method for ten minutes over 21 days building the participant's view of the room; quiet place before. Intervene on expectation, not symptom.

14. Ch 12: positive thinking incompatible with the self-image won't work; Ch 14 Method repaints the picture; Ch 16 recitation obeys the rules; cheatsheet: Method before recitation.

15. Ch 15: not a STOP sign; Ch 8: cooking up failure programs it; Ch 17: the mechanism is impersonal, worry is rehearsal in reverse; replace with correction and a participant rehearsal of the intended result.

16. Tomorrow Illusion: defer everything to a tomorrow nobody has experienced; Yesterday Incorporated: living in the past, equally fatal; the Complex: 60% yesterday, 20% tomorrow, almost nothing left for today. Cure: today (Ch 24 "Every day is a complete lifetime").

17. All three convert ideas into practice: Goal Builders serialized (14 weeks, 6/1) with mirror/word/spoken/erase; Mirror Magic short daily drills attached to existing events; Daily Dozen a non-serialized daily pass.

18. Ch 3: "Whoever told you that you were born to be unhappy?" a disadvantaged background is a fact, not a verdict; consent principle (Ch 1); happiness as habit (Ch 3, 16). Be aware: the notes argue by assertion, not data.

19. Ch 9: relaxation after goal-directed effort; Ch 18: relaxation as precondition. Reconcile: both reject straining; relaxation is a capacity maintained daily (quiet place) and the unpursued goal is itself tension. Ch 14 ignores past performance during rehearsal; Ch 21 recalls past triumphs as a resource; both feed the success mechanism with success pictures and exclude failure pictures.

20. Open-ended; strong choices: self-image as ceiling (Ch 12); negative feedback is never a STOP sign (Ch 15); the Method (Ch 14); forgiveness with no reservations (Ch 24).

Arguments & Evidence

The Essential Psycho-Cybernetics (Maxwell Maltz): Arguments, Stories and Evidence

Source note. This file reflects the skill's chapter notes (SKILL.md, glossary, patterns, cheatsheet and the 24 chapter files under maltz-psycho-cybernetics/), not the book's own wording. Quotations are quoted as the notes record them. Where the notes are silent (for example on publication details, studies, or sample sizes), this file is silent too. Time estimates in Part 1 are planning estimates for studying these notes; they are not facts from the book.

Structural warning. The notes cover an omnibus of five volumes (Book One: The Conquest of Frustration; Book Two: The Search for Self-Respect; Book Three: Live and Be Free Thru Psycho-Cybernetics; Book Four: The Magic Power of Self-Image Psychology; Book Five: Thoughts To Live By). Material repeats across volumes by design. "Ch 1-24" below are the notes' sequential chapter files.

A word on "evidence." The notes contain no controlled studies, datasets or sample sizes. The support in the book, as recorded, is clinical anecdote from Maltz's practice, analogies and illustrations (the elephant, the pike, the two ocean liners), quotations from cited authorities, and an invitation to test the method yourself for 21 days. The "Evidence" paragraphs below say exactly that, chapter by chapter.

PART 2 - Chapter by chapter

Chapter 1 - The Art of Overcoming Frustration (Book One, ch. 1)

Central argument. Frustration is not an event that happens to you; it is a habit of self-relation, broken by changing your opinion of yourself, not your circumstances. Maltz offers Psycho-Cybernetics, steering the mind toward a productive, useful, worthwhile, predetermined goal, and a diagnostic of Twelve Faces of Frustration so that you can catch yourself running the pattern. Because "no one can make you feel frustrated without your consent," the consent is the leverage point. The method is positive doing, not positive thinking.

Full stories.

The cleft-lip boy (Maltz's origin runs through the book). Maltz's path to plastic surgery began when, as an intern, he delivered a baby with a cleft lip; the father fainted, Maltz felt responsible, and the experience steered him toward plastic surgery. Years later, working in Latin America, he repaired the cleft lip of a terrified seventeen-year-old boy who shouted "I'm going to die!" on the table. Two weeks later, Maltz handed him a mirror.
